knowledge_statements.title: Algorithm Assessment Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines single-solver assessment over a prespecified benchmark distribution and performance measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a fixed solver, \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) sampled benchmark instances, and \(Y(A,I_i,s)\) the measured outcome under replicate seed \(s\). An algorithm assessment study estimates a prespecified functional \(\theta_A=T(\mathcal L(Y(A,I,S)))\), such as expected runtime, success probability, or solution quality, using the empirical observations \(\{Y(A,I_i,s_{ij})\}\). The target instance population, resource limit, replicate rule, censoring convention, and estimator \(\widehat\theta_A\) are fixed before interpreting the results.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assessment study estimates a predefined performance quantity for one fixed solver on a declared instance population under fixed measurement and replication rules.
assumptions_latex: \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) represent the declared target population.
\(Y\) is measured under a common resource and censoring convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\theta_A\) estimates the declared assessment target \(\theta_A\).

notation.meaning: measured outcome on instance I with seed s

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this experimental-design definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Algorithm Assessment Studies leaf and its variables and scope are substantially explicit, but no citation or inspectable locator supports this particular experimental-design contract or its required precommitment conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparative Solver Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines paired empirical comparison of multiple solvers under a common experimental contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A=\{A_1,ldots,A_k\}\) be eligible solvers and \(I_1,ldots,I_n\) common benchmark instances. A comparative solver study estimates prespecified contrasts \(\Delta_{ab}=T(\mathcal L(Y(A_a,I,S),Y(A_b,I,S)))\) from measurements obtained with identical instance weights, stopping rules, resource accounting, and outcome definitions. Randomized solvers receive a declared replication and seed-coupling policy. Conclusions are restricted to the solver configurations, instance population, platforms, and performance functionals specified by the comparison contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comparative study estimates predefined paired performance contrasts among eligible solvers tested under the same instances, resources, outcomes, and replication policy.
assumptions_latex: \(k\ge 2\) and every included solver satisfies the eligibility contract.
Each contrast \(\Delta_{ab}\) is specified before analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observations define comparable estimators \(\widehat\Delta_{ab}\) for the declared solver contrasts.

notation.meaning: population contrast between solvers a and b

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this benchmarking-study definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits Comparative Solver Studies, but no source supports the stated comparison contract. In addition, the solver set contains the malformed token `ldots` instead of `\ldots`; this must be corrected once a sourced formulation is established.

children.title: Mechanism Attribution Studies
children.top_down_role: Studies isolating which solver components or processes account for observed outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Mechanism Attribution Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines controlled ablation or intervention studies attributing outcome changes to algorithmic mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A(z)\) denote solver variants indexed by a mechanism setting \(z\in\mathcal Z\), with all non-target design factors held fixed or randomized by a declared design. A mechanism attribution study estimates the intervention contrast \(\tau(z,z')=\mathbb E[Y(A(z),I,S)-Y(A(z'),I,S)]\) over the target instance and seed distribution. Attribution to the mechanism is warranted only relative to the stated intervention, implementation equivalence constraints, randomization or adjustment scheme, and absence of uncontrolled changes between variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mechanism attribution study changes a specified solver mechanism while controlling other factors and estimates the resulting average outcome contrast.
assumptions_latex: \(A(z)\) and \(A(z')\) differ only through declared intervention components.
The instance and seed assignment permits estimation of the stated contrast.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\tau(z,z')\) estimates the outcome change attributable to the declared mechanism intervention.
review_flags: Causal interpretation requires an experimental-methodology source absent from the supplied hints.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Mechanism Attribution Studies, but its causal attribution conclusion depends on intervention and identification conditions that are not supported by any cited experimental-methodology source.

children.title: Behavioral Regime Studies
children.top_down_role: Studies characterizing solver behavior across instance or execution regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Behavioral Regime Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines studies that partition instance conditions into reproducible regions of distinct solver behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x(I)\in\mathcal X\) be prespecified instance features and \(B(A,I,S)\in\mathcal B\) a measurable behavioral summary, such as search-tree size or convergence pattern. A behavioral regime study constructs or tests a partition \(\mathcal X=R_1\cup\cdots\cup R_m\) such that the conditional law \(\mathcal L(B\mid x(I)\in R_j)\) is stable within each region and materially differs across at least two regions under a declared discrepancy criterion. Any data-driven partition is evaluated on observations not used to fit it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A behavioral regime study identifies feature regions where a solver's measurable behavior is internally stable and differs materially between regions.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(B\) are measurable under the study protocol.
The discrepancy criterion and validation rule are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validated regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) characterize distinct conditional behavioral regimes.
review_flags: No supplied source addresses regime discovery and out-of-sample validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Behavioral Regime Studies and distinguishes fitting from out-of-sample evaluation, but no source supports the proposed stability, discrepancy, and validation criteria or establishes that they define this study family.

children.title: Mechanism–Outcome Coupling
children.top_down_role: Evidence connecting internal solver mechanisms with externally measured behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Mechanism–Outcome Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a checkable interaction criterion linking mechanism effects to instance or behavioral regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For mechanism settings \(z,z'\) and regime variable \(R\), mechanism–outcome coupling is present when the conditional intervention contrast \(\tau_r(z,z')=\mathbb E[Y(A(z),I,S)-Y(A(z'),I,S)\mid R=r]\) is not constant in \(r\). Equivalently, there exist supported regimes \(r_1,r_2\) such that \(\tau_{r_1}(z,z')\ne\tau_{r_2}(z,z')\). The coupling claim is relative to the declared outcome, intervention, regime construction, and target population; marginal association between mechanism traces and outcomes alone does not establish it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mechanism–outcome coupling occurs when the causal performance effect of a mechanism differs across supported behavioral or instance regimes.
assumptions_latex: Each compared regime has support under both mechanism settings.
The conditional intervention contrasts are identifiable under the study design.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r_1,r_2:\tau_{r_1}(z,z')\ne\tau_{r_2}(z,z')\) characterizes regime-dependent mechanism effect.

notation.meaning: mechanism contrast conditional on regime r

review_flags: The interaction criterion lacks direct support in the supplied source inventory.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the Mechanism–Outcome Coupling leaf, and the conditional-effect criterion is internally coherent, but its causal interpretation and equivalence criterion lack supporting citations and identifiable-design details from an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Implementation Improvement Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines controlled studies of implementation changes preserving the intended algorithmic specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) be two implementations of the same declared algorithmic specification, differing only by a documented implementation change. An implementation improvement study verifies output equivalence under a stated tolerance and estimates paired resource contrasts \(\Delta_R=\mathbb E[R(P_1,I,S)-R(P_0,I,S)]\) on common instances under identical build, platform, stopping, and measurement conditions. An improvement is reported only for prespecified resources and populations for which the estimated contrast satisfies the declared practical-improvement criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implementation improvement study compares equivalent program versions differing by one documented change and measures paired resource gains under controlled conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) satisfy the same correctness specification.
Only documented implementation factors differ between measurements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A declared improvement holds when \(\Delta_R\) meets the prespecified practical criterion without violating output equivalence.
review_flags: Implementation sections in the supplied books do not directly establish this study-design contract.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Implementation Improvement Studies, but the inventory's algorithm-implementation sections do not support this controlled empirical-study contract, output-equivalence requirement, or practical-improvement criterion.

children.title: Perturbation Robustness Studies
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of solver conclusions to controlled changes in inputs, configurations, or conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Robustness Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines robustness evaluation over a declared family of admissible input or configuration perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) be a distance on instances or configurations and \(\mathcal P_\varepsilon(I)=\{I':d(I,I')\le\varepsilon\}\) the admissible perturbation set. A perturbation robustness study estimates a prespecified degradation functional, for example \(D_A(\varepsilon)=\mathbb E[\sup_{I'\in\mathcal P_\varepsilon(I)}(Y(A,I',S)-Y(A,I,S))]\), using a declared perturbation generator or exhaustive set. Feasibility, semantic equivalence, seed coupling, resource limits, and the direction in which larger outcomes are worse must be specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation robustness study measures worst-case or sampled performance degradation under a precisely bounded family of admissible perturbations.
assumptions_latex: \(d\) and \(\mathcal P_\varepsilon\) preserve the declared instance domain.
Larger values of \(Y\) denote worse outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat D_A(\varepsilon)\) quantifies robustness at perturbation radius \(\varepsilon\) under the declared generator.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports the perturbation-robustness study definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Perturbation Robustness Studies, but no source supports the chosen degradation functional or the methodological requirements for admissible perturbations, seed coupling, and sampled versus exhaustive evaluation.

children.title: Platform Portability Studies
children.top_down_role: Transfer of solver behavior across hardware, software, or execution platforms.

knowledge_statements.title: Platform Portability Studies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cross-platform evaluation separating absolute performance from platform-dependent solver effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be declared hardware-software platforms and \(Y(A,I,h,S)\) a performance outcome measured on platform \(h\). A platform portability study uses common solver semantics, instances, stopping rules, and outcome definitions to estimate platform-conditional performance \(\theta_{A,h}\) and interactions \(\Gamma_{A,B;h,h'}=(\theta_{A,h}-\theta_{B,h})-(\theta_{A,h'}-\theta_{B,h'})\). Absolute runtime ratios are interpreted only with documented platform configurations; nonzero \(\Gamma\) indicates that a solver comparison does not transfer unchanged between platforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A platform portability study repeats a controlled benchmark across documented systems and tests whether solver comparisons change with the platform.
assumptions_latex: Solver semantics and benchmark instances are common across \(h\in\mathcal H\).
Each platform configuration and resource-accounting rule is documented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_{A,B;h,h'}\ne0\) indicates platform-dependent comparative performance.

notation.meaning: performance of solver A on platform h

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports cross-platform benchmarking methodology.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Platform Portability Studies and the interaction contrast is mathematically plausible, but no cited source supports this cross-platform benchmarking formulation or the interpretation assigned to a nonzero interaction.

children.title: Robustness Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which robust findings cease to transfer between environments.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes where an empirical robustness claim ceases to transfer to new perturbations, populations, or platforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(A,e)\) be a declared robustness criterion for solver \(A\) in environment \(e\), where an environment fixes the instance population, perturbation family, platform, and resource policy. For validated environments \(E_0\), a robustness transfer boundary is the set \(\partial T=\{e:C(A,e)\text{ changes truth value relative to nearby }e'\in E_0\}\). Outside the supported domain or across \(\partial T\), evidence for \(C(A,e')\) does not by itself certify \(C(A,e)\); transfer requires new assumptions or validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transfer boundary marks environments where a validated robustness criterion changes or lacks support, so the original claim cannot be carried across unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The environment variables and robustness predicate \(C\) are prespecified.
Neighborhood or ordering among environments is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Crossing \(\partial T\) invalidates unqualified transfer of the robustness claim from \(E_0\).
review_flags: The precise transfer-boundary formalization is not supported by the supplied locators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is appropriate, but the proposed set is not reliably established as a boundary: the environment topology or neighborhood structure is only deferred to an assumption, and the relation between candidate environments and the validated set is ambiguous. No source supports this formalization.

children.title: Eligible Solver Classes
children.top_down_role: Solver categories admitted to the experimental comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Eligible Solver Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the predicate determining which solver classes may enter a baseline comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a study contract \(K\), a solver \(A\) is eligible exactly when \(E_K(A)=1\), where \(E_K\) is a prespecified conjunction requiring: applicability to every claimed instance class; output satisfying the common feasibility and objective convention; compliance with the resource, information, and stopping model; availability of a reproducible fixed configuration; and membership in any declared algorithmic class. Eligibility is determined independently of outcomes observed on the evaluation instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver is eligible only if it satisfies all prespecified scope, correctness, resource, reproducibility, and algorithm-class requirements, without using evaluation outcomes.
assumptions_latex: The comparison contract \(K\) is fixed before evaluation.
Every clause of \(E_K\) is operationally checkable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_K=\{A:E_K(A)=1\}\) is the eligible solver set.
review_flags: No supplied source directly supports this solver-eligibility contract.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Eligible Solver Classes, and the predicate is operationally framed, but no citation supports the asserted conjunction of eligibility requirements or its outcome-independence rule.

children.title: Baseline Solver Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice of reference implementations or competing solvers used as baselines.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Solver Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies outcome-independent selection of representative baselines from the eligible solver set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A_K\) be the eligible solvers and let \(c_1,ldots,c_m\) be prespecified comparison roles, such as incumbent practice, best known general method, or structurally matched method. A baseline set \(B\subseteq\mathcal A_K\) is admissible when each required role has at least one representative in \(B\), every inclusion and exclusion follows a documented rule, and configuration effort is governed by the same declared policy as for the focal solver. Selection must not depend on hidden evaluation-set outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Baselines are selected from eligible solvers to cover predefined comparison roles under documented, outcome-independent inclusion and configuration rules.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A_K\) has been determined before baseline selection.
The required comparison roles \(c_1,\ldots,c_m\) are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An admissible baseline set satisfies \(B\subseteq\mathcal A_K\) and covers every required role.
review_flags: No supplied locator establishes principles for outcome-independent baseline selection.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Baseline Solver Selection, but no source supports the role-coverage and outcome-independent selection policy. The sequence of roles also contains the malformed token `ldots` instead of `\ldots`.

children.title: Scope-Matched Baseline Coverage
children.top_down_role: Alignment between declared solver scope and the capabilities represented by baselines.

knowledge_statements.title: Scope-Matched Baseline Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires baseline coverage for every domain over which comparative conclusions are asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the declared claim domain and \(D_A\subseteq D\) the subset on which solver \(A\) is eligible and executable under the common contract. A selected baseline set \(B\) has scope-matched coverage when, for every \(x\in D\), each comparison role required at \(x\) is represented by some \(Ain B\) with \(x\in D_A\). If this condition fails on \(U\subseteq D\), comparative conclusions must exclude \(U\) or explicitly state the uncovered role.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Baseline coverage is scope-matched when every claimed domain point has an eligible baseline for each required comparison role; uncovered regions must be excluded or disclosed.
assumptions_latex: The claim domain \(D\) and eligibility domains \(D_A\) are declared.
Required comparison roles may vary with \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in D\), every role required at \(x\) is covered by an eligible member of \(B\).
review_flags: No supplied source directly supports this baseline-coverage condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Scope-Matched Baseline Coverage, but no citation supports this quantified coverage contract. The statement also contains the malformed token `Ain B` instead of `A\in B`, so the displayed membership condition is not valid as written.

children.title: Eligible Problem Classes
children.top_down_role: Problem families and formulations admitted to the study.

knowledge_statements.title: Eligible Problem Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the declared universe of problem classes to which a benchmark comparison applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a declared collection of combinatorial-optimization problem classes. An eligibility predicate is a fixed map \(e:\mathcal P\to\{0,1\}\), specified before experiments, whose value may depend only on declared structural properties such as input representation, feasibility model, objective type, and size domain. The eligible class family is \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm{el}}=\{P\in\mathcal P:e(P)=1\}.\] Every reported benchmark instance must belong to a class in \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{el}}\); post-experiment performance may not alter \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eligible classes are selected before experimentation by a declared structural predicate, and every reported instance must belong to one of those classes.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) and all admissible structural descriptors are fixed before observing benchmark outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\text{ reported}\implies I\in P\text{ for some }P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{el}}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but it has no citation. The asserted admissibility rule, permitted eligibility descriptors, and prohibition on outcome-dependent eligibility require an inspectable benchmark-design source.

children.title: Instance Sampling Frame
children.top_down_role: Population sources and inclusion boundaries from which benchmark instances are sampled.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance Sampling Frame
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite or probabilistic population from which benchmark instances may be selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each eligible class \(P\), an instance sampling frame is a pair \((\mathcal F_P,\mu_P)\), where \(\mathcal F_P\) is a declared set of admissible encoded instances of \(P\) and \(\mu_P\) is either a probability measure on \(\mathcal F_P\) or a specified finite-population sampling design. Membership rules, exclusions, strata, and duplicate handling are fixed before algorithm outcomes are inspected. A benchmark sample \((I_1,\ldots,I_n)\) is valid only when every \(I_j\in\mathcal F_P\) and its selection follows \(\mu_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sampling frame declares the admissible instance population and its sampling design before outcomes are observed; valid samples must follow both.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is an eligible problem class.
Each instance has a fixed encoding sufficient to test membership in \(\mathcal F_P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I_1,\ldots,I_n)\text{ valid}\implies I_j\in\mathcal F_P\text{ for all }j\text{ and sampling follows }\mu_P\).

notation.meaning: admissible instance population for class P
declared probability measure or finite-population design

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the sampling-frame leaf, but no evidence supports treating a probability measure or finite-population design as part of the frame or the stated validity condition. An authoritative sampling or experimental-design source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Scope-to-Sample Coverage
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between the declared problem scope and the sampled benchmark population.

knowledge_statements.title: Scope-to-Sample Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when a realized benchmark sample covers every declared stratum of the intended scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the intended scope be partitioned into nonempty declared strata \(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_k\}\), with \(S_h\subseteq\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{el}}}\mathcal F_P\), and let \(m_h\geq 1\) be the required count for stratum \(h\). A realized multiset \(D=(I_1,\ldots,I_n)\) satisfies scope-to-sample coverage exactly when \[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{I_j\in S_h\}\geq m_h\qquad\text{for every }h\in\{1,ldots,k\}.\] Overlapping strata count an instance in each stratum containing it unless the protocol explicitly requires disjoint allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage holds exactly when the realized sample meets the predeclared minimum count in every scope stratum.
assumptions_latex: The strata and minimum counts are fixed before benchmark outcomes are observed.
Every sampled instance belongs to its declared sampling frame.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) has scope-to-sample coverage if and only if every declared stratum count is at least its required minimum.

notation.meaning: minimum required sample count in stratum h

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, but the displayed index set contains the malformed text \(\{1,ldots,k\}\), which should be \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). More importantly, no source supports the minimum-count coverage definition or the overlapping-strata convention, so the mathematical contract remains source-dependent.

children.title: Resource Limits
children.top_down_role: Computational resources bounded during an experiment.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines admissibility of a run under predeclared limits on measured computational resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the finite set of metered resources, including any declared wall time, CPU time, memory, energy, oracle calls, or parallel workers. For each \(r\in R\), fix a limit \(B_r\in[0,\infty]\) and a deterministic accounting rule producing consumption \(C_r(A,I,\omega)\) for algorithm \(A\), instance \(I\), and run seed \(\omega\). The run respects its resource limits exactly when \[C_r(A,I,\omega)\leq B_r\qquad\text{for every }r\in R.\] Setup, preprocessing, and verification costs are included precisely when the declared accounting rule assigns them to \(C_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run respects its limits when every resource consumption, measured by a predeclared accounting rule, stays within its corresponding budget.
assumptions_latex: Resource meters, limits, and accounting boundaries are fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{admissible}(A,I,\omega)\iff \forall r\in R,\ C_r(A,I,\omega)\leq B_r\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the resource-limits leaf and the variables are introduced, but the multidimensional admissibility rule and treatment of setup, preprocessing, and verification costs have no cited support. A benchmark-methodology source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Execution Budget Protocols
children.top_down_role: Time, work, or evaluation allowances assigned to solver executions.

knowledge_statements.title: Execution Budget Protocols
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies deterministic enforcement and recording of a multidimensional execution budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an algorithm \(A\), instance \(I\), seed \(\omega\), resource limits \((B_r)_{r\in R}\), meters \((C_r)_{r\in R}\), and checkpoint rule \(Q\). Initialize every meter to zero, start \(A(I;\omega)\), and update each \(C_r\) according to its declared accounting rule. At every checkpoint prescribed by \(Q\), stop before further algorithmic work if some \(C_r>B_r\), recording resource-limit status and the last accepted output. Otherwise stop when \(A\) declares termination. Return the output, all terminal meter values, the stopping status, seed, and timestamps required by the protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The protocol meters declared resources, enforces limits at fixed checkpoints, and returns the output together with complete terminal accounting and status.
assumptions_latex: All algorithms are subjected to the same declared metering and checkpoint semantics.
A checkpoint can interrupt execution without accepting subsequent work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned run record contains \((A,I,\omega)\), terminal \((C_r)_{r\in R}\), output, and exactly one stopping status.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is an appropriate content kind for this procedural leaf. However, the checkpoint rule tests \(C_r>B_r\), permitting work that reaches the limit and possible overshoot between checkpoints; whether that is intended depends on an uncited enforcement model. Interrupt, last-output, and terminal-accounting semantics also need a specific source.

children.title: Budget Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Comparability of resource allowances across solvers or execution architectures.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines equivalence of execution budgets relative to declared resource-conversion and enforcement rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b=(B_r)_{r\in R}\) and \(b'=(B'_s)_{s\in R'}\) be two execution budgets with enforcement protocols \(Q\) and \(Q'\). Fix a comparison domain \(\mathcal X\) of run traces and a declared normalization map \(N\) from a trace to a common resource vector. The budgets are equivalent on \(\mathcal X\) exactly when, for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \[x\text{ is admitted by }(b,Q)\iff x\text{ is admitted by }(b',Q'),\] and both protocols assign the same normalized terminal consumption \(N(x)\). Equality of nominal wall-time limits alone does not imply equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two budgets are equivalent only when they admit exactly the same declared run traces and yield the same normalized resource accounting.
assumptions_latex: The trace domain and normalization map are fixed before comparing algorithms.
Admission under each protocol is well-defined for every trace in \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((b,Q)\equiv_{\mathcal X,N}(b',Q')\) if and only if admission and normalized terminal consumption agree on every \(x\in\mathcal X\).

notation.meaning: declared comparison domain of run traces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the equivalence leaf, but the proposed tracewise equivalence is a bespoke and unusually strong definition without evidence. Because \(N\) is presented as a single map of the trace, the requirement that both protocols assign the same \(N(x)\) is either automatic or requires protocol-indexed normalization maps; a source is needed to determine the intended formulation.

children.title: Stopping Statuses
children.top_down_role: Recorded categories describing why an execution terminated.

knowledge_statements.title: Stopping Statuses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a mutually exclusive terminal taxonomy for why an experimental run ended.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be the set of completed run records. A stopping-status map is a total function \(\sigma:T\to\Sigma_{\mathrm{stop}}\), where \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{stop}}\) is a finite set of mutually exclusive terminal causes fixed before execution. It must distinguish at least normal algorithm termination, declared target attainment, resource-limit termination, external interruption, and abnormal process termination whenever these causes are possible. Each run receives exactly one primary status, chosen by a predeclared precedence rule if several conditions are detected simultaneously; auxiliary events may be recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every completed run receives exactly one predeclared primary reason for stopping, with a fixed precedence rule resolving simultaneous events.
assumptions_latex: Terminal causes are observable from the run record and environment logs.
The precedence rule is fixed before benchmark execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall t\in T\), there exists exactly one \(s\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{stop}}\) such that \(\sigma(t)=s\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the stopping-status leaf, but the mandatory minimum vocabulary and precedence treatment are uncited. Normal termination and target attainment may overlap rather than denote mutually exclusive causes, so an authoritative taxonomy or protocol specification is needed.

children.title: Success Statuses
children.top_down_role: Recorded categories for executions satisfying the study's success criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Success Statuses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines success through independently checkable acceptance predicates on a run's returned result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\), let \(V_I(y)\in\{0,1\}\) be the declared feasibility verifier and let \(G_I(y)\in\{0,1\}\) encode any required objective, optimality, approximation, or target criterion. A terminal run record \(t\) with returned result \(y(t)\) has success status exactly when \[V_I(y(t))=1\quad\text{and}\quad G_I(y(t))=1.\] Substatuses may distinguish feasible, target-achieving, and certified-optimal results, but algorithm self-report alone is insufficient whenever the protocol requires independent verification. A resource-limit stop may still be successful if its last accepted result satisfies both predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run is successful exactly when its accepted result passes the declared feasibility and performance or certification checks, regardless of the stopping cause.
assumptions_latex: The verifier and target predicate are fixed before observing the run outcome.
The returned result is available to the required verification procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{success}(t)\iff V_I(y(t))=G_I(y(t))=1\).

notation.meaning: accepted result returned by run t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is plausible, but no source supports defining every success status by the conjunction of feasibility and a single aggregate target predicate. The statement also makes success independent of stopping status, so the intended relation between sibling status families must be sourced.

children.title: Failure Statuses
children.top_down_role: Recorded categories for unsuccessful, invalid, or incomplete executions.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Statuses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines failure categories without conflating invalid results, system faults, and unmet targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a terminal run record \(t\) on instance \(I\), define declared predicates \(V_I(y(t))\) for result validity, \(G_I(y(t))\) for target attainment, and \(E(t)\) for protocol-conformant execution. The run has failure status when \[E(t)=0\quad\text{or}\quad V_I(y(t))=0\quad\text{or}\quad G_I(y(t))=0,\] including the case of no returned result when one is required. The recorded subtype must identify protocol or system failure, invalid result, or valid-but-unsuccessful result. Resource exhaustion alone is a stopping cause and becomes failure only when the success predicates are not met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure means protocol violation, invalid output, or failure to meet the declared target; its subtype must preserve that distinction.
assumptions_latex: Validity, target, and execution-conformance predicates are fixed before the run.
Missing required output is assigned a determinate validity value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\operatorname{failure}(t)\iff 
eg E(t)\lor
eg V_I(y(t))\lor
eg G_I(y(t))\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but the proposed disjunction makes any protocol nonconformance a failure even when result predicates pass and treats every unmet target as failure. Those are protocol-specific choices without evidence. The formula also applies \(y(t)\) when no result exists, while the assumptions do not formally extend its domain or define a sentinel value.

children.title: Hardware Contract
children.top_down_role: Processor, memory, accelerator, and machine characteristics fixed or reported for comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Hardware Contract
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the hardware state that must be fixed or recorded for comparable runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hardware contract is a tuple \(H=(C,M,S,A,P)\) describing processor architecture and enabled cores \(C\), memory hierarchy and capacity \(M\), storage \(S\), accelerators \(A\), and power, frequency, and affinity policy \(P\). A run conforms to \(H\) exactly when its observed hardware descriptor \(h(t)\) matches every field declared invariant and every varying field lies within its prescribed admissible set. Shared-machine load, thermal policy, and virtualization are included whenever they can affect the measured resource. Nonconforming runs are excluded or labeled by a rule fixed before analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run conforms only when all invariant hardware fields match and every permitted variation stays within its predeclared range.
assumptions_latex: The hardware fields relevant to measured performance are observable or auditable.
Matching rules and admissible variations are fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conforms}_H(t)\iff h(t)\in\mathcal H(H)\), where \(\mathcal H(H)\) is the hardware set admitted by the contract.

notation.meaning: observed hardware descriptor for run t
set of hardware configurations admitted by H

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record primarily defines a hardware contract and only secondarily states a conformance condition, so definition would better match the exact leaf than condition. The selected tuple fields and claims about load, thermal policy, and virtualization also require an inspectable reproducibility or benchmarking source.

children.title: Software Contract
children.top_down_role: Operating system, compiler, library, runtime, and dependency environment used in execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Software Contract
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies reproducible software identities, configurations, and runtime dependencies for benchmark runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A software contract is a tuple \(W=(K,D,B,L,O,R)\) recording operating system and kernel \(K\), source or executable identity \(D\), build procedure and compiler flags \(B\), linked libraries \(L\), algorithm parameters \(O\), and runtime settings \(R\). A run \(t\) conforms exactly when its observed descriptor \(w(t)\) matches every invariant field and each permitted variation belongs to its declared admissible set \(\mathcal W(W)\). Random-number generator implementation, seed policy, environment variables, and concurrency settings are included whenever they affect outputs or measured resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Software conformance requires auditable agreement with all fixed versions, builds, dependencies, parameters, randomness, and runtime settings declared relevant.
assumptions_latex: Software identities and effective runtime settings can be recorded or reconstructed.
Admissible variations are declared before outcome analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conforms}_W(t)\iff w(t)\in\mathcal W(W)\).

notation.meaning: observed software descriptor for run t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record primarily defines a software contract, making definition a better terminal content kind than condition. Its mandatory software, randomness, and concurrency fields are plausible but uncited and need a reproducibility or benchmark-reporting source with a specific locator.

children.title: Numerical Precision Contract
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic formats and precision modes governing comparable solver runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Precision Contract
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes arithmetic formats, tolerances, rounding, and comparison rules used during execution and validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numerical precision contract \(N\) specifies each arithmetic format, rounding mode, exceptional-value policy, accumulation rule, and tolerance pair \((\tau_{\mathrm{abs}},\tau_{\mathrm{rel}})\). For declared scalar comparisons, computed \(a\) and reference \(b\) agree exactly when \[|a-b|\leq \tau_{\mathrm{abs}}+\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}|b|.\] Integrality, feasibility, and objective checks must state whether they use exact arithmetic, this tolerance rule, or another fixed predicate. A run conforms only if execution and validation use the prescribed formats and predicates; tolerances may not be selected from observed algorithm errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contract fixes arithmetic and validation semantics in advance, including an explicit absolute-relative rule wherever approximate scalar equality is used.
assumptions_latex: Reference quantities and exceptional values have declared representations.
All tolerances and rounding policies are fixed before outcome inspection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conforms}_N(t)\) implies that every arithmetic operation and validation check follows the formats, rounding rules, and predicates prescribed by \(N\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record primarily defines a numerical precision contract, so definition is a better fit than condition. No source supports choosing this asymmetric absolute-relative comparison rule as the contract default, and the nonnegativity and numeric domains of the tolerances, computed value, and reference value are not explicitly stated in the formal statement.

children.title: Environment Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Criteria for treating distinct execution environments as experimentally comparable.

knowledge_statements.title: Environment Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence of benchmark environments relative to a declared computational contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an environment have contract signature \(s(e)=(h(e),w(e),p(e))\), recording all declared hardware, software, and numerical-precision fields that can affect a benchmark. Two environments \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) are environment-equivalent, written \(e_1\sim_E e_2\), exactly when \[s(e_1)=s(e_2).\] Benchmarks obtained in distinct environments may be pooled as contract-equivalent observations only if this equality holds; undeclared fields are outside the equivalence claim. Because equality of signatures is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, \(\sim_E\) is an equivalence relation on the set of fully specified environments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two benchmark environments are equivalent when every declared hardware, software, and precision field in their computational contracts agrees exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(s(e)\) is defined using a fixed field set and fixed normalization conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_1\sim_E e_2\iff s(e_1)=s(e_2)\), and \(\sim_E\) is an equivalence relation.

notation.meaning: declared contract signature of environment e

review_flags: No supplied locator supports computational-environment equivalence; an empirical algorithm-engineering source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Environment Equivalence leaf and is internally coherent, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the proposed contract-signature formalization or the pooling rule. The unrelated local inventory cannot establish this domain-specific definition.

children.title: Paired Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparisons using matched observations across solver or treatment conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Within-instance comparison of two algorithms using paired benchmark observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For benchmark units \(i=1,\ldots,n\), observe both algorithms under matched conditions, producing responses \(Y_{iA}\) and \(Y_{iB}\). A paired comparison uses the within-unit differences \[D_i=Y_{iA}-Y_{iB}\] as its elementary observations. The sample effect is \(\bar D=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n D_i\), with estimated sampling variance \(s_D^2/n\), where \(s_D^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(D_i-\bar D)^2\). Pairing is valid only when the two responses in each pair share the declared benchmark unit and nuisance conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run both algorithms on each matched unit and analyze their within-unit response differences, thereby removing nuisance variation shared by the pair.
assumptions_latex: \((D_i)_{i=1}^n\) are independent across benchmark units.
\(n\ge 2\) and each unit supplies both responses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat{\Delta}=\bar D\) and \(\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar D)=s_D^2/n\).

notation.meaning: response for algorithm a on benchmark unit i

review_flags: Supplied source locators concern optimization algorithms rather than paired experimental designs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and paired-difference formulation fit the Paired Comparisons leaf. However, no experimental-design or statistical source with a specific locator is cited, so the variance formula and validity conditions lack required evidence.

children.title: Blocked Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparisons organized within groups sharing relevant nuisance characteristics.

knowledge_statements.title: Blocked Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm comparison after grouping experimental units by a declared nuisance factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition experimental units into blocks \(b=1,\ldots,B\) that are internally homogeneous with respect to a declared nuisance factor. For treatments or algorithms \(a=1,\ldots,A\), a complete blocked comparison observes every \((a,b)\) combination and models \[Y_{ab}=\mu+\tau_a+\beta_b+\varepsilon_{ab},\qquad \sum_{a=1}^A\tau_a=0,\quad \sum_{b=1}^B\beta_b=0.\] Treatment contrasts are computed after removing block effects; for algorithms \(a\) and \(a'\), the block-adjusted contrast is \(\widehat\tau_a-\widehat\tau_{a'}\). Randomization occurs within each block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group similar benchmark units into blocks, run all compared algorithms within each block, and estimate algorithm effects after accounting for block differences.
assumptions_latex: \(A\ge2\), \(B\ge2\), and every treatment occurs in every block.
\(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{ab}\mid a,b]=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\tau_a-\widehat\tau_{a'}\) is the block-adjusted comparison of algorithms \(a\) and \(a'\).

notation.meaning: response for algorithm a in block b

review_flags: Supplied source locators do not support blocked-design methodology.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition generally matches complete blocked comparisons, but it has no supporting design-of-experiments citation. A source is also needed to clarify that the displayed one-observation-per-treatment-block additive model is the intended scope and not a replicated or interaction model.

children.title: Pairing–Block Interaction
children.top_down_role: Designs combining matched observations with structured comparison blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairing–Block Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition determining whether a common paired effect is stable across benchmark blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_{bi}=Y_{biA}-Y_{biB}\) be the paired algorithm difference for pair \(i\) in block \(b\). In the model \[D_{bi}=\delta+\gamma_b+\varepsilon_{bi},\qquad \sum_{b=1}^B n_b\gamma_b=0,\] the pairing–block interaction is absent exactly when \(\gamma_b=0\) for every block. Equivalently, all conditional mean paired effects coincide: \(\mathbb E[D_{bi}\mid b]=\delta\). A nonzero \(\gamma_b\) means that the algorithm contrast changes with the blocking factor, so a single pooled paired effect does not describe every block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairing and blocking do not interact when the expected within-pair algorithm difference is identical in every block.
assumptions_latex: \(n_b\ge1\) paired observations are available in each block.
\(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{bi}\mid b]=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No pairing–block interaction \(\iff \gamma_b=0\) for all \(b\iff\mathbb E[D_{bi}\mid b]=\delta\) for all \(b\).

notation.meaning: paired difference i in block b
block-specific departure from the overall paired effect

review_flags: The precise intended interaction model is not supported by the supplied locators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is plausible as an algorithm-by-block interaction expressed through paired differences, but no source supports this exact parameterization or terminology. The intended meaning of pairing-block interaction must be confirmed before accepting the equivalences.

children.title: Factorial Designs
children.top_down_role: Experiments varying multiple implementation or configuration factors across structured combinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorial Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-factorial evaluation of algorithm components or experimental factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let factor \(j\) have a finite level set \(L_j\), for \(j=1,\ldots,k\). A full factorial design evaluates every treatment combination in \[\mathcal T=L_1\times\cdots\times L_k.\] With replication index \(r\), the response at treatment \(x\in\mathcal T\) is \(Y_{x r}\). Main effects and interactions are identifiable contrasts among the cell means \(\mu_x=\mathbb E[Y_{x r}\mid x]\), subject to the chosen contrast coding. Randomization assigns execution order within any required benchmark blocks, and replication supplies independent observations for estimating experimental error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full factorial design evaluates every combination of factor levels, permitting main effects and interactions to be estimated from cell-mean contrasts.
assumptions_latex: \(k\ge1\) and every \(L_j\) is finite and nonempty.
Every \(x\in\mathcal T\) is observed at least once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The treatment set is \(\mathcal T=\prod_{j=1}^kL_j\), and factorial effects are contrasts of \((\mu_x)_{x\in\mathcal T}\).

notation.meaning: mean response at treatment combination x

review_flags: Supplied source locators do not address factorial experimental design.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Factorial Designs leaf and the treatment-space formula is standard, but no factorial-design source is cited. The claims about identifiability, randomization, and replication therefore lack inspectable support.

children.title: Ablation Designs
children.top_down_role: Experiments assessing the contribution of removed or disabled solver components.

knowledge_statements.title: Ablation Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled removal of algorithm components for empirical contribution assessment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{1,ldots,k\}\) index optional algorithm components, and let \(Y(S,u)\) be the response of the variant containing component set \(S\subseteq C\) on benchmark unit \(u\). An ablation design declares a reference set \(S_0\) and evaluates controlled deletions. The single-component ablation effect for \(j\in S_0\) is \[\Delta_j=\mathbb E_u\bigl[Y(S_0,u)-Y(S_0\setminus\{j\},u)\bigr].\] The two variants in each contrast must differ only in component \(j\), and they must be evaluated under matched benchmark and environment conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ablation design removes one declared component at a time from a reference algorithm and compares matched responses to estimate that component’s contribution.
assumptions_latex: \(S_0\subseteq C\) is fixed before observing outcomes.
For each \(j\in S_0\), both compared variants are evaluated on the same sampled units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_j=\mathbb E_u[Y(S_0,u)-Y(S_0\setminus\{j\},u)]\) is the reference-conditional ablation effect of component \(j\).

notation.meaning: response of component set S on benchmark unit u

review_flags: Supplied source locators do not support a formal ablation-design definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed reference-conditional ablation estimand. In addition, the component set is malformed as \(C=\{1,ldots,k\}\), where the intended \(\ldots\) command is missing its backslash. Source support is needed before determining the authoritative formulation and issuing a replacement.

children.title: Interaction Attribution
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of component effects that depend on other experimental factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Interaction Attribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorial contrast attributing nonadditivity to a specified pair of binary components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two binary components \(A\) and \(B\), let \(\mu_{ab}=\mathbb E[Y\mid A=a,B=b]\) for \(a,b\in\{0,1\}\), with all other factors fixed or averaged according to a declared design. Their interaction attribution is the difference of differences \[I_{AB}=(\mu_{11}-\mu_{01})-(\mu_{10}-\mu_{00})=\mu_{11}-\mu_{10}-\mu_{01}+\mu_{00}.\] Thus \(I_{AB}=0\) exactly when the mean effect of enabling \(A\) is unchanged by the level of \(B\). Its sign and magnitude depend on the response scale and coding convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interaction attributed to two binary components is the difference between one component’s mean effect when the other is enabled and disabled.
assumptions_latex: All four cells \((a,b)\in\{0,1\}^2\) are observed under a common design.
Cell means are compared on one fixed response scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{AB}=\mu_{11}-\mu_{10}-\mu_{01}+\mu_{00}\), with no additive interaction exactly when \(I_{AB}=0\).

notation.meaning: mean response at binary component levels a and b

review_flags: No supplied locator supports factorial interaction attribution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The difference-of-differences representation fits the Interaction Attribution leaf for two binary factors, and the scope appropriately notes coding and response-scale dependence. No factorial-design citation with a specific locator supports the formula or its interpretation.

children.title: Randomized Designs
children.top_down_role: Experiments randomizing treatment assignment, order, seeds, or instance allocation.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random assignment of algorithm treatments or execution order within an experiment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite set of experimental units and \(T\) a finite set of algorithm treatments. A randomized design specifies a probability distribution \(P\) over admissible assignments \(Z:U\to T\), chosen independently of potential responses \(Y_u(t)\). The realized assignment is sampled from \(P\) before outcomes are observed. In a completely randomized design with fixed treatment counts, \(P\) is uniform over all assignments having those counts. Randomization may instead be restricted within declared blocks, but every permitted assignment must have a known selection probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized design samples treatment assignments from a declared probability distribution independently of unobserved potential outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(T\) are finite and nonempty.
\(P(Z=z)\) is known for every admissible assignment \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z\sim P\) and \(Z\) is independent of \((Y_u(t))_{u\in U,t\in T}\).

notation.meaning: potential response of unit u under treatment t

review_flags: Supplied source locators concern optimization methods, not randomization-based experimental design.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Randomized Designs and consistently introduces assignments and potential responses. Nevertheless, no randomization-based experimental-design source supports the independence formulation, uniform fixed-count special case, or known-probability requirement.

children.title: Repeated-Run Designs
children.top_down_role: Experiments using multiple executions to characterize stochastic solver variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Run Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replication of stochastic algorithm runs under independently controlled random seeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For algorithm \(a\), benchmark unit \(i\), and replication \(r=1,\ldots,R_{ai}\), a repeated-run design records \(Y_{air}\) from separately initialized runs under the same declared treatment and environment. Conditional on \((a,i)\), the random seeds are independently sampled from a declared seed-generating mechanism. The cell mean and within-cell variance are \[\bar Y_{ai}=R_{ai}^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R_{ai}}Y_{air},\qquad s_{ai}^2=(R_{ai}-1)^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R_{ai}}(Y_{air}-\bar Y_{ai})^2.\] Replications estimate run-to-run variability; they do not replace replication across benchmark units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeat each stochastic algorithm–instance run with independently generated seeds to estimate its conditional mean and run-to-run variability.
assumptions_latex: \(R_{ai}\ge2\) for every cell whose variance is estimated.
Runs are conditionally independent given \((a,i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar Y_{ai}\) estimates the conditional run mean and \(s_{ai}^2\) estimates conditional run variance.

notation.meaning: response of replication r for algorithm a on unit i
number of repeated runs in cell (a,i)

review_flags: No supplied locator supports repeated-run benchmark design.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Repeated-Run Designs leaf and distinguishes within-instance runs from replication across benchmark units. No algorithm-engineering or statistical source with an inspectable locator supports the seed-independence contract or the stated interpretation.

children.title: Randomization–Replication Balance
children.top_down_role: Allocation of experimental effort between randomized conditions and repeated observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomization–Replication Balance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allocation principle separating protection against order bias from estimation of stochastic variability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a fixed run budget \(N\) allocated across treatment cells, with \(R_c\) replications in cell \(c\) and randomized execution order within each admissible block. Randomization controls assignment and order confounding, whereas replication controls Monte Carlo uncertainty. If independent runs in cell \(c\) have variance \(\sigma_c^2\), then \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_c\mid c)=\frac{\sigma_c^2}{R_c}.\] Consequently, randomization cannot compensate for \(R_c=1\) when run variance must be estimated, and additional replication cannot remove systematic order bias when execution order is not randomized or otherwise controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization addresses assignment and order bias; replication estimates run variability. Neither substitutes for the other under a fixed experimental budget.
assumptions_latex: \(N=\sum_cR_c\) is fixed.
Within each cell, runs are independent with finite variance \(\sigma_c^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_c\mid c)=\sigma_c^2/R_c\), while unbiased order protection requires a valid randomization scheme.

notation.meaning: replication count in treatment cell c
run-to-run response variance in cell c

review_flags: The supplied locators do not establish the randomization–replication design principle.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle belongs in the Randomization-Replication Balance leaf, but it lacks a supporting source. The wording that randomization controls assignment and order confounding, and the conclusion's reference to unbiased order protection, require a precise estimand and randomization argument before they can be accepted.

children.title: Fixed-Target Designs
children.top_down_role: Evaluations comparing resources required to reach a predetermined outcome level.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Target Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation of resources required to reach a prespecified solution-quality threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_a(t,\omega,i)\) be the quality attained by algorithm \(a\) on instance \(i\) after resource consumption \(t\) in run \(\omega\), with larger values denoting better quality. For a target \(q_i^*\) fixed before the run, define the hitting resource \[T_a(q_i^*,\omega,i)=\inf\{t\ge0:Q_a(t,\omega,i)\ge q_i^*\}.\] A fixed-target design compares algorithms through the distribution or declared summary of \(T_a\). Runs that do not attain the target within an imposed cap are right-censored and must not be recorded as uncensored hitting times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a quality target in advance and compare algorithms by the resources they require to reach it, treating capped failures as censored.
assumptions_latex: \(q_i^*\) is chosen independently of the evaluated run outcomes.
\(Q_a(t,\omega,i)\) and resource \(t\) use common declared conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-target response is \(T_a(q_i^*,\omega,i)=\inf\{t\ge0:Q_a(t,\omega,i)\ge q_i^*\}\).

notation.meaning: prespecified target quality for instance i
resource required to hit the target

review_flags: Supplied source locators do not support fixed-target benchmarking methodology.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hitting-resource definition fits Fixed-Target Designs, but no benchmarking source supports the formal response or the asserted right-censoring treatment of capped failures. That convention is consequential and must be tied to an inspectable locator.

children.title: Fixed-Budget Designs
children.top_down_role: Evaluations comparing outcomes attained under a predetermined resource allowance.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Budget Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation of solution quality after a prespecified resource allowance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_a(t,\omega,i)\) denote the quality achieved by algorithm \(a\) on instance \(i\) in run \(\omega\) after consuming resource \(t\). For a budget \(b_i\ge0\) fixed before the run, the fixed-budget response is \[V_a(b_i,\omega,i)=Q_a(b_i,\omega,i).\] A fixed-budget design compares algorithms through the distribution or a declared summary of \(V_a\). Every algorithm must use the same resource accounting rule and stopping convention; early termination is assigned the quality of its declared incumbent at budget \(b_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a resource budget in advance and compare the solution quality each algorithm has attained when that budget is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: \(b_i\) is selected independently of evaluated run outcomes.
Resource use and incumbent quality follow common declared conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-budget response is \(V_a(b_i,\omega,i)=Q_a(b_i,\omega,i)\).

notation.meaning: prespecified resource budget for instance i
quality observed at the fixed budget

review_flags: Supplied source locators do not support fixed-budget benchmarking methodology.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-budget response fits the leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no benchmarking source supports it. In particular, assigning an early-terminated run its incumbent quality at the full budget is a substantive convention requiring explicit source support.

children.title: Target–Budget Duality
children.top_down_role: Correspondence and divergence between target-conditioned and budget-conditioned conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Target–Budget Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional equivalence of fixed-target and fixed-budget observations for a monotone incumbent process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(b)\) be the best objective value attained by computational budget \(b\ge 0\) in a minimization run, with \(Q\) nonincreasing. For target \(\tau\), define \(T(\tau)=\inf\{b\ge 0:Q(b)\le \tau\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Then, for every \(b\ge 0\), \[\{T(\tau)\le b\}=\{Q(b)\le \tau\},\qquad \Pr(T(\tau)\le b)=\Pr(Q(b)\le \tau).\] Thus the fixed-target runtime distribution and fixed-budget quality distribution determine the same attainment surface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a monotone best-so-far objective, reaching a target by a budget is exactly the event that the quality observed at that budget meets the target.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(b)\) is the best-so-far value in a minimization run.
Budget \(b\) and target \(\tau\) use fixed, prespecified conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(T(\tau)\le b)=\Pr(Q(b)\le \tau)\) for every \(b\ge 0\).

notation.meaning: Best objective value attained by budget b.
First budget at which target tau is attained.
Objective target for a minimization problem.

review_flags: Exact benchmark-design source supporting the attainment-surface formulation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The attainment-event identity is mathematically plausible and fits the duality leaf, but no cited source supports the fixed-target/fixed-budget attainment-surface formulation.

children.title: Cross-Platform Designs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons spanning distinct hardware or software execution platforms.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Platform Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparability condition for benchmarking algorithms on multiple computing platforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cross-platform benchmark design is paired if every algorithm-instance-seed unit \(u\in U\) is executed on every platform \(p\in P\) under a common protocol, producing response \(Y_{u,p}\). Platform-adjusted algorithm comparisons are identifiable when platform assignment is complete or randomized within units and the analysis includes platform effects, for example \[Y_{u,p}=\mu+\alpha_{a(u)}+\beta_p+\gamma_{a(u),p}+\delta_u+\varepsilon_{u,p}.\] Portability requires reporting \(\gamma_{a,p}\), not merely averages over platforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run matched experimental units on every platform, model platform and algorithm-by-platform effects, and report interactions to distinguish general performance from platform-specific behavior.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) uses identical instances, seeds, stopping rules, and measurement definitions across platforms.
Platform order is randomized or otherwise protected against time trends.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Algorithm effects \(\alpha_a\) are separated from platform effects \(\beta_p\) and portability interactions \(\gamma_{a,p}\).

notation.meaning: Measured response for unit u on platform p.

review_flags: No supplied source addresses cross-platform experimental design or interaction modeling.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed cross-platform design or the claim that complete or randomized assignment plus the displayed model identifies platform-adjusted effects. The interaction-model conditions require authoritative specification.

children.title: Longitudinal Designs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons repeated across software versions, hardware generations, or time periods.

knowledge_statements.title: Longitudinal Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated benchmark measurements across time with stable experimental units and version metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A longitudinal benchmark design observes each retained experimental unit \(u\in U\) at ordered times \(t\in T_u\), recording response \(Y_{u,t}\) and all algorithm, compiler, dependency, operating-system, firmware, and hardware versions. A time contrast is interpretable only when the response definition and workload are invariant, or their changes are explicitly modeled. A suitable decomposition is \[Y_{u,t}=\mu+\delta_u+f(t)+\eta_{u,t},\] with dependence among repeated observations incorporated into uncertainty estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly measure stable benchmark units, record the complete software and hardware state, and model temporal trends and within-unit dependence.
assumptions_latex: Experimental units have persistent identifiers across observation times.
Any workload or measurement change is recorded and modeled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The temporal component \(f(t)\) represents change not attributable to stable unit effects \(\delta_u\).

notation.meaning: Response for experimental unit u at time t.

review_flags: No supplied source supports the longitudinal benchmarking formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits longitudinal benchmark design, but no source supports the design requirements or establishes that the temporal component excludes changes attributable to other time-varying factors.

children.title: Platform–Time Drift
children.top_down_role: Changes where platform evolution and observation time cannot be cleanly separated.

knowledge_statements.title: Platform–Time Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-varying platform effects that invalidate static performance normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For response \(Y_{u,p,t}\) from unit \(u\), platform \(p\), and time \(t\), define the platform contrast \(D_{p,q}(t)=\mathbb{E}[Y_{u,p,t}-Y_{u,q,t}\mid u]\). Platform–time drift is present when there exist platforms \(p,q\) and times \(t_1,t_2\) such that \[D_{p,q}(t_1)\ne D_{p,q}(t_2).\] Equivalently, a response model requires a nonzero platform-by-time term. Consequently, a platform correction estimated at one time need not transport to another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Platform–time drift occurs when the performance difference between two platforms changes over time, making a single static platform correction invalid.
assumptions_latex: Responses use a common scale and matched experimental units.
Relevant platform and time states are recorded.

notation.meaning: Response for unit u on platform p at time t.
Matched expected contrast between platforms p and q at time t.

review_flags: No supplied source defines platform-by-time drift in algorithm benchmarks.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source defines platform–time drift in this benchmark setting. The claimed equivalence with requiring a nonzero platform-by-time term depends on the model class and coding and therefore needs sourced qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Selection Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias caused by nonrepresentative inclusion of benchmark instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\sim P\) denote an instance from the target population, let \(S\in\{0,1\}\) indicate inclusion in the benchmark, and let \(L_a(X)\) be algorithm \(a\)'s loss. Benchmark selection bias for \(a\) is \[B_a=\mathbb{E}[L_a(X)\mid S=1]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[L_a(X)].\] It is absent for the mean-performance estimand when \(B_a=0\). For comparisons of algorithms \(a\) and \(b\), selection can also reverse conclusions when the signs of the selected and population mean loss differences disagree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benchmark selection bias is the difference between performance on selected instances and expected performance in the intended instance population; it may reverse algorithm rankings.
assumptions_latex: The target instance distribution \(P\) and selection indicator \(S\) are conceptually defined.
Losses are integrable under both selected and target distributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bias equals \(B_a=\mathbb{E}[L_a(X)\mid S=1]-\mathbb{E}_{X\sim P}[L_a(X)]\).

notation.meaning: Loss of algorithm a on instance X.

review_flags: No supplied source supports this statistical definition of benchmark selection bias.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The estimand-specific definition is coherent and matches benchmark selection bias, but neither the definition nor the ranking-reversal claim has cited support.

children.title: Configuration Leakage
children.top_down_role: Information transfer into solver configuration from evaluation instances or outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Leakage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation contamination caused by configuration choices informed by held-out outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition instances into configuration data \(C\) and evaluation data \(E\). Let \(Z_E\) denote evaluation outcomes and let \(\widehat c\) be the selected algorithm configuration. Configuration leakage occurs when \(E\) is intended to be held out but \(\widehat c\) is not measurable solely with respect to the permitted configuration information; formally, \[\widehat c\notin\sigma(C,R),\] where \(R\) contains only prespecified external randomness and public prior information, because \(Z_E\) or a statistic derived from it influences configuration selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Configuration leakage occurs when information from the held-out evaluation set influences which algorithm configuration is ultimately evaluated.
assumptions_latex: Configuration and evaluation data have distinct declared roles.
Permitted external information and randomness are specified before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Leakage holds when \(\widehat c\notin\sigma(C,R)\) due to dependence on \(Z_E\).
review_flags: No supplied source formalizes configuration leakage for algorithm engineering.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the formulation, and the expression \(\widehat c\notin\sigma(C,R)\) is ill-typed: a random configuration is not an event in a sigma-algebra. Measurability should be expressed using \(\sigma(\widehat c)\subseteq\sigma(C,R)\) or an equivalent sourced formulation.

children.title: Tuning Leakage
children.top_down_role: Evaluation contamination arising from parameter or portfolio tuning on protected data.

knowledge_statements.title: Tuning Leakage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive hyperparameter tuning that improperly consumes evaluation-set feedback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_k\) be the hyperparameter choice at tuning round \(k\), and let \(Z_E(h_k)\) be feedback computed on the held-out evaluation set \(E\). Tuning leakage occurs if a later choice or the reported choice uses such feedback, namely if for some \(k\), \[h_{k+1}=g_k(C,R,Z_E(h_1),\ldots,Z_E(h_k))\] with nonconstant dependence on an evaluation statistic. Repeated evaluation followed by choosing the best observed hyperparameter is therefore leakage unless a fresh untouched evaluation set is used afterward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tuning leakage occurs when evaluation-set results guide later hyperparameter choices or determine which tuned result is reported.
assumptions_latex: The evaluation set \(E\) is declared held out from tuning.
Tuning rounds and all feedback channels are identifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Leakage occurs when some \(h_{k+1}\) depends nontrivially on \(Z_E(h_j)\) for \(j\le k\).

notation.meaning: Hyperparameter choice at tuning round k.
Evaluation-set feedback for hyperparameter choice h.

review_flags: No supplied source formalizes adaptive tuning leakage in benchmark studies.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The adaptive-feedback description matches tuning leakage, but no source supports its formal definition or the asserted fresh-evaluation-set remedy.

children.title: Leakage-Control Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Separation boundaries between configuration development, tuning data, and final evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Leakage-Control Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-flow separation required between development, tuning, validation, and final evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D,T,V,E\) be development, tuning, validation, and final-evaluation data, and let \(A\) denote every artifact fixed before final evaluation, including code, features, configurations, stopping rules, and reporting rules. A leakage-control boundary is valid when \[A\in\sigma(D,T,V,R),\qquad A\notin\sigma(D,T,V,R,Z_E)\setminus\sigma(D,T,V,R),\] where \(R\) is prespecified randomness and \(Z_E\) denotes any evaluation-derived information. After unblinding \(Z_E\), modifying \(A\) requires a new untouched evaluation set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All executable and reporting choices must be fixed without final-evaluation feedback; changes after unblinding require a fresh evaluation set.
assumptions_latex: Dataset roles and permitted information flows are declared prospectively.
All artifacts affecting execution or reporting are versioned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Final-evaluation information \(Z_E\) has no influence on the fixed artifact \(A\).

notation.meaning: Development, tuning, validation, and final-evaluation data.

review_flags: No supplied source establishes this information-flow boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes this boundary, and both displayed membership expressions are ill-typed because the artifact \(A\) is treated as an event belonging to sigma-algebras. A valid formulation must state measurability or conditional independence precisely.

children.title: Machine Confounding
children.top_down_role: Performance distortion attributable to physical machine characteristics.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine Confounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm effects mixed with physical-machine effects by an unbalanced assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be algorithm assignment, \(M\) physical-machine assignment, and \(Y\) the measured response. Machine confounding occurs when algorithm and machine effects cannot be separately identified from the design, as when \(A\) determines \(M\). In the additive model \[Y=\mu+\alpha_A+\beta_M+\varepsilon,\] complete confounding occurs when the design matrix columns for \(\alpha_A\) and \(\beta_M\) are linearly dependent. An observed algorithm contrast may then equal an algorithm effect plus an unidentified machine contrast.
