knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machine confounding occurs when algorithms are assigned to machines so that algorithm effects cannot be distinguished from physical-machine effects.
assumptions_latex: Machines may differ in performance-relevant physical characteristics.
The estimand is an algorithm effect independent of machine assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effects \(\alpha_A\) and \(\beta_M\) are not separately identifiable under a rank-deficient assignment design.
review_flags: No supplied source addresses physical-machine confounding in benchmark experiments.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-deficiency characterization fits machine confounding, but no source supports its application to benchmark experiments or the exact design-matrix formulation.

children.title: System Confounding
children.top_down_role: Performance distortion attributable to operating-system, runtime, or background-service behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: System Confounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm effects mixed with software-system or runtime-environment effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) denote algorithm assignment, \(S\) the software-system state, and \(Y\) the response. The state \(S\) may include compiler, libraries, operating system, scheduler, runtime, and configuration. System confounding occurs when the design cannot separately identify algorithm and system effects. In \[Y=\mu+\alpha_A+\gamma_S+\varepsilon,\] complete confounding occurs when the design columns for \(\alpha_A\) and \(\gamma_S\) are linearly dependent, for example when each algorithm is executed under a distinct system state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: System confounding occurs when algorithms use different software environments, preventing their effects from being separated from compiler, library, operating-system, or runtime effects.
assumptions_latex: Software-system states may affect the measured response.
The desired algorithm contrast is intended to hold system state fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effects \(\alpha_A\) and \(\gamma_S\) are not separately identifiable from the observed design.
review_flags: No supplied source addresses software-system confounding in benchmark experiments.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition fits system confounding, but no cited evidence supports the benchmark-specific formulation or its identifiability characterization.

children.title: Machine–System Entanglement
children.top_down_role: Cases where hardware effects cannot be isolated from system-level execution effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine–System Entanglement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonidentifiability between physical-machine and software-system effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be physical-machine assignment and \(S\) software-system assignment in the response model \[Y=\mu+\beta_M+\gamma_S+\xi_{M,S}+\varepsilon.\] Machine–system entanglement is present when the observed support \(\mathcal O\subseteq M\times S\) does not permit separate estimation of machine, system, and interaction effects. In particular, if each machine is observed with only one system state, then \(\beta_M\) and \(\gamma_S\) are aliased. A crossed or connected assignment is required to separate these components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Machine–system entanglement arises when software states are tied to particular machines, so hardware, software, and their interaction cannot be separated.
assumptions_latex: Both physical-machine and software-system states can affect responses.
Observed machine-system combinations are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate effects are unidentifiable when the support \(\mathcal O\) aliases \(\beta_M\), \(\gamma_S\), or \(\xi_{M,S}\).
review_flags: No supplied source formalizes machine-system assignment entanglement.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source formalizes machine–system entanglement. Moreover, saying that a crossed or connected assignment is required does not fully specify the replication and rank conditions needed to estimate main and interaction effects separately.

children.title: Timeout Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion introduced by the placement or application of execution time limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Timeout Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias from treating timed-out runs as ordinary completed observations or excluding them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be runtime to a prespecified target, let \(c>0\) be the timeout, and observe \(X=\min(T,c)\) with completion indicator \(\Delta=\mathbf 1\{T\le c\}\). Timeout bias occurs when a completed-runtime estimand is estimated by either \(\mathbb E[X]\) or \(\mathbb E[T\mid\Delta=1]\) without a censoring-aware model. Generally, \[\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[T],\] while conditioning on completion preferentially removes long runs and can distort algorithm comparisons, especially when completion probabilities differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Timeout bias results when capped runtimes or completed runs alone are analyzed as ordinary runtimes, typically understating runtime and potentially changing rankings.
assumptions_latex: Runtime \(T\) is nonnegative and the target is fixed.
The timeout \(c\) is finite and timed-out runs are right-censored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Naive use of \(X\) yields \(\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[T]\), and complete-case analysis targets \(\mathbb E[T\mid\Delta=1]\) rather than \(\mathbb E[T]\).

notation.meaning: Runtime required to attain the target.
Indicator that the target was reached before timeout.

review_flags: No supplied source supports the censoring-based formulation of timeout bias.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The censoring formulation and inequality are plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no source supports labeling these naive analyses as timeout bias or the stated implications for algorithm comparisons.

children.title: Censoring Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by incomplete outcome observations for terminated executions.

knowledge_statements.title: Censoring Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Statistical bias caused by performance-dependent observation of benchmark outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in L^1\) be an uncensored performance outcome and let \(R\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether \(Y\) is fully observed. For the target \(\mu=\mathbb E[Y]\), the complete-case estimand is \(\mu_{\mathrm{obs}}=\mathbb E[Y\mid R=1]\), provided \(\mathbb P(R=1)>0\). Its censoring bias is \[B_{\mathrm{cens}}=\mu_{\mathrm{obs}}-\mu.\] Censoring bias is present when \(B_{\mathrm{cens}}\ne0\). In particular, integrability and independence \(Y\perp R\) imply \(B_{\mathrm{cens}}=0\), whereas outcome-dependent censoring can make it nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Censoring bias is the difference between the mean among fully observed runs and the mean that would be obtained from all uncensored outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{cens}}=\mathbb E[Y\mid R=1]-\mathbb E[Y]\).

notation.meaning: Indicator that the outcome is fully observed.

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses statistical censoring bias.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no cited source supports this complete-case formulation of censoring bias or provides an inspectable locator.

children.title: Timeout-Induced Censoring
children.top_down_role: Censoring patterns specifically created by experimental timeout policies.

knowledge_statements.title: Timeout-Induced Censoring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-censoring of algorithm runtime at a declared timeout.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in[0,\infty]\) be the runtime required by an algorithm to finish an instance, and fix a timeout \(\tau\in(0,\infty)\). The timeout-observed data are \[X=\min\{T,\tau\},\qquad \Delta=\mathbf 1\{T\le\tau\}.\] A run with \(\Delta=0\) is right-censored: the observation identifies only \(T>\tau\), not the actual runtime. Treating \(X=\tau\) as an exact completion time replaces censored observations by point values and generally changes runtime means, quantiles, and algorithm comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timeout records only that an unfinished run exceeds the cutoff; its true runtime remains unknown and is right-censored.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in[0,\infty]\).
\(0<\tau<\infty\) is fixed and recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((X,\Delta)=(\min\{T,\tau\},\mathbf 1\{T\le\tau\})\), with \(\Delta=0\) revealing only \(T>\tau\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses survival-style timeout censoring.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The right-censoring representation is standard and the definition fits the leaf, but the claims about affected summaries and comparisons lack a supporting citation and locator.

children.title: Multiple-Comparison Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion arising from evaluating many solvers, metrics, instances, or hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Comparison Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: False-positive inflation from selecting among many unadjusted benchmark comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(m\ge2\) true null hypotheses tested at marginal level \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and report that a difference exists whenever at least one null is rejected. If the test decisions are independent and each rejects with probability \(\alpha\), then the family-wise false-positive probability is \[\operatorname{FWER}=1-(1-\alpha)^m>\alpha.\] Thus interpreting the smallest unadjusted \(p\)-value as if only one comparison had been planned yields an anti-conservative claim. Under arbitrary dependence, the union bound instead gives \(\operatorname{FWER}\le m\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Searching multiple unadjusted comparisons increases the probability of at least one false discovery; under independence it equals one minus the probability that none reject.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge2\) null hypotheses are all true.
Each marginal test has rejection probability \(\alpha\).
For the equality, rejection decisions are independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{FWER}=1-(1-\alpha)^m>\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Probability of at least one false rejection.

review_flags: No supplied source locator covers multiple-testing error inflation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The independent-test FWER formula and union bound are mathematically correct, and property is an acceptable role for the stated inflation phenomenon, but neither claim has cited evidence.

children.title: Selective Reporting Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by preferential disclosure of favorable experimental results.

knowledge_statements.title: Selective Reporting Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias induced when disclosure depends on realized benchmark results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in L^1\) be a benchmark result and let \(S\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that the result is reported. For the target \(\mu=\mathbb E[Y]\), the reported-result estimand is \(\mu_S=\mathbb E[Y\mid S=1]\), assuming \(\mathbb P(S=1)>0\). Selective reporting bias is \[B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mu_S-\mu.\] It vanishes when \(S\) is independent of \(Y\), but can be nonzero when reporting depends on statistical significance, favorable rank, effect direction, or magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selective reporting bias is the difference between the average disclosed result and the average over all eligible results when disclosure depends on outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb E[Y\mid S=1]-\mathbb E[Y]\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses outcome-dependent selective reporting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outcome-dependent reporting formulation is coherent and fits a definition of selective reporting bias, but no source establishes this exact estimand or the listed selection mechanisms.

children.title: Multiplicity-Aware Reporting
children.top_down_role: Reporting structures that expose the breadth of comparisons behind published conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity-Aware Reporting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reporting rule controlling family-wise error across declared benchmark comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a prespecified family of \(m\ge1\) hypotheses with valid marginal \(p\)-values \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\), multiplicity-aware Bonferroni reporting declares hypothesis \(i\) significant only if \(p_i\le\alpha/m\). It reports the family definition, \(m\), the adjustment rule, and adjusted values \(q_i=\min\{1,mp_i\}\). Regardless of dependence among tests, \[\mathbb P\!\left(\text{at least one false rejection}\right)\le\alpha.\] The guarantee applies to the declared family and does not justify unreported post hoc comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declare the comparison family and adjust its p-values; Bonferroni reporting controls the chance of any false rejection without requiring test independence.
assumptions_latex: Each true-null \(p_i\) is super-uniform.
The tested family of size \(m\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_i\le\alpha/m\) implies family-wise error at most \(\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Number of comparisons in the family.

review_flags: No supplied source locator covers multiplicity-adjusted statistical reporting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bonferroni reporting principle is mathematically sound under super-uniform true-null p-values and fits the leaf, but its error-control guarantee requires a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Internal Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing whether observed performance differences support causal study conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Internal Validity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification conditions for causal algorithm effects within the sampled benchmark regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) denote an algorithm assignment, \(X\) recorded instance and system covariates, and \(Y(a)\) the potential outcome under algorithm \(a\). An experimental regime is internally valid for comparing \(a\) and \(b\) when consistency \(Y=Y(A)\), conditional exchangeability \((Y(a),Y(b))\perp A\mid X\), and positivity \(0<\mathbb P(A=a\mid X),\mathbb P(A=b\mid X)\) hold almost surely. Then the within-regime causal contrast is identified by \[\mathbb E[Y(a)-Y(b)]=\mathbb E_X\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid A=a,X]-\mathbb E[Y\mid A=b,X]\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Internal validity holds when assignment, measurement, and overlap conditions make observed within-benchmark differences identify the causal effect of choosing one algorithm over another.
assumptions_latex: Consistency holds for recorded outcomes.
Potential outcomes are conditionally exchangeable given \(X\).
Both compared assignments have positive conditional probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Y(a)-Y(b)]\) is identified by the covariate-adjusted observed contrast.
review_flags: The intended causal-inference formulation requires a directly relevant experimental-design source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, but this causal-identification formalization needs direct support. The domain and assignment mechanism for algorithms a and b are also not fully specified, so the exact identification claim should be checked against an authoritative source.

children.title: External Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing transfer of experimental conclusions beyond the sampled corpus or environment.

knowledge_statements.title: External Validity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportability conditions from a benchmark population to a target instance population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=1\) identify the benchmark population, \(S=0\) a target population, \(X\) effect-modifying covariates, and \(Y(a)\) the potential outcome under algorithm \(a\). External validity for transporting the mean performance of \(a\) holds when \(Y(a)\perp S\mid X\) and target overlap \(\mathbb P(S=1\mid X)>0\) holds for target-almost-every \(X\). Under consistency, \[\mathbb E[Y(a)\mid S=0]=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid A=a,X,S=1]\mid S=0\right].\] Failure of overlap or conditional population invariance prevents this identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benchmark results transport to a target population when relevant covariates overlap and conditional algorithm outcomes are invariant between benchmark and target populations.
assumptions_latex: Consistency holds in the benchmark population.
\(Y(a)\perp S\mid X\).
Benchmark support covers target covariate values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Y(a)\mid S=0]\) is identified by standardizing benchmark outcomes to the target covariate distribution.
review_flags: The intended transportability formulation requires a directly relevant source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, but the displayed transport formula additionally requires identification of the algorithm-specific outcome within the benchmark population, such as conditional exchangeability and treatment positivity. A directly relevant source is needed to determine and state the sufficient assumptions.

children.title: Construct Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Alignment between reported measurements and the performance concepts they are intended to represent.

knowledge_statements.title: Construct Validity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which benchmark measurements represent the intended performance construct.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be the intended algorithm-performance construct, \(M\) the reported metric, and \(U\) nuisance conditions that are outside the construct. A measurement regime has construct validity for a declared scale function \(g\) when \[\mathbb E[M\mid Z=z,U=u]=g(z)\] for every supported \((z,u)\), with \(g\) injective and fixed before analysis. Nuisance invariance ensures that equal construct values have equal expected measurements across admissible systems or measurement procedures; injectivity ensures that distinct construct values remain distinguishable on the reported scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric validly represents a construct when its expected value depends injectively on that construct and not on irrelevant measurement conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is integrable.
\(g\) is prespecified and injective.
The displayed conditional expectation exists on the supported domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[M\mid Z=z,U=u]=g(z)\) independently of \(u\).
review_flags: Construct validity admits multiple formalizations; no relevant source was supplied for this measurement-invariance version.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, but equating construct validity with injective conditional-mean nuisance invariance is a narrow, nonstandard formalization that excludes other accepted validity frameworks. Its intended scope cannot be established without a directly relevant source.

children.title: Benchmark Corpus Engineering
children.top_down_role: Construction, representation, validation, selection, and stewardship of benchmark collections independently of any one problem family.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Shared test libraries, generators, formats, and experimental infrastructure
Selection Methodology and Benchmark Set
Problem-indexed test-data collections

knowledge_statements.title: Real-World Instance Collections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark collections whose instances originate in documented operational systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A real-world instance collection is a finite indexed family \(\mathcal C=\{(I_j,ho_j)
\}_{j=1}^n\) in which each optimization instance \(I_j\) is extracted from a documented operational process rather than sampled from a benchmark generator. Its provenance record \(\rho_j\) identifies the source domain, acquisition procedure, acquisition time or version, preprocessing operations, and deduplication relation. Membership requires that the recorded transformation chain reconstruct the released instance from the acquired source data, subject to explicitly documented privacy-preserving redactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-world collection contains operationally sourced instances with enough provenance to identify acquisition, preprocessing, versioning, and duplicates.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\) is finite.
Each released instance has a provenance record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C=\{(I_j,\rho_j)\}_{j=1}^n\) is real-world exactly when each \(I_j\) has documented operational origin and reconstructible preprocessing provenance.
review_flags: No supplied source locator defines benchmark-instance provenance classes.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the collection-type leaf, but reconstructible preprocessing and the specified provenance fields are normative membership requirements not supported by any cited benchmark-engineering source.

knowledge_statements.title: Synthetic Model Collections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark collections sampled from explicit generative instance models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A synthetic model collection is a finite family \(\mathcal C=\{(I_j,\theta_j,s_j,G_j)
\}_{j=1}^n\) such that \(I_j=G_j(\theta_j,s_j)\), where \(G_j\) is a documented generator, \(\theta_j\) its parameter setting, and \(s_j\) its random seed or complete randomness record. The collection specification includes the design or probability law governing \((G_j,	heta_j,s_j)\). Re-execution with the recorded generator version, parameters, and randomness must reproduce \(I_j\), except where an explicitly declared stochastic replay convention is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A synthetic collection consists of instances produced by documented generators with recorded parameters, sampling design, versions, and reproducible randomness.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\) is finite.
Every generator invocation and its version are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_j=G_j(\theta_j,s_j)\) with a documented collection-level sampling design.
review_flags: No supplied source locator defines synthetic benchmark collection provenance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the collection-type leaf, but exact replay, complete randomness records, and the stated collection-level specification are unsupported normative requirements. No relevant source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Constructed Hard Collections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purpose-built benchmark families satisfying a declared empirical or analytic hardness criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an algorithm class \(\mathcal A\), resource measure \(R(A,I)\), instance-size function \(n(I)\), and threshold \(h:\mathbb N\to[0,\infty)\). A constructed hard collection is a finite family \(\mathcal C\) of deliberately generated or selected instances for which each \(I\in\mathcal C\) satisfies the declared criterion \[\inf_{A\in\mathcal A}R(A,I)\ge h(n(I)),\] or a stated empirical surrogate for this inequality. The construction procedure, target algorithm class, resource, threshold, and any filtering by observed performance are part of the collection definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constructed hard collection is purpose-built against a declared algorithm class and hardness measure, with construction and performance-based filtering fully recorded.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) and \(R\) are declared before classification.
\(h\) is a declared size-dependent threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\in\mathcal C\) only if it meets the stated hardness criterion or its explicitly labeled empirical surrogate.

notation.meaning: Declared resource used on instance I by algorithm A.
Hardness threshold as a function of size.

review_flags: Hardness is relative to an algorithm and resource model; no relevant benchmark-engineering source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the leaf only provisionally. The analytic infimum criterion and an unspecified empirical surrogate are materially different notions of hardness, and a benchmark-engineering source is needed to establish a defensible classification and required metadata.

children.title: Transformed Instance Collections
children.top_down_role: Collections derived through systematic representation-preserving or structure-altering transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Transformed Instance Collections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derived benchmarks obtained by recorded transformations of source instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A transformed instance collection is a finite family \(\mathcal C'=\{(I'_j,I_j,T_j,ho_j)
\}_{j=1}^n\) satisfying \(I'_j=T_j(I_j)\), where \(I_j\) belongs to an identified source collection, \(T_j\) is a deterministic recorded transformation, and \(\rho_j\) links both versions and transformation parameters. The record must state whether feasibility, objective values, or optimal solutions are preserved and provide the corresponding computable map when preservation is claimed. A transformed instance is not treated as provenance-independent of its source.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transformed collection derives each instance from an identified source through a recorded operation and states which feasible or optimal solutions are preserved.
assumptions_latex: Each source instance \(I_j\) is uniquely identified.
Each transformation \(T_j\) and its parameters are reproducible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I'_j=T_j(I_j)\) with an explicit derivative-provenance link and declared solution-preservation relation.
review_flags: No supplied source locator defines transformed benchmark collections or derivative provenance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the transformed-collection leaf, but deterministic transformation, reproducibility, preservation-map, and provenance-dependence requirements lack a cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Perturbed Instance Collections
children.top_down_role: Collections derived through controlled changes to data, coefficients, topology, or constraints.

assumptions_latex: Each perturbation kernel preserves the instance class or explicitly records rejection of invalid outcomes.
Every random seed and kernel parameter is retained in the benchmark metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting collection is a reproducible family of valid instances derived from identified parents by controlled perturbations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reproducible, validity-preserving perturbation collections for empirical benchmarking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a collection of instances from a specified optimization class. A perturbed instance collection is a multiset \(C'=\{I'_{i,j}\}\) for which every element is generated as \(I'_{i,j}\sim K_{\theta_{i,j}}(\cdot\mid I_i)\) from some identified parent \(I_i\in C\). Its provenance record contains the parent identifier, kernel name and version, parameter \(\theta_{i,j}\), random seed, and validity-test result. The collection is admissible only when every retained \(I'_{i,j}\) satisfies the class constraints and the experimental design specifies whether repeated or isomorphic outcomes are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbed collection reproducibly modifies identified parent instances while recording parameters, seeds, validity checks, and the policy for duplicate or isomorphic outcomes.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Instance Collections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, and the notation is coherent, but no source supports the proposed admissibility and provenance requirements. These requirements are design conventions rather than uniquely standard mathematical facts.

children.title: Derivative Provenance Links
children.top_down_role: Traceability between derived instances and their source collections.

assumptions_latex: Instance identifiers are stable within the benchmark corpus.
Each recorded derivation operation has a fixed versioned interpretation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A provenance link permits the child instance and its derivation from the parent to be independently reconstructed or audited.

notation.meaning: versioned derivation operator with parameters theta and seed s

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directed provenance records between benchmark instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A derivative provenance link is a directed record \(e=(I_p,I_c,T,v,\theta,s,h_p,h_c)\) asserting that child instance \(I_c\) was obtained from parent \(I_p\) by the versioned operation \(T_{v,\theta,s}\), so that \(I_c=T_{v,\theta,s}(I_p)\). Here \(\theta\) contains all nonrandom parameters, \(s\) is the random seed when applicable, and \(h_p,h_c\) are integrity digests of the serialized instances. A link is reproducible when executing the recorded operation on the verified parent serialization yields a serialization with digest \(h_c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative provenance link records a directed, versioned transformation from a verified parent instance to a verified child, including parameters, seed, and integrity digests.
knowledge_statements.title: Derivative Provenance Links

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the provenance-link leaf, but no source supports this particular schema. Exact reconstruction also requires the execution environment, serialization convention, and pseudorandom-generator specification, which are not explicitly included.

assumptions_latex: The challenge edition, rules, and original instance identifiers are available.
Any later corrections or format conversions are distinguishable from the original release.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership is determined by documented challenge release provenance rather than by an instance's structural properties alone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses release provenance as the defining criterion for historical challenge corpora.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a documented challenge edition \(q\), its historical challenge collection \(H_q\) is the set of benchmark instances officially released or explicitly incorporated by reference under that edition's rules. Formally, \(H_q=R_q\cup A_q\), where \(R_q\) is the official release and \(A_q\) contains externally hosted instances named by the organizers. Each member retains its original identifier, release role, format, and checksum. A corrected or converted artifact is a derivative of a member of \(H_q\), not the original member, unless the challenge record declares that artifact authoritative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A historical challenge collection consists exactly of instances officially released or incorporated by a documented challenge edition, with later conversions and corrections tracked as derivatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Historical Challenge Collections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A provenance-based definition fits the topic, but no challenge archive, ruleset, or benchmark-corpus authority is cited for the proposed membership and derivative-artifact policy.

children.title: Random Graph Generators
children.top_down_role: Generators sampling graph structures under probabilistic structural regimes.

assumptions_latex: The vertex count and graph-model parameters are admissible.
The pseudorandom generator and its seed are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output graph is a reproducible sample from the declared graph distribution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a general independent-edge random graph generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an integer \(n\geq 1\), probabilities \(p_{ij}\in[0,1]\) for every admissible unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\), and seed \(s\). Initialize \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(E=\varnothing\). Using the seeded pseudorandom stream, draw mutually independent variables \(U_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) in a fixed lexicographic pair order; insert \(\{i,j\}\) into \(E\) exactly when \(U_{ij}\leq p_{ij}\). Output \(G=(V,E)\), together with \(n\), the probability specification, seed, generator version, and pair-order convention. Thus \(\Pr(\{i,j\}\in E)=p_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generator samples each admissible edge independently with its declared probability and records enough ordering, seed, and version information to reproduce the graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Random Graph Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is a precise independent-edge generator and fits the leaf, but no authoritative random-graph source or generator specification is cited. The local inventory does not support this claim.

children.title: Random Network Generators
children.top_down_role: Generators producing network instances with domain-specific attributes such as capacities, costs, or demands.

assumptions_latex: A directed or undirected topology distribution is specified.
Attribute distributions satisfy declared feasibility conditions.
The pseudorandom generator and seed are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a reproducible random network instance whose topology and attributes follow the declared joint generation law.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers topology-plus-attribute generation for flow-style benchmark networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a topology law \(P_G\), conditional attribute laws \(P_A(\cdot\mid G)\), feasibility predicate \(F\), seed \(s\), and retry bound \(R\). Initialize the seeded pseudorandom stream. For \(r=1,\ldots,R\), sample \(G=(V,A)\sim P_G\), then sample capacities \(u_a\), costs \(c_a\), and node balances \(b_v\) from \(P_A(\cdot\mid G)\). Accept and output the first network satisfying \(F(G,u,c,b)=1\); otherwise output failure after \(R\) attempts. The record includes all laws, parameters, draw order, seed, version, and rejection count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random network generator samples topology and flow attributes from declared laws, rejects infeasible samples under a stated predicate, and records the complete reproducibility metadata.
knowledge_statements.title: Random Network Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits the leaf, but rejection changes the accepted output law to a distribution conditioned on feasibility and permits failure after the retry bound. Thus the conclusion's claim that the output follows the declared joint law requires correction or an explicitly conditioned law, supported by a source.

children.title: Graph-to-Network Enrichment
children.top_down_role: Processes that augment sampled graph structures with network-specific instance data.

assumptions_latex: The input graph has stable vertex and edge identifiers.
All attribute rules and random draws are explicitly parameterized.
A feasibility predicate for the target network model is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output preserves the chosen graph topology while adding reproducible network attributes satisfying the target feasibility predicate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maps a graph topology to a feasible attributed network benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a graph \(G=(V,E)\), orientation or arc-expansion rule \(O\), attribute rule \(A_\theta\), feasibility predicate \(F\), and seed \(s\). Initialize \((V,D)=O(G)\). In fixed identifier order, assign each arc \(a\in D\) its capacity, lower bound, and cost, and each vertex \(v\in V\) its balance, using \(A_\theta\) and the seeded random stream. If \(F(V,D,u,\ell,c,b)=0\), apply the declared repair rule or return failure. Otherwise output \(N=(V,D,u,\ell,c,b)\) with the parent graph identifier and complete enrichment metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph-to-network enrichment orients or expands graph edges, assigns network attributes in fixed order, checks feasibility, and preserves a provenance link to the original graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-to-Network Enrichment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits graph-to-network enrichment, but no source supports the schema. The optional repair rule is not defined and may alter attributes in ways not represented by the stated attribute rule or feasibility model.

children.title: Geometric Generators
children.top_down_role: Generators whose combinatorial structure is induced by geometric objects or distance relations.

assumptions_latex: The sampling region is measurable and the point distribution is specified.
The metric and any deterministic tie-breaking convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a reproducible geometric instance consisting of sampled sites and metric-derived data.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines seeded generation of point-based geometric optimization instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a dimension \(d\geq 1\), measurable region \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), site count \(n\), probability law \(\mu\) on \(D\), metric \(\rho\), and seed \(s\). Initialize the seeded pseudorandom stream and sample \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) from \(\mu\) in identifier order, using the declared dependence model. Compute required geometric data, such as \(w_{ij}=\rho(x_i,x_j)\), without unrecorded rounding. Output the sites and derived data with \(d,D,\mu,\rho,s\), numerical precision, coordinate convention, and generator version.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric generator samples identified sites in a declared metric region and derives geometric weights while recording seed, precision, coordinate convention, and sampling law.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits geometric generation and is internally coherent, but no authoritative source supports the general generator specification or its reproducibility requirements.

children.title: Spatial Generators
children.top_down_role: Generators modeling location-dependent distributions, regions, or spatial interaction patterns.

assumptions_latex: The spatial domain and object-placement law are specified.
Object interactions and boundary conventions are deterministic given the sampled objects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a reproducible spatial optimization instance retaining both object geometry and derived interaction data.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers spatial objects and interactions, not merely point-distance matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), object count \(n\), placement-and-shape law \(\mu\), interaction predicate \(R\), boundary rule \(B\), and seed \(s\). Initialize the seeded pseudorandom stream. Generate labeled spatial objects \(S_1,\ldots,S_n\) according to \(\mu\), applying \(B\) to objects meeting the boundary. In fixed pair order, compute all required relations \(R(S_i,S_j)\) and associated spatial attributes. Output the objects, relations, and complete parameters, including coordinate reference, precision, seed, draw order, rejection policy, and generator version.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spatial generator samples extended objects in a declared domain, applies boundary rules, computes their interactions, and records sufficient metadata for exact regeneration.
knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm distinguishes spatial objects from point-only geometric instances and fits the leaf, but its broad placement, boundary, interaction, and exact-regeneration specification has no cited authority.

children.title: Geometry-to-Topology Mapping
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between sampled spatial geometry and resulting combinatorial structure.

assumptions_latex: The geometric objects and coordinate convention are fixed.
The adjacency predicate and tie-breaking rules are deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping produces a uniquely determined topology whose edges are justified by the declared geometric predicate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents topology as a deterministic predicate over geometric objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given indexed geometric objects \(X=(S_1,\ldots,S_n)\) and a symmetric parameterized predicate \(R_\theta\), the geometry-to-topology mapping is \[G_\theta(X)=(V,E),\qquad V=\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad E=\bigl\{\{i,j\}:i<j\text{ and }R_\theta(S_i,S_j)=1\bigr\}.\] Examples of admissible predicates include threshold distance, region intersection, visibility, or membership in a specified geometric complex. The mapping record must include \(\theta\), coordinate precision, boundary inclusivity, degeneracy handling, and tie-breaking, so identical geometric input determines identical topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometry-to-topology mapping creates one vertex per geometric object and an edge exactly when a declared deterministic geometric adjacency predicate holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-to-Topology Mapping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and displayed mapping fit the leaf, with all TeX commands properly delimited. However, no source supports the asserted taxonomy of predicates or the normative mapping-record requirements.

assumptions_latex: The latent structure is sampled or selected before the observable instance.
The conditional instance law guarantees that the selected structure is feasible.
The generator records the latent structure separately from the solver input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated instance has a known feasible planted witness that can be used for controlled evaluation without exposing it to the tested algorithm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies generation conditional on a hidden feasible witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a latent-structure law \(P_Z\), a conditional instance law \(P_{I\mid Z}\), parameters \(\theta\), and seed \(s\). Initialize the seeded pseudorandom stream, sample \(Z\sim P_Z(\theta)\), and then sample \(I\sim P_{I\mid Z}(\theta)\) until the declared predicate \(F(I,Z)=1\) holds or a stated retry limit is reached. Output \(I\) as the benchmark instance and store \(Z\), the seed, parameters, rejection count, and generator version in protected metadata. Planting certifies feasibility of \(Z\); it certifies optimality only when an additional verifiable optimality condition is recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planted-structure generator first chooses a hidden witness, then samples an instance conditioned on that witness, while distinguishing guaranteed feasibility from separately certified optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Planted-Structure Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits planted-structure generation and correctly separates feasibility from optimality, but no planted-model or benchmark-generation source supports the proposed general formulation.

assumptions_latex: The parameter domain and deterministic or stochastic generator are specified.
Each stress coordinate has an operational interpretation.
Resource measurements use a fixed experimental protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family supports controlled stress analysis by varying declared parameters while holding all other generation and measurement conventions fixed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines controlled parameter sweeps designed to expose algorithmic resource sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized stress generator is a family \(\{G_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\) with a declared stress domain \(\Theta\), where each coordinate of \(\theta\) controls an instance feature hypothesized to affect an algorithmic resource. For algorithm \(A\), seed set \(S\), and resource measure \(R_A\), the benchmark design evaluates \(R_A(G_\theta(s))\) over a specified grid or sampling design in \(\Theta\) and \(s\in S\). The generator specification fixes all nonvaried parameters, validity tests, seed coupling across parameter values, retry policy, and output-size accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameterized stress generator varies declared instance features over a controlled design and measures algorithmic resources while fixing seeds, validity rules, and all nonvaried settings.
knowledge_statements.title: Parameterized Stress Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the topic, but it combines a generator-family definition with an experimental measurement design without a source establishing that exact scope. No authority supports the seed-coupling and accounting requirements.

children.title: Adversarial Generators
children.top_down_role: Generators targeting vulnerabilities of specified algorithms, heuristics, or implementation choices.

assumptions_latex: The tested algorithm and observable generation interface are specified.
Every generated object is a valid instance of the optimization problem.
The adversary's information and computational budget are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generator returns a valid instance selected to maximize a declared performance loss within the stated adversarial model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses an explicit adversarial information model and loss objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an algorithm \(A\), valid instance family \(\mathcal{I}\), loss functional \(L(A,I)\), adversarial information model \(\mathcal{M}\), query or time budget \(B\), and seed \(s\). Initialize a valid candidate \(I_0\in\mathcal{I}\). At step \(t\), use only information permitted by \(\mathcal{M}\) to propose \(I'\in\mathcal{I}\), evaluate or estimate \(L(A,I')\), and update \(I_{t+1}\) according to the declared search rule. Stop when budget \(B\) is exhausted and output the best observed instance, its loss, search trace, seed, and validity certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adversarial generator searches valid instances, under a declared information and computation budget, for one maximizing a specified performance loss of the tested algorithm.
knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Generators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits the leaf, but no source defines the adversarial model or search procedure. A budgeted heuristic returns the best observed candidate, not necessarily an instance maximizing the loss over the admissible family, so the conclusion is overstated unless an optimization guarantee is supplied.

children.title: Worst-Case Generators
children.top_down_role: Generators instantiating extremal structural regimes associated with poor solver behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines algorithm-relative asymptotic worst-case benchmark generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I_n\) be the admissible instances of size \(n\), let \(C_A(I)\ge 0\) be the cost of algorithm \(A\), and define \(W_A(n)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_n}C_A(I)\). A generator \(G\), with outputs \(G(n,\omega)\in\mathcal I_n\), is worst-case for \(A\) with factor \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) if there exists \(n_0\) such that, for every \(n\ge n_0\), \[\Pr_{\omega}\!\left[C_A(G(n,\omega))\ge \alpha W_A(n)\right]\ge \alpha.\] For deterministic \(G\), this means \(C_A(G(n))\ge\alpha W_A(n)\) for every \(n\ge n_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A worst-case generator produces admissible instances whose algorithmic cost attains a fixed fraction of the size-specific worst-case cost with uniformly positive probability.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I_n\ne\varnothing\) and \(W_A(n)<\infty\) for all relevant \(n\).
The size map and cost \(C_A\) are fixed before evaluating \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) generates an asymptotically constant-factor worst-case family for \(A\).

notation.meaning: resource cost of algorithm A on instance I
maximum or supremal cost at size n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalization from algorithm-relative worst-case analysis and randomized benchmark generation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm-relative constant-factor/probability definition fits the leaf, but it is a bespoke convention with no inspectable benchmark-methodology source.

children.title: Adversarial–Extremal Alignment
children.top_down_role: Cases where solver-targeted adversarial instances coincide with broader extremal regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial–Extremal Alignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures whether adversarial generation reaches the extremal cost envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For algorithm \(A\), admissible class \(\mathcal I_n\), and adversarial generator \(G(n,\omega)\in\mathcal I_n\), define \(W_A(n)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_n}C_A(I)\) and \[\rho_G(n)=\frac{\mathbb E_{\omega}[C_A(G(n,\omega))]}{W_A(n)}\] whenever \(0<W_A(n)<\infty\). The generator and extremal family are asymptotically aligned when \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\rho_G(n)>0\); they are strongly aligned when \(\rho_G(n)\to1\). Thus alignment is relative to the fixed algorithm, cost measure, admissible class, and size parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alignment is the asymptotic ratio between expected adversarial-instance cost and the true extremal cost; positive limiting ratio gives alignment, while convergence to one gives strong alignment.
assumptions_latex: \(G(n,\omega)\in\mathcal I_n\) almost surely.
\(0<W_A(n)<\infty\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\rho_G(n)>0\) characterizes constant-factor adversarial–extremal alignment.

notation.meaning: extremal algorithmic cost at size n

review_flags: terminology and normalization require benchmark-methodology source
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio is internally coherent and the property role fits, but neither the alignment terminology nor this expectation-based normalization has cited support.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Feature-based diversity selection and benchmark suitability

children.title: Instance Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata based on counts of primary combinatorial objects or constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance Size Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines structural size strata independently of machine performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R_+^d\) be a declared structural size map, such as vertex, edge, variable, or constraint counts. An instance-size regime is a measurable set \(R\subseteq\mathbb R_+^d\), and its benchmark stratum is \(\mathcal I_R=\{I\in\mathcal I:s(I)\in R\}\). A family \((R_k)_{k=1}^K\) is a size-regime taxonomy when the sets are pairwise disjoint and their union contains every reported size vector. Regime boundaries must be fixed independently of observed algorithm outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance-size regime is a predetermined region of structural-size space; disjoint regions stratify the corpus without using measured algorithm performance.
assumptions_latex: A common structural size map \(s\) is defined for every compared instance.
The reported regimes cover all instances included in the comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal I_{R_k})_{k=1}^K\) forms a structural-size stratification of the benchmark corpus.

notation.meaning: declared structural size vector of instance I
instances assigned to size regime k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: mathematical stratification by a prespecified covariate map
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and locally appropriate, but the required outcome-independent regime convention lacks an inspectable benchmark-taxonomy source.

children.title: Operational Scale Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata based on the effective computational scale experienced by solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Operational Scale Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines scale strata through measured resource demand under a fixed protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an algorithm \(A\), execution protocol \(P\), hardware environment \(H\), measured resource vector \(r_{P,H}(A,I)\in(\mathbb R_+\cup\{\infty\})^q\), and scalar summary \(h:(\mathbb R_+\cup\{\infty\})^q\to\mathbb R_+\cup\{\infty\}\). For declared thresholds \(0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_K=\infty\), operational regime \(k\) is \[O_k=\{I:t_{k-1}<h(r_{P,H}(A,I))\le t_k\}.\] Timeouts or resource exhaustion are assigned summary value \(\infty\). Because membership depends on \(A\), \(P\), \(H\), and \(h\), operational regimes are not intrinsic instance classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operational regimes group instances by observed resource demand under a fixed algorithm, protocol, hardware environment, and resource summary, assigning timeouts or exhaustion infinite demand.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm \(A\), protocol \(P\), hardware environment \(H\), and resource summary \(h\) are fixed.
The thresholds \(t_k\) are declared before comparative inference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((O_k)_{k=1}^K\) partitions the evaluated instances by operational resource scale.

notation.meaning: resource vector measured under protocol P and hardware environment H

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resource-based experimental stratification under a controlled protocol

children.title: Size–Scale Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Regimes where nominal instance size poorly represents computational scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Scale Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies failure of structural size to predict operational difficulty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s(I)\) be structural size and \(q(I)=h(r_P(A,I))\) be operational demand under fixed algorithm \(A\) and protocol \(P\). For a size cell \(R\), define its multiplicative operational spread by \[M(R)=\frac{\sup\{q(I):s(I)\in R\}}{\inf\{q(I):s(I)\in R\}},\] provided the denominator is positive. A size–scale mismatch occurs along cells \((R_j)\) when \(M(R_j)\to\infty\), or when one cell contains both a completed instance and a resource-exhausted instance. Then size-regime membership alone cannot give a uniform constant-factor prediction of operational demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mismatch occurs when structurally similar instances have unboundedly different resource demands, or mix successful runs with resource exhaustion, invalidating size-only difficulty prediction.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm, protocol, hardware, and resource summary remain fixed.
Each considered size cell contains at least two evaluated instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No cellwise predictor depending only on size-regime membership approximates all operational demands within one uniform finite factor.

notation.meaning: scalar operational demand of instance I
multiplicative demand spread within size cell R

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: failure criterion based on within-stratum response dispersion
finite-sample and zero-demand conventions need methodological source

children.title: Sparse Instance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata with low incidence, adjacency, or constraint occupancy.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Instance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines asymptotic sparsity for graph-encoded benchmark instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence of simple undirected graph instances \((G_n)\), with \(v_n=|V(G_n)|\to\infty\) and \(m_n=|E(G_n)|\), define density \(\delta_n=2m_n/[v_n(v_n-1)]\). The sequence is in a sparse regime when \(\delta_n\to0\). It is uniformly linearly sparse when, additionally, there exists \(C<\infty\) such that \(m_n\le Cv_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The stronger linear condition implies sparsity but is not equivalent to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph instances are sparse when their occupied-edge fraction tends to zero; linear sparsity additionally requires the edge count to remain at most proportional to vertices.
assumptions_latex: Each \(G_n\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
\(v_n\ge2\) and \(v_n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_n\to0\) defines the sparse density regime, while \(m_n=O(v_n)\) defines its linear subclass.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between vanishing density and linear sparsity is mathematically correct, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Dense Instance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata with high incidence, adjacency, or constraint occupancy.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Instance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines asymptotically dense graph benchmark families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence of finite simple undirected graphs \((G_n)\), let \(v_n=|V(G_n)|\to\infty\), \(m_n=|E(G_n)|\), and \(\delta_n=2m_n/[v_n(v_n-1)]\). The sequence is in a dense regime when \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}\delta_n>0\). Equivalently, there exist constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(m_n\ge c v_n(v_n-1)/2\) for every \(n\ge n_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph family is dense when a positive fraction of all possible edges remains present for every sufficiently large instance.
assumptions_latex: Each \(G_n\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
\(v_n\ge2\) and \(v_n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dense regime is characterized by \(m_n=\Omega(v_n^2)\), equivalently by density bounded away from zero.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dense-regime equivalences are correct for finite simple undirected graphs with vertex count tending to infinity, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Density Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intermediate strata where solver behavior changes as structural occupancy increases.

knowledge_statements.title: Density Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines parameter windows where a structural property changes probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_n(\theta)\) be a random graph model with density-control parameter \(\theta\in\Theta_n\), and let \(Q_n\) be an indicator-valued graph property. For fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), define the transition window \[T_{n,\varepsilon}=\{\theta\in\Theta_n:\varepsilon\le\Pr(Q_n(G_n(\theta))=1)\le1-\varepsilon\}.\] A density transition regime is a benchmark stratum whose parameters lie in \(T_{n,\varepsilon}\). If the probability is nondecreasing in \(\theta\), this window lies between the corresponding lower and upper \(\varepsilon\)-level locations of the threshold curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A density transition regime samples density-control parameters for which a declared graph property has probability bounded away from both zero and one.
assumptions_latex: The random graph model \(G_n(\theta)\), parameter domain \(\Theta_n\), and indicator property \(Q_n\) are declared.
The same \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) is used across compared sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instances with \(\theta\in T_{n,\varepsilon}\) populate the nondegenerate transition region for \(Q_n\).
review_flags: model-specific density parameter must be documented

children.title: Topological Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata based on global graph, hypergraph, or incidence structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stratifies graph instances by declared topology descriptors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau:\mathcal G\to\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal C\) be a declared topology descriptor, possibly containing connectivity, diameter, clustering, genus, or forbidden-structure labels. A topological regime is the inverse image \(T_B=\{G\in\mathcal G:\tau(G)\in B\}\) of a measurable descriptor cell \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal C\). A finite family \((B_k)_{k=1}^K\) defines a topological taxonomy when its cells are disjoint and cover all reported descriptor values. The descriptor and cells must be fixed before algorithm outcomes are inspected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological regime is a prespecified cell in graph-descriptor space, producing outcome-independent strata based on connectivity or other structural features.
assumptions_latex: Every benchmark graph has a well-defined descriptor \(\tau(G)\).
The descriptor cells cover the benchmark corpus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T_{B_k})_{k=1}^K\) partitions the corpus into declared topological regimes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stratification as inverse images of prespecified structural descriptors
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-image stratification is coherent and fits the leaf, but the heterogeneous topology descriptor and outcome-independent cell convention lack domain-specific support.

children.title: Decomposition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata based on separability, block structure, or exploitable component organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies instances by separator-induced component structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|>0\), let \(\mathcal C(G-S)\) denote the set of connected components remaining after removal of \(S\subseteq V\). Given normalized thresholds \(\sigma,\beta\in[0,1]\), the graph belongs to decomposition regime \(D_{\sigma,\beta}\) if some \(S\subseteq V\) satisfies \[|S|\le\sigma|V|\quad\text{and}\quad\max_{C\in\mathcal C(G-S)}|C|\le\beta|V|,\] where the maximum is defined as \(0\) when \(G-S\) has no vertices. Smaller \(\sigma\) and \(\beta\) encode stronger separator-based decomposability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition regime groups finite undirected graphs admitting a separator of bounded relative size whose removal leaves components of bounded relative size.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph with \(|V|>0\).
Thresholds \(\sigma\) and \(\beta\) are fixed across compared instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(D_{\sigma,\beta}\) certifies a separator decomposition at the declared scale.

notation.meaning: removed vertex set serving as a separator

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: balanced-separator formulation adapted to benchmark strata

children.title: Topology-Induced Decomposability
children.top_down_role: Connections between topological structure and the availability of useful decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Induced Decomposability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connects bounded treewidth with small balanced separators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with \(|V|=n\) and treewidth at most \(k\). Then there exists a vertex set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|\le k+1\) such that every connected component of \(G-S\) contains at most \(n/2\) vertices. Consequently, under the normalized decomposition convention, \(G\in D_{(k+1)/n,\,1/2}\). Thus a bounded-treewidth topological regime induces increasingly small relative separators as \(n\) grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every graph of treewidth at most k has a balanced separator of at most k+1 vertices, so bounded treewidth forces strong asymptotic decomposability.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph with \(|V|=n>0\).
The treewidth of \(G\) is at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|\le k+1\) and \(\max_{C\in\mathcal C(G-S)}|C|\le n/2\).
review_flags: authoritative locator required for the treewidth balanced-separator theorem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a balanced-separator theorem, not merely a generic property. Its mathematical statement is standard, but an authoritative theorem locator is required before correcting the role and accepting it.

children.title: Coefficient Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata based on coefficient type, distribution, sign, or granularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stratifies finite optimization instances by coefficient-distribution descriptors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an optimization instance \(I\) have a finite multiset of nonzero numerical coefficients \(C(I)=\{c_1,\ldots,c_m\}\). Define a coefficient descriptor \(\kappa(I)\) from prespecified statistics of \(C(I)\), such as sign proportions, integrality, quantiles of \(|c_i|\), or repeated-value frequencies. For a declared cell \(B\) in descriptor space, the coefficient regime is \[K_B=\{I:\kappa(I)\in B\}.\] A coefficient-regime taxonomy consists of disjoint cells covering all reported instances, with descriptors and boundaries chosen independently of algorithm outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coefficient regime is a predetermined stratum based on coefficient signs, integrality, magnitudes, quantiles, or repetition patterns, independent of measured performance.
assumptions_latex: Each instance has finitely many numerical coefficients and at least one nonzero coefficient.
Coefficient extraction and normalization conventions are fixed across the corpus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((K_{B_j})_j\) partitions instances according to declared coefficient characteristics.

notation.meaning: coefficient regime associated with cell B

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: outcome-independent stratification by prespecified numerical descriptors
normalization and coefficient-extraction conventions need benchmark source
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits coefficient-based corpus stratification, but coefficient extraction, normalization, and descriptor-cell conventions have no inspectable benchmark source.

children.title: Dynamic-Range Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata based on the numerical spread among nonzero values.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Range Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reproducible strata from ratios of nonzero coefficient magnitudes; it does not measure numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\) with finite coefficient multiset \(C\) containing a nonzero element, define \[\rho(I)=\frac{\max\{|c|:c\in C,\ c\ne0\}}{\min\{|c|:c\in C,\ c\ne0\}},\qquad d_b(I)=\log_b\rho(I).\] Given \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K=\infty\), define \[R_k=\{I:\tau_{k-1}\le d_b(I)<\tau_k\},\qquad k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.\] Zero coefficients are excluded from both extrema, and the base \(b>1\), coefficient fields, and thresholds are fixed corpus metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic-range regime bins every eligible instance by the logarithm of the ratio between its largest and smallest nonzero coefficient magnitudes, using thresholds beginning at zero.
assumptions_latex: The instance has a finite coefficient multiset \(C\subset\mathbb R\) with at least one nonzero element.
A fixed base \(b>1\) and thresholds \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K=\infty\) are declared before benchmarking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) belongs to exactly one declared dynamic-range regime \(R_k\).

children.title: Coefficient-Scale Interaction
children.top_down_role: Combined effects of coefficient composition and numerical magnitude spread.

assumptions_latex: Instances \(I_{s,r}\) share one combinatorial structure while size index \(s\) and coefficient-range index \(r\) vary.
A performance statistic \(T(I)>0\), such as median runtime or node count, is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_{s_1,s_2;r_1,r_2}=0\) exactly when the two size effects on log performance agree across the selected coefficient regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a paired log-performance contrast to separate coefficient-range effects from size effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For size levels \(s_1,s_2\) and coefficient-range levels \(r_1,r_2\), define \[\Delta_{s_1,s_2;r_1,r_2}=\bigl(\log T(I_{s_2,r_2})-\log T(I_{s_1,r_2})\bigr)-\bigl(\log T(I_{s_2,r_1})-\log T(I_{s_1,r_1})\bigr).\] The selected coefficient and size factors have no interaction on the log-performance scale precisely when \(\Delta_{s_1,s_2;r_1,r_2}=0\). A benchmark reports the contrast only for structurally matched instances and records its aggregation and censoring conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient-scale interaction is the change in the size effect on log performance when the coefficient dynamic-range regime changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient-Scale Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The difference-in-differences contrast is mathematically coherent for the selected matched 2-by-2 comparison, and the property role fits the interaction leaf. No inspectable source supports this particular empirical interaction definition or its matching, aggregation, and censoring conventions.

children.title: Degeneracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata exhibiting redundant, tied, or structurally non-unique solution features.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses basic-solution degeneracy for LP-based benchmark formulations; the score, aggregation rule, and thresholds must be fixed in corpus metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible basis \(B\), let \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\in\mathbb R^m\). The basis is degenerate when at least one coordinate of \(x_B\) is zero. Define its degeneracy score by \[\delta(B)=\frac{1}{m}\bigl|\{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:(x_B)_j=0\}\bigr|.\] Given fixed thresholds \(0=\eta_0<\eta_1<\cdots<\eta_K=1\), define \[D_k=\{B:\eta_{k-1}\le\delta(B)<\eta_k\}\] for \(k<K\), and \[D_K=\{B:\eta_{K-1}\le\delta(B)\le1\}.\] Instance-level aggregation over feasible or visited bases must be declared separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degeneracy regime bins feasible LP bases by the fraction of coordinates of their basic solution that are zero, using fixed corpus thresholds.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark instance is represented as a linear program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has rank \(m\).
Every recorded basis \(B\) selects \(m\) linearly independent columns, and only feasible bases are scored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every scored feasible basis \(B\) belongs to exactly one declared degeneracy regime \(D_k\).

notation.meaning: Basic solution vector associated with basis B.
Fraction of coordinates of the basic solution equal to zero.

children.title: Symmetry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Corpus strata exhibiting interchangeable objects, assignments, or equivalent formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stratifies finite objective-preserving instance symmetries; the encoding and normalization must remain fixed across the corpus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(I)\) be the finite group of declared encoding automorphisms whose induced action maps \(F(I)\) to itself and preserves \(f\). For a declared normalization constant \(M(I)>1\) satisfying \(|G(I)|\le M(I)\), define \[\sigma(I)=\frac{\log |G(I)|}{\log M(I)}.\] Given fixed thresholds \(0=\gamma_0<\gamma_1<\cdots<\gamma_K=1\), define \[S_k=\{I:\gamma_{k-1}\le\sigma(I)<\gamma_k\}\] for \(k<K\), and \[S_K=\{I:\gamma_{K-1}\le\sigma(I)\le1\}.\] The corpus specification must define \(M(I)\) and the admitted encoding automorphisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetry regime bins instances by a normalized logarithmic measure of their finite objective-preserving automorphism group, with a normalization guaranteed to bound the score by one.
assumptions_latex: For each instance \(I\), a finite declared group \(G(I)\) acts on \(F(I)\) and preserves the objective.
The corpus declares \(M(I)>1\) with \(|G(I)|\le M(I)\), together with thresholds covering \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized score \(\sigma(I)\) assigns every eligible instance \(I\) to exactly one declared symmetry regime \(S_k\).

notation.meaning: Declared objective-preserving symmetry group of the instance.

children.title: Symmetry-Induced Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Regimes where structural symmetry contributes to non-uniqueness or redundant search.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Induced Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite group-action result concerning multiplicity of symmetry-equivalent optima; it does not by itself assert LP basis degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on a feasible set \(F\), preserve feasibility, and satisfy \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in F\). If \(x^*\in F\) is optimal, then every point in \(Gx^*\) is optimal and \[|Gx^*|=\frac{|G|}{|\operatorname{Stab}_G(x^*)|}.\] Thus the orbit contains more than one distinct optimum exactly when \(\operatorname{Stab}_G(x^*)\ne G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective-preserving finite symmetry group maps an optimum to an orbit of optima. The number of distinct optima in that orbit is the group size divided by the stabilizer size.
assumptions_latex: A finite group \(G\) acts on a feasible set \(F\), preserves feasibility, and satisfies \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(x\in F\).
An optimal solution \(x^*\in F\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit \(Gx^*\) consists of exactly \(|G|/|\operatorname{Stab}_G(x^*)|\) distinct optimal solutions.

assumptions_latex: A finite benchmark corpus \(\mathcal I\), solver configuration \(A\), resource limit \(L\), and performance statistic \(T_A(I)\) are fixed.
A scalar instance feature \(h(I)\) and disjoint declared intervals \(J_1,\ldots,J_K\) are fixed before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sets \(H_1,\ldots,H_K\) form reproducible empirical hardness strata relative to \(A\), \(L\), \(T_A\), and the declared aggregation rule.

notation.meaning: Observed performance statistic for solver configuration A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness is empirical and configuration-relative, not an instance's worst-case complexity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An empirical hardness score is a declared statistic \(h:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\) computed from repeated observations of \(T_A(I)\), with timeouts represented by a fixed censoring or penalty rule at limit \(L\). For disjoint intervals \(J_1,\ldots,J_K\) covering the score range, define \[H_k=\{I\in\mathcal I:h(I)\in J_k\}.\] The solver version, hardware, seeds, repetitions, statistic, resource limit, and interval boundaries are components of the regime specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical hardness regimes partition a corpus using a declared performance score measured under one fixed solver, platform, repetition, and timeout protocol.
knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Hardness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly treats empirical hardness as configuration-relative and the definition role fits the topic. No inspectable benchmark-methodology source supports the proposed score, timeout treatment, aggregation rule, or required metadata.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) is the set of abstract instances and \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of finite exchange strings.
A deterministic parser \(P:\Sigma^*\rightharpoonup\mathcal I\) and serializer \(S:\mathcal I\to\Sigma^*\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(I)\) is the unique canonical exchange representation of \(I\), and canonicalization is idempotent on valid strings.

notation.meaning: Deterministic parser from exchange strings to instances.
Canonical serializer from instances to exchange strings.
Canonicalization map on valid exchange strings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines canonicality abstractly; a concrete corpus must separately specify grammar, ordering, numeric syntax, and identifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical exchange format satisfies \[P(S(I))=I\quad\text{for every }I\in\mathcal I,\] and, for every valid string \(w\in\operatorname{dom}P\), \[S(P(w))=S(P(S(P(w)))).\] Thus \(C=S\circ P\) is idempotent on \(\operatorname{dom}P\), and two valid strings \(u,v\) encode the same abstract instance exactly when \(P(u)=P(v)\), equivalently \(C(u)=C(v)\). Invalid strings lie outside \(\operatorname{dom}P\) and must produce a deterministic validation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical exchange format parses and serializes losslessly, gives equivalent encodings one unique string, and makes repeated canonicalization idempotent.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Exchange Formats

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parser-serializer formulation is internally coherent and the representation kind fits the exchange-format container. A concrete or authoritative exchange-format source is needed for the canonicality, validation-error, grammar, and serialization requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Formulation Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses solution-bijection equivalence with a positive affine objective transformation and assumes finite attained optima when asserting optimal-value identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two formulations \((F,f)\) and \((F',f')\) are equivalent variants when there exist a bijection \(\phi:F\to F'\) and constants \(a>0\), \(b\in\mathbb R\) such that \[f'(\phi(x))=af(x)+b\qquad\text{for every }x\in F.\] If both formulations have finite attained minima \(z^*\) and \(z'^*\), then \[\phi\bigl(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f(x)\bigr)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in F'}f'(y),\qquad z'^*=az^*+b.\] A benchmark variant record must store \(\phi\), its inverse or reconstruction rule, and \(a,b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulation variants have a feasible-solution bijection and preserve objective ordering through a positive affine transformation; when finite minima are attained, optimal solutions correspond bijectively and their values transform affinely.
