assumptions_latex: The feasible sets \(F\subseteq X\) and \(F'\subseteq X'\) are nonempty, and the objectives are \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) and \(f':F'\to\mathbb R\).
There are a bijection \(\phi:F\to F'\) and constants \(a>0\), \(b\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \(f'(\phi(x))=af(x)+b\) for every \(x\in F\).
The minima defining \(z^*\) and \(z'^*\) are finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\) maps the optimal-solution sets bijectively, and \(z'^*=az^*+b\).

notation.meaning: Finite attained optimal objective values of the two formulations.

assumptions_latex: A serialized instance \(w\) is intended to encode an instance \(I\) under a declared schema.
A finite ordered collection of deterministic predicates \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\) is fixed for that schema.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance passes integrity validation exactly when \(P(w)\) is defined and \(Q(I)=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers deterministic structural and semantic validation, excluding claims about optimality or solver performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance string \(w\) passes integrity checks if and only if \(P(w)\) is defined and, for \(I=P(w)\), \[Q(I)=\bigwedge_{j=1}^{m}q_j(I)=1.\] The predicates must include all schema-required tests for identifier uniqueness, index and dimension consistency, finite numeric values, declared domains, reference validity, and problem-specific structural invariants. Validation returns \(Q(I)\) together with the ordered set \(\{j:q_j(I)=0\}\); acceptance must not depend on solver behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance passes integrity checks exactly when parsing succeeds and every declared deterministic schema and problem-invariant predicate holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance Integrity Checks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The acceptance condition is mathematically coherent and the condition kind fits the integrity-check container. The mandatory predicate classes and deterministic diagnostic behavior are schema-design claims without an inspectable source.

children.title: Reference Solution Status
children.top_down_role: Archived status labels for known, unknown, feasible, optimal, or otherwise qualified reference outcomes.

assumptions_latex: The optimization sense is minimization and the feasible set \(F(I)\) is well-defined.
Any claimed solution \(x\) is checked independently for membership in \(F(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each status has an explicit mathematical predicate and cannot be inferred solely from a solver's label.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines core minimization statuses; a corpus may extend the vocabulary only with explicit predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reference status \(s(I)\) is assigned only when its predicate is supported: \(\mathrm{feasible}\) requires a recorded \(x\in F(I)\); \(\mathrm{optimal}\) requires a recorded feasible \(x\) and a valid lower bound \(L\) with \(f_I(x)=L\); \(\mathrm{infeasible}\) requires a verifiable infeasibility certificate; and \(\mathrm{unknown}\) applies when none of these claims is certified. If \(F(I)=\varnothing\), no finite reference solution is recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reference status distinguishes feasible, certified optimal, certified infeasible, and unknown cases by explicit predicates and supporting records.
knowledge_statements.title: Reference Solution Status

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The status predicates are coherent for minimization and appropriately distinguish solver labels from certified claims. An authoritative status or benchmark-record standard is needed to support the vocabulary and certificate requirements.

children.title: Reference Objective Records
children.top_down_role: Archived objective values or bounds associated with benchmark instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference Objective Records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the minimization convention; maximization records require the corresponding reversed bound convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reference objective record is \[R(I)=(L,U,g,\varepsilon,\nu),\] where \(L\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is a certified lower bound, \(U\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is the objective value of a verified feasible incumbent when finite, \(\varepsilon\ge0\) is a declared comparison tolerance, and \(\nu\) identifies the numeric representation. When both bounds are finite, define \[g=U-L.\] Consistency requires \(L\le U\), hence \(g\ge0\). Exact certified optimality requires \(g=0\); the weaker condition \(g\le\varepsilon\) records certified additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference objective record stores a certified lower bound, a feasible upper bound, their nonnegative gap when finite, a comparison tolerance, and the numeric representation. Zero gap certifies exact optimality, while a gap within the tolerance certifies additive approximate optimality.
assumptions_latex: The optimization sense is minimization.
Every finite lower bound is certified, every finite upper bound is attained by a verified feasible solution, and numeric values use an exact representation or certified enclosures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever the optimal value \(z^*\) and both recorded bounds are finite, \(L\le z^*\le U\), \(g=U-L\ge0\), and exact certified optimality requires \(g=0\).

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound and feasible-incumbent upper bound.
Nonnegative absolute optimality gap when both bounds are finite.

children.title: Status–Objective Provenance
children.top_down_role: Source and revision history linking reference statuses to objective records.

knowledge_statements.title: Status–Objective Provenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies verifiable lineage for status and objective assertions, not the underlying optimality proof system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A status-objective provenance record is a tuple \[P=(d_I,s,R,m,e,t,\mathcal A),\] containing the instance digest \(d_I\), asserted status \(s\), objective record \(R\), method identifier \(m\), execution-environment identifier \(e\), timestamp \(t\), and a set \(\mathcal A\) of immutable supporting-artifact identifiers. It is valid exactly when \(V(P)=1\), where \(V\) verifies the digest, schema, artifact availability, certificates required by \(s\), and consistency of \(R\). Any changed component produces a new provenance record rather than modifying the prior assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A provenance record immutably links each status and objective claim to the exact instance, method, environment, time, supporting artifacts, and validation result.
assumptions_latex: A status-objective assertion concerns a fixed instance identifier and immutable content digest \(d_I\).
Every supporting computation or certificate has an immutable artifact identifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The provenance record binds a status and objective claim to one instance version, method, environment, evidence set, and validation result.

notation.meaning: Deterministic validation predicate for the provenance record.

children.title: Certificate Archives
children.top_down_role: Stored artifacts supporting verification of recorded benchmark claims.

assumptions_latex: Each benchmark instance has a persistent identifier and a formally specified feasibility and objective convention.
A deterministic verifier is available for every archived certificate type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted archive entry is independently checkable against the identified instance and claimed assertion.

notation.meaning: certificate object and its claimed assertion

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses certificate archives; standard_field_rationale only.
A source specifying archival integrity and verifier requirements is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a verifier-oriented archive of optimization certificates, not a particular certificate format.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certificate archive is a finite set \(\mathcal A_C\) of records \((\operatorname{id}(I),c,q,h,v)\), where \(I\) is a benchmark instance, \(c\) is a certificate, \(q\) is the assertion certified, \(h\) is a cryptographic digest of the canonical instance and certificate encodings, and \(v\) identifies the verifier version. A record is admissible exactly when the referenced encodings reproduce \(h\), the verifier terminates, and \(V_v(I,c,q)=1\). The archive is immutable by version: any change to \(I\), \(c\), \(q\), or \(V_v\) creates a new record rather than overwriting the old one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate archive stores immutable, versioned certificates whose instance binding, integrity, and claimed assertion can be checked by a deterministic verifier.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Archives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Certificate Archives leaf and is internally coherent, but no cited source supports the specific digest, immutability, versioning, and deterministic-verifier requirements.

children.title: Witness Archives
children.top_down_role: Stored feasible solutions, counterexamples, or other instance-specific witness artifacts.

assumptions_latex: Each benchmark instance and each submitted solution object has a canonical encoding.
A deterministic predicate specifies whether a solution object witnesses the claimed property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admitted witness is reproducibly bound to one instance and satisfies its declared witness predicate.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses witness archives; standard_field_rationale only.
A source distinguishing witnesses from certificates in benchmark repositories is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats a witness as a concrete solution object establishing a declared instance property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A witness archive is a finite set \(\mathcal A_W\) of records \((\operatorname{id}(I),w,p,h,v)\), where \(I\) is a benchmark instance, \(w\) is a concrete solution object, \(p\) names the property witnessed, \(h\) is the digest of the canonical instance and witness encodings, and \(v\) identifies the predicate version. A record is admissible exactly when its encodings reproduce \(h\) and \(P_v(I,w,p)=1\). Typical properties include feasibility and attainment of a stated objective value. Versioned records are retained whenever the instance, witness, predicate, or encoding changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A witness archive stores immutable, versioned solution objects that reproducibly satisfy a declared property of an identified benchmark instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Witness Archives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Witness Archives leaf, but the proposed witness semantics, digest binding, predicate versioning, and retention policy have no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Certificate–Witness Linkage
children.top_down_role: Associations among verification artifacts, solution witnesses, instances, and reference records.

assumptions_latex: Certificate and witness records use persistent identifiers and canonical encodings.
The linkage verifier can recompute all instance, witness, and claim fields used by a certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted link proves that the certificate and witness concern the same immutable instance record and that the certificate's claim matches the witness-derived claim.

notation.meaning: instance identifier stored in a record

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses certificate-witness linkage; standard_field_rationale only.
A source for repository linkage semantics and integrity conditions is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies integrity conditions for linking separately archived certificates and witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certificate record \(r_C\) and witness record \(r_W\) are validly linked, written \(r_C\sim r_W\), exactly when \(\iota(r_C)=\iota(r_W)\), both records pass their archive verifiers, their stored instance digests agree, and \(\kappa(r_C)=\kappa(r_W)\). Here \(\kappa(r_W)\) is recomputed from the witness rather than copied from metadata. If a certificate concerns optimality, the linkage additionally requires the certificate's objective value to equal the value obtained by evaluating the archived witness under the identified instance and objective convention. A failed equality makes the link invalid without invalidating either underlying record independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid link joins verified records for the same immutable instance and requires the certificate claim to equal the claim recomputed from the witness.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate–Witness Linkage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is an appropriate kind for this leaf, but the required equalities and optimality-linkage semantics are repository-specific and unsupported by any cited source.

children.title: Diversity-Based Selection
children.top_down_role: Corpus selection emphasizing variation across structural, numerical, or provenance characteristics.

assumptions_latex: The candidate pool is finite and carries a symmetric nonnegative dissimilarity.
A cardinality budget is fixed and deterministic tie-breaking is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a budget-feasible subset constructed by repeated maximum-distance augmentation.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports diversity-based corpus selection; standard_field_rationale only.
The intended diversity objective and approximation guarantee require a domain source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses deterministic farthest-first selection as one precise diversity-based corpus rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite nonempty pool \(U\), a symmetric dissimilarity \(d:U\times U\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) with \(d(x,x)=0\), and an integer \(1\le k\le |U|\), choose a prescribed seed \(x_1\in U\) and set \(S_1=\{x_1\}\). For \(t=1,\ldots,k-1\), select \(x_{t+1}\) from the maximizers of \(\min_{s\in S_t}d(x,s)\) over \(x\in U\setminus S_t\), resolving ties by a fixed total order, and set \(S_{t+1}=S_t\cup\{x_{t+1}\}\). Stop after \(k\) selections and output \(S_k\) together with all selected distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a fixed seed, repeatedly add the candidate farthest from its nearest selected instance until the corpus budget is filled.
knowledge_statements.title: Diversity-Based Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The farthest-first algorithm is precise and fits a diversity-based selection leaf, but no source establishes that this particular rule is the intended corpus-selection method or supplies the relevant metric assumptions or guarantees.

children.title: Representativeness-Based Selection
children.top_down_role: Corpus selection emphasizing correspondence with a declared target population.

assumptions_latex: Candidates and the target population are finite weighted sets in a common feature space.
A nonnegative discrepancy and a cardinality budget are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned subset minimizes the prescribed weighted representation discrepancy among all budget-feasible subsets.

notation.meaning: weighted empirical feature distribution of a set

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports representativeness-based corpus selection; standard_field_rationale only.
The intended discrepancy and weighting protocol require a benchmark-methodology source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines representativeness through explicit empirical-distribution matching under a fixed budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite candidate pool, let \(T\) be a finite weighted target population, let \(\phi\) map instances into a feature space, and let \(D\) be a nonnegative discrepancy between weighted empirical feature distributions. For a budget \(k\), representativeness-based selection returns a deterministically tie-broken minimizer \[S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq U,\ |S|=k}D(\widehat\mu_S,\widehat\mu_T).\] If selected instances may receive weights, the minimization also ranges over nonnegative weights summing to one; otherwise \(\widehat\mu_S\) is uniform. The output includes \(S^*\), its weights, and the attained discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select the budget-feasible corpus whose empirical feature distribution most closely matches a specified weighted target population.
knowledge_statements.title: Representativeness-Based Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the local topic, but it specifies an optimization criterion rather than a procedure for computing its minimizer. The discrepancy, weighting protocol, and intended algorithm are source-dependent and uncited.

children.title: Diversity–Coverage Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Selection tensions between broad variation and faithful population coverage.

assumptions_latex: Every budget-feasible corpus has a real-valued diversity score and a real-valued coverage loss.
Both criteria are evaluated using fixed features, weights, and conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The undominated corpora form the diversity-coverage Pareto frontier; a scalarized optimizer with positive weights must lie on that frontier.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports the benchmark-specific tradeoff; standard_field_rationale only.
A source defining accepted diversity and coverage metrics is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes the tradeoff as finite bicriteria Pareto selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S,T\in\mathcal F\), say that \(T\) dominates \(S\) when \(\Delta(T)\ge\Delta(S)\) and \(L(T)\le L(S)\), with at least one strict inequality. The diversity-coverage frontier is \(\mathcal P=\{S\in\mathcal F: S\text{ is not dominated}\}\). For any \(\alpha,\beta>0\), every maximizer of \(\alpha\Delta(S)-\beta L(S)\) over \(S\in\mathcal F\) belongs to \(\mathcal P\). Consequently, selecting a corpus off \(\mathcal P\) sacrifices either diversity or coverage without improving the other criterion; unsupported Pareto points may nevertheless fail to optimize any linear scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A corpus is tradeoff-efficient exactly when no feasible corpus improves diversity without worsening coverage, or improves coverage without reducing diversity.
knowledge_statements.title: Diversity–Coverage Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto property is mathematically sound for the stated finite bicriteria model and fits the tradeoff leaf, but no source supports the benchmark-specific meanings or accepted definitions of diversity and coverage.

children.title: Solvability-Based Selection
children.top_down_role: Corpus selection based on whether instances yield usable reference or evaluation outcomes.

assumptions_latex: A finite candidate pool, solver set, resource limit, and required success threshold are fixed.
Each candidate has a reproducibly measured solver-success indicator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output maximizes a declared hardness or discrimination score among instances meeting the solvability threshold.

notation.meaning: success indicator for solver on instance

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports solvability-based benchmark selection; standard_field_rationale only.
The intended success threshold, censoring rule, and score need a methodology source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects informative instances subject to a reproducible minimum solvability constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite \(U\) and \(\mathcal A\), define \(Y_{a,x}=1\) exactly when solver \(a\) returns a verifier-accepted result for instance \(x\) within the fixed resource limit, and define \(p(x)=|\mathcal A|^{-1}\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}Y_{a,x}\). For threshold \(\tau\in[0,1]\), budget \(k\), and declared instance score \(H\), form \(E_\tau=\{x\in U:p(x)\ge\tau\}\). If \(|E_\tau|\ge k\), return a deterministically tie-broken maximizer of \(\sum_{x\in S}H(x)\) over \(S\subseteq E_\tau\) with \(|S|=k\); otherwise report infeasibility and the maximum attainable cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Filter candidates by a minimum reproducible solver-success rate, then select the highest-scoring feasible subset under the corpus budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Solvability-Based Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is coherent and locally relevant, but the solver-success threshold, resource and censoring convention, aggregation over solvers, and hardness score are methodological choices without cited support.

children.title: Stability-Based Selection
children.top_down_role: Corpus selection based on consistency across runs, environments, formulations, or measurements.

assumptions_latex: Each candidate instance is evaluated under repeated, independently initialized runs of a fixed experimental protocol.
A bounded performance statistic and an admissible instability threshold are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected corpus contains only instances whose empirical performance variability does not exceed the declared threshold.

notation.meaning: performance observation for instance on repetition

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports stability-based benchmark selection; standard_field_rationale only.
A source is needed for the replication design and accepted stability statistic.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses repeated-run empirical variance as one explicit operational stability criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each candidate \(x\) and repetitions \(r=1,\ldots,m\), record the bounded performance statistic \(Z_{x,r}\) under the same protocol except for declared randomization. Compute \(\overline Z_x=m^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^m Z_{x,r}\) and \(s_x^2=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^m(Z_{x,r}-\overline Z_x)^2\), where \(m\ge2\). Given threshold \(\sigma^2_{\max}\) and budget \(k\), form \(E=\{x:s_x^2\le\sigma^2_{\max}\}\), rank \(E\) by a prespecified utility score with deterministic tie-breaking, and return its first \(\min\{k,|E|\}\) instances together with \(m\), \(s_x^2\), and any shortfall.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate repeated-run variability, exclude candidates above a fixed instability threshold, and select the best remaining instances under the budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Stability-Based Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The repeated-run variance filter is precise and fits the leaf as one possible algorithm, but no source supports variance as the intended stability measure, the replication design, threshold, or ranking protocol.

children.title: Solvability–Stability Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Selection effects arising when tractable instances differ from empirically stable instances.

assumptions_latex: Each feasible corpus has a solvability score and an instability loss computed under one fixed protocol.
The corpus budget and all aggregation weights are fixed before selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The efficient corpora are precisely those not dominated in solvability and stability; positive scalarization selects only efficient corpora.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this benchmark-specific tradeoff; standard_field_rationale only.
A source defining corpus-level solvability and stability aggregation is needed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes solvability versus empirical stability as a finite bicriteria frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S,T\in\mathcal F\), \(T\) dominates \(S\) when \(Q(T)\ge Q(S)\) and \(R(T)\le R(S)\), with at least one strict inequality. The solvability-stability frontier is \(\mathcal P=\{S\in\mathcal F:S\text{ is not dominated}\}\). For every \(\alpha,\beta>0\), each maximizer of \(\alpha Q(S)-\beta R(S)\) over \(\mathcal F\) lies in \(\mathcal P\). Thus any corpus outside \(\mathcal P\) can be replaced by one having at least as much solvability and no greater instability, with a strict improvement in one criterion; nonlinear selection may be required to recover unsupported frontier points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An efficient corpus cannot gain solvability without increasing instability, or reduce instability without losing solvability; dominated corpora are never rational choices.
knowledge_statements.title: Solvability–Stability Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto statement is correct for the stated bicriteria model and property is an appropriate kind, but corpus-level solvability and instability scores lack sourced definitions in the benchmark context.

children.title: Training Partitions
children.top_down_role: Corpus partitions available for fitting configurations, selectors, or learned solver components.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark corpus is partitioned into pairwise disjoint training, validation, and test sets.
All algorithm parameters and learned components are represented by a configuration variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The training partition may determine candidate configurations but cannot, by itself, provide an unbiased final performance estimate.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses dataset partition roles; standard_field_rationale only.
A benchmark-methodology source is needed for formal partition-use requirements.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines training by permitted adaptive use, independently of how instances are generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A training partition \(D_{\mathrm{tr}}\) is the subset of benchmark instances whose features, labels, solutions, certificates, and measured outcomes may be queried adaptively while constructing or fitting an algorithm configuration. Formally, after fixing any external randomness \(\xi\), the trained configuration has the form \(\widehat\theta=T(D_{\mathrm{tr}},\xi)\), commonly with \(\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}L_{\mathrm{tr}}(\theta;D_{\mathrm{tr}})\). Repeated inspection of \(D_{\mathrm{tr}}\) is permitted and is part of training. Performance computed on the same partition estimates training behavior and is not designated as the final out-of-sample benchmark result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The training partition is the data that may be inspected repeatedly and adaptively to fit or construct algorithm configurations.
knowledge_statements.title: Training Partitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the Training Partitions leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no inspectable citation supports its permitted adaptive uses or the stated interpretation of training-set performance.

children.title: Validation Partitions
children.top_down_role: Corpus partitions used for development-time selection without final performance reporting.

assumptions_latex: Training, validation, and test partitions are pairwise disjoint.
A finite candidate set of trained configurations and a deterministic validation score are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validation chooses among candidate configurations without using test observations, but its score is not the final untouched evaluation.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses validation partition semantics; standard_field_rationale only.
A benchmark-methodology source is needed for reuse and stopping-policy requirements.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines validation as configuration selection after training and before final test evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A validation partition \(D_{\mathrm{val}}\) is a benchmark subset used to compare trained candidate configurations and select hyperparameters, stopping rules, or model variants. Given a finite candidate family \(\Theta_0\), the selected configuration is \[\widehat\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta_0}L_{\mathrm{val}}(\theta;D_{\mathrm{val}}),\] with ties resolved by a prespecified rule. The candidates may depend on training data but not on test observations. Because repeated validation queries adapt the selection procedure to \(D_{\mathrm{val}}\), its reported score is a selection statistic and is not substituted for the final score on an isolated test partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The validation partition compares trained candidates and selects settings; repeated use makes its score unsuitable as the untouched final evaluation.
knowledge_statements.title: Validation Partitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Validation Partitions, but the reuse, candidate-dependence, and reporting rules are methodological claims requiring a specific benchmark or statistical-learning source.

children.title: Test Partitions
children.top_down_role: Protected corpus partitions reserved for final performance evaluation.

assumptions_latex: Training, validation, and test partitions are pairwise disjoint.
The complete algorithm-selection protocol is frozen before test outcomes are revealed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The test statistic evaluates the frozen procedure on held-out instances and must not influence any reported configuration choice.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses test partition isolation; standard_field_rationale only.
A benchmark-methodology source is needed for disclosure and reuse rules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a test partition by its nonadaptive role in final performance estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A test partition \(D_{\mathrm{te}}\) is a held-out benchmark subset used only after the configuration \(\widehat\theta\), resource limits, seeds policy, verifier, exclusions, and aggregate statistic \(M\) have been frozen. The reported test result is \(M(\widehat\theta;D_{\mathrm{te}})\), computed for the prespecified evaluation protocol. No outcome derived from \(D_{\mathrm{te}}\) may alter \(\widehat\theta\), the instance set, or the reporting rule for that evaluation. If test outcomes guide any such alteration, the partition has become validation data for the revised procedure and a fresh isolated test partition is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The test partition evaluates a fully frozen procedure once; using its outcomes to revise choices converts it into validation data.
knowledge_statements.title: Test Partitions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Test Partitions and consistently states a nonadaptive evaluation role, but the freezing, reuse, and fresh-test requirements lack an inspectable authoritative citation.

children.title: Partition Isolation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Information-separation boundaries among corpus partitions with different evaluation roles.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Isolation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-flow condition separating training, validation, and final testing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=T\mathbin{\dot\cup}V\mathbin{\dot\cup}E\) be a benchmark corpus, and let \(A\) denote the complete algorithm-selection and tuning procedure. Partition isolation holds when \(T,V,E\) are disjoint at the declared identity-family level, \(A\) may access all permitted information from \(T\), validation feedback only from \(V\), and no labels, reference solutions, scores, or instance-specific summaries derived from \(E\) before \(A\) is frozen. The reported test score is then computed by applying the frozen procedure exactly once to \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partitions are identity-disjoint, test-derived information cannot influence development, and the frozen procedure is evaluated once on the test partition.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is partitioned into training, validation, and test instances.
Identity is evaluated at the declared duplicate-family granularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is independent of test-derived information until frozen, and final evaluation uses only \(E\).

notation.meaning: Complete selection, implementation, and tuning procedure.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational information-flow definition for benchmark partition isolation
A benchmark-methodology source is required to certify the chosen isolation convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but no cited evidence supports the specific identity-family isolation, information-flow, freezing, or single-evaluation convention. The supplied source inventory is unrelated.

children.title: Public Test Sets
children.top_down_role: Evaluation collections whose instances or complete contents are openly available.

knowledge_statements.title: Public Test Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disclosure regime in which test instances are inspectable before submission.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A test set \(E\) is public at time \(t\) if every evaluated instance representation in \(E\) is available to participants before their evaluated procedures are irrevocably submitted. Publicity concerns instance disclosure, not necessarily disclosure of reference solutions or scores. A valid public-test protocol must therefore declare separately which auxiliary artifacts are visible and must forbid using feedback from prior evaluations on \(E\) for the reported development cycle unless that adaptive use is explicitly part of the benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A public test set exposes evaluated instances before submission, while solutions, scores, and permission for adaptive reuse remain separately governed.
assumptions_latex: A submission deadline and an evaluated test set \(E\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every instance representation in \(E\) is disclosed before the evaluated procedure is frozen.

notation.meaning: Time at which disclosure status is assessed.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: disclosure-time definition of a public benchmark test set
Relevant benchmark-governance evidence was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Public Test Sets, but its disclosure-time criterion and restrictions on adaptive reuse are governance conventions requiring benchmark-methodology evidence. No relevant citation is supplied.

children.title: Hidden Test Sets
children.top_down_role: Evaluation collections whose instances or selected attributes remain protected.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Test Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disclosure regime withholding evaluated instance representations until procedures are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A test set \(E\) is hidden for a submission cycle if participants cannot access its evaluated instance representations, reference solutions, or instance-level outcomes before the submitted procedure \(A\) is frozen. Evaluation is performed by a trusted evaluator that runs \(A\) on \(E\). Aggregate feedback released during the cycle must be limited by a declared policy; otherwise repeated submissions can convey information about \(E\) and destroy effective hiddenness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hidden test set is withheld until submission is frozen and evaluated by a trusted party under a controlled feedback policy.
assumptions_latex: A trusted evaluator can execute frozen submissions on \(E\).
The feedback policy is fixed before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No participant-observable information identifies the contents or instance-level outcomes of \(E\) before \(A\) is frozen.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: access-and-feedback definition of hidden test data
Relevant benchmark-governance evidence was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Hidden Test Sets, but the exact requirements concerning representations, trusted evaluation, aggregate feedback, and effective hiddenness are unsupported by a cited benchmark policy or methodology source.

children.title: Test-Set Disclosure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on information exposure needed to preserve independent evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Test-Set Disclosure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-indexed boundary governing which test artifacts participants may observe.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_E\) be all artifacts derived from test set \(E\), including instance encodings, metadata, reference solutions, logs, and scores. A disclosure boundary is a time-indexed family \((D_t)_{t\geq0}\) with \(D_t\subseteq U_E\), where \(D_t\) contains exactly the artifacts authorized for participant access by time \(t\). Compliance requires every participant-visible test-derived message at time \(t\) to be a function only of \(D_t\), and any enlargement of \(D_t\) to be recorded before affected results are interpreted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disclosure boundary specifies, over time, every test-derived artifact participants may observe; all feedback must remain within that declared set.
assumptions_latex: All test-derived artifacts and participant-visible messages are auditable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every time \(t\), participant-visible test information is measurable from authorized artifacts \(D_t\) only.

notation.meaning: Universe of artifacts derived from the test set.
Artifacts authorized for disclosure by time t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: time-indexed access-control formalization of disclosure
A source is needed for the exact disclosure and feedback convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the disclosure-boundary leaf, but the time-indexed artifact-set formalization and its measurability/compliance requirement are bespoke and lack supporting evidence.

children.title: Instance Deduplication
children.top_down_role: Identification and handling of exact or near-duplicate benchmark instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance Deduplication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic removal of repeated benchmark instances under a declared identity relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite multiset \(C\), a canonicalization map \(\kappa\), a duplicate predicate \(R\), and a deterministic priority order \(\prec\). Construct the undirected graph \(G=(C,F)\), where \(\{x,y\}\in F\) exactly when \(R(\kappa(x),\kappa(y))=1\). Compute its connected components \(K_1,\ldots,K_m\); from each \(K_j\), retain its \(\prec\)-minimum member and record every discarded member's identifier and lineage link. Output the retained set and the component-to-representative map. Stop after every input member belongs to exactly one component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalize instances, connect declared duplicates, retain one deterministic representative per component, and preserve an auditable map from discarded instances.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is finite.
\(R\), \(\kappa\), and \(\prec\) are fixed before processing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one representative is retained from each connected duplicate family.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not address benchmark-instance deduplication.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is an appropriate content kind, and the procedure is mathematically intelligible. However, treating connected components of an arbitrary pairwise duplicate predicate as duplicate families is a substantive design choice requiring a benchmark-deduplication source.

children.title: Instance Lineage
children.top_down_role: Parentage and derivation relationships among source, transformed, or revised instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance Lineage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provenance relation connecting benchmark instances to their derivations and sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance-lineage structure for corpus \(C\) is a directed acyclic graph \(L=(N,A)\) whose nodes contain every released instance and every recorded source artifact. An arc \((u,v)\in A\) states that \(v\) was produced directly from \(u\) by a recorded transformation carrying an operation identifier, parameters, software version, and timestamp. Each instance \(x\in C\) must be reachable from at least one source node, and its lineage is the subgraph induced by all ancestors of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Instance lineage is an acyclic provenance graph recording each source and transformation from original artifacts to released benchmark instances.
assumptions_latex: Every derivation step has a stable record.
Cycles in provenance are prohibited.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(x\in C\) has an auditable directed path from a recorded source artifact.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: provenance-DAG definition specialized to benchmark instances
A provenance or benchmark-data source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Instance Lineage, but requiring a DAG, specified transformation metadata, and reachability from a source node is a particular provenance model not supported by any cited provenance standard or benchmark-data source.

children.title: Instance Grouping
children.top_down_role: Organization of related instances into families for sampling, partitioning, or analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance Grouping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment of related instances to indivisible experimental groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a corpus \(C\), an instance grouping is a surjective map \(g:C\to\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Its fibers \(G_j=g^{-1}(j)\) form a partition of \(C\), and membership is determined by a declared relation such as common source, generator seed family, transformation lineage, or duplicate family. For split-sensitive evaluation, grouping is atomic: if \(p:C\to\mathcal P\) assigns experimental partitions, then \(g(x)=g(y)\) implies \(p(x)=p(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Grouping partitions related instances into declared families that must remain intact when assigning training, validation, or test roles.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and finite.
The grouping criterion is fixed before partition assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fibers of \(g\) partition \(C\), and each fiber receives one experimental role.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: grouped-splitting formalization for related benchmark instances
The supplied locators do not support this benchmark-design convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The grouping definition is coherent and locally appropriate, but atomic placement of every group within one experimental partition is a split-policy condition rather than an intrinsic consequence of grouping and requires relevant methodology evidence.

children.title: Duplicate-Family Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Criteria separating harmless similarity from evaluation-compromising overlap.

knowledge_statements.title: Duplicate-Family Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary requiring all exact or declared near-duplicates to share one partition role.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the declared symmetric duplicate relation on corpus \(C\), and let \(\sim_R\) be its transitive closure. The duplicate-family boundary is respected by partition map \(p:C\to\mathcal P\) exactly when \(x\sim_R y\) implies \(p(x)=p(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\). Thus every connected component of the duplicate graph is assigned atomically. The declaration of \(R\), including canonicalization and similarity thresholds, must precede partition construction and remain versioned with the corpus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every connected family of declared duplicates must lie wholly within one experimental partition under a predicate fixed before splitting.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is symmetric and fixed before partitioning.
\(p\) assigns exactly one role to each instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\sim_R y\Rightarrow p(x)=p(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

notation.meaning: Transitive closure of the duplicate relation.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: group-preserving boundary against duplicate leakage
A benchmark-splitting source is needed to certify this condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the leaf and consistently expresses component-preserving partition assignment. No source supports the transitive-family convention or the requirement that predicate parameters be fixed before splitting.

children.title: Corpus Versioning
children.top_down_role: Release identity, change history, and compatibility of benchmark corpus editions.

knowledge_statements.title: Corpus Versioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immutable manifest representation of each released benchmark-corpus state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent corpus version \(C_v\) by an immutable manifest \(M_v=(v,P_v,H_v,ho_v)\), where \(v\) is a unique version identifier, \(P_v\) lists instance identifiers and partition roles, \(H_v(x)\) is a collision-resistant digest of each canonical instance and its evaluation metadata, and \(\rho_v\) identifies the predecessor version and recorded change set. Two releases are the same version exactly when their manifests agree; any change to membership, content, role, metadata, or scoring semantics requires a new identifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each corpus release has an immutable manifest of members, roles, hashes, and predecessor changes; any evaluation-relevant change creates a new version.
assumptions_latex: Canonical serialization and a digest function are fixed for the corpus.
Version identifiers are never reused.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_v=C_w\) as released benchmark states if and only if \(M_v=M_w\).
review_flags: A benchmark-corpus versioning standard or methodology source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate content kind, but the immutable manifest schema, collision-resistant digest requirement, version identity rule, and change-trigger policy are specific design conventions without a relevant source.

children.title: Instance Retirement
children.top_down_role: Removal or deprecation of instances that no longer support reliable evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance Retirement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifecycle state excluding an instance from future headline evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For corpus version \(C_v\), an instance \(x\) is retired at version \(v+1\) when its lifecycle status changes from active to retired, it is excluded from the primary evaluation set of \(C_{v+1}\), and the manifest records a reason, effective version, and successor if one exists. Retirement does not delete \(x\), its historical scores, or its lineage. Results obtained under versions where \(x\) was active remain associated with those versions and are not silently recomputed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retirement removes an instance from future primary evaluation while preserving its provenance, reason, historical scores, and former version membership.
assumptions_latex: Corpus releases have immutable version manifests.
Every active instance has a stable identifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin E_{v+1}\) while its historical records and lineage remain preserved.

notation.meaning: Primary evaluation set in the successor version.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: auditable lifecycle-state definition of retirement
A benchmark lifecycle policy source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Instance Retirement, but exclusion from primary evaluation, preservation requirements, and historical-result handling constitute a lifecycle policy that is not supported by a cited benchmark standard or policy.

children.title: Evaluation Contamination
children.top_down_role: Exposure or reuse that compromises the independence of benchmark conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation Contamination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information dependence that invalidates an instance's role as unseen evaluation data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be the declared evaluation set and \(A\) the submitted procedure, including its code, parameters, learned state, selection decisions, and human design choices. Evaluation contamination occurs when some nonpermitted artifact derived from an instance \(x\in E\), its duplicate family, reference solution, execution, or score influences \(A\) before final evaluation. Equivalently, \(A\) is not measurable solely with respect to the protocol-authorized development information because it also depends on prohibited test-derived information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation is contaminated when prohibited information from a test instance or its duplicate family influences the submitted procedure before final scoring.
assumptions_latex: The protocol identifies authorized development information.
The procedure includes human and automated adaptation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x\in E\) such that prohibited information derived from \(x\) or its family influences \(A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: information-dependence definition of test contamination
Relevant benchmark-validity evidence was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Evaluation Contamination, but the scope of prohibited influence—including duplicate families and human design choices—and the asserted measurability equivalence require benchmark-validity evidence.

children.title: Retirement-by-Contamination
children.top_down_role: Lifecycle decisions triggered by excessive solver, tuning, or reporting exposure.

knowledge_statements.title: Retirement-by-Contamination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifecycle rule retiring compromised evaluation instances and their dependent families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input corpus version \(C_v\), active evaluation set \(E_v\), duplicate-family map \(g\), and auditable contamination predicate \(q\). Form \(R=\{x\in E_v:q(x)=1\}\), expand it to \(R^+=\{y\in E_v:g(y)=g(x)\text{ for some }x\in R\}\), and mark every member of \(R^+\) retired. Create successor version \(C_{v+1}\) whose primary evaluation set is \(E_{v+1}=E_v\setminus R^+\); record evidence, effective date, affected results, and any replacements. Output \(C_{v+1}\) and the retirement log.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Detect contaminated instances, expand retirement to their duplicate families, issue a new corpus version, and retain an auditable retirement record.
assumptions_latex: The contamination predicate \(q\) and duplicate-family map \(g\) are fixed and auditable.
Retirement cannot mutate an already released manifest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{v+1}=E_v\setminus R^+\), and every contaminated duplicate family is absent from future primary evaluation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: family-closed lifecycle response to evaluation contamination
A published benchmark-retirement policy is required to certify this algorithm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct role for the proposed lifecycle procedure, but mandatory family-closed retirement, successor-version construction, and affected-result logging are policy choices unsupported by any published retirement protocol in the supplied evidence.

children.title: Solver Implementation-Observability Interface
children.top_down_role: Implementation choices that affect experimental comparability and observable solver behavior.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Shortest-path data structures and network-simplex implementation sections
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Simplex and weighted-matching implementation sections

children.title: Reference Implementations
children.top_down_role: Implementations emphasizing canonical behavior, auditability, or comparison against optimized variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition for correctness-oriented benchmark baselines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance class \(\mathcal I\) with solution verifier \(V\), a reference implementation is a deterministic program \(R\) with a documented configuration such that, for every supported instance \(I\in\mathcal I\), it returns an output \(s_R(I)\) satisfying \(V(I,s_R(I))=1\), or a documented failure status. Its algorithmic rules, numeric conventions, tie breaking, input interpretation, and stopping conditions are fixed before measurement. Benchmark results using \(R\) identify its version, build, configuration, and execution environment; performance beyond correctness and reproducibility is not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference implementation is a frozen, documented, correctness-oriented baseline whose outputs are verifiable and whose algorithmic and execution conventions are reproducible.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) has a specified input format and verifier \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is an auditable baseline on its documented supported domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Reference Implementations leaf and is internally consistent, but it is a project-specific operational definition rather than a universally standard mathematical definition. No inspectable citation supports the selected correctness, failure-status, freezing, and reporting criteria; the local inventory does not contain a benchmark-methodology source for them.

children.title: Pedagogical Implementations
children.top_down_role: Implementations emphasizing transparent organization and instructional accessibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Pedagogical Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition emphasizing transparent correspondence with an algorithm specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an algorithm specification \(A=(S_0,U,T,O)\), a pedagogical implementation is a program \(P\) whose exposed state, initialization, update, termination, and output operations correspond respectively to \(S_0\), \(U\), \(T\), and \(O\). For each supported instance \(I\), its execution trace can be mapped to a valid abstract trace of \(A\), and its output passes the designated verifier. Optimizations that obscure this correspondence may be omitted; consequently, timing results for \(P\) characterize that implementation and are not automatically estimates of optimized algorithm performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pedagogical implementation exposes the specification’s states and operations, enabling trace-level inspection while making no claim to optimized performance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has explicit initialization, update, termination, and output rules.
Supported outputs admit an independent correctness check.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Executions of \(P\) are inspectable realizations of \(A\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Pedagogical Implementations leaf, and the plain and LaTeX statements agree. However, the trace-correspondence and verifier requirements are substantive operational choices with no inspectable supporting source in the record or local inventory.

children.title: Reference–Pedagogy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Differences between canonical experimental baselines and teaching-oriented code structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference–Pedagogy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multi-criteria comparison of baseline fidelity and explanatory transparency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each implementation \(x\) have measured attributes \(q(x)=(c(x),r(x),t(x),p(x))\), representing correctness coverage, reproducibility, trace transparency, and performance representativeness, with larger values preferred. An implementation \(x\) dominates \(y\) only if every component of \(q(x)\) is at least the corresponding component of \(q(y)\), with one strict inequality. Selection between reference and pedagogical implementations shall therefore report \(q\) and the intended benchmark purpose; absent a declared scalar utility, incomparable attribute vectors do not determine a unique preferred baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reference and pedagogical baselines should be compared by explicit correctness, reproducibility, transparency, and performance-fidelity criteria rather than an undeclared aggregate ranking.
assumptions_latex: All four attributes are measured on declared, directionally consistent scales.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Componentwise-incomparable implementations have no unique ranking without an additional preference rule.

notation.meaning: coverage, reproducibility, transparency, and performance representativeness

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Pareto comparison for competing benchmark attributes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly describes componentwise Pareto comparison and fits the tradeoff leaf. The recommendation to use these four particular attributes as benchmark criteria is nevertheless an uncited methodological prescription; the standard-field rationale does not establish that selection empirically or authoritatively.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimized Research Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Research prototype optimized for a declared experimental question.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For benchmark domain \(\mathcal I\), an optimized research implementation is a versioned program \(R_\theta\) realizing a declared algorithmic method under configuration \(\theta\), with performance-oriented choices such as specialized data structures, preprocessing, parallelism, or machine-specific tuning. Its admissible instances, correctness verifier, resource limits, build options, dependencies, random seeds, and hardware environment are recorded. Measurements are attributed to the complete pair \((R_\theta,E)\), where \(E\) is the execution environment; they do not by themselves identify the performance of the abstract algorithm independently of implementation and environment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimized research implementation is a versioned experimental artifact whose tuning, correctness checks, configuration, and environment are disclosed with every performance claim.
assumptions_latex: The experimental domain \(\mathcal I\) and correctness criterion are fixed before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Observed performance is an attribute of \((R_\theta,E)\), not solely of the abstract method.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: artifact-centered empirical algorithm engineering convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Optimized Research Implementations and appropriately attributes observations to implementation, configuration, and environment. Its disclosure requirements and treatment interpretation are methodology claims for which no specific, inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Production Solver Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deployed solver treated as a versioned configurable benchmark system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A production solver implementation is a released solver system \(S=(B,C,D)\), comprising executable build \(B\), admissible configuration space \(C\), and runtime dependency environment \(D\). A benchmark observation is indexed by \((B,c,D,I)\) for configuration \(c\in C\) and instance \(I\), and records termination status, certified solution information, elapsed resources, and any solver-reported bounds. Comparisons must fix or disclose automatic tuning, preprocessing, parallelism, randomization, licensing restrictions, and resource limits. Results from distinct builds or configurations are observations of distinct solver treatments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A production solver is benchmarked as a complete versioned system; build, configuration, dependencies, tuning, parallelism, and resource limits define the treatment.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark harness can identify the build, configuration, dependencies, and termination status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each distinct tuple \((B,c,D)\) constitutes a distinct experimental treatment.

notation.meaning: build, selected configuration, and dependency environment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Production Solver Implementations, and treating distinct builds and configurations as distinct experimental treatments is coherent. No cited solver-benchmarking or experimental-design source supports the exact system tuple, mandatory disclosures, or treatment rule.

children.title: Shared-Kernel Implementations
children.top_down_role: Solver variants built upon common data structures, utilities, or computational kernels.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Kernel Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementations sharing executable infrastructure on measured computational paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) be solver implementations and let \(K\) be an executable component. They are shared-kernel implementations with respect to \(K\) when every \(P_i\) invokes the same version and configuration of \(K\) on at least one measured execution path, and the work or outputs of \(K\) contribute to the recorded response. Shared parsers, allocators, graph primitives, relaxation routines, presolvers, or optimization libraries qualify only when their execution lies inside the declared measurement boundary. Common specifications or independently rewritten code do not constitute a shared executable kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implementations share a kernel when the same executable component contributes within each measured path; merely sharing specifications does not qualify.
assumptions_latex: The measurement boundary and dynamic or static component provenance are observable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) share \(K\) exactly relative to the declared measured paths.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Shared-Kernel Implementations leaf and clearly distinguishes executable sharing from specification sharing. The range and minimum value of k are only implicit, and the operational measurement-boundary criterion lacks an inspectable software-experimentation source.

children.title: Independent Implementations
children.top_down_role: Solver variants developed with separate codebases or implementation stacks.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational code-provenance independence, distinct from statistical independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Implementations \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) are implementation-independent on a measured domain \(\mathcal I\) when no pair shares executable solver code, generated object code, mutable runtime state, or solver-specific library components on the measured paths, and each was produced from a separately maintained code base. They may share the mathematical specification, input instances, file formats, operating system, and benchmark harness, provided those common elements are disclosed. This definition concerns implementation provenance and does not imply statistical independence of their errors or running times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent implementations use separately maintained solver code and share no executable solver components on measured paths; their outcomes need not be statistically independent.
assumptions_latex: Code provenance and measured execution paths are available for audit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Implementation independence excludes shared solver machinery but not disclosed common experimental infrastructure.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Independent Implementations and correctly separates provenance independence from statistical independence. The domain of the implementation index is implicit, while the strong exclusions concerning object code, state, libraries, and code-base maintenance are uncited operational choices.

children.title: Kernel-Sharing Confounds
children.top_down_role: Comparison effects attributable to shared infrastructure rather than algorithmic differences.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel-Sharing Confounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-identifiability of solver effects when an influential kernel is shared.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the measured response of implementation \(i\) on instance \(j\) satisfies \(Y_{ij}=\alpha_i+\kappa_j+\gamma_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}\), where \(\kappa_j\) is the contribution of a kernel shared by all implementations and \(\gamma_{ij}\) is an implementation-kernel interaction. If the experiment observes only \(Y_{ij}\), uses one kernel version, and does not separately instrument kernel time or vary kernel assignment, then \(\alpha_i\) and \(\gamma_{ij}\) are not separately identifiable. Consequently, an observed difference cannot be attributed solely to the implementation-level algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one uninstrumented shared kernel, implementation effects and implementation–kernel interactions cannot be separated, so performance differences lack algorithm-only attribution.
assumptions_latex: All compared implementations use one kernel version on the measured path.
No kernel-level response or alternative kernel assignment is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decomposition into \(\alpha_i\) and \(\gamma_{ij}\) is non-identifiable from \(Y_{ij}\) alone.

notation.meaning: observed response for implementation i on instance j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identifiability argument for shared components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf, and the stated additive model does exhibit confounding between implementation effects and unrestricted implementation-kernel interactions. However, the implementation and instance index sets are not explicit, and no statistical-design source supports the model or the resulting attribution boundary.

children.title: Implementation-Independence Variance
children.top_down_role: Behavioral variation introduced by independently chosen engineering decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Implementation-Independence Variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-effects decomposition for variability across independent implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For algorithm \(a\), independent implementation \(i\), and benchmark instance \(j\), represent a response by \(Y_{aij}=\mu+\alpha_a+u_{ai}+\beta_j+\varepsilon_{aij}\). Assume the centered random terms are mutually uncorrelated, with variances \(\sigma_I^2\), \(\sigma_B^2\), and \(\sigma_E^2\) for \(u_{ai}\), \(\beta_j\), and \(\varepsilon_{aij}\), respectively. Then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_{aij}\mid a)=\sigma_I^2+\sigma_B^2+\sigma_E^2\). Using only one implementation per algorithm aliases \(u_{ai}\) with the algorithm effect and prevents estimation of \(\sigma_I^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random-effects model separates implementation, instance, and residual variance; one implementation per algorithm cannot identify implementation variance.
assumptions_latex: Random terms are centered, mutually uncorrelated, and have finite second moments.
Implementations satisfy the declared provenance-independence criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_{aij}\mid a)=\sigma_I^2+\sigma_B^2+\sigma_E^2\), while one implementation per algorithm leaves \(\sigma_I^2\) unidentified.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional additive random-effects variance decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A random-effects representation is appropriate for the variance leaf, and the variance sum follows under the stated uncorrelatedness assumptions. The claim that one implementation per algorithm prevents estimation of implementation variance depends on the nesting, replication, and treatment of algorithm effects; those design conditions and an authoritative statistical source are absent.

children.title: Graph Storage Layouts
children.top_down_role: Storage layouts for vertices, edges, incidence records, attributes, plus traversal metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Storage Layouts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compressed adjacency representation for finite weighted or unweighted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed graph with \(V=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and \(m=|E|\). A compressed sparse row layout consists of an offset array \(p\) of length \(n+1\) and a head array \(h\) of length \(m\), where \(p_0=0\), \(p_n=m\), and the outgoing neighbors of vertex \(v\) occupy \(h[p_v],\ldots,h[p_{v+1}-1]\). Optional edge attributes use aligned arrays of length \(m\). An undirected edge is stored as two directed incidences unless another convention is declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compressed adjacency stores each vertex’s outgoing incidences in one contiguous range, with aligned arrays for weights or other edge attributes.
assumptions_latex: Vertices and stored directed incidences have contiguous integer identifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The layout uses \(n+1\) offsets and \(m\) adjacency entries and enumerates the neighbors of \(v\) in \(O(p_{v+1}-p_v)\) time.

notation.meaning: numbers of vertices and stored directed incidences

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional compressed sparse row representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and CSR statement fit Graph Storage Layouts, and the array dimensions and adjacency ranges are standard. No record citation or inventory locator supports this exact layout and complexity statement; the listed algorithm chapters are not storage-layout references.

children.title: Hypergraph Storage Layouts
children.top_down_role: Storage layouts for hyperedges, pins, incidence records, attributes, plus traversal metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraph Storage Layouts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional compressed-incidence representation of a finite hypergraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) have \(n=|V|\), \(m=|\mathcal E|\), and incidence count \(L=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}|e|\). A bidirectional compressed-incidence layout stores edge offsets \(p^E\) and vertex identifiers \(a^E\), so the members of edge \(e\) occupy one contiguous range, together with vertex offsets \(p^V\) and edge identifiers \(a^V\), so incident edges of vertex \(v\) occupy one contiguous range. The offset arrays have lengths \(m+1\) and \(n+1\); both identifier arrays have length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bidirectional hypergraph layout stores contiguous vertex lists per hyperedge and contiguous hyperedge lists per vertex, using space linear in total incidence count.
assumptions_latex: Vertices, hyperedges, and incidences have finite index sets.
Repeated incidences are either forbidden or retained under a declared multiplicity convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation occupies \(O(n+m+L)\) words and enumerates either side of an incidence neighborhood in time proportional to its size.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bidirectional compressed-incidence representation fits the Hypergraph Storage Layouts leaf, with consistent dimensions and space bounds. The record supplies no inspectable hypergraph data-structure source for the representation or its enumeration guarantees.

children.title: Cross-Representation Conversion Costs
children.top_down_role: Memory, preprocessing, update, plus traversal costs arising when converting between graph-oriented or hypergraph-oriented layouts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Representation Conversion Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear conversion between incidence arrays and incidence bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) have \(n\) vertices, \(m\) hyperedges, and \(L\) incidences stored in compressed edge-to-vertex form. In the unit-cost RAM model, constructing its incidence bipartite graph \(B_H=(V\cup\mathcal E,F)\), where \((v,e)\in F\) exactly when \(v\in e\), takes \(O(n+m+L)\) time and \(O(n+m+L)\) words. Conversely, given \(B_H\), its bipartition, and adjacency arrays, counting degrees, prefix-summing offsets, and scattering incidences constructs bidirectional compressed hypergraph arrays within the same bounds. Every conversion must inspect all \(L\) incidences, giving an \(\Omega(L)\) time lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hypergraph incidence arrays and a partitioned incidence bipartite graph convert in linear time and space, and every conversion must inspect all incidences.
assumptions_latex: Input arrays are valid and their lengths are available in constant time.
Machine words hold vertex, hyperedge, incidence, and offset indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conversion costs \(\Theta(n+m+L)\) time and \(O(n+m+L)\) auxiliary output space in the worst case.

notation.meaning: incidence bipartite graph of the hypergraph

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: linear scan and prefix-sum conversion analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the conversion-cost leaf, and linear construction is plausible in the stated RAM model. The text explicitly establishes only an Omega(L) inspection lower bound while concluding Theta(n+m+L); an output-size argument for Omega(n+m+L) is needed. No inspectable source supports the exact conversion model and bounds.

assumptions_latex: The priority keys lie in a totally ordered set \(K\).
Each live item has a stable identifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every family member implements a common minimum-priority interface while differing in its supported updates and resource bounds.

notation.meaning: finite set of live item identifiers

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract interface for comparing priority-queue implementations in combinatorial solvers.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Performance of Label Setting Methods p. 68
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A priority-queue family over a totally ordered key set \(K\) consists of data structures maintaining a finite set \(Q\) of live item identifiers and a key map \(k:Q\to K\). Every member supports \(\operatorname{insert}(v,a)\), \(\operatorname{findMin}()\), and \(\operatorname{deleteMin}()\); a member may additionally support \(\operatorname{decreaseKey}(v,a)\), deletion by identifier, or key increases. When \(Q\neq\varnothing\), \(\operatorname{findMin}()\) returns some \(v\in Q\) satisfying \(k(v)=\min_{u\in Q}k(u)\), and \(\operatorname{deleteMin}()\) removes such an item. A benchmark distinguishes family members by supported operations, tie policy, amortized or worst-case operation costs, and measured memory and locality behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A priority-queue family shares minimum-key insertion and extraction semantics; implementations differ in update operations, tie handling, theoretical costs, memory use, and locality.
knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Queue Families

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Performance of Label Setting Methods p. 68
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Dynamic-Tree Support
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-tree representations, operation profiles, implementation choices, plus engineering costs.

assumptions_latex: The maintained object is a forest on a fixed vertex set.
Updates preserve the forest invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The structure maintains path aggregates under link and cut operations and answers path queries without rebuilding the forest.

notation.meaning: aggregate on the path from \(u\) to \(v\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface-level dynamic-forest support, independent of a particular link-cut or topology-tree implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a forest \(F=(V,E)\), edge or vertex values from a set carrying an associative aggregate operation, initialize one singleton tree per vertex. Support \(\operatorname{link}(u,v,w)\) only when \(u\) and \(v\) are in distinct trees, support \(\operatorname{cut}(u,v)\) only when \(uv\in E\), and support \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\). For vertices in one tree, \(\operatorname{pathAggregate}(u,v)\) returns the ordered aggregate \(A_F(u,v)\) of values on their unique path. After each update, the represented edge set equals the current \(E\). The algorithm outputs query answers online and stops when the supplied operation stream ends.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic-tree support maintains a changing forest, permits valid links and cuts, tests connectivity, and returns aggregates on unique tree paths.
knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Tree Support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic interface fits Dynamic-Tree Support and is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source is supplied for the supported operations or aggregate semantics.

children.title: Disjoint-Set Support
children.top_down_role: Disjoint-set representations, operation profiles, implementation choices, plus engineering costs.

assumptions_latex: The universe \(V\) is finite.
Updates only merge sets and never split them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned representatives characterize exactly the partition generated by all processed unions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental-connectivity interface with union by rank or size and path compression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a parent forest on a finite universe \(V\) with \(p(v)=v\) and rank or size metadata for every \(v\in V\). The operation \(\operatorname{find}(v)\) follows parent pointers to a root and may replace traversed pointers by that root. The operation \(\operatorname{union}(u,v)\) computes \(r_u=\operatorname{find}(u)\) and \(r_v=\operatorname{find}(v)\); if \(r_u\neq r_v\), it attaches the lower-rank or smaller root below the other and updates metadata. At every time, \(u\) and \(v\) occupy the same block of \(\mathcal P\) if and only if \(\operatorname{find}(u)=\operatorname{find}(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint-set support represents a merge-only partition through representative queries and unions, commonly using weighted linking and path compression.
