knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint-Set Support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and merge-only partition semantics fit Disjoint-Set Support, but the record has no source for weighted linking, path compression, or the representation invariant.

children.title: Support-Structure Selection Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Workloads, mutation patterns, plus query demands that favor either support family.

assumptions_latex: Connectivity operations are processed online.
The required query semantics are fixed before selecting the support structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disjoint sets suffice only in the merge-only regime; deletions, cuts, or path aggregates require stronger dynamic-connectivity support.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic boundary between merge-only partition support and fully dynamic forest support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sigma\) be an online sequence of connectivity operations on \(n\) vertices. If every update only inserts an edge whose effect is to merge two current components and every query asks whether two vertices share a component, disjoint-set support represents all required state. This selection fails once \(\sigma\) contains an effective deletion or cut: a union operation irreversibly coarsens its represented partition and cannot recover the refined components. Likewise, component representatives do not determine path aggregates. Therefore workloads requiring cuts, deletions, or queries on unique forest paths lie beyond the disjoint-set interface and require a dynamic-tree or another dynamic-connectivity structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint sets fit merge-only connectivity. Effective deletions, cuts, or path queries cross their semantic boundary and require a stronger dynamic structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Structure Selection Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct content kind and the semantic distinction is plausible, but no source supports the asserted selection boundary between disjoint sets and dynamic connectivity structures.

children.title: Sparse-Matrix Storage
children.top_down_role: Compressed sparse layouts, indexing choices, mutation support, plus factorization-facing access.

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has \(z\) explicitly stored nonzero entries.
Row and column indices use fixed finite integer domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation stores exactly the nonzeros using \(O(m+z)\) CSR space or \(O(n+z)\) CSC space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compressed sparse row and compressed sparse column representations for solver matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(z\) stored nonzeros, compressed sparse row storage consists of values \(a_0,\ldots,a_{z-1}\), corresponding column indices \(j_0,\ldots,j_{z-1}\), and row pointers \(r_0,\ldots,r_m\) with \(r_0=0\), \(r_m=z\), and entries for row \(i\) occupying positions \(r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1\). Compressed sparse column storage is the transposed convention with column pointers and row indices. Duplicate coordinates must be combined or explicitly distinguished by the interface; omitted coordinates denote zero. Thus sequential traversal by the compressed dimension touches every stored entry once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CSR or CSC stores nonzeros, indices, and segment pointers, giving linear storage in the relevant dimension plus the number of stored entries.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Matrix Storage

children.title: Basis Storage
children.top_down_role: Representations for basis membership, basis factors, update metadata, plus restoration state.

assumptions_latex: The basis matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
All factor permutations and update metadata are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stored factors and updates must reproduce solves with both \(B\) and \(B^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor-based storage contract for a nonsingular simplex basis.

source_refs.locator: 5.2 The Basic Simplex Algorithm p. 186
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonsingular basis \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), a basis-storage representation comprises either an explicit current factorization \(PBQ=LU\) or a reference factorization together with an ordered sequence of nonsingular update transformations. Here \(P\) and \(Q\) are permutations and \(L\) and \(U\) are triangular factors. The representation is valid when its solve procedures return \(x\) satisfying \(Bx=b\) and \(y\) satisfying \(B^{\mathsf T}y=c\), up to the declared numerical tolerance, for every supplied \(b,c\in\mathbb R^m\). It must also identify the current basic-column ordering so factor coordinates remain consistent with solver variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis storage retains factors, permutations, updates, and column ordering sufficient to solve systems with a nonsingular basis and its transpose.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Storage

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 The Basic Simplex Algorithm p. 186
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Basis Storage, but the cited basic-simplex section does not yet establish the stated factorization alternatives, update sequence, transpose-solve contract, and numerical-tolerance requirements. The mathematical version therefore remains source-dependent.

children.title: Matrix-to-Basis Data Exchange
children.top_down_role: Data movement, indexing compatibility, ownership, plus synchronization across matrix storage or basis storage.

assumptions_latex: The matrix store exposes every requested basis column.
The assembled basis is nonsingular before factorization is requested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exchange preserves equality between the solver's selected columns and the basis module's assembled matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency contract between sparse matrix storage and a factorized basis module.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a matrix store for \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), an ordered tuple \(I=(i_1,\ldots,i_m)\) of distinct basic-column indices, and an optional replacement \((p,j)\). If a replacement is supplied, set \(i_p\leftarrow j\). Retrieve each selected sparse column in a declared index convention, canonicalize duplicate coordinates, and assemble \(B=[A_{i_1}\ \cdots\ A_{i_m}]\). Pass \(B\), \(I\), and any scaling or permutation metadata to the basis module; refactorize or apply a validated column update. Reject the exchange if dimensions, indices, or nonsingularity checks fail. Output a basis handle whose recorded ordering is exactly \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exchange assembles selected sparse columns in a fixed order, transfers metadata, validates the basis, and returns a consistently indexed basis handle.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-to-Basis Data Exchange

children.title: Memory-Locality Layouts
children.top_down_role: Spatial or temporal placement choices affecting solver data access.

assumptions_latex: A fixed logical record set is stored in memory.
A cache line contains \(L\) consecutive addressable bytes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A locality layout is characterized by its address map and the resulting cache-line footprint of each access sequence.

notation.meaning: finite set of stored logical item-fields
starting byte address assigned to a stored item-field

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Address-map model covering array-of-structures, structure-of-arrays, blocking, and ordering choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A memory-locality layout for a finite set \(D\) of stored logical item-fields assigns each \(d\in D\) a nonoverlapping byte interval whose starting address is \(\lambda(d)\), together with alignment, ordering, and blocking rules. For cache-line size \(L\), an access sequence \(s=(d_1,\ldots,d_t)\) has starting-line trace \((\lfloor\lambda(d_1)/L\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor\lambda(d_t)/L\rfloor)\). Array-of-structures places fields of one record adjacently; structure-of-arrays places equal fields of successive records adjacently; a blocked layout applies either rule within bounded groups. Two layouts are semantically equivalent when decoding yields the same logical records, although their line traces and storage overhead may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A memory-locality layout maps logical fields to aligned, nonoverlapping byte intervals; record ordering, field grouping, and blocking determine the cache lines touched by an access sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Locality Layouts

children.title: Cache-Behavior Profiles
children.top_down_role: Cache residency, miss patterns, reuse behavior, plus hierarchy-level sensitivity.

assumptions_latex: All runs use the same cache hierarchy and measurement protocol.
Counters are attributed to a specified benchmark region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized counter vector defines a comparable cache-behavior profile for that region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized empirical profile for a fixed execution region and hardware cache hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a benchmark region, input, hardware cache hierarchy, counter semantics, and work normalizer \(W>0\). A cache-behavior profile is the vector \(\pi=(C_e/W)_{e\in E}\), where \(E\) is a declared set of events such as references, misses, writebacks, or stall cycles at specified cache levels and \(C_e\) is the measured count of event \(e\). Each component must state its event definition and scope. Repeated-run profiles additionally report an aggregation rule and dispersion statistic. Profiles are comparable only when region boundaries, event meanings, normalization, cache state policy, and hardware configuration are held fixed or explicitly modeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cache profile is a declared vector of normalized hardware-event counts, comparable only under compatible regions, counter meanings, cache policies, and hardware.
knowledge_statements.title: Cache-Behavior Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is a suitable role for Cache-Behavior Profiles and the quantities are introduced, but no source supports the normalization and comparability requirements. Hardware-counter semantics are sufficiently platform-sensitive that standard-field rationale alone is inadequate.

children.title: Locality-Induced Performance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance sizes, access patterns, plus execution architectures that change locality benefits.

assumptions_latex: The executed instruction path and problem instance are fixed for the comparison.
Cache penalties and miss counts are measured under a declared protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A locality-induced regime is a parameter region where memory-stall cost determines the observed ordering of implementations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational condition for classifying benchmark regions as locality dominated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the additive diagnostic model \(T=T_{\mathrm{core}}+\sum_{\ell=1}^h p_\ell M_\ell\), a benchmark point lies in a locality-induced performance regime at threshold \(\theta\in(0,1)\) when \(\sum_{\ell=1}^h p_\ell M_\ell\geq\theta T\). A parameter region is assigned one regime only if this inequality and the ordering of compared implementation times persist under the declared replication and uncertainty rule throughout that region. A claimed layout-induced regime change additionally requires that changing the layout changes the miss term enough to reverse or materially alter the implementation ordering while logical outputs remain identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locality-induced regime occurs when estimated cache-miss cost supplies a declared fraction of runtime and persistently controls implementation rankings across a parameter region.
knowledge_statements.title: Locality-Induced Performance Regimes

children.title: Default Configurations
children.top_down_role: Maintainer-supplied settings intended for broad, low-intervention use.

assumptions_latex: The solver exposes a finite configuration space \(\Theta\).
The release fixes a declared default selector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A default configuration is selected without instance-specific expert intervention and is reproducible from the recorded release context.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark-facing definition of a solver-supplied, non-expert configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be the solver's finite or finitely encoded configuration space and let \(r\) record the solver release, build, and platform context. A default configuration is \(\theta_0=d(r)\in\Theta\), selected by the solver's documented default rule before inspecting benchmark-instance identity, hidden labels, or measured outcomes. If the solver performs automatic instance analysis as part of its default behavior, that analysis belongs to \(d\) and must be recorded. Repeated executions with identical \(r\), input, and random seed must select the same \(\theta_0\), unless declared nondeterminism is itself part of the evaluated default policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A default configuration is the release-defined setting chosen without expert instance tuning, including any documented automatic selection performed by the solver itself.
knowledge_statements.title: Default Configurations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits Default Configurations and is internally precise, but the restrictions on instance inspection, reproducibility, automatic analysis, and nondeterminism constitute a benchmark policy taxonomy with no cited source.

children.title: Expert Configurations
children.top_down_role: Specialized settings intended for workload-aware or implementation-aware control.

assumptions_latex: The admissible configuration space \(\Theta\) and information available to the expert are declared.
The selected setting is fixed before scoring the evaluation instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expert configuration is a reproducibly recorded admissible setting with explicitly bounded human authority.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark-facing definition of a human-selected configuration under a declared information regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be the admissible solver-configuration space and \(\mathcal I\) the information disclosed before evaluation, including any permitted training instances and preliminary runs. An expert configuration is \(\theta_E=e(\mathcal I)\in\Theta\), where \(e\) includes human judgment and is applied within a declared time, computation, and trial budget. The benchmark record must identify whether \(\theta_E\) is global, class-specific, or instance-specific, and must store every overridden parameter. Evaluation outcomes unavailable at selection time may not enter \(\mathcal I\). Reproduction uses the recorded \(\theta_E\), solver release, build, platform, and random-seed policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expert configuration is a human-selected admissible setting chosen under declared information and tuning budgets, then frozen and fully recorded for evaluation.
knowledge_statements.title: Expert Configurations

children.title: Configuration Override Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions, risks, plus reproducibility implications associated with replacing defaults.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark fixes an instance set \(I\), configuration space \(\Theta\), and admissible override set \(O\subseteq\Theta\).
Each run records its effective configuration and the authority that supplied every overridden coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A run is compliant exactly when its effective configuration belongs to the declared override boundary.

notation.meaning: admissible values for coordinate j under authority a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal compliance boundary for benchmark-visible configuration overrides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite ordered set of configuration authorities, with higher authorities taking precedence. For each \(a\in A\), let \(J_a\) be its declared coordinate domain and let \(O_{a,j}\subseteq\Theta_j\) contain its admissible values for \(j\in J_a\). Starting from \(\theta^0\), process authorities in increasing precedence and replace coordinate \(j\) only when \(j\in J_a\). The resulting effective configuration \(\theta\) respects the override boundary precisely when every applied value satisfies \(\theta_j\in O_{a,j}\), no authority modifies a coordinate outside \(J_a\), and the recorded provenance identifies the highest-precedence authority applied to each modified coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An override is compliant only when each authority changes permitted coordinates to permitted values, precedence is respected, and the effective configuration retains complete provenance.
knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Override Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports this benchmark-specific compliance condition. The meaning of increasing precedence and the relationship between the assumed override set O and the coordinatewise sets O_{a,j} also require authoritative specification.

assumptions_latex: A finite training set \(T\) and configuration space \(\Theta\) are fixed before test evaluation.
The loss \(L(\theta,i)\) includes the declared timeout and failure penalties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuner returns a configuration minimizing its training objective without using test-instance outcomes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static tuning performed before evaluation on held-out benchmark instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(T\), \(\Theta\), a budget \(B\), and loss \(L:\Theta\times T\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), initialize an evaluated set \(E_0=\varnothing\). At iteration \(t\), a search rule selects \(\theta_t\in\Theta\) using only observations in \(E_{t-1}\); execute the prescribed training runs, append their losses to obtain \(E_t\), and charge their declared cost against \(B\). Stop before the next evaluation would exceed \(B\). Output \(\hat\theta\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta_t}\widehat R_T(\theta)\), where \(\Theta_t\) is the evaluated configuration set and \(\widehat R_T(\theta)=|T|^{-1}\sum_{i\in T}L(\theta,i)\). Test outcomes may not influence any selection or update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Offline tuning searches configurations using only training runs and a fixed budget, then returns the evaluated configuration with minimum declared empirical training loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Offline Parameter Tuning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No algorithm-configuration source is cited. The proposed search procedure is only one possible offline tuner, and the empirical objective is undefined unless every configuration in Theta_t has losses for all instances in T.

assumptions_latex: Every instance \(i\in I\) has an observable feature vector \(\phi(i)\in\mathcal X\).
Configuration performance is measured by a declared loss \(L:\Theta\times I\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A per-instance configurator is a feature-measurable mapping from instances to admissible configurations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feature-based static configuration chosen separately for each unseen instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an instance domain, \(\Theta\) an admissible configuration space, and \(\phi:I\to\mathcal X\) a feature map computable before the configured solver run. A per-instance configurator is a mapping \(g:\mathcal X\to\Theta\); instance \(i\) is solved with \(\theta(i)=g(\phi(i))\). Its population risk under distribution \(D\) is \(R_D(g)=\mathbb E_{i\sim D}[L(g(\phi(i)),i)]\), including feature-computation cost or failure penalties when the benchmark protocol requires them. Training determines \(g\) without observing outcomes from held-out test instances, and \(g(\phi(i))\) remains fixed throughout the run on \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Per-instance configuration maps pre-run instance features to one admissible, run-fixed solver configuration and is evaluated by its expected protocol-defined loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Per-Instance Configuration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the stated definition or risk formulation. Calling the mapping feature-measurable would require measurable structures, and protocol-dependent feature costs and penalties need a cited convention.

assumptions_latex: A solver exposes an observable state space \(S\), action space \(A\), and admissible-action correspondence \(A(s)\subseteq A\).
The benchmark specifies a stopping rule and accounts for configuration-decision overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adaptive configuration is a causal policy whose choices may change during a solver run.

notation.meaning: observed run history through decision time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Causal within-run configuration based on solver observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decision times \(t=0,1,\ldots\), let \(H_t=(s_0,a_0,\ldots,s_t)\) be the information observed by time \(t\). An adaptive configurator is a causal policy \(\pi\) selecting \(a_t=\pi(H_t)\in A(s_t)\); it may alter parameters, heuristics, or allocated resources during the run. Causality requires that equal histories produce the same action distribution, so \(\pi\) cannot depend on future states or unobserved outcomes. Execution terminates under the benchmark stopping rule and returns the solver output together with the action history. Its measured loss includes solver work, decision overhead, and declared penalties for invalid actions or failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive configuration uses only the observed run history to change admissible solver settings, while benchmark loss includes decision overhead and failures.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Configuration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No adaptive-configuration source is supplied. The statement defines pi as a deterministic mapping but subsequently refers to an action distribution, so the intended deterministic or randomized policy model is unresolved.

children.title: Algorithm Portfolio Construction
children.top_down_role: Candidate diversity, complementarity, coverage, plus portfolio maintenance.

assumptions_latex: A finite candidate set \(\mathcal A\) and representative training set \(T\) are given.
Each candidate has a protocol-defined loss \(L(a,i)\) on every \(i\in T\), including failure penalties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Portfolio construction returns a budget-feasible subset selected by its aggregate instancewise coverage.

notation.meaning: resource cost of a portfolio member

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite portfolio construction under a declared resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\mathcal A\), \(T\), costs \(c:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R_+\), and budget \(C\), initialize \(P_0=\varnothing\). At step \(k\), choose an unselected candidate maximizing the decrease in \(F(P)=|T|^{-1}\sum_{i\in T}\min_{a\in P}L(a,i)\) among additions satisfying \(\sum_{a\in P}c(a)\le C\); use a declared deterministic tie rule. Stop when no feasible addition strictly decreases \(F\), and output \(P=P_k\). For \(P=\varnothing\), define \(F(P)=+\infty\). Any validation used to choose portfolio size or stopping thresholds must be separated from the final test set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Portfolio construction greedily adds budget-feasible candidates that improve training-instance coverage, stopping when no admissible addition reduces aggregate oracle loss.
knowledge_statements.title: Algorithm Portfolio Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No portfolio-construction source supports this particular greedy algorithm. With F(empty)=+infinity, every finite singleton has an infinite decrease, so the first-step maximization and tie semantics are not mathematically well-defined as written.

children.title: Per-Instance Algorithm Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection based on instance features, historical performance, resource limits, plus deployment constraints.

assumptions_latex: A finite portfolio \(P\) and pre-run feature map \(\phi:I\to\mathcal X\) are fixed.
The loss \(L(a,i)\) accounts for feature cost, timeout, and failure according to the protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selector assigns each instance one portfolio member using only information available before its run.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static selection of one portfolio member for each instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From training observations \(\{(\phi(i),L(a,i)):i\in T,\ a\in P\}\), fit a selector \(s:\mathcal X\to P\) by minimizing a declared empirical or cross-validated surrogate for \(L\). For a held-out instance \(i\), compute \(x=\phi(i)\), choose \(a_i=s(x)\), execute only \(a_i\) under the common run budget, and return its output. Ties and missing-feature behavior must be fixed before test evaluation. The selector's test loss is \(L(s(\phi(i)),i)\), augmented by feature and selection overhead when those costs are not already included in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trained selector uses pre-run features to choose one portfolio member per held-out instance under fixed tie, missing-feature, and cost-accounting rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Per-Instance Algorithm Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No algorithm-selection source is cited. The record describes a family of training procedures rather than a definite algorithm because neither the surrogate nor its optimization rule is specified; evidence is needed to determine whether this leaf should contain a definition or a particular algorithm.

children.title: Portfolio-to-Selector Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Coverage gaps, redundant candidates, feature availability, plus selection overhead.

assumptions_latex: The selector emits labels in a decision space \(Y\), and the executable portfolio is \(P\).
Every selected member must support the benchmark's instance representation, resource limits, and output contract.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds exactly when every possible selector decision resolves to a valid executable member with comparable outcomes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total interface contract between selector outputs and executable portfolio members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A portfolio \(P\) is compatible with a selector \(s:\mathcal X\to Y\) when there exists a total resolution map \(\rho:Y\to P\) such that, for every admissible feature vector \(x\), the member \(\rho(s(x))\) accepts the benchmark instance encoding, obeys the declared resource and configuration constraints, and returns an output in the common result space. Furthermore, all members use the same loss convention, failure coding, and stopping semantics. If \(s(x)\) is missing or invalid, a predeclared fallback in \(P\) must be resolved by \(\rho\); otherwise compatibility fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selector and portfolio are compatible when every decision, including fallbacks, resolves to an executable member obeying common input, resource, output, and loss contracts.
knowledge_statements.title: Portfolio-to-Selector Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this interface condition. A total map rho:Y-to-P already resolves every value in Y, while a missing selector output is not defined as an element of Y; the fallback domain and common comparability contract require an authoritative specification.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic transition map \(F:S\times U\to S\) and initial state \(s_0\in S\) are fixed.
Exactly one transition is completed at each step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sequential execution produces a totally ordered state trajectory determined by the initial state and control sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-worker operational model for benchmarked solver execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequential execution of a solver is a trajectory \((s_t)_{t=0}^{\tau}\) satisfying \(s_{t+1}=F(s_t,u_t)\), where each control \(u_t\in U\) is chosen only after transition \(t-1\) has completed. The stopping index is \(\tau=\inf\{t\ge 0:q(s_t)=1\}\), subject to the benchmark resource limit; if the limit occurs first, the run returns the prescribed censored or timeout outcome. No two transitions overlap in execution time, and the event log is ordered by \(0<1<\cdots<\tau\). Under deterministic controls and arithmetic, \(s_0\) uniquely determines the recorded trajectory and output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential execution completes one state transition at a time, yielding a total event order and, under deterministic controls, a uniquely determined trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Execution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No execution-model source is cited. The trajectory indexed through tau is not defined when the stopping predicate is never reached, and the benchmark resource-limit stopping time is not incorporated into the formal index.

assumptions_latex: There are \(p\ge2\) workers sharing one address space.
The synchronization semantics and treatment of conflicting memory accesses are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Shared-memory execution is valid when concurrent worker actions are consistent with the specified synchronization model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiple workers operating concurrently in one shared address space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shared-memory parallel execution consists of worker event sequences \(E_1,\ldots,E_p\) acting on shared state \(s\), together with a synchronization relation \(\prec\). Each \(E_k\) is locally ordered, synchronization events add cross-worker order, and every conflicting non-atomic access must be ordered by \(\prec\); otherwise the execution is invalid under the benchmark model. Atomic updates take effect according to their declared memory semantics. The run stops when the global stopping predicate or resource limit is observed under the specified synchronization rule. Reported resources include \(p\), elapsed time, aggregate work when available, and synchronization overhead required by the protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared-memory execution uses concurrent workers over one state, with declared synchronization ordering all conflicting accesses and benchmark reports identifying parallel resources and overhead.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Memory Parallel Execution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No parallel-execution source is supplied. Requiring all conflicting non-atomic accesses to be synchronization-ordered defines a particular data-race-free model, not shared-memory execution generally, so the intended benchmark semantics need evidence.

assumptions_latex: There are \(p\ge2\) processes with disjoint local address spaces.
Processes communicate only through messages governed by a declared delivery model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distributed execution is defined by local computations plus explicit send, receive, and collective events.

notation.meaning: message sent from process k to process l

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Message-passing solver execution across disjoint process memories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distributed-memory execution comprises local trajectories \((s_{k,t})_t\) for processes \(k=1,\ldots,p\) and communication events. A receive of \(m_{k\ell}\) may affect \(s_\ell\) only after the corresponding send, and the global event relation \(\prec\) is the transitive closure of each process's local order, send-before-receive edges, and declared collective synchronization edges. Termination requires the protocol's global completion condition or resource limit. Benchmark accounting records process count, placement, elapsed time, communicated bytes or messages when observable, and failures. An execution trace is admissible only if every receive and collective is consistent with the declared communication semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed-memory execution combines locally ordered process computations through explicit messages and collectives, with admissible traces respecting send-before-receive and declared termination semantics.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed-Memory Execution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No distributed-execution source supports the proposed admissibility and accounting rules. Message matching, collective ordering, failure handling, and global termination are model-dependent and require a specific cited protocol.

assumptions_latex: A host solver offloads designated kernels to one or more accelerators.
Transfer, kernel, synchronization, and accelerator-memory costs are measurable under the protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accelerator-backed execution includes host-device interaction and all required synchronization in the measured run.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Host-controlled solver execution with measured accelerator offloads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An accelerator-backed execution is a sequence of host operations, transfers, kernel launches, and synchronization events acting on joint state \((h_t,d_t)\). A kernel \(K_t\) may consume accelerator-resident inputs only after their producing transfers or kernels complete under the declared device ordering semantics; host-visible outputs may be used only after required synchronization. The measured interval includes all transfers, compilation or warm-up designated by the protocol, kernel execution, synchronization, and fallback computation. The report specifies accelerator model and count, host resources, numerical mode, memory limits, and whether operations are deterministic. Output feasibility and objective evaluation use the same benchmark contract as nonaccelerated executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerator-backed execution measures the complete host-device workflow, respects device dependencies, and reports hardware, numerical mode, memory, determinism, and common output validity.
knowledge_statements.title: Accelerator-Backed Execution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No accelerator-benchmarking source is cited. Inclusion of compilation, warm-up, transfers, fallback work, and synchronization depends on the benchmark protocol and cannot be established from standard-field rationale alone.

children.title: Asynchronous Execution
children.top_down_role: Execution with independently progressing workers, delayed communication, or relaxed synchronization.

assumptions_latex: Concurrent tasks generate events subject to a dependency partial order \(\prec\).
The runtime may schedule any currently enabled event and need not reproduce a fixed total order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Asynchronous execution permits every dependency-respecting interleaving and therefore may expose schedule-dependent states or outputs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency-respecting execution without globally synchronized rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\prec)\) be the finite event poset of one run. An asynchronous runtime may realize any linear extension \(\sigma\) of \(\prec\): whenever \(e\prec f\), event \(e\) precedes \(f\) in \(\sigma\), while incomparable events may occur in either order or overlap. Workers progress without a mandatory global barrier between successive updates. If every pair of incomparable state transformations commutes on every reachable state, then all admissible linear extensions yield the same final state. Without this commutativity, or an equivalent confluence property, asynchronous execution can produce schedule-dependent intermediate states, termination times, or outputs even from identical inputs and configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asynchronous runtimes may realize any dependency-respecting event order; schedule independence follows from commutation or confluence, but otherwise states, time, or output may vary.
knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Execution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No asynchronous-execution source is supplied. The leaf is primarily given a definition although marked as a property, and a linear extension represents a total ordering rather than overlapping events. The stated commutativity condition and its claimed consequences also require a precise operational model and citation.

children.title: Nondeterministic Execution Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Run-to-run variation in schedules, search trajectories, output choices, plus measured performance.

assumptions_latex: A fixed instance, solver build, configuration, input state, and execution environment are specified.
The execution architecture permits at least one uncontrolled scheduling, ordering, random, or hardware-dependent choice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated executions may produce distinct elements of \(\mathcal{O}\), even when every outcome satisfies the solver's correctness specification.

notation.meaning: Set of observable execution outcomes, including solution, trace, counters, and runtime.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses empirical execution nondeterminism or its observability semantics.
Terminology and observable-outcome boundary require an algorithm-engineering source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines operational nondeterminism by observable variation across nominally identical solver executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For repeated executions indexed by \(r\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(O_r\in\mathcal{O}\) contain all benchmark-visible outputs. The execution has nondeterministic outcomes when there exist admissible executions \(r\neq s\) with identical recorded inputs and controls but \(O_r\neq O_s\). The difference may occur in the returned optimum representative, search trajectory, event counts, timing, or termination state. Nondeterminism does not itself imply incorrectness: every returned solution may still satisfy the same feasibility and optimality requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Execution outcomes are nondeterministic when identical recorded inputs and controls can yield different benchmark-visible solutions, traces, counts, timings, or termination states without necessarily violating correctness.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondeterministic Execution Outcomes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but no cited source supports the proposed observable-outcome boundary or the listed manifestations of execution nondeterminism.

children.title: Reproducibility Controls
children.top_down_role: Controls for repeatable experiments, trace comparison, schedule capture, plus result auditing.

assumptions_latex: All benchmark-relevant inputs and environmental controls can be recorded or fixed.
The solver exposes seeds and deterministic modes for every controllable randomized or concurrent subsystem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the control record is complete and the platform honors it, executions sharing \(C\) are expected to produce the same designated observables.

notation.meaning: Designated observable projection of execution r.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifies solver reproducibility controls.
The strength of cross-platform reproducibility requires source review.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a controlled-execution condition for reproducing designated benchmark observables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reproducibility control record \(C\) consists of the instance and preprocessing data, executable and library versions, parameter values, random seeds, thread count, scheduling or deterministic-mode settings, numerical environment, hardware identifier, and stopping rule relevant to the experiment. For a declared observable projection \(\pi\), the controls are sufficient when any two compliant executions \(r,s\) using the same \(C\) satisfy \(\pi(O_r)=\pi(O_s)\). The declaration must distinguish exact trace reproducibility from equality only of objective value or solution status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Controls are sufficient when their complete recorded configuration makes the declared observables identical across compliant reruns, with the required reproducibility level stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Reproducibility Controls

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but the completeness of the control record and the claimed reproducibility implication depend on platform and solver semantics for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Event Counters
children.top_down_role: Counters for state transitions, triggers, exceptions, callbacks, plus lifecycle events.

assumptions_latex: The solver defines a finite set \(E\) of named event types.
Every occurrence has an unambiguous attribution scope and counting rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(e\in E\), the counter equals the cardinality of the recorded occurrences of \(e\) in the selected scope.

notation.meaning: Finite set of instrumented event types.
Number of occurrences of event e in scope S.

review_flags: No supplied source defines event-counter semantics for solver instrumentation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines counters for discrete, semantically named solver events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an event type \(e\in E\) and execution scope \(S\), let \(I_e(S)\) be the finite multiset of instrumented occurrences classified as \(e\). The event counter is \(N_e(S)=|I_e(S)|\), initialized to zero and incremented exactly once for each qualifying occurrence. Its specification must state the event predicate, attribution scope, treatment of retries and nested events, and whether suppressed, failed, or speculative occurrences are included. Examples include incumbent updates, node expansions, cuts accepted, and restarts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An event counter records how many qualifying occurrences of a named solver event happen within a declared scope under an explicit inclusion rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Event Counters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit Event Counters, but the once-per-occurrence, retry, nesting, and speculative-event conventions lack supporting instrumentation evidence.

children.title: Operation Counters
children.top_down_role: Counters for solver primitives, data-structure operations, oracle calls, plus numerical work.

assumptions_latex: The solver defines instrumented primitive or composite operation classes \(Q\).
Each executed operation has a declared multiplicity and attribution scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operation counter is the sum of declared multiplicities over all executions of the selected operation class.

notation.meaning: Multiplicity assigned to executed operation j of class q.
Weighted count of operations of class q in scope S.

review_flags: No supplied source defines operation-counter granularity or weighting conventions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines weighted counts of declared computational operations performed by a solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For operation class \(q\in Q\) and execution scope \(S\), enumerate its instrumented executions by \(j\in J_q(S)\). Given a declared nonnegative multiplicity \(w_{q,j}\), the operation counter is \(M_q(S)=\sum_{j\in J_q(S)}w_{q,j}\). Unit multiplicity counts invocations; other choices may count processed elements, arithmetic operations, comparisons, or oracle calls. The counter specification must fix the operation boundary, multiplicity rule, handling of vectorized or batched work, and inclusion of failed or repeated work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operation counter sums declared multiplicities over executions of a specified computational operation, with batching, retries, and operation boundaries fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.title: Operation Counters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-counter definition fits the leaf, but operation granularity, multiplicities, batching, and repeated-work conventions are methodology choices unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Counter Aggregation Semantics
children.top_down_role: Scoping, nesting, thread aggregation, reset behavior, plus cross-run comparability.

assumptions_latex: Counters use identical event or operation definitions across the scopes being combined.
The scopes form either disjoint partitions or explicitly overlapping collections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Additive aggregation is valid on disjoint scopes; overlapping scopes require deduplication or an explicitly nonexclusive interpretation.

notation.meaning: Counter value on execution scope S.

review_flags: No supplied source specifies aggregation semantics for hierarchical or concurrent solver counters.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when solver counters may be summed across runs, threads, phases, or components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A counter \(C\) has additive aggregation semantics when, for every finite family of pairwise disjoint scopes \((S_i)_{i=1}^k\), \(C(\biguplus_{i=1}^k S_i)=\sum_{i=1}^k C(S_i)\). If scopes overlap, direct summation double-counts occurrences in their intersections unless occurrences carry unique identities and are deduplicated. Aggregation across repeated runs must retain the run count and use a declared statistic, such as sum, mean, median, or empirical distribution; such summaries are not interchangeable with within-run additive totals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counters add exactly across disjoint scopes. Overlapping scopes need deduplication, while repeated-run aggregation must name the summary statistic and retain the number of runs.
knowledge_statements.title: Counter Aggregation Semantics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive statement is mathematically coherent and property is an appropriate kind, but its application to hierarchical, concurrent, and repeated-run solver counters requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Solver-Phase Timing
children.top_down_role: Timing organized by preprocessing, initialization, search, refinement, certification, or cleanup phases.

assumptions_latex: The execution is partitioned into declared solver phases \(P\).
Each timed interval has a monotone clock and a phase attribution rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Phase time is the measure of intervals attributed to that phase; phase totals equal total attributed time only under exclusive exhaustive attribution.

notation.meaning: Union of intervals attributed to phase p.
Measured duration of a set of intervals.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses solver-phase timing or concurrent attribution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines timing attributed to coarse sequential or concurrent solver phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each declared phase \(p\in P\), let \(I_p\) be the union of measured execution intervals attributed to \(p\), and define \(T_p=\mu(I_p)\). The timing specification must identify the clock, thread or process scope, nesting policy, and treatment of blocked or asynchronous work. If the sets \(I_p\) are pairwise disjoint and cover the measured execution interval \(I\), then \(\sum_{p\in P}T_p=\mu(I)\). With concurrent or overlapping phases, the sum may exceed wall-clock duration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver-phase timing measures intervals attributed to each declared phase; phase totals match elapsed time only when attribution is exclusive and exhaustive.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Phase Timing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Solver-Phase Timing, but the interval-measure model and its treatment of clocks, blocking, concurrency, and asynchronous work are not supported by a cited specification.

children.title: Solver-Component Timing
children.top_down_role: Timing organized by modules, data structures, numerical kernels, plus external services.

assumptions_latex: The solver defines a finite component set \(K\).
Every measured activation has a component attribution and nesting convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each component receives inclusive or exclusive duration according to the declared convention; the two forms generally differ for nested calls.

notation.meaning: Finite set of instrumented solver components.
Activation intervals attributed to component k.

review_flags: No supplied locator defines component timing, nesting, or concurrency conventions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines timing attributed to instrumented solver modules or routines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For component \(k\in K\), let \(A_k\) be its activation intervals. Inclusive time is \(T_k^{\mathrm{inc}}=\sum_{J\in A_k}\mu(J)\). Exclusive time is the measure of portions of those intervals during which no timed descendant component is active. The profile must declare whether concurrent activations are accumulated as thread time or merged as wall-clock intervals, and whether waiting, runtime services, and instrumentation are attributed to \(k\). Inclusive component times are not generally additive because nested activation intervals overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component timing assigns inclusive or exclusive duration to solver modules, with nesting, concurrency, waiting, and instrumentation handled by a declared convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Component Timing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusive/exclusive timing distinction fits the leaf, but the activation, descendant, concurrency, waiting, and instrumentation conventions lack source support.

children.title: Timing Attribution Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Overlapping work, nested scopes, asynchronous activity, plus unattributed runtime.

assumptions_latex: Every timed interval has labeled start and end boundaries.
Boundary events are consistently ordered within each clock domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid attribution policy assigns every measured interval according to explicit ownership, nesting, concurrency, and transition rules.

notation.meaning: Attribution label assigned to time t.

review_flags: No supplied source establishes attribution-boundary conventions.
Clock-domain and asynchronous-boundary semantics require authoritative specification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the boundary rules needed for unambiguous timing ownership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=(b_0<\cdots<b_m)\) be ordered timing boundaries within one clock domain. A timing attribution policy is well-defined when it assigns a constant label \(a(t)\) on every half-open interval \([b_i,b_{i+1})\), specifies ownership at phase and component transitions, resolves nesting as inclusive or exclusive, and states how asynchronous work and distinct clock domains are treated. Exclusive exhaustive attribution additionally requires exactly one owner for almost every measured instant; inclusive attribution may assign multiple owners but must report that overlap explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Timing boundaries are valid when every interval receives ownership under explicit transition, nesting, concurrency, and clock-domain rules, with overlap disclosed whenever attribution is inclusive.
knowledge_statements.title: Timing Attribution Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is locally appropriate and internally consistent, but ownership at asynchronous transitions and across clock domains requires an authoritative timing specification.

children.title: Memory-Usage Tracing
children.top_down_role: Resident footprint, working-set evolution, object retention, plus memory-pressure episodes.

assumptions_latex: Memory observations share a declared address-space and allocator scope.
Allocation and release events are timestamped or sampled against a monotone execution coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trace represents current and peak measured memory within the declared scope, subject to its stated sampling and accounting rules.

notation.meaning: Measured live memory at execution coordinate t.
Signed memory-size change at event i.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifies memory-tracing accounting or sampling semantics.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents live and peak memory from scoped allocation changes or samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a complete event trace with initial measured usage \(M_0\) and signed size changes \(\Delta_i\) at coordinates \(t_i\), live measured memory is represented by \(M(t)=M_0+\sum_{i:t_i\le t}\Delta_i\), and peak usage by \(M_{\max}=\sup_t M(t)\). A sampled trace instead records estimates \(\widehat M(t_j)\) and need not capture the true peak. The trace specification must identify logical requested bytes versus allocator-resident or process-resident bytes, address-space scope, sampling frequency, and treatment of shared memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory tracing represents live and peak usage from allocation changes or samples, with byte metric, process scope, shared memory, and sampling limitations declared.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Usage Tracing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate kind, but the live-memory recurrence, peak interpretation, allocator-versus-resident accounting, and sampling limitations require a cited tracing specification.

children.title: Allocation-Activity Tracing
children.top_down_role: Allocation frequency, object sizes, allocator sources, lifetimes, plus deallocation activity.

assumptions_latex: Allocation events expose a time, operation kind, requested size, and scope identifier.
Object identities are available whenever lifetime reconstruction is claimed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trace determines activity totals and, with matched identities, object lifetimes under the declared allocation semantics.

notation.meaning: Requested size attached to event i.

review_flags: No supplied locator defines allocation-event schemas or lifetime matching.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines event-level tracing of allocation, reallocation, and release activity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An allocation-activity trace is an ordered sequence \(\mathcal{A}=((t_i,q_i,s_i,u_i))_{i=1}^n\), where \(t_i\) is an execution coordinate, \(q_i\) identifies allocation, reallocation, or release, \(s_i\ge0\) is the declared byte quantity, and \(u_i\) is a scope or object identifier. Counts and requested-byte totals are obtained by filtering and summing the corresponding events. Lifetime reconstruction additionally requires that allocation and release records be matched by stable object identity and that reallocations have an explicit replacement convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocation-activity tracing records ordered allocation, reallocation, and release events; stable object identities are additionally required to reconstruct lifetimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Allocation-Activity Tracing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Allocation-Activity Tracing, but the proposed event schema, byte semantics, identity matching, and reallocation convention have no supporting source.

children.title: Tracing Overhead Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sampling, full tracing, concurrency, plus workload regimes that affect measurement distortion.

assumptions_latex: The untraced and traced executions use the same instance, solver controls, and resource limits.
Runtime and trace volume are measured using declared clocks and storage units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tracing is negligible, bounded, or intrusive only relative to declared overhead thresholds; intrusive tracing may invalidate direct performance comparison.
review_flags: No supplied source provides standard tracing-overhead regime thresholds.
Regime boundaries are policy-dependent and require benchmark-methodology evidence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when tracing perturbation becomes material to benchmark interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_0>0\) and \(T_1\) be comparable runtimes without and with tracing, and define \(\rho_T=(T_1-T_0)/T_0\). Let \(V\) be trace volume and \(N\) the number of recorded events, with \(\rho_V=V/N\) when \(N>0\). Given preregistered thresholds \(0\le\varepsilon<\delta\), runtime overhead is negligible when \(|\rho_T|\le\varepsilon\), bounded when \(\varepsilon<|\rho_T|\le\delta\), and intrusive when \(|\rho_T|>\delta\). Any change in solver outcome, timeout status, or memory exhaustion also makes tracing intrusive regardless of \(\rho_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tracing regimes compare instrumented and baseline executions using declared thresholds; changed outcomes, timeouts, or memory exhaustion make tracing intrusive regardless of measured runtime overhead.
knowledge_statements.title: Tracing Overhead Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas are coherent, but the negligible, bounded, and intrusive regimes are policy-defined and unsourced. The leaf describes all overhead regimes, so failure_boundary may be too narrow unless the intended terminal role specifically emphasizes invalidating perturbation.

assumptions_latex: The processor exposes a finite event set \(H\) with documented counting semantics.
Measurements specify process, thread, privilege, sampling, and multiplexing scopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile reports raw or scaled event counts together with enough metadata to determine their measurement scope and comparability.

notation.meaning: Raw observed count for hardware event h.
Enabled and running measurement times for event h.

review_flags: No supplied locator covers hardware performance counters.
Scaling, sampling, and cross-platform comparability require architecture-specific sources.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines scoped profiling from processor performance-monitoring events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hardware-counter profile selects events \(H\) and records, for each \(h\in H\), a raw count \(R_h\) over a declared execution scope. If counters are multiplexed and \(0<U_h\le E_h\), a conventional scaled estimate is \(\widehat R_h=R_hE_h/U_h\), where \(E_h\) and \(U_h\) are enabled and running times. The profile must retain event encodings, processor model, counting domain, sampling or counting mode, multiplexing data, and attribution scope. Counts with different encodings or unsupported scaling assumptions are not directly comparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardware-counter profiling records scoped processor-event counts and metadata; multiplexed estimates require enabled and running times, and differing event encodings are not directly comparable.
knowledge_statements.title: Hardware-Counter Profiling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Hardware-Counter Profiling, but multiplexing scaling, event encodings, attribution scope, and comparability are architecture-specific claims requiring authoritative documentation.

children.title: Solver-State Logging
children.top_down_role: Snapshots or changes involving incumbent state, bounds, queues, bases, partitions, plus internal status.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver-State Logging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reproducible snapshots of internal solver state during benchmark runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a solver run on instance \(I\), solver-state logging is a finite sequence \(L=((t_k,s_k))_{k=0}^{m}\), where \(0=t_0<\cdots<t_m\), each \(t_k\) is measured in a declared run clock, and each state record \(s_k\) has a fixed schema. The schema identifies every recorded field and may include the incumbent value, valid bound, queue size, iteration count, memory use, and termination status. Each field must be either measured at \(t_k\) or explicitly marked unavailable; records must not depend on nondeterministic formatting. The logging interface includes the clock definition, schema version, sampling rule, and run identifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solver-state logging records timestamped, schema-defined snapshots of internal algorithmic state, together with the clock, sampling rule, schema version, and run identity.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a fixed benchmark instance and the solver execution has a unique run identifier.
The run clock and sampling rule are declared before measurements are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=((t_k,s_k))_{k=0}^{m}\) is a reproducible, schema-defined state trace.

notation.meaning: declared run-clock value of snapshot k

review_flags: benchmark instrumentation definition lacks an authoritative supplied source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but its reproducibility requirements, mandatory metadata, and sampling conventions are unsupported benchmark-methodology claims.

children.title: Progress Logging
children.top_down_role: Milestones, elapsed resources, objective movement, work completed, plus termination progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Progress Logging
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines objective-and-bound traces used to compare optimization progress over time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization run, a progress log is a time-ordered sequence \(P=((t_k,u_k,\ell_k))_{k=0}^{m}\), where \(u_k\) is the best feasible objective value known by time \(t_k\), \(\ell_k\) is a valid lower bound known by that time, and missing values are represented explicitly. Validity requires \(u_{k+1}\le u_k\), \(\ell_{k+1}\ge \ell_k\), and \(\ell_k\le u_k\) whenever both values are finite. For maximization, the inequalities are reversed. The log declares whether timestamps denote discovery, validation, or emission time and records a final entry at termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A progress log is a timestamped trace of incumbent values and valid bounds, with monotonicity, missing-value, timestamp, and termination conventions declared.
assumptions_latex: Every reported incumbent is feasible and every reported bound is valid for the benchmark instance.
All entries use the same objective orientation and declared clock.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For minimization, \(u_{k+1}\le u_k\), \(\ell_{k+1}\ge \ell_k\), and \(\ell_k\le u_k\) whenever defined.

notation.meaning: incumbent objective value at time k
valid lower bound at time k

review_flags: benchmark progress-log convention lacks an authoritative supplied source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf and definition role fit, but the proposed timestamp, termination, monotonicity, and missing-value conventions require an authoritative source.

children.title: Log Volume Control
children.top_down_role: Sampling, filtering, compression, retention, plus verbosity choices for solver logs.

knowledge_statements.title: Log Volume Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a bounded-overhead admissibility condition for benchmark logging policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=(e_1,\ldots,e_N)\) be the ordered stream of loggable solver events. A log-volume policy \(\pi\) is admissible for limits \((R,B,\delta)\) if it emits a subsequence \(L_\pi(E)\) containing every mandatory event, including initialization, incumbent improvement, and termination, while satisfying \(|L_\pi(E)|\le R\), encoded size \(\operatorname{bytes}(L_\pi(E))\le B\), and logging time \(T_\pi\le\delta T_0\). Here \(T_0\) is the runtime under the declared uninstrumented or minimally instrumented baseline. The policy, limits, encoding, buffering behavior, and treatment of truncated logs must be fixed before comparing solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A volume-control policy preserves mandatory events while respecting declared record, byte, and runtime-overhead budgets under a fixed encoding and baseline.
assumptions_latex: \(R,B\ge 0\) and \(\delta\ge 0\) are fixed before the benchmark run.
Mandatory event types and the runtime baseline are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|L_\pi(E)|\le R\), \(\operatorname{bytes}(L_\pi(E))\le B\), and \(T_\pi\le\delta T_0\), with all mandatory events retained.
review_flags: the precise benchmark overhead convention requires a source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but the mandatory-event set and the interpretation of logging time as relative overhead are methodology choices requiring support.

children.title: Single-Source Instances
children.top_down_role: Instances centered on distances or routes from one source to a broad destination set.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Source Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines shortest-path benchmarks requiring distances from one source to every vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-source shortest-path instance is a tuple \((G,w,s)\), where \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph, \(w:A\to\mathbb{R}\) assigns arc lengths, and \(s\in V\) is the designated source. Its required output is the distance map \(d_s:V\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), defined by \(d_s(v)=\inf\{w(P):P\text{ is an }s\text{-}v\text{ directed path}\}\), together with an optional predecessor representation of shortest paths. The value is \(+\infty\) when \(v\) is unreachable. The instance is well posed when no negative-length directed cycle is reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-source instance requests the shortest-path distance from one designated source to every vertex, using infinity for unreachable vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
No negative-length directed cycle is reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The requested output is \(d_s(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: sum of arc lengths along path P
shortest-path distance from s to v

children.title: Point-to-Point Instances
children.top_down_role: Instances centered on a specified source-target query.

knowledge_statements.title: Point-to-Point Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines shortest-path benchmarks with one designated source-target query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point-to-point shortest-path instance is a tuple \((G,w,s,t)\), where \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph, \(w:A\to\mathbb{R}\) assigns arc lengths, and \(s,t\in V\) are designated terminals. Its required output is \(d(s,t)=\inf\{w(P):P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ directed path}\}\), optionally accompanied by a path attaining this value. If no such path exists, \(d(s,t)=+\infty\). The instance is well posed when no negative-length directed cycle lies on any directed walk from \(s\) to \(t\). Benchmark timing must state whether preprocessing is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point-to-point instance requests the shortest distance, and optionally a shortest path, between one designated source and target.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
No negative-length directed cycle can occur on an \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk.

children.title: Query-Reuse Regimes
children.top_down_role: One-shot, repeated-source, repeated-target, plus batched-query benchmark settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Query-Reuse Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies shortest-path workloads by reuse of graph data and query terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed weighted graph \((G,w)\), a query-reuse regime is a finite ordered workload \(Q=((s_i,t_i))_{i=1}^{q}\) together with a declaration of which state may persist between queries. The regime is cold if no query-derived state persists; graph-reuse if graph-dependent preprocessing may persist but terminal-dependent state may not; source-reuse if consecutive queries sharing \(s_i\) may reuse source-dependent state; and warm if all explicitly declared state may persist. Reported cost must separate one-time preprocessing \(T_{\mathrm{pre}}\) from query costs \(T_i\), with amortized cost \((T_{\mathrm{pre}}+\sum_{i=1}^{q}T_i)/q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A query-reuse regime declares the query sequence, permitted persistent state, and separation of preprocessing, per-query, and amortized costs.
assumptions_latex: All queries use the same declared weighted graph \((G,w)\).
The permitted persistent state is fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The amortized time is \((T_{\mathrm{pre}}+\sum_{i=1}^{q}T_i)/q\) under the declared persistence rule.
review_flags: reuse-regime terminology and cost-accounting convention require benchmark-methodology support

children.title: All-Pairs Instances

knowledge_statements.title: All-Pairs Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines shortest-path benchmarks requiring distances for every ordered vertex pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An all-pairs shortest-path instance is a pair \((G,w)\), where \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph and \(w:A\to\mathbb{R}\) assigns arc lengths. Its required output is the matrix \(D\in(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\})^{V\times V}\) with \(D_{uv}=\inf\{w(P):P\text{ is a directed }u\text{-}v\text{ path}\}\). Set \(D_{uv}=+\infty\) if \(v\) is unreachable from \(u\), and \(D_{uu}=0\) when the empty path is optimal. Finite-valued well-posedness requires that \(G\) contain no negative-length directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An all-pairs instance requests a complete matrix of shortest-path distances between every ordered pair of vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(G\) contains no negative-length directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output satisfies \(D_{uv}=d(u,v)\) for every \((u,v)\in V\times V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Terminal Instances

The benchmark specification must distinguish terminal-set input from any algorithmically chosen auxiliary landmarks.

No negative-length directed cycle affects a requested pair.

children.title: Terminal-Coverage Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Coverage Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how densely a workload covers possible ordered terminal pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given nonempty terminal sets \(S,T\subseteq V\) and requested pairs \(Q\subseteq S\times T\), the terminal-coverage ratio is \(\rho(Q)=|Q|/(|S||T|)\). A coverage regime is the pair consisting of this ratio and a declared sampling rule for \(Q\). It is complete when \(Q=S\times T\), source-complete when each \(s\in S\) is paired with every \(t\in T\), and sampled when \(Q\) is generated by a specified deterministic or probabilistic design. For probabilistic designs, the distribution, seed policy, and treatment of duplicate pairs are part of the regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal-coverage regime specifies the fraction and sampling design of source-target terminal pairs included in a shortest-path workload.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(T\) are finite and nonempty.
\(Q\subseteq S\times T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le\rho(Q)=|Q|/(|S||T|)\le1\), with \(\rho(Q)=1\) exactly when \(Q=S\times T\).

children.title: Dijkstra Method Family
children.top_down_role: Dijkstra-style label-setting implementations across relevant graph or weight regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Dijkstra Method Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Label-setting shortest paths for finite graphs with nonnegative arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), nonnegative lengths \(w:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and source \(s\in V\). Initialize \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and settled set \(S=\varnothing\). While an unsettled vertex of finite label exists, choose \(u\in V\setminus S\) minimizing \(d(u)\), insert \(u\) into \(S\), and for every arc \((u,v)\in A\) replace \(d(v)\) by \(\min\{d(v),d(u)+w(u,v)\}\), recording a predecessor after strict improvement. Stop when no finite unsettled label remains, or when a designated target is settled. Output the labels and predecessor forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dijkstra's family repeatedly settles a minimum tentative-distance vertex and relaxes its outgoing arcs; nonnegative lengths make settled labels final.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(w(a)\ge0\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(d(v)=d_G(s,v)\) for every settled vertex \(v\), and for every vertex when the full run terminates.

notation.meaning: tentative distance label of vertex v
length of arc from u to v

children.title: Heap-Based Realizations
children.top_down_role: Priority-queue realizations using binary, d-ary, pairing, Fibonacci, radix, or related heaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Heap-Based Realizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Priority-queue implementations of Dijkstra's label-setting method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Implement Dijkstra's unsettled-label selection with a min-priority queue \(H\). Initialize \(H\) with \((0,s)\). Whenever relaxing \((u,v)\) strictly decreases \(d(v)\), perform \(\operatorname{DecreaseKey}(H,v,d(v))\), or insert a new keyed copy and discard stale copies when extracted. Repeatedly extract a vertex with minimum key, skipping settled or stale entries, then relax its outgoing arcs. With a binary heap and adjacency lists, a full single-source run uses \(O((|V|+|A|)\log |V|)\) time under explicit decrease-key, or \(O((|V|+|A|)\log(|V|+|A|))\) time with duplicate entries, and \(O(|V|+|A|)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A heap realization uses a min-priority queue for Dijkstra selection, either decreasing keys or inserting duplicate entries and later skipping stale copies.
assumptions_latex: Arc lengths are nonnegative.
The graph is finite, is represented by adjacency lists, and heap operations use comparison-based binary-heap costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implementation returns Dijkstra distances in \(O((|V|+|A|)\log |V|)\) time with explicit decrease-key, or \(O((|V|+|A|)\log(|V|+|A|))\) time with duplicate entries.

children.title: Dial Method Family
children.top_down_role: Bucket-based shortest-path implementations for bounded or structured edge weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Dial Method Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bucket-based Dijkstra realization for bounded nonnegative integer arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), a source \(s\in V\), a positive integer \(C\), and integer lengths \(w:A\to\{0,1,\ldots,C\}\). Run Dijkstra's relaxation rule, but store every unsettled vertex of finite label in a bucket indexed by its integer label. Initialize \(d(s)=0\) and place \(s\) in bucket zero. Repeatedly scan bucket indices upward, extract a vertex from the first nonempty bucket, settle it, and move any unsettled vertex whose label decreases to the bucket for its new label. Since every reachable vertex has a simple shortest path of length at most \((|V|-1)C\), scanning through this index range yields \(O(|A|+|V|C)\) time and \(O(|A|+|V|C)\) storage when the graph and direct bucket array are both counted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dial's method implements Dijkstra with direct integer-indexed buckets and runs in time proportional to the arc count plus the number of vertices times the positive maximum arc length.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(s\in V\).
\(C\ge 1\) is an integer and every arc length lies in \(\{0,1,\ldots,C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm computes all distances from \(s\) in \(O(|A|+|V|C)\) time using direct distance buckets.

notation.meaning: positive integer upper bound on arc lengths

children.title: Bellman–Ford Family
children.top_down_role: Bellman–Ford implementations, scanning variants, plus workload sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Bellman–Ford Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous and early-stopping Bellman–Ford for single-source shortest paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), source \(s\), and arc lengths \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), initialize \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and predecessors undefined. For each of at most \(|V|-1\) passes, relax every arc \((u,v)\) by replacing \(d(v)\) with \(d(u)+w(u,v)\) and setting \(p(v)=u\) whenever this value is smaller; stop if a pass makes no change. If a further complete pass permits an improvement, report a negative cycle reachable from \(s\); otherwise output \(d\) and \(p\), where \(d(v)\) is the shortest-path length from \(s\) to every reachable \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly relax every arc, stopping after stabilization or detecting a reachable negative cycle through an improvement after the standard number of passes.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed.
\(w(e)\in\mathbb R\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,v)\) when no negative cycle is reachable from \(s\); otherwise an extra-pass improvement detects one.

notation.meaning: current distance label of vertex v

children.title: D'Esopo–Pape Family

knowledge_statements.title: D'Esopo–Pape Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deque-based label correction with history-dependent insertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize shortest-path labels as in Bellman–Ford and place \(s\) in a deque \(Q\). Remove the front vertex \(u\), scan every outgoing arc \((u,v)\), and perform each improving relaxation. If improved \(v\notin Q\), append \(v\) to the rear when it has never previously been removed from \(Q\), but prepend it when it has previously been removed; an already queued \(v\) is not duplicated. Continue until \(Q\) is empty. Provided no negative cycle is reachable from \(s\), the final labels are the single-source shortest-path distances; predecessor arcs define corresponding paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Improved vertices enter a deque at the rear before their first scan and at the front after they have previously been scanned.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with real arc lengths.
No negative cycle is reachable from the source \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\implies d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,v)\text{ for all }v\in V.

children.title: SLF Queue Discipline
