knowledge_statements.title: SLF Queue Discipline
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small-label-first insertion rule for a label-correcting deque.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a deque \(Q\) of vertices having improved labels but awaiting scans. When a relaxation improves \(d(v)\) and \(v\notin Q\), insert \(v\) at the front if \(Q\ne\varnothing\) and \(d(v)<d(\operatorname{front}(Q))\); otherwise insert it at the rear. Remove and scan vertices from the front, never storing two copies of a vertex. Combined with valid label-correcting relaxations, this rule changes only scan order: if the process terminates with \(Q=\varnothing\), every arc satisfies \(d(v)\le d(u)+w(u,v)\), and the labels are shortest-path distances when no reachable negative cycle exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A newly eligible vertex goes to the front when its label is smaller than the current front label; otherwise it goes to the rear.
assumptions_latex: Queue membership is updated after every improving relaxation.
No negative cycle is reachable from the source.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\implies d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,v)\text{ for every reachable }v.

children.title: LLL Queue Discipline

knowledge_statements.title: LLL Queue Discipline
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-label-last extraction rule for a label-correcting queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty queue \(Q\), compute its mean label \(\bar d_Q=|Q|^{-1}\sum_{x\in Q}d(x)\). Before scanning, while \(d(\operatorname{front}(Q))>\bar d_Q\), move the front vertex to the rear and recompute the mean if labels or membership have changed; then remove and scan the front vertex. Improving relaxations insert vertices according to the underlying label-correcting method without duplication. The rotations alter only processing order. If no negative cycle is reachable from \(s\), termination with an empty queue yields the shortest-path labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rotate a front vertex to the rear while its label exceeds the mean label of queued vertices, then scan the resulting front.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is finite and contains no duplicate vertex.
No negative cycle is reachable from the source \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\implies d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,v)\text{ for every reachable }v.

children.title: Threshold Queue Families

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Queue Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric label-correcting selection by a moving label threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a set \(Q\) of vertices awaiting scans and choose a parameter \(\theta\ge0\). At each selection, let \(m=\min_{x\in Q}d(x)\) and scan any eligible vertex \(u\in Q\) satisfying \(d(u)\le m+\theta\); improving relaxations update labels and restore improved unqueued vertices to \(Q\). A threshold implementation may partition queued vertices into eligible and deferred groups, but it must eventually select every vertex that remains queued. With this fairness condition and no reachable negative cycle, termination yields shortest-path labels. The case \(\theta=0\) restricts selection to minimum-label vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan queued vertices whose labels lie within a chosen threshold of the current minimum, while ensuring that persistently queued vertices are eventually processed.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta\ge0\) and the queue-selection rule is fair.
No negative cycle is reachable from the source.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q=\varnothing\implies d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,v)\text{ for every reachable }v.

children.title: A* Search Family
children.top_down_role: Heuristic-guided shortest-path implementations, heuristic quality regimes, plus benchmark costs.

knowledge_statements.title: A* Search Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-search A* with a consistent goal heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For source \(s\), target \(t\), and heuristic \(h:V\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), initialize \(g(s)=0\), \(g(v)=+\infty\) otherwise, and key \(f(v)=g(v)+h(v)\). Repeatedly extract an unsettled vertex of minimum \(f\), relax its outgoing arcs, and update predecessor and key values. Stop when \(t\) is extracted or the queue is empty. If \(h(t)=0\) and \(h(u)\le w(u,v)+h(v)\) for every arc, then extracted labels are final; when \(t\) is extracted, \(g(t)\) equals the shortest \(s\)-to-\(t\) path length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A* extracts the vertex minimizing known path length plus heuristic remainder; a consistent heuristic makes target extraction certify optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite with \(w(e)\ge0\).
\(h(t)=0\) and \(h(u)\le w(u,v)+h(v)\) for every \((u,v)\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\text{ extracted}\implies g(t)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,t).

notation.meaning: consistent estimate from v to the target

children.title: Bidirectional Search Family
children.top_down_role: Forward-reverse search implementations, meeting policies, plus stopping-policy variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional Search Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional Dijkstra search with a valid frontier stopping test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run Dijkstra searches simultaneously from \(s\) in \(G\) and from \(t\) in the reversed graph, maintaining labels \(d_f,d_b\), minimum unsettled keys \(k_f,k_b\), and an incumbent \(\mu\). Whenever an arc \((u,v)\) joins vertices reached from opposite directions, update \(\mu\) with \(d_f(u)+w(u,v)+d_b(v)\). Expand either frontier according to a fixed valid policy. Stop when \(k_f+k_b\ge\mu\), or when a frontier is empty. In the first case \(\mu=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,t)\); if no finite incumbent exists when a frontier empties, no \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and reverse Dijkstra searches share an incumbent path and stop when the sum of frontier lower bounds reaches that incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(w(e)\ge0\).
Both searches use exact minimum-key extraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k_f+k_b\ge\mu\implies\mu=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,t).

notation.meaning: minimum unsettled keys of the two searches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bidirectional Dijkstra formulation and frontier-bound stopping condition require an authoritative source with a specific theorem, section, or page locator; none is supplied.

children.title: Bidirectional A* Variants
children.top_down_role: Combined heuristic-guided bidirectional variants plus their implementation tradeoffs.

knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional A* Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced-potential bidirectional A* reducible to bidirectional Dijkstra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose potentials \(p_f,p_b:V\to\mathbb R\) with \(p_f(v)+p_b(v)=C\) for every \(v\). Require \(w(u,v)+p_f(v)-p_f(u)\ge0\) and \(w(u,v)+p_b(u)-p_b(v)\ge0\) for every arc \((u,v)\). Run forward and reverse Dijkstra searches using these reduced arc lengths, while evaluating incumbent complete paths in original lengths. Apply the corresponding bidirectional reduced-key lower-bound stopping test. Because every complete \(s\)-to-\(t\) path receives the same potential offset, minimizing reduced length is equivalent to minimizing original length; thus the reported incumbent is an original shortest path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced consistent forward and backward potentials turn bidirectional A* into bidirectional Dijkstra without changing the ordering of complete path lengths.
assumptions_latex: The forward and backward potentials are balanced by a vertex-independent constant.
All forward and reverse reduced arc lengths are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \arg\min_P\sum_{e\in P}w(e)=\arg\min_P\sum_{e\in P}w_p(e)\text{ over }s\text{-to-}t\text{ paths }P.

children.title: Negative-Cycle Certificates
children.top_down_role: Witness representation, extraction costs, validation coverage, plus malformed-certificate cases.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable certificate of source-reachable negative-cycle unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A negative-cycle certificate consists of a directed path \(P\) from the source \(s\) to a vertex \(v_0\), together with a directed cycle \(C=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k=v_0)\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})<0\). Verification checks adjacency of consecutive vertices, the endpoint agreement, and the displayed weight sum. Repeating \(C\) arbitrarily many times proves that every vertex reachable from \(C\) has source distance \(-\infty\); in particular, no finite shortest path exists from \(s\) to any such vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source path plus a directed cycle of negative total length certifies unboundedly decreasing walks to the cycle and all its descendants.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with real arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\leadsto C,\ \sum_{e\in C}w(e)<0,\ C\leadsto x\implies\operatorname{dist}_G(s,x)=-\infty.

notation.meaning: witness path from the source to the cycle

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The witness has the correct certificate role and states the standard reachability qualification, but the certificate and negative-unboundedness claim lack a cited source and locator.

children.title: Feasible-Potential Certificates
children.top_down_role: Potential-vector representation, validation coverage, numerical tolerance, plus malformed-certificate cases.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Potential Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-path and dual-potential certificate for finite shortest-path distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every vertex be reachable from \(s\). A proposed distance vector \(d\) is certified by \(d(s)=0\), inequalities \(d(v)\le d(u)+w(u,v)\) for all arcs \((u,v)\), and, for each \(v\ne s\), a predecessor \(p(v)\) such that repeated predecessors reach \(s\) and \(d(v)=d(p(v))+w(p(v),v)\). The inequalities make \(d(v)\) a lower bound on every \(s\)-to-\(v\) path length, while the predecessor chain realizes a path of length \(d(v)\). Hence \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_G(s,v)\) for every vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global arc inequalities give lower bounds, and tight predecessor paths attain them, jointly certifying all proposed shortest-path distances.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and every vertex is reachable from \(s\).

children.title: Certificate Outcome Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Outcome Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertexwise boundary among unreachable, finite-distance, and negative-unbounded outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph with source \(s\), each vertex \(v\) has exactly one outcome. If no directed \(s\)-to-\(v\) path exists, then \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)=+\infty\). If some negative directed cycle is reachable from \(s\) and can reach \(v\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(s,v)=-\infty\), certified by the access path, cycle, and exit path. Otherwise \(v\) has a finite shortest-path distance, certifiable by feasible arc inequalities and an attaining predecessor path on the relevant reachable subgraph. A negative cycle unreachable from \(s\), or unable to reach \(v\), does not by itself invalidate the finite outcome for \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is unreachable, negative-unbounded, or has a finite certifiable distance; only source-reachable negative cycles leading to that vertex cause unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite with real arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(s,v)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}\cup\mathbb R\text{ with the three stated cases mutually exclusive and exhaustive}.

notation.meaning: existence of a directed path from s to v
infimum of lengths of directed s-to-v walks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three vertexwise outcomes are stated with the necessary source-to-cycle-to-vertex qualification and fit a failure-boundary container, but the exhaustive classification has no supporting citation.

children.title: Source–Sink Flow Instances

knowledge_statements.title: Source–Sink Flow Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard capacitated single-source, single-sink maximum-flow instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A source–sink flow instance is a tuple \((G,u,s,t)\), where \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph, \(u:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) gives capacities, and \(s,t\in V\) are distinct terminals. A feasible flow is a function \(f:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) satisfying \(0\le f(e)\le u(e)\) and flow conservation \(\sum_{(x,v)\in E}f(x,v)=\sum_{(v,y)\in E}f(v,y)\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\). Its value is net outflow from \(s\); the maximum-flow problem maximizes this value over all feasible flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-source, single-sink flow instance specifies a capacitated directed graph and maximizes conserved feasible flow sent from the source to the sink.

\(u(e)\ge0\) for every arc and \(s\ne t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\left\{\sum_{(s,v)\in E}f(s,v)-\sum_{(v,s)\in E}f(v,s):f\text{ is feasible}\right\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Terminal Flow Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines single-commodity benchmark instances with multiple source or sink terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multi-terminal flow instance is a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), disjoint nonempty terminal sets \(S,T\subseteq V\), and a feasible flow \(f:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) satisfying \(f(e)\le u(e)\) and flow conservation on \(V\setminus(S\cup T)\). Its value is \(\sum_{s\in S}(f(\delta^+(s))-f(\delta^-(s)))\), which equals the total net inflow into \(T\). It reduces to ordinary maximum flow by adjoining a supersource connected to \(S\) and a supersink connected from \(T\), with sufficiently large or prescribed terminal-arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multi-terminal instance has several sources and sinks, conserves flow elsewhere, and can be represented as an ordinary source–sink instance using superterminals.

\(S\cap T=\varnothing\).

children.title: Terminal-Balance Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Balance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies transshipment-style benchmarks by the prescribed terminal imbalance vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be the terminal set and let \(b:K\to\mathbb{R}\) prescribe net terminal outflow, with \(b(v)=0\) for \(v\notin K\). A terminal specification is globally balanced when \(\sum_{v\in K}b(v)=0\); it is supply dominated when this sum is positive and demand dominated when it is negative. Without an external superterminal, feasibility of the conservation equations \(f(\delta^+(v))-f(\delta^-(v))=b(v)\) requires global balance. Benchmark regimes may additionally distinguish unit balance, where every nonzero \(|b(v)|=1\), from heterogeneous balance, where terminal magnitudes vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terminal regimes distinguish zero total imbalance from excess supply or demand, and unit terminal requirements from heterogeneous ones.

\(b(v)=0\) outside the terminal set \(K\).

children.title: Ford–Fulkerson Family
children.top_down_role: Augmenting-path implementations distinguished by path choice, capacity regime, plus residual representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Ford–Fulkerson Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-path schema for finite-capacity single-source maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=(V,E)\), capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), source \(s\), and sink \(t\), initialize a feasible flow \(f=0\). Form the residual network with forward residual capacity \(u(e)-f(e)\) and reverse residual capacity \(f(e)\). While an \(s\)-to-\(t\) residual path \(P\) exists, set \(\Delta=\min_{a\in P}u_f(a)\) and augment \(f\) by \(\Delta\) along \(P\), subtracting on arcs traversed in reverse. Stop when no residual \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists and output \(f\); the path-selection rule distinguishes members of the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment along any residual source–sink path by its bottleneck capacity; absence of such a path certifies maximality.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and directed.
Capacities are nonnegative; finite termination is guaranteed for integral capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the procedure terminates, its output \(f\) is a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.

notation.meaning: residual capacity of residual arc a
bottleneck residual capacity of the selected path

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), and capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), initialize the flow \(f=0\). At each iteration, run breadth-first search from \(s\) in the positive-capacity residual network of \(f\). If \(t\) is unreachable, output \(f\). Otherwise, choose an \(s\)-to-\(t\) residual path \(P\) having the minimum number of arcs, set \(\Delta=\min_{a\in P}u_f(a)\), and augment along \(P\) by \(\Delta\). Writing \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\), the algorithm performs \(O(nm)\) augmentations and, with an \(O(m)\)-time breadth-first search, runs in \(O(nm^2)\) time independently of the capacity magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a finite directed capacitated graph with a source and sink, Edmonds-Karp repeatedly augments along a residual path with the fewest arcs. It returns a maximum flow after O(nm) augmentations and O(nm²) total time.

children.title: Augmenting-Path Selection Effects
children.top_down_role: Performance consequences of path-selection policy across capacity, topology, plus degeneracy regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmenting-Path Selection Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts arbitrary, shortest, and capacity-scaled residual-path selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Ford–Fulkerson, the selected residual path can determine both termination and work. With integral capacities, every augmentation raises the flow value by at least one, giving at most \(\operatorname{val}(f^*)\) augmentations, a pseudopolynomial bound. With irrational capacities, an admissible sequence of augmenting paths can converge without attaining a maximum flow. Selecting a minimum-arc residual path yields Edmonds–Karp and the strongly polynomial bound \(O(|V||E|^2)\); selecting paths only through arcs above a decreasing residual-capacity threshold gives capacity-scaling bounds polynomial in the encoded capacity magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary path choice can be pseudopolynomial or nonterminating, while shortest-path or scaling rules provide polynomial control.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and directed.
Augmentations use residual-path bottleneck values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Path selection changes the termination guarantee and worst-case augmentation count without changing the residual optimality criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), and capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), initialize the flow \(f=0\). In each phase, compute the residual distances \(d(v)\) from \(s\) and form the level graph \(L_f\) from the positive-capacity residual arcs \((v,w)\) satisfying \(d(w)=d(v)+1\). Compute a blocking flow \(g\) in \(L_f\), meaning that every \(s\)-to-\(t\) path in \(L_f\) contains an arc saturated by \(g\), and augment \(f\) by this residual flow. Stop when \(t\) is unreachable in the residual network. The algorithm uses fewer than \(|V|\) phases, and the standard current-arc blocking-flow implementation runs in \(O(|V|^2|E|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a finite directed capacitated graph with a source and sink, Dinic repeatedly computes a blocking flow in the residual level graph. It returns a maximum flow in fewer than n phases and O(n²m) time with the standard implementation.

knowledge_statements.title: Karzanov Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preflow-based construction of blocking flows in acyclic level networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each Dinic phase, let \(L\) be the acyclic residual level graph. Initialize zero flow on \(L\), then process active internal vertices using admissible forward pushes while residual outgoing level arcs remain. When an active vertex cannot push its excess forward, return its excess through residual reverse arcs toward earlier levels; delete vertices or arcs that can no longer lie on an unsaturated \(s\)-to-\(t\) path. Continue until no internal vertex is active. The resulting feasible flow blocks every \(s\)-to-\(t\) path of \(L\); augment the original flow and rebuild the level graph until \(t\) is unreachable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karzanov constructs each blocking flow by forward preflow pushes, backward excess returns, and elimination within the acyclic level graph.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is the positive-capacity residual level graph.
Pushes respect residual capacities and level order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each completed phase supplies a blocking flow in \(L\), and repeated phases yield a maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Fujishige Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocking-flow construction through balanced augmentation in the level graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a Dinic phase, work on the acyclic residual level graph \(L	o t\). Maintain a feasible partial flow and residual capacities on \(L\). Select admissible source-to-sink chains and augment them, while balancing intermediate excess by additional admissible pushes; when a vertex cannot transmit further flow, remove the unusable incident residual structure from the current search. Continue until every residual \(s\)-to-\(t\) path in \(L\) contains a saturated arc. The phase output is therefore a blocking flow; add it to the current flow, reconstruct \(L\), and terminate when the sink has no residual level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fujishige’s family constructs a blocking flow by balanced admissible augmentations and elimination in each residual level graph.
assumptions_latex: The current level graph \(L\) is finite and acyclic.
Every augmentation and balancing push respects residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The phase output blocks all \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths in \(L\); iterated phases produce a maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), and capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), let \(n=|V|\). Initialize a preflow by setting \(h(s)=n\), setting \(h(v)=0\) for every \(v\ne s\), and saturating every arc leaving \(s\). While an active vertex \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\) with \(e(v)>0\) exists, push \(\Delta=\min\{e(v),u_f(v,w)\}\) on a positive-capacity residual arc \((v,w)\) satisfying \(h(v)=h(w)+1\). If no such arc exists, set \(h(v)=1+\min\{h(w):u_f(v,w)>0\}\). When no active internal vertex remains, output the resulting preflow, which is then a feasible maximum flow. FIFO, highest-label, and vertex-discharge selection rules define members of the family.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), a reported value \(F\in\mathbb{R}\), and a claimed flow \(f:E\to\mathbb{R}\), verify \(0\le f(e)\le u(e)\) for every \(e\in E\). For every \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\), verify \(\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}f(e)=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}f(e)\). Finally, verify that the net outflow from \(s\) and the net inflow into \(t\) both equal \(F\). knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Certificate Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation of a source-side cut and its reported capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A claimed cut certificate is a set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), together with a reported capacity \(C\). Validate terminal separation, then compute \(c(S,\bar S)=\sum_{(v,w)\in E:\,v\in S,\,w\notin S}u(v,w)\) and check \(C=c(S,\bar S)\). These checks certify an \(s\)-to-\(t\) cut of capacity \(C\), hence the upper bound \(\operatorname{val}(f)\le C\) for every feasible flow \(f\). Given a proposed flow of value \(C\), the same cut also certifies that the flow is maximum and the cut is minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check that the set separates source from sink and recompute its outgoing capacity; equality with a feasible flow value certifies both optima.

Capacities are nonnegative and exactly summable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible flow satisfies \(\operatorname{val}(f)\le c(S,\bar S)=C\); equality certifies max-flow/min-cut optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic statistics for augmenting-path maximum-flow implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f^0,\ldots,f^K\) be the feasible-flow sequence produced by an augmenting-path algorithm. At iteration \(k\), let \(P_k\) be the selected residual source–sink path and let \(\delta_k=\min_{a\in P_k}r_{f^{k-1}}(a)\). The augmentation diagnostic record is \(D_{\mathrm{aug}}=((\delta_k,|P_k|,q_k))_{k=1}^K\), where \(q_k\) is the measured work for finding and applying \(P_k\). It satisfies \(|f^k|=|f^{k-1}|+\delta_k\); hence \(\sum_{k=1}^K\delta_k=|f^K|-|f^0|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Record each augmentation’s bottleneck, path length, and measured work; the bottlenecks sum to the total increase in flow value.

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Flow Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-level diagnostics for blocking-flow maximum-flow methods.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible capacitated circulation \(x\). Construct its residual network, assigning cost \(c_a\) to each forward residual arc corresponding to an original arc \(a\), and cost \(-c_a\) to the corresponding reverse residual arc. While the residual network contains a directed cycle \(C\) with \(c(C)=\sum_{a\in C}c_a<0\), choose such a cycle, set \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}r_x(a)\), and augment \(\delta\) units around \(C\). Stop when no negative-cost residual cycle exists and output \(x\). For rational input data, exact arithmetic, and any terminating cycle-selection rule, the output is a minimum-cost feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible circulation, repeatedly augment by the bottleneck amount around a negative-cost residual cycle. When a terminating selection rule reaches a residual network with no negative-cost cycle, the current circulation is minimum-cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible capacitated circulation \(x\in\mathbb Q^A\). At each iteration, among all directed cycles \(C\) in the residual network, select one minimizing the mean residual cost \(\mu(C)=|C|^{-1}\sum_{a\in C}c_a\). If \(\mu(C)\ge 0\), stop and output \(x\). Otherwise set \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}r_x(a)\), augment \(\delta\) units around \(C\), update the residual network, and repeat. At the stopping test no negative-cost residual cycle exists, so the output circulation is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible rational circulation, repeatedly cancel a residual cycle of minimum mean cost by its bottleneck amount. When the minimum mean is nonnegative, no negative-cost residual cycle exists and the current circulation is minimum-cost.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Progress-per-work decomposition for comparing negative-cycle selection rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose cancellation iteration \(k\) selects a negative residual cycle \(C_k\), augments \(\delta_k\) units around it, and incurs measured work \(w_k>0\). The objective decrease in that iteration is exactly \(g_k=-\delta_kc(C_k)>0\). Thus the cumulative progress per unit of measured work through iteration \(K\) is \[\rho_K=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^K g_k}{\sum_{k=1}^K w_k}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^K[-\delta_kc(C_k)]}{\sum_{k=1}^K w_k}.\] Cycle-selection regimes can therefore be compared by jointly reporting cycle cost, bottleneck augmentation, and measured selection and augmentation work rather than iteration count alone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input integral balances \(b_v\), integral capacities, arc costs, and a capacity-feasible pseudoflow \(x\). For each \(v\in V\), define \(e(v)=b_v-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a\). While some vertex \(s\) has \(e(s)>0\), choose a vertex \(t\) with \(e(t)<0\), compute a minimum-cost residual path \(P\) from \(s\) to \(t\), and augment \(\delta=\min\{e(s),-e(t),\min_{a\in P}r_x(a)\}\). Stop when all excesses vanish and output \(x\). If feasible potentials are maintained so that residual reduced costs are nonnegative before every shortest-path computation, the resulting feasible transshipment is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a capacity-feasible pseudoflow, repeatedly send as much flow as possible from an excess vertex to a deficit vertex along a shortest residual path. Under an anticycling ordering, choose eligible entering and leaving arcs by their prescribed global indices, including ties among simultaneously blocking arcs. Record whether \(T_{k+1}\neq T_k\), the number of consecutive zero-augmentation pivots, and any repeated basis. The variant terminates normally only when the reduced-cost optimality condition holds; detection of a repeated ordered basis under a non-anticycling policy is reported as a cycling failure rather than as optimal termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy policies specify tie-breaking for zero-flow pivots, preserve a valid basis, count degenerate runs, and either guarantee anticycling or explicitly report repeated bases.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Handling Variants

source_witnesses.locator: 2.7 Degeneracy and Bland's Anticycling Algorithm p. 51

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but the citation covers generic simplex degeneracy rather than the bounded-variable network-simplex specialization. Source uncertainty affects the exact entering/leaving ordering and the hypotheses under which repeated bases are prevented, so the network-specific version needs an authoritative locator.

children.title: Initialization-Induced Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Interactions between starting-basis choice, early pivots, stalling, plus numerical sensitivity.

assumptions_latex: An initializer produces a feasible tree basis \((f^0,T^0)\) for a capacitated minimum-cost-flow instance.
A basic arc is degenerate when its flow equals one of its active bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Initialization-induced degeneracy is measured by \(d_0\) and by the subsequent zero-augmentation prefix under a fixed pivot and tie-breaking policy.

notation.meaning: Initial number of bound-valued basic arcs.
Length of the initial zero-augmentation pivot prefix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational metric linking initial tree construction to early degenerate network-simplex behavior.

source_refs.locator: 2.7 Degeneracy and Bland's Anticycling Algorithm p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an initial state \((f^0,T^0)\), define \(d_0=|\{e\in T^0:f_e^0=0\text{ or }f_e^0=u_e\}|\). Fix the subsequent pivot and tie-breaking policies, and let \(z_0\) be the largest integer such that the first \(z_0\) pivots all have augmentation \(\theta_k=0\). Two initialization variants exhibit different initialization-induced degeneracy when their distributions of \((d_0,z_0)\) differ on the same instance set. The metric attributes only the initial condition and early zero-augmentation behavior; it does not by itself establish a runtime ordering.

children.title: Basis-Update Variants
children.top_down_role: Representations plus maintenance strategies for basis membership, factors, pricing state, or update history.

assumptions_latex: The current network-simplex state has a feasible flow \(f\) and a spanning-tree basis \(T\).
An entering arc creates a fundamental cycle and a leaving arc is selected among the blockers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every basis-update variant must produce the same mathematical exchange \(T'=(T\cup\{e_{\mathrm{in}}\})\setminus\{e_{\mathrm{out}}\}\) and a basis consistent with the updated flow.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical interface shared by alternative data structures for executing a network-simplex basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((f,T)\), an entering arc \(e_{\mathrm{in}}\), and a selected leaving arc \(e_{\mathrm{out}}\), augment \(f\) by \(\theta\) around the fundamental cycle with signs determined by its orientation. If \(e_{\mathrm{in}}=e_{\mathrm{out}}\), retain \(T'=T\); otherwise set \(T'=(T\cup\{e_{\mathrm{in}}\})\setminus\{e_{\mathrm{out}}\}\). Recompute or incrementally update all basis-dependent quantities. Output \((f',T')\) only if \(T'\) spans \(V\), every tree arc has zero reduced cost under the stored potentials, and the stored arc states agree with their lower-bound, upper-bound, or basic status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis-update variants may use different representations but must implement the same cycle augmentation and tree exchange and return mutually consistent flow, basis, potentials, and arc states.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Update Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits basis-update variants, but no source supports the asserted update contract, particularly the \(e_{\mathrm{in}}=e_{\mathrm{out}}\) case and the required consistency conditions for bounded-arc states and potentials. These are implementation-critical mathematical semantics and require a network-simplex source.

children.title: Tree-Maintenance Variants
children.top_down_role: Representations plus maintenance strategies for spanning-tree topology, paths, depths, or subtree data.

assumptions_latex: The basis tree supports path queries, arc exchange, and node-potential or reduced-cost maintenance.
The mathematical pivot specifies one entering arc, one leaving arc, and an oriented fundamental-cycle update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A tree-maintenance variant is correct when every query and update is observationally equivalent to recomputing the new spanning tree and its derived quantities from scratch.

notation.meaning: Unique tree path between vertices v and w.
Updated basis tree after an exchange.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness contract for alternative static or dynamic representations of the network-simplex basis tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree-maintenance representation stores a spanning tree \(T\) and enough auxiliary data to return \(P_T(v,w)\), path bottlenecks, orientations, and basis-derived potentials. After exchanging \(e_{\mathrm{out}}\in T\) with \(e_{\mathrm{in}}\notin T\), it must represent \(T'=(T\cup\{e_{\mathrm{in}}\})\setminus\{e_{\mathrm{out}}\}\). For every subsequent legal query \(q\), the returned value must equal the value obtained by rebuilding \(T'\) and all auxiliary quantities exactly from the arc set. Runtime and memory may differ among variants, but this observational equivalence is invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different tree data structures are valid only when their paths, bottlenecks, orientations, and potentials match a complete rebuild after every basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Maintenance Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the exact leaf, and observational equivalence to rebuilding is a coherent correctness condition. No evidence supports the claimed common query interface or establishes that all listed basis-derived quantities are maintained by the intended variant family.

children.title: Basis–Tree Synchronization Failures
children.top_down_role: Stale state, inconsistent indices, invalid topology, plus recovery costs across coupled structures.

assumptions_latex: A pivot has declared mathematical state \((f,T,\pi)\) and an implementation-maintained tree representation \(D\).
An independent rebuild from \(T\) can evaluate paths, potentials, reduced costs, and arc statuses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any mismatch between \(D\) and the rebuilt basis state is a synchronization failure, even if the current objective value appears valid.

notation.meaning: Flow, basis tree, and node potentials.
Reduced cost computed from costs and potentials.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detectable boundary where incremental basis-tree state ceases to represent the mathematical network-simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After every pivot, rebuild auxiliary state from \((f,T)\). A basis-tree synchronization failure occurs if at least one of the following holds: the arcs represented by \(D\) differ from \(T\); \(D\) returns a path different from \(P_T(v,w)\); a stored parent, depth, orientation, or subtree value disagrees with the rebuild; some tree arc has nonzero reduced cost under stored \(\pi\); or a stored basic or bound status contradicts \(f\). Such a state invalidates subsequent pivot decisions because path bottlenecks or reduced costs may be computed for a basis other than \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization fails whenever incremental tree data disagree with an independent basis rebuild; this invalidates later paths, bottlenecks, reduced costs, or pivot choices despite a plausible objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis–Tree Synchronization Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the leaf and the checks are internally consistent. However, the record supplies no source or marked standard-field rationale for treating every listed discrepancy, including cached subtree metadata, as part of the mathematical synchronization boundary. Evidence is required for this nontrivial diagnostic specification.

children.title: Auction Families
children.top_down_role: Auction-style implementations, bidding regimes, price management, plus parallelization choices.

assumptions_latex: The problem is an integral assignment or unit-supply transportation instance with nonempty feasible set.
The accuracy parameter satisfies \(\epsilon>0\), and prices and assignments are updated using a fixed deterministic tie rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm terminates with an \(\epsilon\)-complementary-slack assignment; under the standard integral-cost threshold, that assignment is optimal.

notation.meaning: Benefit of assigning object j to bidder i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward auction family for assignment-like minimum-cost-flow subfamilies; general transshipment extensions are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize prices \(p_j\) and a partial assignment. While some bidder \(i\) is unassigned, compute \(v_i=\max_j(a_{ij}-p_j)\), choose a maximizing object \(j_i\), and let \(w_i=\max_{j\neq j_i}(a_{ij}-p_j)\). Raise \(p_{j_i}\) by \(v_i-w_i+\epsilon\), assign \(j_i\) to \(i\), and unassign its previous owner if one exists. Stop when every bidder is assigned. Output the assignment and prices; they satisfy \(a_{ij_i}-p_{j_i}\geq\max_j(a_{ij}-p_j)-\epsilon\) for every bidder \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward auction repeatedly lets an unassigned bidder raise the price of its best object beyond its second-best alternative, producing an approximately complementary assignment and prices.
knowledge_statements.title: Auction Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the auction-family leaf and the displayed update is recognizable for forward assignment auction. No source supports the termination and exact-optimality claims, the conclusion invokes an unspecified integral-cost threshold, and \(w_i=\max_{j\neq j_i}(a_{ij}-p_j)\) is undefined when a bidder has only one available object. These details require a sourced, domain-complete formulation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual objectives are nondecreasing; termination with a primal feasible flow satisfying complementary slackness certifies primal and dual optimality.

Chosen dual-feasible ascent direction and step.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a dual-feasible vector \(y^0\). Update the associated primal candidate by the family-specific augmentation or recovery rule. Stop when the candidate flow is primal feasible and complementary slackness holds with \(y^k\); output both. If no improving admissible step exists before these conditions hold, report failure rather than optimality.

children.title: Relaxation Families
children.top_down_role: Relaxation-based implementations, candidate management, scaling choices, plus benchmark regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian dual-price relaxation for bounded minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given  directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), solve \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) by relaxing \(Bx=b\). Initialize prices \(p^0\) and, at iteration \(t\), compute \[x_e^t\in\arg\min_{\ell_e\le z\le u_e}\bigl(c_e+(B^{\mathsf T}p^t)_e\bigr)z.\] Let \(g(p)=-p^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_e\min_{\ell_e\le z\le u_e}(c_e+(B^{\mathsf T}p)_e)z\). Update \(p^{t+1}=p^t+\alpha_t(Bx^t-b)\), optionally using coordinate, ascent, or scaling variants. Stop when a prescribed dual-improvement, feasibility, or iteration criterion holds; return the best dual bound and any recovered feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relax flow balance with node prices, minimize independently over arcs, update prices using balance violations, and return the best dual bound plus any recovered feasible flow.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell,u,c\in\mathbb R^E\) with \(\ell_e\le u_e\) for every arc \(e\).
\(\alpha_t>0\), with the step rule specified as part of the tested family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(p^t)\le z^*\) for every iterate whenever the primal minimum \(z^*\) is finite.

children.title: Reduced-Cost Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation coverage for reported reduced costs, residual arcs, tolerances, plus sign conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduced-cost optimality test for bounded minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) satisfy \(Bx=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), and let \(p\in\mathbb R^V\). Define \(r=c+B^{\mathsf T}p\). Validate every arc \(e\) by requiring \(r_e\ge0\) when \(x_e=\ell_e<u_e\), \(r_e=0\) when \(\ell_e<x_e<u_e\), and \(r_e\le0\) when \(x_e=u_e>\ell_e\); a fixed arc with \(\ell_e=u_e\) imposes no sign condition. If all tests hold exactly, then \(x_e\) minimizes \(r_ez\) over \([\ell_e,u_e]\) for every arc, so primal feasibility and the node-price vector jointly certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible bounded flow is optimal when each arc's reduced cost has the sign required by whether its flow is at its lower bound, interior, or upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is exactly feasible for \(Bx=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
All costs, prices, and comparisons use exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}y:By=b,\ \ell\le y\le u\}\).

children.title: Dual-Certificate Validation

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Certificate Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual objective equality certificate using the separable dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), take a primal candidate \(x\) and node prices \(p\). Compute \[g(p)=-p^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_{e\in E}\min_{\ell_e\le z\le u_e}\bigl(c_e+(B^{\mathsf T}p)_e\bigr)z.\] Validate that \(Bx=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), every displayed scalar minimum is attained by \(x_e\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=g(p)\). Then \(g(p)\) is a valid lower bound on \(P\), while \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) is a valid upper bound; equality certifies that both \(x\) and \(p\) are optimal certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate primal feasibility, independently recompute the price-based dual bound, and certify optimality when primal and dual objective values agree exactly.
assumptions_latex: The bounded minimum-cost-flow problem is feasible and has finite data.
All feasibility and objective equalities are evaluated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(p)=c^{\mathsf T}x=P\).

children.title: Numerical Certificate Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Tolerance sensitivity, overflow, rounding, inconsistent scaling, plus borderline validation outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Certificate Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based reduced-cost checks need not certify exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two parallel arcs from \(s\) to \(t\), each with capacity one, costs \(0\) and \(\delta>0\), and demand one. The flow sending one unit on the costly arc is feasible but has objective gap \(\delta\). Its exact reduced-cost optimality conditions contain a violation of magnitude \(\delta\). Consequently, any validator declaring every violation of magnitude at most \(\varepsilon\) acceptable will accept this nonoptimal flow whenever \(0<\delta\le\varepsilon\). Thus a floating-point tolerance alone yields only an approximate certificate unless accumulated residual and objective errors are bounded and translated into an explicit optimality-gap guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tolerance can hide a small reduced-cost violation: a two-parallel-arc instance may pass the numerical test while remaining nonoptimal by the hidden cost difference.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\delta\le\varepsilon\).
The validator treats reduced-cost violations of magnitude at most \(\varepsilon\) as zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x-z^*=\delta>0\) although the tolerance-based sign test accepts \(x\).

notation.meaning: Cost difference and exact optimality gap.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-parallel-arc construction establishes the stated failure mechanism

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit two-parallel-arc construction correctly demonstrates that a tolerance-based sign test can accept a nonoptimal flow. The failure-boundary content kind is appropriate, but a source is still required for the broader claim about numerical certification conventions and conversion of residual errors into optimality-gap guarantees.

children.title: Gain Network Instances
children.top_down_role: Generalized-flow benchmarks dominated by amplifying arcs or gain-oriented structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Gain Network Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-flow instances whose arc multipliers never diminish flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gain-network instance is a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with capacities \(u_e\ge0\), node balances \(b_v\), and arc multipliers \(\gamma_e\ge1\), with at least one \(\gamma_e>1\). A feasible generalized flow is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R_+^E\) satisfying \(x_e\le u_e\) and, for every node \(v\), \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e=(w,v)\in\, E}\gamma_e x_e=b_v.\] Sending \(x_e\) units on arc \(e=(v,w)\) removes \(x_e\) at \(v\) and delivers \(\gamma_e x_e\) at \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every arc weakly amplifies transmitted flow, at least one arc strictly amplifies it, and feasibility accounts for multiplied inflow at each receiving node.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and every multiplier satisfies \(\gamma_e>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_e\ge1\) for all \(e\in E\), and \(\gamma_e>1\) for some \(e\in E\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generalized-flow conservation with multiplicative arc gains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generalized-flow equations and multiplier convention are internally consistent, and definition is the appropriate content kind. However, the requirement that all multipliers be at least one with at least one strict gain is a benchmark-family boundary that needs an inspectable source.

children.title: Loss Network Instances

knowledge_statements.title: Loss Network Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-flow instances whose arc multipliers never amplify flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A loss-network instance is a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with capacities \(u_e\ge0\), node balances \(b_v\), and arc multipliers \(0<\gamma_e\le1\), with at least one \(\gamma_e<1\). A feasible generalized flow is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R_+^E\) satisfying \(x_e\le u_e\) and, for every node \(v\), \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e=(w,v)\in E}\gamma_e x_e=b_v.\] Thus transmission on every arc preserves or loses flow, and at least one arc strictly loses flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every arc preserves or diminishes transmitted flow, at least one strictly diminishes it, and node feasibility uses the diminished quantity delivered by incoming arcs.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and every multiplier satisfies \(\gamma_e>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\gamma_e\le1\) for all \(e\in E\), and \(\gamma_e<1\) for some \(e\in E\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lossy generalized-flow formulation is mathematically coherent and the definition content kind fits the instance-family container. The precise family boundary, including the strict-loss requirement, lacks an inspectable source.

children.title: Mixed Gain–Loss Networks
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks combining amplification, attenuation, cycles, plus varied gain-factor ranges.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and \(\gamma_e>0\) for every arc \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\exists e\in E:\gamma_e>1)\land(\exists f\in E:0<\gamma_f<1)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-flow instances containing both amplifying and diminishing arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed gain-loss network is a generalized-flow instance \((G,u,b,\gamma)\) with positive arc multipliers for which there exist arcs \(e,f\in E\) satisfying \(\gamma_e>1\) and \(0<\gamma_f<1\). Feasibility requires \(0\le x_e\le u_e\) and \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e=(w,v)\in E}\gamma_e x_e=b_v\qquad(v\in V).\] Arcs with \(\gamma_e=1\) may also occur. The classification is invariant under the presence of such neutral arcs but depends on the chosen arc orientations and multiplier convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed instance contains at least one amplifying arc and at least one lossy arc, while neutral arcs may also be present.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Gain–Loss Networks

assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(K\) are finite.
Each balance vector satisfies \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v^k=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R_+^{E\times K}\), with conservation per commodity and capacity coupling across commodities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous arc-flow formulation of capacitated multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fractional multicommodity-flow instance consists of a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), capacities \(u_e\ge0\), and commodities \(k\in K\) with balance vectors \(b^k\). Its feasible set contains arrays \(x=(x_e^k)\in\mathbb R_+^{E\times K}\) such that \[Bx^k=b^k\quad(k\in K),\qquad \sum_{k\in K}x_e^k\le u_e\quad(e\in E).\] No integrality restriction is imposed: each commodity may split across multiple routes. Costs, when present, are evaluated as \(\sum_{k,e}c_e^k x_e^k\), and feasibility is independent of how a fractional arc flow is decomposed into paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each commodity obeys flow conservation, all commodities share arc capacities, and real-valued flows may split a commodity among several routes.
knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Multicommodity Instances
Integral Multicommodity Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer arc-flow formulation of capacitated multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integral multicommodity-flow instance consists of a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), integral capacities \(u_e\ge0\), and commodities \(k\in K\) with integral balance vectors \(b^k\). Its feasible set contains arrays \(x=(x_e^k)\in\mathbb Z_+^{E\times K}\) satisfying \[Bx^k=b^k\quad(k\in K),\qquad \sum_{k\in K}x_e^k\le u_e\quad(e\in E).\] Integrality applies to every commodity-arc variable; it does not by itself require an unsplittable commodity, because an integer demand larger than one may be divided among several paths in integer amounts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commodity flows, capacities, and balances are integral; conservation and shared capacities hold, but integer flow may still use multiple paths.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(K\) are finite.
\(u\) and every \(b^k\) are integral, with \(\sum_v b_v^k=0\).

children.title: Decomposition Comparisons

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired empirical comparison of decomposition algorithms under a common mathematical model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_1,D_2\) solve the same instance set \(I\), using the same formulation, feasibility tolerance, objective convention, hardware, stopping rule, and resource limit. For each commonly solved instance \(i\), record runtime \(T_j(i)\), subproblem calls \(N_j(i)\), final feasible value \(U_j(i)\), and valid lower bound \(L_j(i)\). Compare performance by paired quantities such as \(\log(T_1(i)/T_2(i))\) and normalized gaps \((U_j(i)-L_j(i))/\max\{1,|U_j(i)|\}\); separately report timeouts and failures. A decomposition comparison is valid only when subproblem accuracy and bound validity are matched or explicitly stratified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare decomposition methods on identical instances and controls, using paired runtime, subproblem work, certified gaps, and separately reported failures.
assumptions_latex: Both methods use the same objective sense and instance data.
Every reported lower bound is valid for the original minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_j(i)-L_j(i)\ge0\) on every successfully certified minimization run.

notation.meaning: Feasible upper bound and valid lower bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paired-comparison requirements and certified-gap quantities are coherent, and principle is an appropriate role for this empirical comparison container.
