children.title: Relaxation Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparisons among linear, Lagrangian, surrogate, penalty, plus integrality relaxation choices.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq Q_1\cap Q_2\).
All displayed minima are finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_1\subseteq Q_2\Longrightarrow L_2\le L_1\le z^*\le U\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: feasible-set inclusion implies bound dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound dominance and computational comparison for minimization relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with feasible set \(P\) and optimum \(z^*\), let relaxations have feasible regions \(Q_1,Q_2\) with \(P\subseteq Q_j\), and let \(L_j=\min_{x\in Q_j}c^{\mathsf T}x\). Then \(L_j\le z^*\). If \(Q_1\subseteq Q_2\), relaxation \(1\) dominates relaxation \(2\) and \(L_1\ge L_2\). An empirical comparison records both strength, for example \((U-L_j)/\max\{1,|U|\}\) for a common feasible value \(U\), and the time or oracle work required to compute \(L_j\). Bound strength alone does not determine total algorithmic performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tighter feasible-region relaxation gives a no-weaker lower bound, but comparisons must report both bound strength and the work required to obtain it.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Comparisons

children.title: Decomposition–Relaxation Couplings
children.top_down_role: Performance, bound quality, coordination cost, plus recovery behavior for combined approaches.

assumptions_latex: Each commodity set \(X_k\) is nonempty and each priced subproblem has a finite minimum.
\(\alpha_t>0\), with the step and primal-recovery rules fixed by the tested method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(\lambda^t)\le z^*\) for every \(t\), where \(z^*\) is the coupled minimization optimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian decomposition of shared multicommodity capacity constraints.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.4 Decomposition of Infeasible Network Problems p. 124
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{\sum_k(c^k)^{\mathsf T}x^k:x^k\in X_k,\ \sum_kx^k\le u\}\). Initialize \(\lambda^0\ge0\). At iteration \(t\), independently compute \[x^{k,t}\in\arg\min_{x\in X_k}(c^k+\lambda^t)^{\mathsf T}x,\] giving the relaxation bound \[q(\lambda^t)=-(\lambda^t)^{\mathsf T}u+\sum_k(c^k+\lambda^t)^{\mathsf T}x^{k,t}.\] Update \[\lambda^{t+1}=\bigl[\lambda^t+\alpha_t(\sum_kx^{k,t}-u)\bigr]_+.\] Optionally recover a capacity-feasible primal flow from the subproblem solutions. Stop by a bound-gap or iteration rule and return the best dual bound and feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualize shared capacities, solve one priced flow problem per commodity, update capacity prices from violations, and retain the best bound and feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition–Relaxation Couplings

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.4 Decomposition of Infeasible Network Problems p. 124
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Random Sparse Networks
children.top_down_role: Random-network benchmarks with low edge density, varied connectivity, plus sparse local structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Sparse Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the loopless directed independent-arc model with bounded expected degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random sparse network is a loopless directed random graph \(G_n=(V_n,A_n)\) with \(V_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), in which every ordered pair \((i,j)\) with \(i\ne j\) is included in \(A_n\) independently with probability \(p_n=c/n\), where \(c>0\) is fixed independently of \(n\) and \(n\ge\max\{2,\lceil c\rceil\}\). Capacities or costs, when required by a flow benchmark, are assigned after the topology is sampled and do not alter membership in this density regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse random network independently includes each possible directed arc with probability c/n for a fixed positive c and sufficiently large n, yielding bounded expected degree and linearly many expected arcs.
assumptions_latex: The parameter \(c>0\) is fixed independently of \(n\).
The vertex count satisfies \(n\ge\max\{2,\lceil c\rceil\}\).
Arc selections are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected arc count is \(\mathbb{E}|A_n|=n(n-1)p_n=c(n-1)=\Theta(n)\), and the expected out-degree is \((n-1)p_n=c(n-1)/n=\Theta(1)\).

notation.meaning: random directed network on n labeled vertices
independent probability of including an ordered arc

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical independent-arc sparse random-network regime

children.title: Random Dense Networks
children.top_down_role: Random-network benchmarks with high edge density, broad connectivity, plus dense local structure.

assumptions_latex: The vertex count satisfies \(n\ge 2\).
Arc selections are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected arc count is \(\mathbb{E}|A_n|=n(n-1)p_n=\Theta(n^2)\), and the expected out-degree is \((n-1)p_n=\Theta(n)\).

notation.meaning: random directed network on n labeled vertices
independent probability of including an ordered arc

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical independent-arc dense random-network regime
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the loopless directed independent-arc model with density bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random dense network is a loopless directed random graph \(G_n=(V_n,A_n)\) with \(V_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), in which every ordered pair \((i,j)\) with \(i\ne j\) is included independently with probability \(p_n\). The dense regime requires a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\varepsilon\le p_n\le 1\) for every \(n\). Capacities or costs may subsequently be sampled independently or conditionally on the realized topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense random network includes every possible directed arc with probability bounded away from zero, producing linear expected degree and quadratically many arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Random Dense Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The independent-arc dense-regime definition and its asymptotic conclusions are mathematically consistent, but no inspectable citation supports the selected benchmark convention.

children.title: Density-Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Intermediate densities where storage, traversal, shortest-path, or flow behavior changes materially.

assumptions_latex: The vertex count tends to infinity.
Arc selections are mutually independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameter \(d_n=(n-1)p_n\) interpolates between vanishing, bounded, and diverging expected-degree regimes, while \(p_n\ge\varepsilon>0\) gives the dense regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: asymptotic density classification by expected degree and arc count
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies independent-arc benchmarks by asymptotic expected degree, including the sparse-to-dense crossover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For loopless directed independent-arc networks, density-transition regimes are represented by a sequence \(p_n\in[0,1]\) through \(d_n=(n-1)p_n\) and \(m_n=n(n-1)p_n\). The regimes are subcritical-density when \(d_n\to0\), bounded-degree sparse when \(d_n=\Theta(1)\), intermediate when \(d_n\to\infty\) and \(p_n\to0\), and dense when \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}p_n>0\). A benchmark sweep crosses regimes by varying \(p_n\) with \(n\) and recording the resulting \(d_n\) or \(m_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Density transitions are parameterized by expected degree: it may vanish, remain bounded, diverge while edge probability vanishes, or become linear in the dense regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Density-Transition Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas are consistent, but the named density classification, especially “subcritical-density,” requires a source establishing the intended terminology and benchmark partition.

children.title: Grid Networks
children.top_down_role: Regular lattice benchmarks with dimensional, boundary, obstacle, plus capacity variations.

knowledge_statements.title: Grid Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite rectangular grids; benchmark orientation and arc data are additional parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(d\)-dimensional rectangular grid network has vertex set \(V=\prod_{r=1}^d\{1,\ldots,k_r\}\). Distinct vertices \(x,y\in V\) are grid neighbors exactly when \(y=x+e_r\) or \(y=x-e_r\) for some \(r\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Its directed arc set \(A\) contains one or both orientations of every grid-neighbor pair and contains no other arcs. Capacities, costs, supplies, and designated terminals are benchmark attributes attached to this topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A grid network places vertices on a finite rectangular integer lattice and represents every pair of vertices differing by one in exactly one coordinate by one or both directed arcs.
assumptions_latex: The dimension satisfies \(d\ge1\).
The side lengths satisfy \(k_1,\ldots,k_d\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The underlying undirected graph has \(\prod_{r=1}^d k_r\) vertices and adjacency given exactly by unit coordinate moves.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Cartesian grid-graph definition adapted to directed flow networks

children.title: Geometric Networks
children.top_down_role: Spatially embedded benchmarks generated from proximity, distance, or geometric adjacency.

assumptions_latex: The sampled points lie in a metric space \((X,\delta)\).
The connection radius satisfies \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adjacency is determined by the geometric predicate \(\delta(x_i,x_j)\le r\), with orientation and flow data specified separately.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard radius-based geometric graph definition adapted to network benchmarks
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the radius-based geometric graph model rather than arbitrary spatial embeddings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric network is obtained from points \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X\) in a metric space \((X,\delta)\) and a radius \(r>0\). Distinct vertices \(i,j\) are adjacent exactly when \(\delta(x_i,x_j)\le r\). A directed benchmark replaces each qualifying undirected edge by either or both orientations. Arc lengths may equal \(\delta(x_i,x_j)\), while capacities and other costs may be assigned independently of the adjacency rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric network connects embedded points whose metric distance is at most a prescribed radius, then separately assigns directions, capacities, and costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record consistently defines a radius-threshold geometric network, but “geometric network” is broader in common usage. A source is needed to establish that this narrower model is the intended terminal-container sense.

children.title: Road Networks
children.top_down_role: Road-derived benchmarks with sparse connectivity, hierarchy, directionality, plus metric structure.

assumptions_latex: Every road segment has specified endpoints and permitted travel direction.
Every arc length is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting directed embedded multigraph preserves segment incidence, travel direction, and nonnegative traversal length.

notation.meaning: nonnegative arc length or travel cost

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard directed-graph representation of road-segment data
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows parallel arcs and grade-separated crossings, so planarity is not imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A road network is represented by a directed multigraph \(G=(V,A)\) embedded in a geographic space. Vertices represent junctions or segment endpoints, and each arc represents one permitted direction of travel along a road segment between its endpoints. The function \(\ell:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) assigns length or nonnegative traversal cost. Geometric crossings without a common junction need not define a shared vertex, and parallel arcs are permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A road network is a geographically embedded directed multigraph whose vertices are junctions and whose arcs are permitted travel directions with nonnegative lengths or costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Road Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directed embedded-multigraph representation is coherent and the content kind fits, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Layered Networks
children.top_down_role: Networks organized into levels with controlled interlevel or intralevel connectivity.

assumptions_latex: The layer count satisfies \(L\ge 1\).
The vertex layers are pairwise disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The layer map \(\lambda(v)=i\) for \(v\in V_i\) constrains every arc to move from a lower to a higher permitted layer.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permits specified forward layer skips; consecutive-layer networks use \(S=\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A layered network is a directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with a partition \(V=V_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_L\) and an allowed-offset set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}\) such that every arc \((u,v)\in A\) satisfies \(\lambda(v)-\lambda(u)\in S\), where \(\lambda(v)=i\) for \(v\in V_i\). Sources are ordinarily selected in \(V_0\) and sinks in \(V_L\); capacities and costs are additional arc data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered network partitions vertices into ordered layers and permits arcs only forward by specified layer offsets, commonly from each layer to the next.
knowledge_statements.title: Layered Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward-offset layered-network definition is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but the convention is unsupported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: Acyclic Networks
children.top_down_role: Directed acyclic benchmark networks with varied depth, width, plus branching structure.

assumptions_latex: The directed graph is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A directed graph is acyclic exactly when it admits a topological ordering.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the finite directed-graph characterization by topological ordering.

source_refs.locator: Section 4. Acyclic Networks p. 68

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) is acyclic when it contains no directed cycle. Equivalently, there exists a bijection \(\pi:V\to\{1,\ldots,|V|\}\) such that \(\pi(u)<\pi(v)\) for every arc \((u,v)\in A\). Such a map is a topological ordering and supplies an explicit representation of the acyclic structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite directed network is acyclic precisely when its vertices can be ordered so every arc points from an earlier vertex to a later one.
knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Networks

source_witnesses.locator: Section 4. Acyclic Networks p. 68

children.title: Layered DAG Regimes
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks combining strict layering with acyclicity across varied depth-width profiles.

assumptions_latex: The depth satisfies \(L\ge1\).
All arcs are sampled independently conditional on the layers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every sampled graph is acyclic, has expected arc count \(p\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}w_iw_{i+1}\), and varies systematically with depth, widths, and density.

notation.meaning: number of vertices in layer i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: natural parametric benchmark regime for random consecutive-layer DAGs
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a reproducible consecutive-layer random DAG benchmark family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A consecutive-layer DAG regime is parameterized by \((L,w_0,\ldots,w_L,p)\). It has disjoint layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_L\) with \(|V_i|=w_i\), and each possible arc in \(V_i\times V_{i+1}\) is included independently with probability \(p\); no other arcs occur. Thus every arc increases the layer index, and the expected number of arcs is \(p\sum_{i=0}^{L-1}w_iw_{i+1}\). Benchmark regimes vary depth \(L\), width profile \((w_i)\), and density \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered DAG benchmark varies depth, layer widths, and the probability of arcs between consecutive layers; forward-only arcs guarantee acyclicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Layered DAG Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consecutive-layer random-DAG regime and expected-arc formula are correct under the stated model, but the benchmark family has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Bipartite Networks
children.top_down_role: Two-part network benchmarks with varied partition balance, density, weights, plus capacities.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite.
The vertex classes are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every edge has one endpoint in \(U\) and one in \(W\); hence each class is an independent set.

notation.meaning: directed arc set when orientations are present

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bipartite topology; directed flow networks orient the cross-class edges.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Bipartite matchings p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bipartite network has a vertex partition \(V=U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W\) such that every undirected edge belongs to \(\{\{u,w\}:u\in U,\ w\in W\}\). In a directed bipartite network, each arc has endpoints in different classes, although either orientation may be allowed. Capacities, costs, supplies, and demands are additional data and do not affect whether the topology is bipartite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite network partitions its vertices into two classes, with every edge or arc joining vertices from different classes.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Networks

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Bipartite matchings p. 65

children.title: Transportation Networks
children.top_down_role: Supply-demand bipartite benchmarks with balanced or unbalanced node quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the balanced uncapacitated transportation representation on an allowed bipartite shipment graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A balanced transportation network has finite supply and demand vertex sets \(I\) and \(J\), allowed shipment arcs \(E\subseteq I\times J\), supplies \(a_i\ge0\) for \(i\in I\), and demands \(b_j\ge0\) for \(j\in J\), with \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). A feasible transportation flow assigns \(x_{ij}\ge0\) to each \((i,j)\in E\) such that \(\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=a_i\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=b_j\) for every \(j\in J\). Given per-unit costs \(c_{ij}\) on \(E\), the standard objective is \(\min\sum_{(i,j)\in E}c_{ij}x_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced transportation network sends supply from one finite vertex class to demand in another through allowed shipment arcs, with each supply and demand balance imposed over its incident allowed arcs.
assumptions_latex: The sets \(I\) and \(J\) are finite and disjoint.
The supplies and demands satisfy \(a_i\ge0\), \(b_j\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\).
Allowed shipment pairs form \(E\subseteq I\times J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible transportation flow satisfies \(x_{ij}\ge0\) for every \((i,j)\in E\), \(\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=a_i\) for every \(i\in I\), and \(\sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=b_j\) for every \(j\in J\).

notation.meaning: finite supply and demand vertex sets
shipment on the allowed arc from i to j
per-unit shipment cost on an allowed arc

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical balanced transportation problem as a bipartite flow network

children.title: Transportation-Specific Bipartite Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural restrictions, balance patterns, sparsity, plus cost organization distinguishing transportation cases.

assumptions_latex: The transportation network has supply class \(I\) and demand class \(J\).
Every shipment arc is oriented from \(I\) to \(J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every directed path contains at most one shipment arc, and the node-arc incidence column for \((i,j)\) has exactly one \(-1\) in row \(i\) and one \(+1\) in row \(j\).

notation.meaning: shipment arc from supply i to demand j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate incidence structure of the canonical transportation network
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the directed bipartite incidence structure distinguishing transportation networks from general bipartite digraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a transportation network with \(V=I\mathbin{\dot\cup}J\) and \(E\subseteq I\times J\), all arcs leave supply vertices and enter demand vertices. Consequently, no two shipment arcs can be consecutive on a directed path. Under the incidence convention assigning \(-1\) to an arc tail and \(+1\) to its head, the column of \(B\) for \(e=(i,j)\) has \(B_{i,e}=-1\), \(B_{j,e}=1\), and zeros in every other row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transportation arcs all run from supplies to demands, so shipment paths have one arc and each incidence column contains one negative and one positive entry.
knowledge_statements.title: Transportation-Specific Bipartite Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-length and incidence-column properties follow correctly from the stated supply-to-demand arc orientation, and property is the appropriate content kind, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: High-Diameter Networks
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks with long path structure, deep search fronts, plus delayed information propagation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite strongly connected directed graph.
Arc lengths satisfy \(\ell:E\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is high-diameter at threshold \(D_0\) exactly when \(D_\ell(G)\ge D_0\).

notation.meaning: Shortest-path distance induced by the arc lengths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a thresholded weighted-diameter benchmark class; the threshold must be fixed before comparing algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a prescribed threshold \(D_0>0\), a network instance \((G,\ell)\) is a high-diameter network when its directed weighted diameter satisfies \[D_\ell(G):=\max_{u,v\in V}d_\ell(u,v)\ge D_0,\] where \(d_\ell(u,v)\) is the minimum \(\ell\)-length of a directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) path. For a size-indexed benchmark family \(\{(G_n,\ell_n)\}\), a scale-free version requires \(D_{\ell_n}(G_n)/\min_{e\in E_n}\ell_n(e)\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network is high-diameter when its largest directed shortest-path distance exceeds a fixed threshold; a family is asymptotically high-diameter when normalized diameter diverges.
knowledge_statements.title: High-Diameter Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record combines a fixed-threshold definition with a distinct asymptotic normalized-diameter definition, while the conclusion covers only the first. No source supports either benchmark convention or its normalization.

children.title: Bottleneck Networks
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks with narrow cuts, restricted corridors, concentrated capacity, plus critical arcs.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite capacitated directed network with source \(s\) and sink \(t\).
Capacities satisfy \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and the maximum flow value \(F^*>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance has a \(\beta\)-bottleneck when some minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut contains an arc carrying at least the fraction \(\beta\) of that cut's capacity.

notation.meaning: Capacity of the directed cut induced by a source-side set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses capacity concentration on a minimum cut as the bottleneck criterion.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Network Flow Models - Examples p. 8
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\beta\in(0,1]\). A capacitated \(s\)-\(t\) network is a \(\beta\)-bottleneck network if there exists a minimum cut \(S\subset V\), with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), such that \[U(S)=F^*\quad\text{and}\quad \max_{e\in\delta^+(S)}u_e\ge\beta U(S).\] Thus at least a \(\beta\) fraction of the limiting cut capacity is concentrated on one arc. The value of \(\beta\) is part of the benchmark specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bottleneck network has a minimum source-sink cut whose capacity is substantially concentrated on one arc, according to a declared concentration threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck Networks

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Network Flow Models - Examples p. 8
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited network-flow examples may support cuts and capacities but do not specifically support defining a bottleneck network by single-arc concentration on some minimum cut. A benchmark source for this criterion is required.

children.title: Long-Corridor Bottleneck Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances combining large diameter with narrow or capacity-constrained passage structure.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite capacitated directed network with terminals \(s,t\).
Every directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path meets the designated cut \(\delta^+(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance lies in the \((L_0,\beta)\) long-corridor bottleneck regime when both \(L(S)\ge L_0\) and \(\max_{e\in\delta^+(S)}u_e\ge\beta U(S)\) hold.

notation.meaning: Minimum number of arcs needed to reach the bottleneck cut from the source

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines a long access corridor with concentrated capacity at a separating cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(L_0\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(\beta\in(0,1]\), a network is in the \((L_0,\beta)\) long-corridor bottleneck regime if there is an \(s\)-\(t\) cut \(S\) such that every \(s\)-to-\(t\) path crosses \(\delta^+(S)\), the corridor depth satisfies \(L(S)\ge L_0\), and \[\max_{e\in\delta^+(S)}u_e\ge\beta U(S).\] Both parameters must be reported, because corridor length and bottleneck concentration represent distinct geometric stresses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime combines a long route from the source to a separating cut with strong concentration of that cut's capacity on one arc.
knowledge_statements.title: Long-Corridor Bottleneck Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The corridor-depth statistic and its conjunction with cut-capacity concentration are bespoke and unsourced. The path-crossing clause is also automatic for an ordinary source-side s-t cut and does not independently characterize a corridor.

children.title: Degenerate Network Instances
children.top_down_role: Network instances featuring ties, redundant structure, or nonunique intermediate choices.

assumptions_latex: A feasible minimum-cost-flow instance is represented in network-simplex form.
\(T\) is a feasible spanning-tree basis with basic flow \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis \(T\) is degenerate exactly when some basic arc is at a capacity bound.

notation.meaning: Tree arcs defining the current network-simplex basis
Flow and upper capacity on arc e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses basis degeneracy for capacitated network simplex, not merely nonuniqueness of an optimal flow.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232
2.7 Degeneracy and Bland's Anticycling Algorithm p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible network-simplex basis \(T\) is degenerate when at least one basic tree arc is at a bound, namely \[d(T):=\left|\{e\in T:x_e=0\text{ or }x_e=u_e\}\right|>0.\] A network instance is degenerate relative to this representation if it admits such a feasible basis. The integer \(d(T)\) is a local degeneracy multiplicity and may vary across bases of the same instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network-simplex instance is degenerate when a feasible tree basis has at least one basic arc already at zero or at its upper capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Network Instances

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232
2.7 Degeneracy and Bland's Anticycling Algorithm p. 51

children.title: Adversarial Network Instances
children.top_down_role: Purpose-built networks that expose unfavorable algorithmic behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a fixed deterministic network-flow algorithm with operation count \(T_{\mathcal A}(I)\).
\(n(I)\) is the declared instance-size measure, and \(B(n)\) is a declared reference growth function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A family is adversarial for \(\mathcal A\) when its normalized operation count has positive asymptotic lower limit.

notation.meaning: Operation count of the fixed algorithm on an instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adversariality is explicitly relative to an algorithm, implementation model, size measure, and reference rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A size-indexed family \(\{I_n\}_{n\ge1}\) is adversarial for \(\mathcal A\) at reference rate \(B\) when \(n(I_n)\to\infty\) and \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{T_{\mathcal A}(I_n)}{B(n(I_n))}>0.\] The operation counted by \(T_{\mathcal A}\), preprocessing included or excluded, tie-breaking rule, size measure \(n\), and reference function \(B\) are part of the benchmark definition. Without these declarations, adversariality is not an intrinsic property of the network alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance family is adversarial only relative to a fixed algorithm and measurement model, when its operation count asymptotically matches a declared adverse reference rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Network Instances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is formally explicit but an arbitrary reference function B can make the classification vacuous or conventional. A source or established benchmark protocol must justify the adverse rate and measurement model.

children.title: Degeneracy-Sensitive Stress Regimes
children.top_down_role: Benchmark regimes where small structural changes amplify degeneracy effects.

assumptions_latex: \(I(\theta)\) is a controlled family of network-flow instances.
\(d(\theta)\) is a declared degeneracy statistic and \(T_{\mathcal A}(I(\theta))\) is a fixed algorithmic cost measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family is degeneracy-sensitive when unbounded degeneracy forces an unbounded normalized algorithmic cost along the controlled sequence.

notation.meaning: Algorithmic cost normalized by instance size

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes sensitivity as a controlled asymptotic response, not as degeneracy alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A controlled family \(\{I(\theta)\}\) is a degeneracy-sensitive stress regime for \(\mathcal A\) if all declared nondegeneracy covariates are held fixed or normalized, while there exists a sequence \(\theta_k\) such that \[d(\theta_k)\to\infty\quad\text{and}\quad R(\theta_k):=\frac{T_{\mathcal A}(I(\theta_k))}{n(I(\theta_k))}\to\infty.\] The basis convention defining \(d\), cost counter defining \(T_{\mathcal A}\), and controlled covariates must be included in the benchmark protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stress family is degeneracy-sensitive when increasing a declared degeneracy measure, with other factors controlled, makes normalized algorithmic work diverge.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Sensitive Stress Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The divergence condition is a bespoke empirical sensitivity definition. No source establishes the degeneracy statistic, normalization, controlled covariates, or divergence criterion as a degeneracy-sensitive stress regime.

children.title: Capacity Overflow
children.top_down_role: Capacity ranges that exceed supported arithmetic or representation limits.

assumptions_latex: Capacities are stored in a signed integer type with representable maximum \(M\).
The implementation evaluates capacity aggregates using that same type without checked widening.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any required capacity aggregate exceeding \(M\) lies beyond the implementation's exact numeric range.

notation.meaning: A set of capacities accumulated by the implementation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Addresses overflow of capacity aggregates, even when every input capacity is individually representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Capacity overflow is possible whenever the implementation must exactly evaluate an aggregate \(U(F)=\sum_{e\in F}u_e\) for which \[0\le u_e\le M\quad\text{for every }e\in F,\qquad U(F)>M.\] Although every input field is representable, evaluation in the same signed integer type cannot represent the mathematical sum. A benchmark witness must identify the overflowing expression and distinguish checked failure from wraparound, saturation, or undefined arithmetic behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity overflow occurs when an algorithm must accumulate individually valid capacities whose exact sum exceeds the largest representable integer.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Overflow

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The range argument is mathematically plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no source or explicit standard-field rationale supports the implementation arithmetic model and overflow classification.

children.title: Cost Overflow
children.top_down_role: Objective-coefficient ranges that trigger arithmetic overflow or loss of reliability.

assumptions_latex: Arc costs and flows are stored in signed integer arithmetic with range \([-M,M]\).
Cost products and sums are evaluated without a wider checked accumulator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If an objective term or required objective sum has magnitude above \(M\), exact evaluation in the chosen type is impossible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers overflow in cost-flow products and their accumulation for linear minimum-cost flow.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cost overflow is possible if a feasible flow \(x\) requires evaluation of either an arc contribution or an accumulated objective satisfying \[|c_ex_e|>M\quad\text{for some }e\in E,\qquad\text{or}\qquad \left|\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\right|>M.\] Bounds \(|c_e|\le M\) and \(|x_e|\le M\) do not prevent either failure. The benchmark must state whether multiplication, accumulation, and comparisons use the same numeric type.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cost overflow arises when a cost-flow product or the accumulated flow objective exceeds the representable range, despite individually representable inputs.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost Overflow

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited minimum-cost-flow section supports the objective expression but does not, as cited, support the bounded multiplication and accumulation failure boundary. A numeric-arithmetic source or explicit standard-field rationale is needed.

children.title: Distance Overflow
children.top_down_role: Path-label ranges that exceed finite distance representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Overflow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to shortest-path subroutines used within network-flow algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Distance overflow is possible at a relaxation of arc \((u,v)\) whenever \[0\le d(u)\le M,\qquad 0\le \ell_{uv}\le M,\qquad d(u)+\ell_{uv}>M.\] Equivalently, a reachable path whose exact length exceeds \(M\) cannot be represented by the chosen finite-distance type. If \(M\) or another in-range value is also used as infinity, the implementation additionally loses the distinction between an unreachable vertex and a reachable vertex having that label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance overflow occurs when a shortest-path relaxation adds two valid nonnegative values whose exact sum exceeds the largest finite distance representation.
assumptions_latex: Arc lengths are nonnegative integers represented in a type with maximum \(M\).
Shortest-path relaxations add labels and arc lengths in that type without checked widening.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A relaxation requiring \(d(u)+\ell_{uv}>M\) crosses the exact distance-arithmetic boundary.

notation.meaning: Tentative distance label at vertex v
Length of arc from u to v

source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models
source_refs.locator: 2.2 A Generic Shortest Path Algorithm p. 57

source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Compound Numeric Range Failures
children.top_down_role: Instances where multiple numeric ranges jointly stress implementation limits.

assumptions_latex: A network-flow implementation uses bounded numeric types for capacities, costs, flows, distances, and potentials.
Its executed arithmetic trace is interpreted over exact integers or reals for comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A compound failure occurs when the trace violates at least two declared numeric range predicates, or one mixed expression violates its range predicate.

notation.meaning: Exact arithmetic trace on instance I
Representable set for numeric channel q
Exact intermediate values in channel q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unifies simultaneous and mixed-expression range failures across numeric channels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance \(I\) causes a compound numeric range failure if either \[\left|\{q:X_q(\tau(I))\nsubseteq R_q\}\right|\ge2,\] or a single executed expression combines values from distinct channels and its exact result lies outside the expression's declared representable set. Relevant channels may include capacity, cost, flow, distance, and potential. The failure report must identify the first offending operation in \(\tau(I)\); merely having large input fields does not establish a compound failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compound range failure crosses multiple numeric channel bounds, or overflows one expression that mixes channels such as cost, flow, distance, or potential.
knowledge_statements.title: Compound Numeric Range Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-trace and numeric-channel framework is coherent but bespoke. No source supports the definition of a compound failure, particularly the alternative involving a single mixed-channel expression.

assumptions_latex: Reduced costs are computed in floating-point arithmetic as \(\widehat r_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(c_{ij}+\widehat\pi_i-\widehat\pi_j)\).
The absolute evaluation error is bounded by \(|\widehat r_{ij}-r_{ij}|\le\eta_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reduced-cost sign decision is uncertified whenever \(|\widehat r_{ij}|\le\eta_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: Exact reduced cost under exact potentials

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a local sign-instability boundary for potential-based reduced-cost tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arc \((i,j)\), suppose the implementation decides eligibility or dual feasibility from the sign of \(\widehat r_{ij}\). If \(|\widehat r_{ij}|>\eta_{ij}\), then \(r_{ij}\) has the same sign as \(\widehat r_{ij}\). If \[|\widehat r_{ij}|\le\eta_{ij},\] the error interval contains zero, so the sign of the exact reduced cost is not certified. Repeated potential updates may therefore change pivot or relaxation decisions unless the implementation uses verified bounds, exact arithmetic, or a declared tolerance rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A floating-point reduced-cost sign is unstable when its computed magnitude is no larger than its certified evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Potential Instability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local error-interval implication is mathematically sound, but the record has no source for the floating-point reduced-cost model, certified error bound, or claimed potential-update instability.

children.title: Degenerate Pivot Behavior
children.top_down_role: Benchmark cases dominated by pivots that produce little or no objective progress.

assumptions_latex: A network-simplex iteration starts from a feasible tree basis \(T\).
An entering arc creates a fundamental cycle, and the ratio test chooses augmentation \(\theta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pivot is degenerate exactly when \(\theta=0\), so the basis may change while the primal flow and objective remain unchanged.

notation.meaning: Current feasible flow and its cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-simplex characterization of a degenerate pivot and its immediate primal effect.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232
2.7 Degeneracy and Bland's Anticycling Algorithm p. 51

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a network-simplex pivot, let \(\theta\) be the maximum feasible augmentation around the fundamental cycle created by the entering arc. The pivot is degenerate precisely when \[\theta=0.\] In that case the leaving and entering arcs may produce a different tree basis \(T'\ne T\), but the primal flow satisfies \(x'=x\) and hence \(C(x')=C(x)\). Consequently, a sequence of degenerate pivots can perform basis changes without primal or objective progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network-simplex pivot is degenerate when its feasible augmentation is zero; it can change the basis without changing the flow or objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Pivot Behavior

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232
2.7 Degeneracy and Bland's Anticycling Algorithm p. 51

children.title: Algorithmic Stalling Behavior
children.top_down_role: Instances exhibiting prolonged lack of measurable solver progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Algorithmic Stalling Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition for instrumented network-simplex benchmark runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For indices \(p<q\), a network-simplex run stalls on \([p,q]\) when \(B_{k+1}\ne B_k\) for every \(k=p,\ldots,q-1\) while \(z_p=z_{p+1}=\cdots=z_q\). Its stall length is \(q-p\). A pivot with \(\theta_k=0\) is degenerate; if every pivot in the stalled interval is degenerate, the maintained basis changes while the represented primal flow and its objective value remain unchanged. A benchmark reports each stall length and the maximum stall length observed before termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stall is a consecutive interval of basis-changing pivots with constant objective value. Its length is the number of pivots in that interval; a benchmark reports the observed lengths and their maximum, and may identify stalls consisting entirely of zero-step degenerate pivots.
assumptions_latex: A network-simplex implementation records the basic feasible solution and objective value after every pivot.
Pivot arithmetic is exact, or zero step lengths are detected using a fixed declared tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recorded interval is classified as a stall.

notation.meaning: basis and objective value after pivot k
primal step length of pivot k

source_refs.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232

children.title: Cycling-Prone Pivot Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance regimes that expose repeated basis or state patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycling-Prone Pivot Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic network-simplex cycling caused by basis repetition during a constant-objective pivot sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pivot regime is cycling-prone if there exists a feasible instance and indices \(p<q\) such that \(B_p=B_q\), every pivot from \(p\) through \(q-1\) is admissible, and \(z(B_p)=z(B_{p+1})=\cdots=z(B_q)\). Because the state and deterministic pivot rule agree at \(p\) and \(q\), the subsequent basis sequence repeats with period \(q-p\). Thus termination is not guaranteed unless the rule is modified, for example by a provably anti-cycling tie-breaking scheme.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic pivot rule cycles when it revisits an identical basis under the same state-dependent rules and therefore repeats the same future basis sequence.
assumptions_latex: The pivot rule and all tie-breaking rules are deterministic functions of the current basis.
The implementation does not apply an anti-cycling perturbation or basis-history test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repeated basis initiates a nonterminating periodic pivot cycle.

notation.meaning: objective value associated with basis B

source_refs.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.6. The Network Simplex Algorithm p. 232

assumptions_latex: A generator \(G\) induces a probability distribution \(P_G\) on network-flow instances.
A target workload induces a comparison distribution \(P_*\) on the same measurable instance space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generator is biased for the stated algorithm comparison.

notation.meaning: measured resource cost of algorithm a on instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-relative bias in empirical network-flow algorithm rankings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For algorithms \(a,b\), define the expected cost difference under a distribution \(P\) by \(\Delta_P(a,b)=\mathbb{E}_{I\sim P}[T_a(I)-T_b(I)]\), whenever the expectations exist. Generator \(G\) exhibits algorithm-selection bias relative to \(P_*\) if \(\operatorname{sign}\Delta_{P_G}(a,b)\ne\operatorname{sign}\Delta_{P_*}(a,b)\) for at least one tested pair, with zero treated as a tie. The claim is meaningful only after fixing the resource metric, parameter distribution, failure handling, and target workload.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generator is algorithmically biased when its induced instance distribution reverses an algorithm ranking obtained on the declared target workload.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator-Induced Algorithm Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distribution-relative ranking-reversal definition is coherent and fits the topic, but no source supports this particular definition of generator-induced algorithm bias or its required benchmark controls.

assumptions_latex: Two encodings describe the same abstract network-flow instance and use the same arithmetic model.
The tested implementation accepts both encodings without changing the mathematical optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implementation exhibits representation-dependent performance on the instance.

notation.meaning: two equivalent encodings of abstract instance I
measured resource vector on an encoding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding sensitivity of otherwise equivalent network-flow benchmark inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(E)\) contain declared resources such as elapsed time, memory, pivot count, or cache misses. Performance is representation-dependent at \(I\) when \(E_1(I)\) and \(E_2(I)\) encode identical vertices, arcs, capacities, costs, and supplies, yet \(R(E_1(I))\ne R(E_2(I))\) beyond the benchmark's declared measurement tolerance. A representation study must vary ordering, adjacency layout, numeric type, or parallel-arc treatment while holding the abstract instance and stopping criterion fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent encodings reveal representation dependence when they produce materially different resource measurements under a fixed implementation and stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Dependent Network Performance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically coherent and locally appropriate, but the record has no source supporting its encoding-equivalence criterion, tolerance rule, or prescribed representation study controls.

children.title: Bipartite Matching Instances
children.top_down_role: Unweighted or cardinality-focused benchmark instances on bipartite graphs.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and bipartite, with vertex classes \(U\) and \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((G,M)\) supplies a bipartite-matching benchmark instance and a feasible matching.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted finite bipartite matching instances.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246
Chapter 5. Bipartite Matching p. 182

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bipartite matching instance is a finite graph \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}V,E)\) with \(E\subseteq U\times V\). A feasible matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) satisfying \(\lvert M\cap\delta(x)\rvert\le 1\) for every \(x\in U\mathbin{\dot\cup}V\). The maximum-cardinality problem asks for \(M\) maximizing \(\lvert M\rvert\). A benchmark instance records \(\lvert U\rvert\), \(\lvert V\rvert\), \(\lvert E\rvert\), and whether a matching saturating the smaller vertex class exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite matching benchmark asks for the largest set of edges sharing no endpoint and records graph size and saturation feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Matching Instances

source_witnesses.locator: Section 10.1. Bipartite Matching p. 246
Chapter 5. Bipartite Matching p. 182

children.title: Assignment Instances
children.top_down_role: Weighted one-to-one allocation benchmarks with bipartite structure.

assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph is finite and balanced, with \(U\) representing agents and \(V\) representing tasks.
Every admissible pair has a real-valued cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal assignment is a minimum-cost perfect matching.

notation.meaning: cost of assigning u to v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced linear assignment as minimum-cost perfect bipartite matching.

source_refs.locator: Section 8. The Hungarian Method for Weighted Matching p. 201
3.3 Weighted matchings of bipartite graphs p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite sets \(U,V\) with \(\lvert U\rvert=\lvert V\rvert=n\), an assignment instance consists of admissible edges \(E\subseteq U\times V\) and costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\). Its feasible solutions satisfy \(x_{uv}\in\{0,1\}\), \(\sum_{v:uv\in E}x_{uv}=1\) for every \(u\in U\), and \(\sum_{u:uv\in E}x_{uv}=1\) for every \(v\in V\). The objective is \(\min\sum_{uv\in E}c_{uv}x_{uv}\); infeasibility means that the admissible graph has no perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assignment instance seeks a minimum-cost perfect matching between equally many agents and tasks, subject to admissible-pair restrictions.
knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Instances

source_witnesses.locator: Section 8. The Hungarian Method for Weighted Matching p. 201
3.3 Weighted matchings of bipartite graphs p. 111

children.title: Rectangular Assignment Regimes
children.top_down_role: Assignment benchmarks with unequal partition sizes or optional assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Assignment Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full assignment of the smaller side in an unbalanced bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rectangular assignment instance has finite sides \(U,V\), admissible edges \(E\subseteq U\times V\), costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\), and cardinalities \(m=\lvert U\rvert\le \lvert V\rvert=n\). Feasibility requires \(x_{uv}\in\{0,1\}\), \(\sum_{v:uv\in E}x_{uv}=1\) for every \(u\in U\), and \(\sum_{u:uv\in E}x_{uv}\le 1\) for every \(v\in V\). The objective is \(\min\sum_{uv\in E}c_{uv}x_{uv}\). Equivalently, one may add \(n-m\) dummy vertices to \(U\), join every dummy vertex to every vertex of \(V\) with zero-cost edges, and solve the resulting balanced assignment instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectangular assignment injectively matches every vertex on the smaller side into the larger side while minimizing total cost; it can be reduced to a balanced assignment by adding fully adjacent zero-cost dummy vertices to the smaller side.
assumptions_latex: The finite bipartite sides have unequal sizes, with \(m=\lvert U\rvert\le \lvert V\rvert=n\).
Each admissible edge carries a real-valued cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible rectangular assignment injectively assigns every vertex of the smaller side.

source_refs.locator: Section 8. The Hungarian Method for Weighted Matching p. 201

source_witnesses.locator: Section 8. The Hungarian Method for Weighted Matching p. 201

children.title: General Graph Matching Instances
children.top_down_role: Matching benchmarks on nonbipartite graph structures.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, undirected, and may contain odd cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance asks for a maximum-cardinality matching without assuming bipartiteness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted matching instances on arbitrary finite undirected graphs.

source_refs.locator: Section 10.5. Edmonds' Matching Algorithm p. 259
Section 5. Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 193

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A general graph matching instance is a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\). A feasible solution is an edge set \(M\subseteq E\) satisfying \(\lvert M\cap\delta(v)\rvert\le 1\) for every \(v\in V\), and the cardinality objective is to maximize \(\lvert M\rvert\). Unlike a bipartite instance, \(G\) may contain odd cycles; therefore benchmark metadata should include bipartiteness, connected-component sizes, and an odd-cycle or blossom-related structural statistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general graph matching instance maximizes disjoint edges in an arbitrary undirected graph, including graphs with odd cycles.
knowledge_statements.title: General Graph Matching Instances

source_witnesses.locator: Section 10.5. Edmonds' Matching Algorithm p. 259
Section 5. Cardinality Matching Algorithm p. 193

children.title: Weighted Matching Instances
children.top_down_role: Matching benchmarks with edge weights governing solution quality.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and undirected.
Every edge has a real-valued weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is a feasible matching of maximum total edge weight.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight matching with optional nonperfect solutions.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 11. Weighted Matching p. 277
Section 11.2. Outline of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 280

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weighted matching instance is a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\). A feasible matching \(M\subseteq E\) satisfies \(\lvert M\cap\delta(v)\rvert\le 1\) for every \(v\in V\), and its value is \(w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). The maximum-weight matching problem asks for \(M\) maximizing \(w(M)\). If perfectness or maximum cardinality has priority over weight, that alternative objective convention must be declared separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted matching instance seeks a vertex-disjoint edge set of maximum total weight under an explicitly stated cardinality convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Matching Instances

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 11. Weighted Matching p. 277
Section 11.2. Outline of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 280

children.title: Weighted General Graph Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonbipartite weighted instances combining blossom structure with numerical variation.

assumptions_latex: The finite undirected graph is not required to be bipartite.
Edge weights belong to a declared numeric domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark belongs to the weighted general-graph regime.

notation.meaning: set of odd cycles of G

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted matching regimes where odd-cycle structure is algorithmically relevant.

source_refs.locator: Section 11.3. Implementation of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 283
Chapter 11. Weighted Matching p. 277

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance \((G,w)\) is in a weighted general-graph regime when \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected, \(w:E\to D\) for a declared domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), and the required output maximizes total matching weight without a bipartiteness assumption. A benchmark is odd-cycle-active when \(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{odd}}(G)\ne\varnothing\); it should separately report weight range, integrality, sign pattern, graph density, and statistics describing odd cycles or contracted blossoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime combines arbitrary undirected graph structure with edge weights and records both numeric difficulty and odd-cycle structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted General Graph Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Section 11.3. Implementation of the Weighted Matching Algorithm p. 283
Chapter 11. Weighted Matching p. 277

children.title: Factor Instances
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks centered on prescribed spanning subgraph factor structures.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and undirected.
A set of allowed degrees is specified for every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible factor is a spanning subgraph satisfying every local degree requirement.

notation.meaning: allowed degree set at vertex v
spanning subgraph induced by selected edges F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General allowed-degree factors in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A factor instance consists of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and allowed degree sets \(B(v)\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,d_G(v)\}\) for all \(v\in V\). A feasible factor is a spanning subgraph \((V,F)\), where \(F\subseteq E\), such that \(d_F(v)\in B(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). Special cases include an \(f\)-factor with \(B(v)=\{f(v)\}\) and a matching with \(B(v)=\{0,1\}\). A benchmark must state whether feasibility, maximum weight, or another objective is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor instance selects a spanning edge set whose degree at every vertex belongs to that vertex's declared allowed set.
knowledge_statements.title: Factor Instances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is a coherent definition of a general allowed-degree factor, but no factor-specific source is cited. Standard-field rationale alone cannot resolve whether this leaf intends general factors, f-factors, or another narrower benchmark family.

children.title: Degree-Constrained Instances
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks governed by vertex-specific degree restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and undirected.
Integer lower and upper degree bounds satisfy \(0\le \ell(v)\le u(v)\le d_G(v)\) for every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution is a spanning subgraph obeying all degree intervals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval-bounded degree-constrained spanning subgraph instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A degree-constrained instance is a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) together with integer functions \(\ell,u:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\). A feasible solution is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(\ell(v)\le d_F(v)\le u(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). Exact prescribed degrees arise when \(\ell(v)=u(v)\), while matching-type capacities arise when \(\ell(v)=0\) and \(u(v)=1\). Weighted variants additionally specify \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\) and optimize \(\sum_{e\in F}w(e)\) under the same constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-constrained instance selects edges so every vertex degree lies between its specified integer lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Constrained Instances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval-bounded degree formulation is mathematically coherent, but no cited source establishes this exact interpretation of the leaf or the included weighted variant. A degree-constrained-subgraph or general-factor source is required.

children.title: Irregular Degree Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances with heterogeneous or tightly restrictive degree requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Irregular Degree Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines degree-heterogeneous benchmark sequences for factor and degree-constrained matching instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph sequence \((G_n,b_n)\), where \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\) and \(b_n:V_n\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) gives factor degree requirements, define \(d_n(v)=\deg_{G_n}(v)\), \(\bar d_n=|V_n|^{-1}\sum_{v\in V_n}d_n(v)\), and \(H_n=\max_{v\in V_n}d_n(v)/\max\{1,\bar d_n\}\). The sequence is an irregular degree regime when \(|V_n|\to\infty\), \(H_n\to\infty\), and every instance admits at least one \(b_n\)-factor. A benchmark must report \(|V_n|\), \(|E_n|\), \(H_n\), and the empirical distribution of \(d_n(v)-b_n(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An irregular regime is a feasible factor-instance sequence whose maximum degree grows unboundedly relative to its average degree, with degree slack distributions reported.
assumptions_latex: \(G_n\) is a finite undirected graph and \(b_n(v)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).
Each \((G_n,b_n)\) has a \(b_n\)-factor.
\(|V_n|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_n\to\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed irregularity ratio, divergence threshold, feasibility requirement, and reporting fields form a plausible local benchmark convention, but no source supports this particular definition.

children.title: Hungarian Method Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Assignment instances selected to compare Hungarian-method implementations.

knowledge_statements.title: Hungarian Method Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies primal-dual benchmarks for square minimum-cost assignment solved by the Hungarian method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), a Hungarian-method benchmark runs a fixed implementation on the assignment problem \(\min_{\pi\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n c_{i,\pi(i)}\). Besides time and memory, it records dual-label updates, equality-graph searches, and augmentations. The output \((\pi,u,v)\) passes verification when \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\) for all \(i,j\), \(u_i+v_{\pi(i)}=c_{i,\pi(i)}\) for all \(i\), and the reported objective equals \(\sum_i u_i+\sum_j v_j\). Instances must state size, cost representation, sparsity convention, and tie-breaking policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These benchmarks measure Hungarian-method resources and verify each assignment through feasible dual labels that are tight on every selected edge.
assumptions_latex: \(C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) has finite entries.
The benchmark implementation and tie-breaking policy are fixed.

children.title: Path-Length Stress Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Length Stress Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes augmenting-path instances that force searches through paths linear in graph size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider benchmark runs on bipartite graphs \(G_n=(L_n\cup R_n,E_n)\) with a specified initial matching and deterministic augmenting-path rule. Let \(P_{n,k}\) be the path selected at augmentation \(k\), and let \(N_n=|L_n|+|R_n|\). The runs form a path-length stress regime with parameters \((\rho,\alpha)\in(0,1]^2\) when, for all sufficiently large \(n\), at least \(\alpha N_n\) augmentation steps are executed and at least \(\alpha N_n\) selected paths satisfy \(|E(P_{n,k})|\ge\rho N_n\). Initialization, adjacency ordering, and tie-breaking must remain fixed across the sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path-length stress regime forces linearly many augmentations to use alternating paths whose lengths are linear in the instance size.
assumptions_latex: \(G_n\) is finite and bipartite.
The initialization and deterministic path-selection rule are fixed.
\(N_n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl|\{k:|E(P_{n,k})|\ge\rho N_n\}\bigr|\ge\alpha N_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Edmonds Blossom Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies cardinality-matching benchmarks for implementations using blossom contraction and expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an Edmonds-blossom benchmark applies a fixed blossom implementation to compute a maximum-cardinality matching. Each run records alternating-forest growth, examined edges, detected blossoms, blossom contractions, blossom expansions, augmentations, time, and peak memory. Whenever a valid blossom \(B\) detected by the algorithm is contracted, the contraction must preserve the existence of an augmenting path; after augmentation, expansion must produce a matching in \(G\). The output \(M\) is accepted only if it is a matching and its cardinality agrees with an independently checked optimality certificate or trusted reference value.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted-Matching Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines certified benchmarks for primal-dual maximum-weight matching implementations.

The run must declare whether its admissible family \(\mathcal A\) consists of all matchings, maximum-cardinality matchings, or perfect matchings. Its reported matching \(M\) is accepted only when \(M\in\mathcal A\) and a feasible dual certificate for the declared formulation has value \(D=w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w_e\). The benchmark must also report the weight encoding and arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The benchmark measures a declared weighted-matching variant and accepts an output only when the matching is admissible and an equal-valued feasible dual certificate for that variant is reported.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Blossom Stress Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines benchmark runs whose laminar blossom hierarchy has unbounded nesting depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence of fixed blossom-algorithm runs on graphs \(G_n\), let \(T_n\) be the finite set of recorded event indices and let \(\mathcal B_n(t)\) be the active contracted blossoms at \(t\in T_n\). Search order and tie-breaking are fixed.

children.title: Matching-Polytope Representations
children.top_down_role: Benchmark encodings based on matching-polytope formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Polytope Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds' finite-graph linear description of the convex hull of matching incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(P_M(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}\). Then
\[P_M(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\ge0\ (e\in E),\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le1\ (v\in V),\ \sum_{e\in E(S)}x_e\le\frac{|S|-1}{2}\ (S\subseteq V,\ |S|\text{ odd})\right\}.\]
Thus every vector satisfying nonnegativity, vertex-degree inequalities, and all odd-set inequalities is a convex combination of matching incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matching polytope consists exactly of nonnegative edge vectors satisfying every vertex-degree inequality and every odd-cardinality vertex-set inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_M(G)=\{x\ge0:x(\delta(v))\le1\ \forall v,\ x(E(S))\le(|S|-1)/2\ \forall S\subseteq V\text{ odd}\}\).

notation.meaning: edges with both endpoints in S

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Relaxation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines comparisons between the degree relaxation and the odd-set-complete matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(G=(V,E)\), define the degree relaxation \(Q(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^E:x(\delta(v))\le1\text{ for every }v\in V\}\). A matching-relaxation benchmark supplies \((G,w)\), solves \(\max\{w^Tx:x\in Q(G)\}\), and compares its value and resources with the exact matching formulation obtained by adding violated odd-set inequalities. It reports the relaxation value \(z_Q\), integer optimum \(z_M\), additive gap \(z_Q-z_M\), separation rounds, generated odd-set inequalities, time, and memory; ratios are reported only when \(z_M>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These benchmarks compare the vertex-degree relaxation with the exact matching formulation, recording gaps and the work needed to separate odd-set inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(w\in\mathbb Q^E\) has a declared encoding.
Both formulations use the same objective and arithmetic convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_Q\ge z_M\), with equality after all necessary odd-set inequalities are enforced.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Extreme-Point Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd cycles exhibit fractional extreme points of the vertex-degree matching relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_k\) be the disjoint union of \(k\) odd cycles, each of length \(2r+1\), and define \(x_e=1/2\) for every edge. Then \(x\) is an extreme point of \(Q(G_k)=\{y\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{E(G_k)}:y(\delta(v))\le1\text{ for every }v\}\), because every degree constraint is tight and uniquely determines the edge values on each odd cycle. With unit weights, the relaxation value is \(k(2r+1)/2\), whereas a maximum matching has value \(kr\); hence the additive gap is \(k/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half-valued edges on disjoint odd cycles are fractional extreme points of the degree relaxation and create an additive gap of one half per cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(k\ge1\) and \(r\ge1\) are integers.
Every edge has unit weight.

notation.meaning: disjoint union of k odd cycles

children.title: Matching Dual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Dual evidence used to validate matching objectives or bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Dual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual certificate for maximum-weight matching using vertex and odd-set multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have weights \(w_e\), and let \(M\) be a matching. A dual certificate consists of \(y_v\ge0\) and \(z_S\ge0\) for odd sets \(S\subseteq V\), with only finitely many nonzero \(z_S\), such that \(y_u+y_v+\sum_{S:e\in E(S)}z_S\ge w_e\) for every \(e=uv\). Its value is \(D=\sum_v y_v+\sum_{S\text{ odd}}((|S|-1)/2)z_S\). If \(D=\sum_{e\in M}w_e\), weak duality certifies that \(M\) is a maximum-weight matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is optimal when feasible vertex and odd-set dual multipliers have objective value equal to the matching's weight.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(M\) is a matching.
The displayed dual inequalities and nonnegativity conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{e\in M}w_e=D=\max\{\sum_{e\in N}w_e:N\text{ is a matching}\}\).

children.title: Matching Barrier Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Barrier Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte–Berge barrier certificate for maximum-cardinality matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(U\subseteq V\), let \(q(G-U)\) be the number of odd connected components of \(G-U\). Every matching leaves at least \(q(G-U)-|U|\) vertices unmatched, so \(\nu(G)\le\bigl(|V|-q(G-U)+|U|\bigr)/2\). A pair \((M,U)\) is a matching barrier certificate when \(M\) is a matching and \(|M|=\bigl(|V|-q(G-U)+|U|\bigr)/2\). The component parities, absence of intercomponent edges in \(G-U\), and matching feasibility are directly checkable and certify \(|M|=\nu(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex set whose odd-component upper bound equals a matching's size certifies that the matching has maximum cardinality.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(U\subseteq V\).
\(M\subseteq E\) is a matching.

notation.meaning: number of odd components after deleting U

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The barrier certificate is mathematically standard and precisely stated, but it has no citation. An authoritative section, theorem, or page locator for the Tutte–Berge formula is required.

children.title: Certificate Verification Stress Cases
children.top_down_role: Instances designed to test certificate parsing, scaling, or independent checking.

assumptions_latex: A weighted bipartite graph \(G=(U\dot\cup V,E)\) has rational weights \(w_e\).
A claimed certificate consists of a matching \(M\subseteq E\) and rational vertex potentials \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^{U\cup V}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stress-case verifier computes every residual \(s_{uv}=y_u+y_v-w_{uv}\) exactly and accepts precisely when \(M\) is a matching, \(y\ge 0\), \(s_{uv}\ge 0\) for every \(uv\in E\), and \(\sum_{e\in M}w_e=\sum_{z\in U\cup V}y_z\). A certificate stress family contains instances with zero residuals, residuals of minimum nonzero magnitude \(\delta\), and single-coordinate corruptions of magnitude less than \(\delta\); it tests whether verification distinguishes exact feasibility and equality from tolerance-based acceptance.

notation.meaning: Slack of the dual inequality for edge \(uv\).
Smallest nonzero absolute residual represented in a stress instance.

review_flags: benchmark-specific stress-family formulation needs an authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic stress cases for weighted bipartite matching certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The stress-case verifier computes every residual \(s_{uv}=y_u+y_v-w_{uv}\) exactly and accepts precisely when \(M\) is a matching, \(y\ge 0\), \(s_{uv}\ge 0\) for every \(uv\in E\), and \(\sum_{e\in M}w_e=\sum_{z\in U\cup V}y_z\). A certificate stress family contains instances with zero residuals, residuals of minimum nonzero magnitude \(\delta\), and single-coordinate corruptions of magnitude less than \(\delta\); it tests whether verification distinguishes exact feasibility and equality from tolerance-based acceptance.

An authoritative source is required before fixing the statement and knowledge kind.

children.title: Cographic Matroid Instances
children.top_down_role: Matroid benchmarks represented through graph cut structure.

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and \(M(G)\) is its graphic matroid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cographic matroid of \(G\) is the dual matroid \(M^*(G)=M(G)^*\) on \(E\). A set \(F\subseteq E\) is independent in \(M^*(G)\) if and only if deleting \(F\) does not increase the number of connected components, equivalently \(c(V,E\setminus F)=c(V,E)\). Its rank is \(r^*(F)=|F|+r_G(E\setminus F)-r_G(E)\).

children.title: Regular Matroid Instances
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks from the field-independent regular matroid class.

assumptions_latex: The matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) is finite.

assumptions_latex: The finite matroid is \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), with rank function \(r_M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and an independence oracle, order \(E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_m\}\) so that \(w(e_1)\ge\cdots\ge w(e_m)\). Initialize \(S_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\) when \(w(e_i)<0\); when \(w(e_i)\ge0\), set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\cup\{e_i\}\) if this set is independent, and otherwise set \(S_i=S_{i-1}\). Output \(S_m\). Then \(S_m\) maximizes \(w(S)=\sum_{e\in S}w(e)\) over \(S\in\mathcal I\), using at most \(|E|\) independence-oracle calls after sorting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort elements by decreasing weight, skip negative-weight elements, and retain each nonnegative-weight element exactly when independence is preserved. The resulting independent set has maximum weight and requires at most one independence query per element.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid-Polytope Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-polytope optimization and separation benchmark representation.

A matroid-polytope benchmark may request linear optimization over \(P(M)\), membership testing, or separation: given \(x\), return either confirmation that \(x\in P(M)\) or a subset \(A\subseteq E\) satisfying \(x(A)>r(A)\), with negative coordinates reported separately.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid.
The rank function is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(P(M)\) is equivalent to nonnegativity and all inequalities \(x(A)\le r(A)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Rank Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subset witnesses for violated independence-polytope rank inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) have rank function \(r\), and let \(x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}\). A rank-violation certificate is a subset \(A\subseteq E\) together with the integer \(r(A)\) such that \(x(A)>r(A)\). It certifies \(x\notin P(M)\), because every point of the independence polytope satisfies \(y(A)\le r(A)\). The certificate is verifiable by summing the coordinates indexed by \(A\) and independently validating \(r(A)\), for example by greedily constructing a maximal independent subset of \(A\) using an independence oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset whose coordinate sum exceeds its matroid rank certifies nonmembership in the independence polytope and can be checked using rank or independence queries.

\(x\) is coordinatewise nonnegative.
