knowledge_statements.title: Facet-Separation Stress Cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative near-boundary cases for rank-inequality separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a matroid \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\), rank function \(r\), candidate point \(x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), define the maximum rank-inequality violation by \[v_M(x)=\max_{A\subseteq E}\bigl(x(A)-r(A)\bigr).\] The pair \((M,x)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-facet-separation stress case when \(0<|v_M(x)|\le\varepsilon\), or when several distinct subsets attain values within \(\varepsilon\) of \(v_M(x)\). The first condition places \(x\) close to the polytope boundary; the second creates nearly tied candidate separators. A correct exact separator rejects precisely when \(v_M(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stress case lies within a chosen tolerance of the rank-inequality boundary or has many nearly tied separating subsets; exact separation rejects exactly for positive maximum violation.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid.
\(x\ge0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact rank separator rejects \(x\) if and only if \(v_M(x)>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Minor Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Decomposition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark strata parameterized by certified recursive matroid compositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matroid-decomposition benchmark instance is a pair \((M,T)\), where \(M
ingroup\) is a finite matroid and \(T\) is a rooted tree whose leaves encode base matroids and whose internal nodes encode specified composition operations. Evaluating \(T\) bottom-up must produce a matroid isomorphic to \(M\). A decomposition regime fixes the permitted leaf classes, permitted operations, maximum adhesion parameter \(k\), and optional bounds on the depth or degree of \(T\). A decomposition certificate consists of \(T\), its local interfaces, and isomorphism data sufficient to check that the composed result is \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition regime fixes allowed leaf matroids, composition operations, interface size, and tree shape; each instance carries a checkable tree reconstructing the target matroid.

Each permitted composition operation has specified interface semantics.

children.title: Matroid Width Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Width Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-width stratification using the matroid connectivity function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite matroid \(M
ingroup\) on \(E\), define \(\lambda_M(X)=r(X)+r(E\setminus X)-r(E)\). A branch decomposition is a subcubic tree whose leaves are bijective with \(E\); each tree edge induces a bipartition \((X,E\setminus X)\). Its width is \(\max_X\lambda_M(X)\), with the maximum over induced bipartitions, and the branch-width \(\operatorname{bw}(M)\) is the minimum width over all branch decompositions. A width regime \([a,b]\) consists of instances satisfying \(a\le\operatorname{bw}(M)\le b\), together with a decomposition witness when one is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width regime groups matroids by branch-width, computed from connectivity values across cuts induced by a subcubic leaf-labeled decomposition tree.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite matroid.
The stated convention uses \(\lambda_M\) without an additive-one shift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) lies in regime \([a,b]\) exactly when \(a\le\operatorname{bw}(M)\le b\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits a width-regime leaf, but the immutable title does not select branch-width over other matroid width measures. The additive-shift convention also varies in the literature and requires a source. The statement contains the undefined command \ningroup. A specific authoritative branch-width definition and locator are needed before this provisional interpretation can be reviewed.

children.title: Decomposition Boundary Cases
children.top_down_role: Instances near transitions between tractable and difficult decomposition structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Boundary Cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between fixed-width decomposability and unbounded structural width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((M_n)_{n\ge1}\) be finite matroids with \(|E(M_n)|\to\infty\). Relative to branch-width, this family is a decomposition boundary family when \(\operatorname{bw}(M_n)\to\infty\), while every proper minor \(N\) selected by the benchmark satisfies \(\operatorname{bw}(N)<\operatorname{bw}(M_n)\). For every fixed \(k\), sufficiently large members then admit no branch decomposition of width at most \(k\). Consequently, any algorithm whose guarantee assumes a supplied width-\(k\) decomposition falls outside that guarantee on the tail of the family, although nearby designated minors may remain within it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded-branch-width family eventually escapes every fixed-width decomposition guarantee, while designated proper minors can provide nearby lower-width comparison instances.
assumptions_latex: \((M_n)\) is a family of finite matroids.
Branch-width uses the connectivity convention stated for the benchmark.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed \(k\), there exists \(n_0\) such that \(n\ge n_0\) implies \(\operatorname{bw}(M_n)>k\).

notation.meaning: n-th matroid in the boundary family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and unbounded branch-width does imply escape from every fixed-width regime. However, the additional condition imposed on every benchmark-selected proper minor is a provisional benchmark convention and does not establish that those minors remain in any fixed-width comparison class. No source supports the selected boundary-family definition or its minor condition.

children.title: Local Cut Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances evaluating cuts constrained by locality, seeds, or volume.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Cut Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Seeded, volume-bounded cuts provide a reproducible local-versus-global benchmark convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,c)\) be an undirected graph with nonnegative edge capacities, seed \(s\in V\), and budget \(0<B\leq \operatorname{vol}(V)/2\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(c(\delta(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c_e\) and \(\operatorname{vol}(S)=\sum_{v\in S}\sum_{e\ni v}c_e\). A local-cut benchmark instance asks for a nonempty set \(S\) satisfying \(s\in S\) and \(\operatorname{vol}(S)\leq B\) that minimizes \(c(\delta(S))\); ties are resolved by a declared deterministic rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local-cut instance minimizes boundary capacity among sets containing a designated seed and having volume at most a prescribed local budget.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\geq 0\) for every \(e\in E\).
\(0<B\leq \operatorname{vol}(V)/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{s\in S\subseteq V\\0<\operatorname{vol}(S)\leq B}}c(\delta(S)).\]

notation.meaning: Edges with exactly one endpoint in S.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited cut-functions section does not support the seeded volume-budget benchmark convention. The statement permits positive-volume-free feasible sets, while the conclusion excludes them, and feasibility is not guaranteed when the seed volume exceeds B.

children.title: Cut-Scale Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graphs where relevant cut structure shifts between local and global scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Scale Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regimes are indexed by the permitted smaller-side volume as a fraction of total volume.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacitated undirected graph \(G=(V,E,c)\) and cut-volume budget \(B\), set \(\rho=2B/\operatorname{vol}(V)\), where \(0<B\leq\operatorname{vol}(V)/2\). A benchmark sequence is local-scale when \(\rho\to0\), transition-scale when constants \(0<a\leq b<1\) satisfy \(a\leq\rho\leq b\), and global-scale when \(\rho\to1\). Every feasible cut is represented by its smaller-volume shore, so increasing \(B\) produces nested feasible families and at \(\rho=1\) recovers unrestricted nontrivial cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized smaller-side budget separates vanishing local scales, intermediate transition scales, and the unrestricted global-cut scale.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and has positive total volume.
\(0<B\leq\operatorname{vol}(V)/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal F(B_1)\subseteq\mathcal F(B_2)\quad\text{whenever}\quad B_1\leq B_2,\qquad \mathcal F(\operatorname{vol}(V)/2)=\{S:\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V\}/\!\sim,\] where \(S\sim V\setminus S\).

notation.meaning: Cuts whose smaller shore has volume at most B.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local, transition, and global regime thresholds are introduced conventions not supported by the cited general cut-functions section. A source or explicit standard-field rationale is required, including the treatment of equal-volume shores.

children.title: Cut-Tree Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances assessing tree-based representations of pairwise cut information.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Tree Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gomory–Hu representation for all pairwise minimum cuts in an undirected capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,c)\) be an undirected graph with nonnegative capacities. A cut tree is a weighted tree \(T=(V,F,w)\) such that, for every distinct \(s,t\in V\), the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut value in \(G\) equals the minimum edge weight on the unique \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(T\). Moreover, deleting any minimum-weight path edge partitions \(V\) into the shores of a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in \(G\). A benchmark validates both equalities for every vertex pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut tree stores every pairwise minimum-cut value as the lightest edge on the corresponding tree path and supplies a realizing cut.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\geq0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lambda_G(s,t)=\min_{e\in P_T(s,t)}w_e\qquad(s\neq t).\]

notation.meaning: Minimum s-t cut capacity in G.

source_refs.locator: 6.3 Computing a minimum cut of an undirected graph p. 219

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Computing a minimum cut of an undirected graph p. 219

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation claim is standard, but the cited locator only identifies a general minimum-cut section and is not shown to support the all-pairs cut-tree value and realizing-cut properties.

children.title: Cactus-Representation Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances assessing cactus encodings of minimum-cut families.

knowledge_statements.title: Cactus-Representation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cactus encoding of all global minimum cuts of an undirected capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,c)\) be an undirected capacitated graph with global minimum-cut value \(\lambdam{>0}\). A cactus representation consists of a cactus multigraph \(Km{=(W,F)}\) and a map \(\phi:V\to W\) such that every global minimum cut of \(G\) is the inverse image under \(\phi\) of either a cactus bridge cut or a cut obtained by deleting two edges from one cactus cycle, and every such represented nontrivial partition has capacity \(\lambda\) in \(G\). Benchmark validation requires completeness and soundness of this correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cactus compactly and exactly encodes all global minimum cuts through bridge deletions or pairs of edge deletions on one cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
\(c_e\geq0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_{\min}(G)=\{\phi^{-1}(X):X\text{ is a nontrivial bridge or two-edge cycle shore of }K\}.\]

notation.meaning: Map from original vertices to cactus vertices.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Cactus representation of minimum cuts p. 228

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Cactus representation of minimum cuts p. 228

children.title: Representation Size Stress Cases
children.top_down_role: Graphs producing compact, large, or structurally intricate cut representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Size Stress Cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive cases measure encoding size independently of input graph density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an input graph \(Gm{=(V,E)}\) and an exact cut representation \(R(G)m{=(W,F)}\), define its representation size by \(L(R)=|W|+|F|\) and normalized expansion by \(q(G)=L(R(G))/|V|\). A representation-size stress family is a sequence \((G_n)\) with \(|V(G_n)|\to\infty\) for which \(q(G_n)\) approaches the supremum permitted by the chosen representation class. Implementations are compared using construction time, peak memory, and serialized size as functions of both input size and \(L(R)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stress family drives the exact cut encoding toward its class-specific maximum size and reports output-sensitive time, memory, and storage.
assumptions_latex: Each \(R(G_n)\) is exact under a fixed representation convention.
\(|V(G_n)|\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}q(G_n)=\sup_G q(G)\quad\text{within the declared representation class}.\]

notation.meaning: Number of vertices plus edges in the representation.
Representation size normalized by input vertices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the chosen size normalization, class-specific supremum criterion, or output-sensitive reporting convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Connectivity-Certificate Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-preserving sparse certificates for undirected edge connectivity up to threshold k.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected multigraph and let \(k\) be a positive integer. A sparse \(k\)-connectivity certificate is a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) with \(|F|\leq k(|V|-1)\) such that, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \(|\delta_H(S)|\geq\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\). Since \(H\subseteq G\), this is equivalent to \(\min\{k,|\delta_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\); hence all cut values below \(k\) and all connectivity decisions up to \(k\) are certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse certificate uses at most k times n−1 edges while preserving every cut value after truncation at k.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected multigraph.
\(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(k\geq1\).
\(H\) is a spanning subgraph of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|F|\leq k(|V|-1),\qquad \min\{k,|\delta_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\quad(S\subseteq V).\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate formulation and k(|V|-1) edge bound require an authoritative sparse-certificate source, particularly for the stated multigraph convention.

children.title: Spanning-Tree Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Undirected spanning-tree instances covering diverse graph geometries.

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted and unweighted spanning-tree instances with independently checkable feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), a spanning-tree benchmark asks for a set \(T\subseteq E\) such that \((V,T)\) is connected and \(|T|=|V|-1\). In the weighted variant the objective is to minimize \(w(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w_e\); in the unweighted variant only construction and feasibility are measured. The benchmark declares whether parallel edges are retained and specifies a deterministic policy for equal weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning-tree benchmark constructs a connected acyclic spanning subgraph, minimizing total weight in the weighted variant.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
\(w_e\in\mathbb R\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{T\subseteq E\\(V,T)\text{ connected}\\|T|=|V|-1}}\sum_{e\in T}w_e.\]

source_refs.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

children.title: Arborescence Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Directed rooted spanning-structure instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Arborescence Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted directed spanning-tree benchmarks use the out-arborescence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed graph, let \(r\in V\) be a root, and let \(w:A\to\mathbb R\). An out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) is a set \(B\subseteq A\) such that \(r\) has indegree zero in \((V,B)\), every \(v\neq r\) has indegree one, and every vertex is reachable from \(r\). A weighted arborescence benchmark minimizes \(w(B)=\sum_{a\in B}w_a\) over all such \(B\), reporting infeasibility when no rooted arborescence exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted rooted-arborescence benchmark gives every nonroot vertex one incoming arc and a directed path from the root while minimizing total arc weight.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite directed graph.
\(r\in V\) is fixed.
\(w_a\in\mathbb R\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{B\text{ an out-arborescence rooted at }r}\sum_{a\in B}w_a,\] provided the feasible family is nonempty.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

children.title: Tree-Packing Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances involving multiple edge-disjoint or capacity-limited spanning structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Packing Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted undirected edge-disjoint spanning-tree packing under the Nash-Williams–Tutte partition criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph, and let \(\tau(G)\) be the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees. For a partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\) into at least two nonempty parts, let \(E(\mathcal P)\) contain the edges joining distinct parts. Then \(G\) contains \(k\) edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if \(|E(\mathcal P)|\geq k(|\mathcal P|-1)\) for every such partition. Consequently, the optimum packing number equals the minimum partition ratio rounded down.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum number of edge-disjoint spanning trees is the floor of the minimum, over vertex partitions, of the cross-edge count divided by one less than the number of parts.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected multigraph.
Partitions have at least two nonempty parts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\tau(G)=\min_{\mathcal P:\,|\mathcal P|\geq2}\left\lfloor\frac{|E(\mathcal P)|}{|\mathcal P|-1}\right\rfloor.\]

notation.meaning: Maximum number of edge-disjoint spanning trees.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

children.title: Packing-Density Regimes
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks stratified by attainable packing multiplicity or structural scarcity.

knowledge_statements.title: Packing-Density Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density normalizes the achieved tree packing by the elementary edge-count upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|\geq2\), let \(\tau(G)\) be its maximum number of edge-disjoint spanning trees and define \(U(G)=\lfloor |E|/(|V|-1)\rfloor\). The packing density is \(d(G)=\tau(G)/U(G)\). A benchmark sequence is sparse-packing when \(\tau(G)=O(1)\), underutilized when \(d(G)\to0\), and edge-saturated when \(d(G)\to1\). These labels must be reported together with \(\tau(G)\), \(|V|\), and \(|E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Packing density compares the maximum number of edge-disjoint spanning trees with the upper bound imposed solely by the available edge count.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0<\tau(G)\leq U(G),\qquad 0<d(G)\leq1.\]

notation.meaning: Edge-count upper bound on packing size.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.4. Packing Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 147

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary upper bound is correct, but the sparse-packing, underutilized, and edge-saturated regime labels are benchmark conventions not supported by the cited tree-packing section.

children.title: Graph Orientation Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances assessing orientation choices subject to connectivity targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Orientation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility benchmark for k-arc-connected orientations of undirected multigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph and let \(k\geq1\). An orientation \(D\) of \(G\) is \(k\)-arc-connected when every nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\) has at least \(k\) arcs entering \(S\), equivalently at least \(k\) arcs leaving \(S\). Such an orientation exists if and only if every nontrivial undirected cut of \(G\) has at least \(2k\) edges. A benchmark output is feasible precisely when it satisfies these directed cut inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected multigraph admits a k-arc-connected orientation exactly when every nontrivial cut contains at least 2k edges.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected multigraph.
\(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(k\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G\text{ has a }k\text{-arc-connected orientation}\iff |\delta_G(S)|\geq2k\quad(\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V).\]

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orientation theorem is a nontrivial existence characterization and requires an authoritative citation covering the multigraph and k-arc-connected conventions.

children.title: Connectivity-Augmentation Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances assessing added edges or arcs needed to meet connectivity targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Augmentation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost undirected edge-connectivity augmentation with an explicit admissible-link set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)angle\) be an undirected multigraph, let \(L\) be a set of admissible additional links with nonnegative costs \(c:L\to\mathbb R_{geq0}\), and let \(k\geq1\). A connectivity-augmentation benchmark asks for \(F\subseteq L\) of minimum cost such that \(G+F\) is \(k\)-edge-connected. Equivalently, every nonempty proper \(S\subset V\) must satisfy \(|\delta_G(S)|+|F\cap\delta_L(S)|\geq k\). A budgeted variant asks whether such an \(F\) exists with total cost at most \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose minimum-cost admissible links so every nontrivial cut reaches the required edge-connectivity, or decide feasibility under a stated budget.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected multigraph.
\(c_\ell\geq0\) for every \(\ell\in L\).
\(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(k\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{F\subseteq L}\left\{\sum_{\ell\in F}c_\ell:\ |\delta_G(S)|+|F\cap\delta_L(S)|\geq k\ \text{for all }\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V\right\}.\]

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Cut functions and connectivity concepts p. 19

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general cut-functions section does not support the augmentation optimization model. The statement also contains malformed mathematics: \(G=(V,E)\rangle\) and \(\mathbb R_{geq0}\) must be corrected once an appropriate augmentation source is supplied.

children.title: Orientation Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graphs spanning feasible, marginal, or obstructed orientation conditions.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) admits a strongly connected orientation if and only if \(G\) is connected and has no bridge, equivalently \(\lambda(G)\ge 2\) when \(|V|\ge 2\).

notation.meaning: Edge connectivity of the undirected graph.
An orientation obtained by directing every edge exactly once.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies feasibility of strong orientations for finite undirected benchmark graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an orientation \(D\) of \(G\), call the instance feasible when \(D\) can be chosen strongly connected. The feasibility regimes are: disconnected graphs are infeasible; connected graphs containing a bridge are infeasible; and connected bridgeless graphs are feasible. Thus, for \(|V|\ge 2\), strong-orientation feasibility is characterized exactly by \(\lambda(G)\ge 2\). This predicate separates structurally impossible instances from those on which orientation algorithms may be compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite undirected graph has a strongly connected orientation exactly when it is connected and bridgeless; disconnected graphs and graphs with bridges form the infeasible regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Feasibility Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong-orientation characterization is mathematically standard and fits the feasibility-regime container, but no source or inspectable locator supports the nontrivial equivalence.

children.title: Augmentation Budget Regimes
children.top_down_role: Connectivity instances stratified by augmentation cost or cardinality limits.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph.
Candidate augmentation edges are drawn from a specified set \(F\subseteq \binom{V}{2}\setminus E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The budget-\(b\) regime is feasible exactly when \(b\ge \tau(G,F)\); it is tight when \(b=\tau(G,F)\) and overbudget when \(b>\tau(G,F)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of admissible edges needed to make the graph connected and bridgeless.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses unweighted admissible-edge augmentation toward strong-orientation feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\tau(G,F)=\min\{\lvert A\rvert:A\subseteq F,\ (V,E\cup A)\text{ is connected and has no bridge}\},\] with \(\tau(G,F)=+\infty\) if no such \(A\) exists. An augmentation instance with budget \(b\) is infeasible when \(b<\tau(G,F)\), tight when \(b=\tau(G,F)<+\infty\), and overbudget when \(b>\tau(G,F)\). Because connected bridgeless graphs admit strong orientations, these regimes couple augmentation budget directly to orientation feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum admissible augmentation size defines infeasible, tight, and overbudget regimes according to whether the available budget is below, equal to, or above that minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation Budget Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The budget classification is internally consistent and the definition kind fits the container, but the particular admissible-edge augmentation model and its coupling to strong orientation have no cited support.

children.title: Graph Partitioning Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances for balanced, weighted, or multiway graph partitioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Partitioning Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies balanced minimum-cut partitioning as a reproducible benchmark problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible \(k\)-way partition is an ordered family \((V_1,\ldots,V_k)\) of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \(V\) and for which \(\ell_i\le |V_i|\le u_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its objective is \[\operatorname{cut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)=\sum_{\substack{\{x,y\}\in E:\;x\in V_i,\ y\in V_j\text{ for some }i,j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},\ i\ne j}}w(\{x,y\}).\] The benchmark optimum is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible partitions, with value \(+\infty\) if none exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the vertices into k size-bounded blocks while minimizing the total weight of edges whose endpoints belong to different blocks; the optimum is infinite if no feasible partition exists.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\).
The integers \(k\ge 2\) and bounds \(0\le \ell_i\le u_i\le |V|\) are specified for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A benchmark solution minimizes \(\operatorname{cut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)\) over all feasible ordered partitions.

notation.meaning: Weight of edges whose endpoints lie in different blocks.
Lower and upper cardinality bounds for block i.

children.title: Clique Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances for maximum, weighted, or constrained clique computation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark objective is \(\omega(G)=\max\{|C|:C\subseteq V,\ \binom{C}{2}\subseteq E\}\).

notation.meaning: Clique number, equal to the maximum clique cardinality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unweighted maximum-clique benchmark on finite simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(C\subseteq V\) is a clique when every two distinct vertices in \(C\) are adjacent, equivalently \(\binom{C}{2}\subseteq E\). The maximum-clique benchmark asks for a clique of greatest cardinality and reports \[\omega(G)=\max\{|C|:C\subseteq V,\ \binom{C}{2}\subseteq E\}.\] A reported solution is feasible precisely when its vertices induce a complete subgraph; its objective value is \(|C|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the largest vertex subset whose distinct pairs are all adjacent; feasibility is checked by verifying every induced pair is an edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Clique Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-clique definition is precise and appropriate for the benchmark container, but no citation or specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Graph Coloring Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances for chromatic, weighted, or constrained coloring tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Coloring Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses minimum proper vertex coloring for finite simple benchmark graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\), let \([q]=\{1,\ldots,q\}\) when \(q\ge 1\), and let \([0]=\varnothing\). A proper \(q\)-coloring is a map \(c:V\to[q]\) satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\). The minimum-coloring benchmark reports \[\chi(G)=\min\{q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}:\text{a proper }q\text{-coloring of }G\text{ exists}\}.\] A candidate assignment is feasible exactly when all edge constraints hold, and its measured objective is the number of colors it uses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign labels to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different labels, minimizing the number of colors used; the empty graph may use zero colors.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark objective is \(\chi(G)=\min\{q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}:\exists\text{ a proper }q\text{-coloring of }G\}\).

notation.meaning: A vertex-color assignment using labels from the explicitly defined set [q].

children.title: Independent-Set Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances for maximum, weighted, or constrained independent-set computation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark objective is \(\alpha(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ \binom{S}{2}\cap E=\varnothing\}\).

notation.meaning: Independence number, equal to the maximum independent-set cardinality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unweighted maximum independent-set benchmark on finite simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq V\) is independent when no edge has both endpoints in \(S\), equivalently \(\binom{S}{2}\cap E=\varnothing\). The maximum-independent-set benchmark asks for a feasible set of greatest cardinality and reports \[\alpha(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ \binom{S}{2}\cap E=\varnothing\}.\] Feasibility is verified by inspecting the subgraph induced by \(S\), which must contain no edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the largest vertex subset containing no adjacent pair; feasibility is checked by confirming that its induced subgraph has no edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Set Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-independent-set definition is precise and appropriate for the benchmark container, but it lacks a citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Complementary Problem Pairs
children.top_down_role: Matched graph instances supporting cross-comparison among complementary formulations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph, and \(\overline G\) is its complement on the same vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\), \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\), and \(\chi(G)=\theta(\overline G)\).

notation.meaning: Complement graph, containing exactly the nonedges between distinct vertices of G.
Minimum number of cliques partitioning the vertex set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairs classical vertex-subset and covering problems through graph complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq V\), \(S\) is independent in \(G\) if and only if \(S\) is a clique in \(\overline G\). Consequently, \[\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\quad\text{and}\quad\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G).\] Moreover, the color classes of a proper coloring of \(G\) are independent sets, hence cliques of \(\overline G\); therefore \(\chi(G)=\theta(\overline G)\), where \(\theta\) denotes the minimum cardinality of a partition of the vertices into cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementation exchanges independent sets with cliques and proper color classes with clique partitions, yielding exact correspondences between their optimum values.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Problem Pairs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complement correspondences are mathematically coherent, and duality is the correct content kind, but the nontrivial identities have no supporting source or locator.

children.title: Metric TSP Instances
children.top_down_role: Traveling-salesperson benchmarks satisfying metric cost structure.

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite set with \(|V|\ge 3\).
The cost function \(d:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is symmetric, vanishes on the diagonal, and satisfies the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric TSP optimum is the minimum of \(\sum_{i=1}^{|V|}d(v_i,v_{i+1})\) over cyclic permutations, with \(v_{|V|+1}=v_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines complete symmetric metric TSP benchmark instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric TSP instance is the complete graph on \(V\) with costs \(d\) satisfying \(d(u,v)=d(v,u)\), \(d(u,u)=0\), and \(d(u,w)\le d(u,v)+d(v,w)\) for all \(u,v,w\in V\). A feasible tour is a cyclic ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) containing every vertex once. Its cost is \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}d(v_i,v_{i+1})\), where \(v_{n+1}=v_1\), and the benchmark minimizes this cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric TSP instance uses symmetric, nonnegative, triangle-inequality costs, and seeks the cheapest cycle visiting every vertex exactly once.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric TSP Instances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the metric-TSP instance container and is internally consistent under the common TSP convention permitting zero costs between distinct vertices, but that convention and the formulation need an authoritative citation.

children.title: Euclidean TSP Instances

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean TSP Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coordinate-induced TSP instances using Euclidean distance, with any precision and rounding convention included in the instance specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Euclidean TSP instance assigns vertex \(i\) the point \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and defines \(c(i,j)=\lVert p_i-p_j\rVert_2\). A feasible tour is a cyclic permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with cost \[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lVert p_{\pi(i)}-p_{\pi(i+1)}\rVert_2,\qquad \pi(n+1)=\pi(1).\] The benchmark seeks a tour of minimum cost. Any coordinate precision and distance-rounding rule is part of the instance specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices are points in Euclidean space, travel costs are their Euclidean distances, and the objective is the shortest cyclic ordering; precision and rounding belong to the benchmark specification.
assumptions_latex: \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\) are points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), with \(n\ge 3\).
The dimension \(d\ge 1\) is fixed for the instance family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lVert p_{\pi(i)}-p_{\pi(i+1)}\rVert_2\) over cyclic permutations \(\pi\), with \(\pi(n+1)=\pi(1)\).

notation.meaning: Location of vertex i in Euclidean coordinate space.

children.title: Asymmetric TSP Instances

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite set with \(|V|\ge 2\).
The directed cost function \(c:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{+\infty\}\) need not be symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymmetric TSP optimum is the minimum directed Hamiltonian-cycle cost, or \(+\infty\) when no finite-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle exists.

notation.meaning: Cost of traveling from u to v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines asymmetric TSP with optional forbidden arcs represented by infinite cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An asymmetric TSP instance specifies ordered-arc costs \(c(u,v)\), allowing \(c(u,v)\ne c(v,u)\). A feasible tour is a cyclic ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) of all vertices for which every used arc has finite cost. Its directed cost is \[\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(v_i,v_{i+1}),\qquad v_{n+1}=v_1.\] The benchmark minimizes this quantity; its optimum is defined as \(+\infty\) if no finite-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymmetric TSP permits different costs in opposite directions and seeks a minimum-cost directed Hamiltonian cycle, with infinite cost representing forbidden arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric TSP Instances

children.title: Metricity Boundary Cases
children.top_down_role: Instances near or beyond metric assumptions used by routing methods.

assumptions_latex: \(V=\{a,b,c\}\) and costs are symmetric with zero diagonal.
The positive costs satisfy \(c(a,b)=c(b,c)=1\) and \(c(a,c)=M\) for some \(M>2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The triangle inequality fails, and shortcutting the walk \(a,b,c\) from cost \(2\) to the arc \((a,c)\) raises its cost to \(M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits the failure of cost-nonincreasing shortcutting outside metric TSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the stated three-vertex family, \(c(a,c)=M>2=c(a,b)+c(b,c)\), so the triangle inequality fails. Replacing the two-edge segment \((a,b),(b,c)\), whose cost is \(2\), by the direct shortcut \((a,c)\) produces cost \(M\). Hence shortcutting is not cost-nonincreasing once metricity is removed. Any TSP analysis whose guarantee uses repeated shortcutting therefore requires the triangle inequality or another explicit condition controlling direct-arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-vertex cost matrix with two unit edges and a direct edge costing more than two shows that shortcutting can increase cost outside the metric regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Metricity Boundary Cases

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly exhibits failure of cost-nonincreasing shortcutting and failure_boundary is the appropriate kind, but neither the selected boundary case nor the general methodological claim has a cited source.

children.title: Tour-Construction Method Families
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks for methods that directly build initial tours.

knowledge_statements.title: Tour-Construction Method Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses nearest-neighbor construction as a representative deterministic tour-construction method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U=V\setminus\{v_1\}\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n-1\), choose \[v_{i+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in U}c(v_i,u),\] resolve ties by the specified order, and replace \(U\) by \(U\setminus\{v_{i+1}\}\). If the selected cost is infinite, report failure. After all vertices are selected, output the cycle \((v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n,v_1)\) when \(c(v_n,v_1)<+\infty\); otherwise report failure. The output cost is \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}c(v_i,v_{i+1})\), with \(v_{n+1}=v_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a fixed vertex, repeatedly visit the cheapest unvisited vertex using deterministic tie-breaking, then close the cycle or report failure if a required arc is forbidden.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite with \(|V|=n\ge 2\), and \(c:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{+\infty\}\) gives travel costs.
A start vertex \(v_1\in V\) and deterministic tie-breaking order are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method outputs the cycle \((v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n,v_1)\), or reports construction failure when no finite admissible continuation or closing arc exists.

notation.meaning: Set of vertices not yet inserted into the partial tour.
Vertex selected at construction step i.

children.title: Local-Search Method Families

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Search Method Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical improving neighborhood search for symmetric TSP benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a complete undirected graph with edge costs and an initial Hamiltonian cycle \(T_0\), choose a neighborhood map \(N\) such as \(k\)-opt. At iteration \(t\), select \(T'\in N(T_t)\) with \(c(T')<c(T_t)\) and set \(T_{t+1}=T'\). Stop when no improving neighbor exists, and output the locally optimal tour \(T_t\). A benchmark specification must fix \(N\), the improving-move selection rule, tie breaking, initialization, and stopping tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly replace a TSP tour by a cheaper neighboring tour until the specified neighborhood contains no improving move.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is complete and undirected.
\(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\) assigns finite edge costs.
\(T_0\) is a Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(T_{t+1})<c(T_t)\) for every accepted move, and \(c(T')\ge c(T_t)\) for all \(T'\in N(T_t)\) at termination.

notation.meaning: total edge cost of tour T

knowledge_statements.title: Exact TSP Method Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic branch-and-cut specification for exact symmetric TSP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Formulate the symmetric TSP with binary edge variables, degree equations, and subtour-elimination inequalities. Solve an LP relaxation; if its optimum is fractional, add violated valid inequalities when available and otherwise branch on an unfixed variable. Prune a node when its relaxation is infeasible or its lower bound is at least the incumbent tour cost. When no active nodes remain, output the incumbent Hamiltonian cycle and its bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch-and-cut combines LP bounds, valid cuts, branching, and incumbent pruning to return a provably optimal TSP tour.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite complete undirected graph.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) is the edge-cost vector.
LP subproblems and separation routines are solved exactly for certification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned tour \(T^*\) satisfies \(c(T^*)=\min\{c(T):T\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle of }G\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Heuristic-to-Exact Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparable reporting regime for minimization TSP benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each instance \(i\), run every heuristic under the same declared resource budget and compare its feasible tour value \(U_{i,a}\) with an exact optimum \(z_i^*\), or with a certified lower bound \(L_i\) when the optimum is unavailable. Report runtime, success rate, and the relative optimality gap \((U_{i,a}-z_i^*)/|z_i^*|\); bound-only comparisons must instead report \((U_{i,a}-L_i)/|U_{i,a}|\) and must not label it an exact optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare heuristics under equal budgets using certified optima when available, while clearly distinguishing exact gaps from bound-based gaps.
assumptions_latex: All reported tour values are feasible for the same instance.
\(z_i^*\ne0\) for exact relative gaps.
\(L_i\le z_i^*\le U_{i,a}\) for bound-based reporting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_{i,a}=z_i^*\) implies zero exact gap, while \(U_{i,a}-L_i\) is only a certified upper bound on absolute suboptimality.

certified lower bound for instance i

children.title: Subtour Relaxation Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.title: Subtour Relaxation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard subtour-elimination LP for symmetric TSP benchmarking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a complete undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the subtour relaxation is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=2\ \forall v\in V,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge2\ \forall\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,\ 0\le x_e\le1\ \forall e\in E\right\}.\]
Every Hamiltonian cycle has an incidence vector feasible for this relaxation, so its optimum is a lower bound on the minimum tour cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subtour LP enforces degree two and at least two selected boundary edges for every proper nonempty vertex subset.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, complete, and undirected.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) is the edge-cost vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{SEP}}\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S

children.title: Cutting-Plane Relaxation Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances used to assess cut families, separation burden, or relaxation strengthening.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Relaxation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic valid-inequality loop for measuring TSP relaxation strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize an LP relaxation \(P_0\) containing the degree constraints and variable bounds. At iteration \(t\), solve \(\min\{c^\top x:x\in P_t\}\). If a separation routine finds a valid inequality \(a^\top x\le b\) violated by the optimizer \(x^t\), set \(P_{t+1}=P_t\cap\{x:a^\top x\le b\}\); otherwise stop. Record bound improvement, cuts by class, separation time, LP time, and termination reason.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve an LP, separate violated valid inequalities, add them, and repeat while recording bound and computational progress.
assumptions_latex: Every generated inequality is valid for all TSP tour-incidence vectors.
Each LP is solved to the declared numerical tolerance.
The cut-selection and stopping rules are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For minimization, \(z(P_t)\le z(P_{t+1})\le z_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) at every successful cut iteration.

notation.meaning: LP feasible region after t cut rounds

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and relative LP-gap strata for minimization TSP instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_R(I)\) be the optimum of a relaxation for a minimization instance \(I\), and let \(z^*(I)>0\) be its integer optimum. Define the absolute gap by \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}(I)=z^*(I)-z_R(I)\) and the relative gap by \(g_{\mathrm{rel}}(I)=(z^*(I)-z_R(I))/z^*(I)\). Given predetermined thresholds \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_m\), regime \(j\) contains precisely those instances satisfying \(\tau_{j-1}\le g_{\mathrm{rel}}(I)<\tau_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classify instances by predetermined intervals of the relative difference between an integer optimum and a relaxation lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}(I)\ge0\) and \(g_{\mathrm{rel}}(I)\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Vehicle-Routing Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A capacitated vehicle-routing benchmark instance consists of a depot \(0\), customers \(V\), nonnegative demands \(d_i\), vehicle capacity \(Q>0\), and travel costs \(c_{ij}\). A feasible solution is a collection of depot-rooted routes that visits every customer exactly once and whose customer demand on each route is at most \(Q\). Its objective value is the sum of traversed arc costs; the benchmark seeks a feasible collection of minimum value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition customers among depot tours so every customer is visited once, vehicle capacity is respected, and total travel cost is minimized.

\(Q>0\) and \(d_i\le Q\) for every customer.

knowledge_statements.title: Steiner Network Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected Steiner-tree instance is a graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and a terminal set \(R\subseteq V\). A feasible solution is a connected subgraph containing every vertex of \(R\); nonterminal vertices may be included as Steiner vertices. The objective is to minimize the sum of selected edge costs. With nonnegative costs, a feasible optimum may be chosen to be a tree after deleting cycle edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a minimum-cost connected subgraph spanning all required terminals, with optional nonterminal Steiner vertices.

\(c_e\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\).
All terminals in \(R\) lie in one connected component.

children.title: Prize-Collecting Network Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Collecting Network Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted prize-collecting Steiner-tree benchmark formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A rooted prize-collecting network instance consists of an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), root \(r\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and nonnegative vertex penalties \(\pi_v\). A feasible solution is any connected subgraph \(T\) containing \(r\). Its objective is the selected-edge cost plus penalties for excluded vertices:
\[C(T)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}c_e+\sum_{v\in V\setminus V(T)}\pi_v.\]
The benchmark optimum is the minimum of \(C(T)\) over all such rooted connected subgraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a rooted connected subgraph while balancing purchased edge costs against penalties for omitted vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge0\) and \(\pi_v\ge0\).
The root \(r\in V\) must be included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*=\min\{C(T):T\text{ is connected and }r\in V(T)\}.\)

\(R\subseteq V(G)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Prize-Cost Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric penalty scaling for prize-collecting network benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For scale \(\lambda\ge0\), define the parametric prize-collecting objective
\[F_\lambda(T)=\sum_{e\in E(T)}c_e+\lambda\sum_{v
otin V(T)}\pi_v,\]
where \(T\) is rooted and connected. If \(0\le\lambda_1<\lambda_2\), and \(T_1,T_2\) are respective optimal solutions, then the excluded base penalty satisfies \(\sum_{v
otin V(T_2)}\pi_v\le\sum_{v
otin V(T_1)}\pi_v\). Thus increasing penalty weight admits an optimum excluding no greater total prize.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: As omitted-prize penalties receive greater weight, an optimal solution can be chosen with no larger total excluded base penalty.

Each feasible subgraph is connected and contains the fixed root.
An optimum exists for every tested value of \(\lambda\).

knowledge_statements.title: Survivable Network-Design Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected cut formulation with pairwise connectivity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A survivable network-design instance consists of an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative edge costs \(c_e\), and symmetric integer requirements \(r_{ij}\ge0\). A selected edge set \(F\subseteq E\) is feasible when every vertex cut separating some pair \(i,j\) contains at least \(r_{ij}\) selected edges. Equivalently, for every nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\),
\[|F\cap\delta(S)|\ge \max\{r_{ij}:i\in S,\ j\notin S\}.\]
The objective is to minimize \(\sum_{e\in F}c_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-cost subgraph whose cuts provide the prescribed number of edge-disjoint connections between every required vertex pair.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(c_e\ge0\) for all edges.
\(r_{ij}=r_{ji}\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible \(F\) contains at least \(r_{ij}\) edge-disjoint \(i\)-to-\(j\) paths for each pair \(i,j\).

knowledge_statements.title: Facility-Location Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated metric facility-location benchmark instances with explicit opening and assignment costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A facility-location benchmark is a tuple \(I=(F,D,d,f,w)\), where \(F\) is a finite facility set, \(D\) is a finite demand set, \(d:(F\cup D)^2\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) is a metric, \(f:F\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) gives opening costs, and \(w:D\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) gives demands. Its reference optimum is \[\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}(I)=\min_{S\subseteq F,\,S\ne\varnothing}\left\{\sum_{i\in S}f(i)+\sum_{j\in D}w(j)\min_{i\in S}d(i,j)\right\}.\] A reported solution must specify \(S\) and its objective value under this formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark specifies metric assignment costs, facility opening costs, and demands; solutions choose open facilities and pay opening plus nearest-facility assignment cost.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(D\) are finite and nonempty.
\(d\) is a nonnegative metric on \(F\cup D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}(I)\) is the minimum opening-plus-assignment cost.

notation.meaning: opening costs, demands, and metric distances

children.title: k-Center Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances focused on minimizing worst-case client distance under a center limit.

knowledge_statements.title: k-Center Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete metric \(k\)-center instances using the maximum assignment distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete metric \(k\)-center benchmark is a tuple \(I=(F,D,d,k)\), where \(F\) and \(D\) are finite nonempty sets, \(d:(F\cup D)^2\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) is a metric, and \(k\in\{1,\ldots,|F|\}\). A feasible solution is \(S\subseteq F\) with \(1\le |S|\le k\), and its radius is \(r_I(S)=\max_{j\in D}\min_{i\in S}d(i,j)\). The benchmark optimum is \[\operatorname{OPT}_{k\mathrm C}(I)=\min_{S\subseteq F,\,1\le |S|\le k}r_I(S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most k facilities to minimize the greatest distance from any demand point to its nearest chosen facility.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(D\) are finite and nonempty.
\(d\) is a metric and \(1\le k\le |F|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{k\mathrm C}(I)\) is the least achievable covering radius.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The discrete metric k-center formulation is precise and appropriate as a benchmark definition, but it has no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: k-Median Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances focused on aggregate client distance under a facility limit.

knowledge_statements.title: k-Median Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted discrete metric \(k\)-median instances with sum-of-distances objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weighted discrete metric \(k\)-median benchmark is a tuple \(I=(F,D,d,w,k)\), where \(F,D\) are finite nonempty sets, \(d:(F\cup D)^2\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) is a metric, \(w:D\to\mathbb R_{>0}\), and \(k\in\{1,\ldots,|F|\}\). A feasible solution is \(S\subseteq F\) with \(1\le |S|\le k\). Its cost and the benchmark optimum are \[C_I(S)=\sum_{j\in D}w(j)\min_{i\in S}d(i,j),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_{k\mathrm M}(I)=\min_{S\subseteq F,\,1\le |S|\le k}C_I(S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most k facilities to minimize the demand-weighted sum of distances to nearest selected facilities.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(D\) are finite and nonempty.
\(d\) is a metric, \(w(j)>0\), and \(1\le k\le |F|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{k\mathrm M}(I)\) is the minimum weighted assignment distance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted discrete metric k-median formulation is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but an authoritative source and specific locator are absent.

children.title: Outlier-Robust Location Regimes
children.top_down_role: Location benchmarks incorporating outliers, penalties, or robust service criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Outlier-Robust Location Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Location benchmarks permitting a prescribed number or weight of unserved demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a location instance with facility set \(F\), demand set \(D\), distances \(d\), weights \(w\), center budget \(k\), and outlier budget \(z\ge0\), a feasible robust solution is a pair \((S,O)\) satisfying \(S\subseteq F\), \(1\le |S|\le k\), \(O\subseteq D\), and \(\sum_{j\in O}w(j)\le z\). Its robust median cost is \(\sum_{j\in D\setminus O}w(j)\min_{i\in S}d(i,j)\); its robust center radius is \(\max_{j\in D\setminus O}\min_{i\in S}d(i,j)\), with maximum over the empty set defined as \(0\). A benchmark regime fixes how \(z\) scales with total demand weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime permits discarding bounded total demand weight, then evaluates median cost or center radius only on retained demands.
assumptions_latex: \(F,D\) are finite, \(w(j)>0\), and \(d\) is a metric.
\(1\le k\le |F|\) and \(0\le z\le\sum_{j\in D}w(j)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((S,O)\) is feasible exactly when its center and excluded-weight budgets are respected.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record clearly distinguishes robust median cost from robust center radius, but the weighted-outlier budget, empty-retained-set convention, and regime-scaling claim require a cited source.

children.title: Routing Relaxation Validation
children.top_down_role: Benchmark evidence concerning feasibility, strength, or numerical behavior of routing relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Routing Relaxation Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual validation of a routing relaxation and its reported integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a routing minimization instance have integer formulation \(X_I\subseteq\{0,1\}^m\) with cost \(c\), relaxation \(P_I\supseteq X_I\), and a dual formulation for \(L_I=\min\{c^Tx:x\in P_I\}\). A validation certificate consists of an integer-feasible route vector \(\hat x\in X_I\), a relaxation-feasible vector \(\bar x\in P_I\), and a dual-feasible vector \(y\) such that \(b^Ty=c^T\bar x\). Weak duality then makes \(L_I=b^Ty\) a certified relaxation value and yields \[L_I\le \operatorname{OPT}(I)\le c^T\hat x,\qquad \frac{c^T\hat x}{L_I}\ge\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{L_I}\] when \(L_I>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching primal and dual relaxation solutions certify the lower bound; an integer route supplies an upper bound and observed gap.
assumptions_latex: \(P_I\) contains every integer-feasible routing vector.
The displayed primal and dual programs satisfy weak duality.
\(L_I>0\) when a ratio is reported.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b^Ty=L_I\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\le c^T\hat x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct content kind, and the primal-dual inequalities are valid under the stated assumptions. However, the routing relaxation and its dual are not specified sufficiently to inspect feasibility or the expression b^T y, and no source is cited.

children.title: Approximation-Guarantee Validation
children.top_down_role: Benchmark evidence used to check claimed routing approximation performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Guarantee Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-level validation of a claimed multiplicative guarantee for routing minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a routing minimization instance \(I\), let algorithm \(A\) return a feasible solution of cost \(C_A(I)\), and let \(L(I)>0\) be a certified lower bound on \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). The tuple containing the feasible solution, the lower-bound witness, and a claimed factor \(\alpha\ge1\) validates the guarantee on \(I\) if \[C_A(I)\le \alpha L(I).\] Since \(L(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\), this check certifies \(C_A(I)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). If an exact optimum \(U(I)=\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is independently certified, the exact observed ratio is \(C_A(I)/U(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible routing solution costs at most α times optimum whenever it costs at most α times a certified positive lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) returns a feasible solution for \(I\).
\(0<L(I)\le\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
\(\alpha\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_A(I)\le\alpha L(I)\) implies \(C_A(I)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct role, and C_A(I)≤αL(I) with L(I)≤OPT(I) is a valid sufficient instance-level certificate. No authoritative source with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Worst-Case Ratio Stress Instances
children.top_down_role: Routing instances selected to approach difficult approximation-ratio behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Ratio Stress Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for benchmark sequences approaching an algorithm's worst-case routing ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a routing-instance class with \(0<\operatorname{OPT}(I)<\infty\), and let feasible algorithm \(A\) have ratio \(\rho_A(I)=C_A(I)/\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). A sequence \((I_n)_{n\ge1}\subseteq\mathcal I\) is a worst-case ratio stress sequence if \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}\rho_A(I_n)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\rho_A(I).\] For a claimed upper bound \(\alpha\), a finite instance \(I\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-tight stress instance when \(\alpha-\varepsilon\le\rho_A(I)\le\alpha\); an instance with \(\rho_A(I)>\alpha\) falsifies the claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stress instances make an algorithm's measured ratio approach its worst-case supremum; any ratio above a claimed bound refutes that bound.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) returns a feasible solution on every \(I\in\mathcal I\).
\(0<\operatorname{OPT}(I)<\infty\) for every tested instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_A(I)>\alpha\) is a countercertificate to the claimed factor \(\alpha\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stress-sequence criterion is mathematically plausible and condition is a suitable content kind, but the convention lacks a source and the finite-instance definition does not explicitly quantify ε>0.
