children.title: Knapsack Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Single-capacity or closely related selection benchmarks.

knowledge_statements.title: Knapsack Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary single-capacity knapsack benchmark instances and their reference objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary knapsack benchmark is a tuple \(I=(n,p,w,C)\), where \(n\in\mathbb N\), profits \(p_i\ge0\), weights \(w_i>0\), and capacity \(C>0\). Its feasible set and optimum are \[X(I)=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i\le C\right\},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm K}(I)=\max_{x\in X(I)}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i x_i.\] A benchmark report must identify the numeric representation of \(p_i,w_i,C\) and compare returned objective values using this feasibility convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select a profit-maximizing subset of items whose total positive weight does not exceed one capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) is positive, \(p_i\ge0\), \(w_i>0\), and \(C>0\).
Each item is selectable at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm K}(I)\) is the maximum feasible total profit.

notation.meaning: profit and weight of item i

source_refs.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization
source_refs.locator: 7.2 Knapsack Programs and Group Relaxation p. 184

source_witnesses.source_title: A First Course in Combinatorial Optimization
source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Knapsack Programs and Group Relaxation p. 184

children.title: Multidimensional-Packing Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Packing benchmarks with multiple resource dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multidimensional-Packing Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary multidimensional knapsack benchmarks with componentwise capacity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(d\)-dimensional packing benchmark is a tuple \(I=(n,d,p,A,b)\), where \(n,d\in\mathbb N\), \(p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{d\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R_{>0}^d\). Each item may be chosen at most once. The feasible set and optimum are \[X(I)=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\le b\},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_{d\mathrm K}(I)=\max_{x\in X(I)}p^Tx,\] where the inequality is componentwise. Benchmark metadata must report \(d\), capacities, item resource vectors, and profits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a maximum-profit item subset while respecting every component of a multidimensional capacity vector.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\) are positive integers.
\(p,A\) are componentwise nonnegative and \(b\) is componentwise positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{d\mathrm K}(I)\) is the maximum profit subject to all \(d\) capacities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula correctly defines binary multidimensional knapsack, but the leaf title says multidimensional packing and no source establishes that this is the intended benchmark convention rather than vector packing or another packing variant.

children.title: Capacity-Tightness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances stratified by resource scarcity and aggregate item load.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Tightness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-free capacity regimes for single-capacity knapsack benchmark generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a knapsack instance with positive weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\) and capacity \(C\), define normalized capacity tightness by \[\tau(I)=\frac{C}{\sum_{i=1}^n w_i}.\] A capacity-tightness benchmark regime restricts instances to a declared interval \(T\subseteq(0,1)\) through \(\tau(I)\in T\), after deleting items with \(w_i>C\) when such individually infeasible items are excluded by convention. Smaller \(\tau(I)\) permits a smaller fraction of aggregate item weight; comparisons across regimes must hold the item-generation law and profit regime fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity tightness is capacity divided by total item weight; benchmark strata restrict this normalized quantity to declared intervals.
assumptions_latex: The handling of items satisfying \(w_i>C\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(I)\in(0,1)\) provides a scale-free capacity-stratification parameter.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized ratio is well-defined under the assumptions, but its designation as capacity tightness, the interval convention, and the preprocessing prescription require an authoritative benchmark-generation source.

children.title: Profit-Correlation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances varying the relationship between item value and resource consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Profit-Correlation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Knapsack benchmark strata defined by dependence between item profits and weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For item pairs \((w_i,p_i)\), a profit-correlation benchmark regime is specified by a conditional generation law \(p_i=g(w_i)+\varepsilon_i\), together with the distribution and dependence assumptions for \(\varepsilon_i\). An uncorrelated regime has \(p_i\) independent of \(w_i\). A weakly correlated regime uses bounded centered noise around a nonconstant increasing \(g\). A strongly correlated regime uses \(p_i=g(w_i)+c\), possibly followed by a declared rounding rule, where \(c\) is fixed. Every generated instance must retain \(p_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Profit-correlation regimes prescribe whether profits are independent of weights, noisy increasing functions of weights, or deterministic shifted functions.
assumptions_latex: \((w_i,p_i)\) are generated under a declared joint law.
Profits are nonnegative after any declared rounding or truncation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditional law of \(p_i\) given \(w_i\) determines the benchmark's correlation regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generalized conditional-law description is coherent, but canonical uncorrelated, weakly correlated, and strongly correlated knapsack regimes depend on specific generation and noise conventions that are not sourced here.

children.title: Bin-Packing Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances minimizing the number or cost of capacity-limited containers.

knowledge_statements.title: Bin-Packing Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional identical-bin packing benchmarks minimizing the number of bins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-dimensional bin-packing benchmark is a tuple \(I=(n,s,B)\), where \(n\in\mathbb N\), bin capacity \(B>0\), and item sizes satisfy \(0<s_i\le B\). A feasible packing is a partition \((P_1,\ldots,P_m)\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(\sum_{i\in P_j}s_i\le B\) for every \(j\). Its objective is the number of nonempty parts, and \[\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{BP}}(I)=\min\left\{m:(P_1,\ldots,P_m)\text{ is a feasible packing}\right\}.\] Benchmark reporting must declare whether sizes are integral, rational, or normalized by setting \(B=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition all items into the fewest identical bins so that each bin's total size does not exceed capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) is positive and \(B>0\).
Every item satisfies \(0<s_i\le B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{BP}}(I)\) is the minimum number of feasible bins.

children.title: Cutting-Stock Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Demand-driven cutting instances based on reusable production patterns.

assumptions_latex: Stock length and all item lengths are positive integers.
Demand vector entries are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark optimum is \(z^*=\min\{\mathbf 1^T x:Ax\ge d,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^{|P|}\}\).

notation.meaning: number of items of type i in pattern p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional, identical-stock cutting-stock instances in the standard pattern formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cutting-stock benchmark instance consists of a stock length \(L\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), item lengths \(\ell_i\in\{1,\ldots,L\}\), and demands \(d_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Its feasible pattern set is \(P=\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m \ell_i a_i\le L\}\). With pattern matrix \(A=(a_{ip})\), the benchmark asks for \(x\in\mathbb Z_+^{|P|}\) minimizing \(\mathbf 1^T x\) subject to \(Ax\ge d\). A benchmark record must provide \(L\), \(\ell\), \(d\), and either the complete pattern set or an unambiguous rule for generating it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting-stock benchmark minimizes the number of identical stock rolls used to meet integer item demands through feasible cutting patterns.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Stock Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is mathematically standard and the definition content kind fits the benchmark leaf, but no inspectable source supports either the formulation or the asserted benchmark-record requirements.

children.title: Pattern-Diversity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances varying the number and similarity of useful packing or cutting patterns.

assumptions_latex: All instances use the same pattern definition and feasibility tolerance.
The diversity statistic is computed before algorithm-dependent pattern elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regime \(R_k\) contains precisely the instances satisfying \(\tau_{k-1}<D(I)\le\tau_k\).

notation.meaning: feasible pattern set of the instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stratification by the number or normalized richness of feasible packing patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\), let \(P(I)\) be its feasible pattern set and let \(D(I)\) be a declared diversity statistic, such as \(D(I)=|P(I)|\) or \(D(I)=\log(1+|P(I)|)/m\), where \(m\) is the number of item types. Given fixed thresholds \(-\infty=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K=+\infty\), the pattern-diversity regimes are \(R_k=\{I:\tau_{k-1}<D(I)\le\tau_k\}\). The statistic, normalization, enumeration method, and thresholds must be fixed before solver outcomes are observed and applied identically to every compared algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pattern-diversity regimes partition packing instances using a prespecified statistic for the size or normalized richness of their feasible pattern sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Pattern-Diversity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and covers all real statistic values, but the proposed diversity statistics, normalization choices, and regime protocol are uncited and not canonical enough to validate without a source.

children.title: Waste-Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances where small packing choices substantially affect unused capacity.

assumptions_latex: Every feasible solution uses stock objects of common capacity \(L>0\).
The instance has positive total packed size \(S(I)>0\), so every feasible solution has \(B(x)\ge 1\).
Reported waste excludes unused stock objects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes are \(R_1=\{I:0\le\rho(I)\le\tau_1\}\) and \(R_k=\{I:\tau_{k-1}<\rho(I)\le\tau_k\}\) for \(k=2,\ldots,K\).

notation.meaning: number of used stock objects in solution x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-normalized waste stratification for one-dimensional packing and cutting instances with positive total packed size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\) with positive total packed size \(S(I)>0\), let \(F(I)\) be its feasible set. For each \(x\in F(I)\), let \(B(x)\ge 1\) be the number of used stock objects of common capacity \(L>0\), and define \(W(x)=LB(x)-S(I)\) and \(w(x)=W(x)/(LB(x))\). Define the intrinsic waste sensitivity by \(\rho(I)=\min_{x\in F(I)}w(x)\). For fixed thresholds \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K=1\), define \(R_1=\{I:0\le\rho(I)\le\tau_1\}\) and \(R_k=\{I:\tau_{k-1}<\rho(I)\le\tau_k\}\) for \(k=2,\ldots,K\). Any computable surrogate for \(\rho(I)\) must be identified separately and must not be mixed with exact values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Waste-sensitivity regimes partition positive-load instances by the minimum capacity-normalized unused material attainable by a feasible packing or cutting solution, including zero-waste instances in the first regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Waste-Sensitivity Regimes

children.title: Set-Covering Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances selecting subsets to cover required elements.

assumptions_latex: Every required element belongs to at least one available set.
Set costs are finite real numbers, normally nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark value is \(z^*=\min\{c^Tx:Ax\ge\mathbf 1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted finite set covering in binary incidence-matrix form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set-covering benchmark instance consists of a finite universe \(U=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), subsets \(S_j\subseteq U\), and costs \(c_j\in\mathbb R\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\). Define \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(i\in S_j\). The optimization problem is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax\ge\mathbf 1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\). A valid benchmark record specifies \(m\), \(n\), all nonzero incidences, costs, and the convention for infeasible instances; performance comparisons must use the same presolve and feasibility tolerances or report their differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-covering benchmark selects minimum-cost subsets so that every required element is contained in at least one selected subset.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Covering Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary weighted set-covering formulation is precise, and definition is the correct content kind, but no source supports the formulation together with the additional benchmark and comparison protocol requirements.

children.title: Set-Partitioning Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances selecting subsets to cover each required element exactly once.

assumptions_latex: The incidence matrix is binary.
The benchmark declares whether infeasible instances are excluded or retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark value is \(z^*=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=\mathbf 1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted finite set partitioning with exact single coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set-partitioning benchmark instance consists of a finite universe \(U=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), subsets \(S_j\subseteq U\), and costs \(c_j\in\mathbb R\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\). With \(A_{ij}=1\) if and only if \(i\in S_j\), it asks for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) minimizing \(c^Tx\) subject to \(Ax=\mathbf 1\). Thus every element must occur in exactly one selected subset. The benchmark record must specify dimensions, nonzero incidences, costs, and the treatment of infeasibility and duplicate columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-partitioning benchmark selects minimum-cost subsets so that every required element belongs to exactly one selected subset.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Partitioning Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-cover formulation is mathematically consistent and appropriate as a benchmark definition, but the formulation and asserted record conventions have no inspectable citation.

children.title: Generalized-Assignment Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances assigning tasks to capacity-limited agents with assignment-specific costs.

assumptions_latex: Each job must be assigned to exactly one agent.
Agent capacities and job resource requirements are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark value is \(z^*=\min\{\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\sum_i x_{ij}=1,\ \sum_j a_{ij}x_{ij}\le b_i,\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\}\).

notation.meaning: assignment cost of job j to agent i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-resource generalized assignment with binary job-to-agent decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized-assignment benchmark has agents \(i=1,\ldots,m\), jobs \(j=1,\ldots,n\), assignment costs \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\), resource requirements \(a_{ij}\ge0\), and capacities \(b_i\ge0\). It asks for binary variables \(x_{ij}\) minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}\), subject to \(\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ij}=1\) for every job \(j\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_{ij}\le b_i\) for every agent \(i\). The record must provide every cost, requirement, and capacity, including forbidden-assignment conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized-assignment benchmark assigns every job to one agent at minimum cost without exceeding any agent's resource capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Assignment Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-resource generalized-assignment formulation is precise and matches the leaf, but no source supports its formulation or the required benchmark-record conventions.

children.title: Coverage-Density Regimes
children.top_down_role: Set-system benchmarks stratified by incidence density or overlap.

assumptions_latex: The incidence matrix has at least one row and one column.
Density is measured before presolve removes rows or columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes are \(R_1=\{I:0\le\delta(A(I))\le\tau_1\}\) and \(R_k=\{I:\tau_{k-1}<\delta(A(I))\le\tau_k\}\) for \(k=2,\ldots,K\).

notation.meaning: binary coverage or assignment incidence matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Presolve-independent stratification by binary incidence density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\) with binary incidence matrix \(A(I)\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), where \(m,n\ge 1\), define coverage density by \(\delta(A(I))=\operatorname{nnz}(A(I))/(mn)\). Choose fixed thresholds \(0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K=1\). Define \(R_1=\{I:0\le\delta(A(I))\le\tau_1\}\) and \(R_k=\{I:\tau_{k-1}<\delta(A(I))\le\tau_k\}\) for \(k=2,\ldots,K\). Empty rows, empty columns, and duplicate columns remain included unless the benchmark protocol explicitly defines a common preprocessing transformation. If transformed density is also reported, it is a separate statistic and must identify the transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage-density regimes partition incidence-based instances by the fraction of nonzero entries in their original binary matrix, with zero-density instances included in the first regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Coverage-Density Regimes

assumptions_latex: Each instance has a finite rational mixed-integer linear formulation.
Objective sense and all variable types are explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical benchmark task is to determine \(z^*=\inf\{c^Tx:Ax\,\square\,b,\ \ell\le x\le u,\ x_j\in\mathbb Z\text{ for }j\in J\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent specification of a finite mixed-integer linear-programming instance library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-integer library benchmark is a finite collection \(\mathcal L\) of rational instances, each specifying \(A\), \(b\), \(c\), bounds \(\ell,u\), row senses \(\square\in\{\le,=,\ge\}\), and integer index set \(J\). The associated problem is \(\inf\{c^Tx:Ax\,\square\,b,\ \ell\le x\le u,\ x_j\in\mathbb Z\text{ for }j\in J\}\). A reproducible library fixes instance versions, objective sense, infeasibility and unboundedness conventions, numerical tolerances, resource limits, and aggregation rules; solver-specific reformulations are recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer library benchmark is a versioned collection of rational MILP instances accompanied by fixed feasibility, resource, and result-aggregation conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Library Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic rational MILP-library definition fits the topic, but it identifies no actual library and cites no source for either the mathematical specification or the extensive reproducibility conventions.

children.title: Tree-Based Bounding Search
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks emphasizing branching decisions, node bounds, or search-tree growth.

assumptions_latex: The initial mixed-integer feasible region is bounded or node bounds are otherwise well defined.
Each branching disjunction covers every integer-feasible point at its parent node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When no live nodes remain, the incumbent is optimal; if none exists, the problem is infeasible.

notation.meaning: relaxation lower bound at node N

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization branch-and-bound with valid node relaxations and exhaustive branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(Q\) with the root relaxation and set incumbent value \(U=+\infty\). While \(Q\ne\varnothing\), select a node \(N\), solve a relaxation giving a valid lower bound \(L(N)\), and discard \(N\) if it is infeasible or \(L(N)\ge U\). If its relaxation solution is integer feasible, update \(U\) and the incumbent. Otherwise choose a violated integrality condition, create children whose disjunction contains every integer-feasible point of \(N\), and insert them into \(Q\). Stop when \(Q=\varnothing\), returning the incumbent, or when a declared gap or resource limit is reached, returning bounds and status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch-and-bound repeatedly bounds, prunes, and branches on live nodes, returning an optimal incumbent when the exhaustive search tree closes.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Based Bounding Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind and the minimization branch-and-bound template is coherent under its stated validity assumptions, but the algorithm and its exhaustive-termination claim have no inspectable source.

children.title: Cut-Enhanced Tree Search
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks emphasizing integration of cutting planes within tree search.

assumptions_latex: Every added inequality is valid for the integer-feasible set of its node.
Node relaxations provide valid lower bounds for minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exhaustive termination certifies the returned incumbent as optimal, while limited termination returns valid global bounds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-and-cut for mixed-integer minimization with locally or globally valid cutting planes.

source_refs.locator: 5.21 The integer hull and cutting planes p. 83

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a branch-and-bound tree with root relaxation \(R(N_0)\) and incumbent value \(U=+\infty\). At a selected node \(N\), solve \(R(N)\); prune it when infeasible or when its lower bound is at least \(U\). Otherwise, separate one or more valid inequalities violated by the relaxation solution, add them to \(R(N)\), and reoptimize until the declared separation rule stops. Update \(U\) at integer-feasible solutions; if fractional, branch using an exhaustive disjunction. Stop at tree exhaustion or a declared gap or resource limit, and report the incumbent, global bound, node count, and generated cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch-and-cut augments branch-and-bound node relaxations with valid cutting planes before branching, while preserving valid global bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Enhanced Tree Search

source_witnesses.locator: 5.21 The integer hull and cutting planes p. 83

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section on integer hulls and cutting planes is relevant background, but the supplied locator does not specifically support the complete branch-and-cut workflow, termination statuses, global-bound claim, or reporting protocol stated here. children.title: Node-Selection Stress Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances sensitive to search-node ordering or queue discipline.

assumptions_latex: All compared policies use identical branching, bounding, and pruning rules.
Stress classes are fixed without reference to measured policy performance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each instance belongs to the unique class determined by its declared stress vector \(s(I)\) and fixed partition \(\{C_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled benchmark strata for comparing live-node selection policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a reference tree-generation protocol independent of node selection. For instance \(I\), define a prespecified stress vector \(s(I)=(W(I),D(I),V(I))\), where \(W(I)\) is maximum live-tree width, \(D(I)\) is maximum depth, and \(V(I)\) is a declared dispersion statistic of valid live-node bounds under that protocol. Given a fixed measurable partition \(\{C_1,\ldots,C_K\}\) of the statistic space, regime \(R_k\) is \(\{I:s(I)\in C_k\}\). The protocol, tie-breaking, limits, statistic definitions, and class boundaries must be fixed before policies are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node-selection stress regimes classify instances using prespecified tree width, depth, and bound-dispersion measurements under a common reference protocol.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Selection Stress Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits a regime leaf, but maximum live-tree width and the set of live-node bounds generally depend on node-selection order. The claimed node-selection-independent reference protocol does not define how those quantities are obtained, and no source resolves the ambiguity.

children.title: Cut-Tree Interaction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances exposing tradeoffs between relaxation strengthening and tree size.

assumptions_latex: The baseline and cut-enabled runs use identical branching and node-selection rules.
Cut families, separation schedules, and numerical tolerances are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interaction regime is the cell containing \((\gamma_B(I),\gamma_T(I))\) under a fixed partition of \(\mathbb R_{>0}^2\).

notation.meaning: processed-node count with cut mode q
elapsed time with cut mode q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-dimensional stratification of cut effects on search-tree size and running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instance \(I\), run a fixed tree search with cuts disabled and enabled, denoted by \(q=0\) and \(q=1\). When both runs reach the same declared termination status, define node ratio \(\gamma_B(I)=(N_1(I)+1)/(N_0(I)+1)\) and time ratio \(\gamma_T(I)=(T_1(I)+\varepsilon)/(T_0(I)+\varepsilon)\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed. A cut-tree interaction regime is a cell of a partition of \(\mathbb R_{>0}^2\) applied to \((\gamma_B(I),\gamma_T(I))\). Censored runs must occupy separately declared classes rather than receiving fabricated ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut-tree interaction regimes classify whether cuts shrink or enlarge the search tree and whether that change improves or worsens running time.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Tree Interaction Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outcome-based two-dimensional regime is internally coherent, handles censored runs explicitly, and fits the leaf as a definition, but its ratios, smoothing convention, and classification protocol are uncited and nonstandard.

children.title: Cutting-Plane Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances assessing dynamically generated valid inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark specification for iterative valid-inequality separation in discrete optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance with integer-feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) and initial relaxation \(P_0\supseteq X\), a cutting-plane benchmark is a tuple \((X,P_0,\mathcal S,\varepsilon,T)\). At iteration \(t<T\), the master problem minimizes the objective over \(P_t\), producing \(x^t\); the separator \(\mathcal S\) either returns a valid inequality \(a_t^Tx\leq b_t\) with violation \(a_t^Tx^t-b_t>\varepsilon\), or declares none found. The update is \(P_{t+1}=P_t\cap\{x:a_t^Tx\leq b_t\}\). Report bound progression, separation time, master time, added-cut count, and termination reason under fixed tolerances and resource limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting-plane benchmark fixes the relaxation, separator, tolerance, and limits, then records valid-cut violations, bound progress, model growth, timing, and termination.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq P_0\) and every inequality returned by \(\mathcal S\) is valid for \(X\).
\(T\in\mathbb N\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\) are fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{t+1}\subseteq P_t\) and \(X\subseteq P_t\) for every completed iteration \(t\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this benchmark specification.
Benchmark reporting conventions require an algorithm-engineering source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The benchmark definition fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports its protocol or reporting fields. The minimized objective is not included in the tuple or otherwise defined.

children.title: Constraint-Generation Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Generation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark specification for optimization with an initially restricted constraint set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\leq0\text{ for every }i\in I\}\), where \(I\) is too large to enumerate initially. A constraint-generation benchmark fixes \((D,I,I_0,\mathcal O,\varepsilon,T)\), with \(I_0\subseteq I\). At iteration \(t\), solve the restricted master over constraints indexed by \(I_t\), obtaining \(x^t\). The oracle \(\mathcal O\) returns an index \(i_t\) satisfying \(g_{i_t}(x^t)>\varepsilon\), when one is found, and the update is \(I_{t+1}=I_t\cup\{i_t\}\). Otherwise the run terminates. Record objective values, maximum detected violation, oracle time, master time, and \(|I_t|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint-generation benchmark repeatedly solves a restricted model, requests a violated omitted constraint, adds it, and records feasibility, timing, objective, and model growth.
assumptions_latex: \(I_0\subseteq I\) and \(T\in\mathbb N\).
The oracle returns only indices belonging to \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\mathcal O\) certifies \(g_i(x^t)\leq\varepsilon\) for all \(i\in I\), then \(x^t\) is \(\varepsilon\)-feasible for the full system.

children.title: Separation-Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Benchmarks stratified by the expense or ambiguity of identifying useful violations.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Cost Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime regimes comparing separation effort with restricted-master solution effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For benchmark instance \(n\), let \(S_n\) be total time spent in separation or violation-oracle calls and let \(M_n>0\) be total restricted-master solution time, measured under the same clock and excluding common preprocessing. Define \(r_n=S_n/M_n\). A benchmark sequence is separation-light when \(r_n\to0\), balanced when \(0<\liminf r_n\leq\limsup r_n<\infty\), and separation-dominated when \(r_n\to\infty\). Sequences not satisfying one of these predicates remain unclassified. Timeouts and failed oracle calls must be reported separately rather than encoded as finite observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation cost is classified by its runtime ratio to master optimization: vanishing, comparable, or diverging along a benchmark sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(M_n>0\) for every measured instance.
\(S_n\) and \(M_n\) use a common timing convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic behavior of \(r_n=S_n/M_n\) determines the separation-cost regime.

notation.meaning: total separation time on instance n
total master-solution time on instance n

children.title: Master-Size Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances exposing formulation growth during iterative constraint addition.

knowledge_statements.title: Master-Size Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Growth classification for restricted masters in iterative separation algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run lasting \(T\) iterations, let \(m_t\) denote the number of distinct active generated rows in the master after iteration \(t\), after any explicitly specified deletion policy. For a sequence of runs with \(T\to\infty\), master growth is bounded when \(\sup_T m_T<\infty\), sublinear when \(m_T\to\infty\) and \(m_T/T\to0\), and linear when \(0<\liminf m_T/T\leq\limsup m_T/T<\infty\). Superlinear growth is recorded when \(m_T/T\to\infty\). Duplicate rows and reactivated rows must be counted according to one fixed, disclosed convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Master growth is classified from the number of active generated rows as bounded, sublinear, linear, or superlinear in completed iterations.
assumptions_latex: The row-counting and deletion conventions are fixed across the benchmark sequence.
\(T\to\infty\) along the sequence being classified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal ratio \(m_T/T\), together with boundedness of \(m_T\), determines the stated growth regime.

notation.meaning: active generated-row count after iteration t

children.title: Lagrangian Relaxation Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Relaxation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark specification for dual bounds obtained by relaxing coupling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(z^*=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\in X\}\), where optimization over \(X\) is tractable relative to the full problem. A Lagrangian-relaxation benchmark fixes the multiplier method, initialization, stopping rules, tolerances, and resource limits for maximizing \(\theta(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\{c^Tx+u^T(Ax-b)\}\). Each run reports the best dual bound \(L_T=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\theta(u^t)\), any primal incumbent \(U_T\), the relative or absolute gap under a stated convention, subproblem counts, and time. Multiplier tuning and primal-recovery time are reported separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian benchmark fixes a multiplier algorithm and records dual-bound progress, primal recovery, gaps, subproblem work, timing, and termination.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\) and \(z^*\) is finite.
Each value \(\theta(u^t)\) is computed to the disclosed accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_T\leq z^*\leq U_T\) whenever \(U_T\) is the value of a feasible primal incumbent.

notation.meaning: best dual bound through iteration T

A direct decomposition reference is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Decomposition Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the variables be partitioned as \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_K)\), with local feasible sets \(X_k\), local objectives \(c_k^Tx_k\), and coupling system \(\sum_{k=1}^K A_kx_k=b\). A structural-decomposition benchmark provides this partition explicitly and fixes the master-subproblem protocol, parallelism, tolerances, and limits. It reports per-block dimensions and nonzeros, coupling-row count, load imbalance, subproblem and coordination times, communication volume, bound progression, and final feasibility. Comparisons are valid only when competing methods use the same decomposition or when decomposition-construction cost is separately included.

All cross-block restrictions are represented by the disclosed coupling system.

children.title: Column-Generation Benchmarks

knowledge_statements.title: Column-Generation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark specification for restricted-master optimization with pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the master problem \(\min\{\sum_{j\in J}c_j\lambda_j:\sum_{j\in J}a_j\lambda_j=b,\ \lambda_j\geq0\}\), with a large column set \(J\). A column-generation benchmark fixes an initial set \(J_0\), a restricted-master solver, a pricing oracle, tolerance \(\varepsilon\), and resource limits. At iteration \(t\), dual prices \(\pi^t\) define reduced costs \(c_j-(\pi^t)^Ta_j\). Columns with reduced cost below \(-\varepsilon\) are added to \(J_t\). Report restricted-master bounds, pricing bounds, generated and duplicate columns, pricing and master times, degeneracy indicators, and termination reason.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A column-generation benchmark fixes the restricted master and pricing oracle, then measures reduced costs, bounds, generated columns, degeneracy, timing, and termination.
assumptions_latex: The initial restricted master is feasible or a specified feasibility phase is used.
Pricing evaluates reduced costs consistently with the restricted-master dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If exact pricing finds \(c_j-(\pi^t)^Ta_j\geq-\varepsilon\) for every \(j\in J\), the restricted-master solution is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal under the stated convention.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports column generation or its benchmarking conventions.

children.title: Decomposition Coupling Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Coupling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic regimes measuring interaction among optimization blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decomposed instance \(n\), form the block-interaction graph \(G_n\): vertices are blocks, and two vertices are adjacent when some disclosed constraint contains variables from both blocks. Let \(K_n\) be the block count, \(E_n\) the edge set, and \(d_n=2|E_n|/[K_n(K_n-1)]\) for \(K_n>1\). Coupling is vanishing when \(d_n\to0\), persistent sparse when \(d_n\to0\) but the average degree has positive limit inferior, and dense when \(\liminf d_n>0\). The benchmark must additionally report coupling-row nonzeros because graph density alone does not measure numerical coupling strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling regimes use the block-interaction graph to distinguish vanishing, persistent sparse, and dense interaction, supplemented by coupling-row nonzeros.
assumptions_latex: \(K_n>1\) and the block partition is fixed before constructing \(G_n\).
Cross-block adjacency uses one disclosed constraint-incidence convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limits of \(d_n\) and \(2|E_n|/K_n\) determine the stated coupling regime.

children.title: Primal Solution Certificates
children.top_down_role: Feasible-solution evidence used to validate incumbent objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactly checkable feasible-solution and objective certificate for integer minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the rational-data problem \(z^*=\min\{c^Tx:Ax\geq b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\}\), a primal solution certificate is a rationally encoded vector \(\hat x\). Verification checks componentwise that \(\hat x\geq0\), that every component of \(\hat x\) is integral, and that \(A\hat x\geq b\), using exact arithmetic or certified interval arithmetic. If all checks pass, \(U=c^T\hat x\) is a valid primal upper bound. The certificate establishes feasibility and its stated objective value, but it establishes optimality only when accompanied by a valid lower-bound certificate with the same value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exactly checked nonnegative integer vector satisfying every constraint certifies feasibility and its objective as an upper bound, but not optimality by itself.
assumptions_latex: \(A\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(\hat x\) have finite rational encodings.
The optimization problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\hat x\geq b\) and \(\hat x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\) imply \(z^*\leq c^T\hat x\).
review_flags: The supplied primal-dual locators do not directly document integer-solution certificate verification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and upper-bound conclusion are mathematically appropriate, but no certificate-system source is supplied. The statement should also distinguish exact integrality checking from interval verification of inequalities.

children.title: Dual-Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence supporting lower or upper bounds on optimal objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-dual certificate providing a checkable lower bound for integer minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z^*=\min\{c^Tx:Ax\geq b,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\}\) with rational data, a dual-bound certificate is a rational vector \(y\) satisfying \(y\geq0\) and \(A^Ty\leq c\). Exact verification of these inequalities certifies \(L=b^Ty\) as a lower bound: every primal-feasible \(x\) also belongs to the nonnegative continuous relaxation, so weak duality gives \(L\leq c^Tx\). Consequently \(L\leq z^*\). Together with a primal certificate of value \(U\), it certifies the gap \(U-L\); equality \(U=L\) certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible rational dual vector for the continuous relaxation certifies a lower bound; matching it with a primal upper bound certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(y\) have finite rational encodings.
The primal variables are constrained by \(x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\geq0\) and \(A^Ty\leq c\) imply \(b^Ty\leq z^*\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 104

children.title: Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Evidence supporting the absence of feasible solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite split-tree certificate excluding every integer-feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\geq b,\ x\geq0\}\), an integer-infeasibility certificate is a finite rooted binary tree whose root represents \(P\). Each internal node chooses an integer-constrained coordinate \(i\) and integer \(k\), with children adding \(x_i\leq k\) and \(x_i\geq k+1\); these children cover every integer point of the parent. Every leaf supplies exact Farkas multipliers proving its associated linear system infeasible. Verification checks every split, every multiplier sign and equality, and each strict Farkas contradiction. If all leaves verify, then \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite tree of exhaustive integer splits, with an exact Farkas infeasibility certificate at every leaf, certifies integer infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) have finite rational encodings.
Every branching coordinate is required to be integral in the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Verified exhaustive splits and infeasible leaves imply \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\).
review_flags: No supplied locator supports split-tree integer-infeasibility certificates.
A source for exact leaf-level Farkas verification is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite split-tree construction plausibly certifies integer infeasibility, but no source supports the formulation. The conclusion uses P intersect Z^n, while the assumptions refer only to selected integer-constrained coordinates, leaving pure-integer versus mixed-integer scope unclear.

children.title: Certificate Robustness Cases
children.top_down_role: Instances stressing numerical scaling, serialization, or independent certificate checking.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Robustness Cases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for tolerance-based verification of optimization certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Certificate validity is not preserved by unchecked feasibility tolerances. For any \(\delta>0\), consider \(z^*=\min\{0x:x\geq1,\ x\in\mathbb Z_+\}=0\). The continuous dual requires \(0\leq y\leq0\), but an approximate verifier accepting dual violations up to \(\delta\) may accept \(y=\delta\) and report the false lower bound \(b^Ty=\delta>z^*\). Thus benchmark robustness cases must include coefficients near tolerances, scaling extremes, and independently recomputable rational witnesses. A certificate is accepted only after exact checking or outward-rounded interval checking proves every required sign, equality, integrality, and inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tolerance-only checking can validate false bounds; robust cases require near-boundary data and exact or outward-rounded verification of every certificate condition.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta>0\) is the verifier's accepted dual-feasibility violation.
The claimed lower bound is computed from the accepted approximate vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepting \(y=\delta\) yields \(\delta>z^*=0\), so tolerance acceptance alone is unsound.
review_flags: The counterexample is directly checkable, but no supplied source addresses certificate robustness conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally valid and failure_boundary is the correct role, but the broader robustness requirements and acceptance policy lack a cited numerical-verification source.

children.title: Single-Machine Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances, corpora, metrics, plus evaluation regimes for a single processing machine.

assumptions_latex: Jobs are nonpreemptive and all processing times are nonnegative.
At most one job may be processed at any time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting optimization problem is \(\min_{\pi} F(C_1(\pi),\ldots,C_n(\pi))\) over feasible single-machine schedules \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: processing time and completion time of job i
benchmark objective applied to completion times

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the benchmark-instance convention or objective family.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a common deterministic, nonpreemptive single-machine benchmark class with a configurable completion-time objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-machine benchmark instance consists of a finite job set \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), processing times \(p_i\geq 0\), optional release dates \(r_i\geq 0\), and an objective \(F:\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}\). A feasible schedule assigns each job \(i\) a start time \(S_i\geq r_i\) such that the half-open intervals \([S_i,S_i+p_i)\) are pairwise disjoint. Its completion times are \(C_i=S_i+p_i\), and its benchmark value is \(F(C_1,\ldots,C_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-machine benchmark schedules nonpreemptive jobs without overlap and evaluates the resulting completion times using a stated objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Machine Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is plausible, but no inspectable citation supports this particular single-machine instance convention or the unrestricted completion-time objective F.

children.title: Parallel-Machine Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances, corpora, metrics, plus evaluation regimes for multiple processing machines.

assumptions_latex: Jobs are nonpreemptive and processing times are nonnegative.
Each machine processes at most one job at a time, and each job uses at most one machine at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark optimum is \(\min_{a,S} F(C_1,\ldots,C_n)\) subject to eligibility and machine-capacity constraints.

notation.meaning: processing time of job i on machine k

review_flags: No supplied locator distinguishes identical, uniform, unrelated, and eligibility-constrained parallel-machine benchmark conventions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unrelated-machines model, which contains identical and uniform parallel machines as special cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parallel-machine benchmark instance consists of jobs \(J=\{1,ldots,n\}\), machines \(M=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), eligible pairs \(E\subseteq J\times M\), processing times \(p_{ik}\geq 0\) for \((i,k)\in E\), and an objective \(F\). A feasible schedule chooses \(a(i)\in M\) with \((i,a(i))\in E\) and start times \(S_i\), with no overlap among jobs assigned to the same machine. Completion times satisfy \(C_i=S_i+p_{i,a(i)}\), and the benchmark minimizes \(F(C_1,\ldots,C_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parallel-machine benchmark jointly assigns jobs to eligible machines, sequences jobs on each machine, and evaluates a declared completion-time objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Machine Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports choosing the unrelated-machines model as the benchmark definition. In addition, the job-set expression contains the malformed token `ldots` rather than `\ldots`.

children.title: Machine-Environment Transfer Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparisons of solver behavior as benchmark environments move from one machine to multiple machines.

assumptions_latex: The single- and parallel-machine instance families share a declared feature map.
Every reported algorithm is run under the same stopping rule and hardware-accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transfer is summarized by \(T(A)=\operatorname{Agg}_{I\in\mathcal{P}}\bigl(q(A,I)-q(A,\rho(I))\bigr)\), with aggregation and sign convention declared in advance.

notation.meaning: declared reduction to a single-machine instance
normalized performance score of algorithm A on instance I

review_flags: No supplied source fixes a canonical reduction, normalization, or aggregation rule for machine-environment transfer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes paired empirical transfer; it does not assert equivalence of the two scheduling environments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be parallel-machine instances and let \(\rho:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{S}\) map each instance to a declared single-machine counterpart preserving selected features. For algorithm \(A\), let \(q(A,I)\) be a dimensionless score, such as relative objective gap at a fixed resource budget. A machine-environment transfer comparison is the paired sample \(\{(q(A,I),q(A,\rho(I))):I\in\mathcal{P}\}\), together with the declared aggregate \(T(A)=\operatorname{Agg}_{I\in\mathcal{P}}(q(A,I)-q(A,\rho(I)))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transfer comparison pairs parallel-machine instances with declared single-machine counterparts and aggregates normalized within-pair performance differences under identical resource rules.
knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Environment Transfer Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction rho, normalized score q, pairing rule, and aggregate are methodological choices rather than a standard machine-environment transfer representation; they require a specific source.

children.title: Flow-Shop Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Benchmark corpora and evaluation regimes for flow-shop scheduling.

assumptions_latex: Every job visits every machine exactly once in the common machine order.
Operations are nonpreemptive, and each job and machine process at most one operation at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The makespan benchmark is \(\min C_{\max}\), where \(C_{\max}=\max_{i,k} C_{ik}\).

notation.meaning: processing time of job i on machine k

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the flow-shop benchmark definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the permutation-independent flow-shop feasibility model with makespan objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flow-shop benchmark instance has jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), machines \(M=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and processing times \(p_{ik}\geq 0\). Operation \((i,k)\) requires machine \(k\), and each job follows the common route \(1,\ldots,m\). A feasible nonpreemptive schedule respects \(C_{i,k}\geq C_{i,k-1}+p_{ik}\) and prevents overlap between operations using the same machine. For makespan benchmarks, the objective is \(\min C_{\max}\), with \(C_{\max}=\max_{i,k}C_{ik}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a flow shop, every job traverses all machines in one common order; the standard benchmark minimizes the final makespan.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Shop Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical flow-shop makespan formulation is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Job-Shop Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Benchmark corpora and evaluation regimes for job-shop scheduling.

assumptions_latex: Each job has a prescribed ordered route through its operations.
Operations are nonpreemptive, and machines have unit capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The makespan benchmark is \(\min C_{\max}\) over schedules satisfying job-route precedence and machine disjunctive constraints.

notation.meaning: required machine and processing time of operation o

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the job-shop benchmark definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the classical deterministic job shop with arbitrary job-specific machine routes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A job-shop benchmark instance consists of jobs \(J\), an ordered operation list \(O_i=(o_{i1},\ldots,o_{i\ell_i})\) for each job \(i\), a required machine \(\mu(o)\), and processing time \(p_o\geq 0\) for each operation. A feasible schedule assigns start times so successive operations of each job obey \(S_{o_{i,t+1}}\geq S_{o_{it}}+p_{o_{it}}\), while operations sharing a machine do not overlap. The standard makespan objective is \(\min C_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A job-shop benchmark schedules job-specific operation routes while enforcing route precedence and exclusive machine use, commonly minimizing makespan.
knowledge_statements.title: Job-Shop Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical job-shop formulation is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Open-Shop Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Benchmark corpora and evaluation regimes for open-shop scheduling.

assumptions_latex: Each job requires one nonpreemptive operation on every machine.
Each job and each machine can participate in at most one operation at a time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The open-shop makespan benchmark is \(\min C_{\max}\) without precedence constraints among operations of the same job.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the open-shop benchmark definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the classical open shop, where operation order within each job is a scheduling decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An open-shop benchmark instance has jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), machines \(M=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and one operation \((i,k)\) of duration \(p_{ik}\geq 0\) for every \((i,k)\in J\times M\). A feasible nonpreemptive schedule assigns start times so no two operations of one job overlap and no two operations on one machine overlap. There are no prescribed within-job precedence constraints. The standard objective is \(\min C_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open shop schedules one operation per job-machine pair with no prescribed job route, enforcing exclusive use of both jobs and machines.
knowledge_statements.title: Open-Shop Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical open-shop formulation is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Cross-Shop Benchmark Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparative behavior across flow-shop, job-shop, plus open-shop instance regimes.

assumptions_latex: Compared instances have matched numbers of jobs and machines and matched processing-time multisets.
Algorithms use identical resource budgets and objective normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each algorithm \(A\), report \(R_A^{r,s}=\operatorname{Agg}_{I}(q(A,I^{r})-q(A,I^{s}))\) for every declared regime pair \(r,s\).

notation.meaning: shop regimes flow, job, and open

review_flags: No supplied source establishes a canonical cross-shop matching or aggregation protocol.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matched empirical contrasts among flow-, job-, and open-shop regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each base data set \(I\), construct regime variants \(I^F,I^J,I^O\) with identical job count, machine count, and processing-time multiset, changing only the route constraints that define flow, job, or open shops. Given a normalized score \(q(A,I^r)\) measured under a common resource budget, a cross-shop comparison reports paired contrasts \(q(A,I^r)-q(A,I^s)\) and a prespecified aggregate \(R_A^{r,s}=\operatorname{Agg}_{I}(q(A,I^r)-q(A,I^s))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-shop comparisons hold basic instance data fixed, vary route constraints, and aggregate paired normalized performance differences between shop regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Shop Benchmark Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Matching processing-time multisets while changing route constraints does not by itself define a canonical cross-shop comparison, and the proposed score and aggregation protocol lack cited support.

assumptions_latex: The project precedence graph is acyclic.
Each activity is executed nonpreemptively in exactly one available mode.
Renewable resource capacities are constant over the scheduling horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resource-constrained project-scheduling benchmark minimizes \(C_{\max}=\max_{i\in V}(S_i+p_{i,m_i})\) over feasible mode choices and start times.

notation.meaning: duration and renewable-resource demand of activity i in mode m

review_flags: The cited section is provisional support; its exact project-scheduling variant requires full-text confirmation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the multimode renewable-resource-constrained project-scheduling model; the single-mode model is its special case.

source_refs.locator: Section 13. Application to Project Scheduling p. 165

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A project-scheduling benchmark consists of an acyclic precedence graph \(G=(V,A)\), activity modes \(M_i\), durations \(p_{im}\), renewable demands \(d_{imk}\), and capacities \(R_k\). A feasible schedule chooses \(m_i\in M_i\) and start times \(S_i\geq0\) such that \(S_j\geq S_i+p_{i,m_i}\) for \((i,j)\in A\), and \(\sum_{i:S_i\leq t<S_i+p_{i,m_i}}d_{i,m_i,k}\leq R_k\) for every resource \(k\) and time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A project-scheduling benchmark chooses activity modes and start times while respecting precedence and renewable-resource capacities, typically minimizing project makespan.

children.title: Timetabling Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Educational, examination, transport, plus event-timetabling corpora and evaluation regimes.

assumptions_latex: Events have fixed durations and declared feasible room-period assignments.
No room, instructor, or student group may attend overlapping assigned events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark minimizes \(\sum_{h\in H} w_h v_h(x)\) over assignments satisfying all hard constraints.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports a specific educational timetabling benchmark formulation or penalty convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a generic weighted-penalty educational timetabling benchmark with explicit hard and soft constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A timetabling benchmark specifies events \(E\), periods \(T\), rooms \(R\), feasible assignment sets \(D_e\subseteq T\times R\), hard conflict pairs \(K\subseteq E\times E\), and weighted soft violations \(v_h\). A feasible timetable chooses \(x_e=(t_e,r_e)\in D_e\) so conflicting events receive nonoverlapping periods and no room hosts overlapping events. Its objective is \(\min_{x}\sum_{h\in H}w_hv_h(x)\), with every hard constraint and penalty definition supplied by the instance format.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timetabling benchmark assigns events to allowed periods and rooms, enforces conflicts as hard constraints, and minimizes declared weighted soft violations.
knowledge_statements.title: Timetabling Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Educational timetabling formats differ materially in conflicts, room constraints, event duration, and penalty definitions. No source supports this selected generic formulation.

children.title: Rostering Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Personnel, shift, crew, plus service-rostering corpora and evaluation regimes.

assumptions_latex: Each worker has a declared set of feasible shifts or duty patterns.
Coverage requirements and all hard labor or contractual rules are instance data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark minimizes \(\sum_{i,s}c_{is}x_{is}+\sum_{k,t}(\alpha_{kt}u_{kt}+\beta_{kt}v_{kt})\) subject to roster feasibility and coverage balance.

notation.meaning: binary assignment of worker i to shift or pattern s
required coverage for skill k at time t

review_flags: No supplied locator supports a canonical rostering benchmark formulation, labor-rule set, or penalty scale.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a generic skill-based rostering model with penalized coverage deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rostering benchmark specifies workers \(N\), shifts or patterns \(S_i\), assignment costs \(c_{is}\), coverage coefficients \(a_{is,kt}\), and requirements \(b_{kt}\). Binary variables \(x_{is}\) satisfy each worker's hard assignment and labor constraints. Coverage balance is \(\sum_{i,s}a_{is,kt}x_{is}+u_{kt}-v_{kt}=b_{kt}\), where \(u_{kt},v_{kt}\geq0\). A standard objective minimizes assignment cost plus declared penalties \(\sum_{k,t}(\alpha_{kt}u_{kt}+\beta_{kt}v_{kt})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rostering benchmark assigns workers to feasible duties and minimizes assignment costs plus penalties for undercoverage and overcoverage.
knowledge_statements.title: Rostering Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The skill-based coverage-balance model is plausible, but no citation supports the selected duty representation, labor constraints, or deviation-penalty convention.

children.title: Schedule-Coverage Tradeoff Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Instances exposing tradeoffs between temporal placement quality and coverage quality.

assumptions_latex: Every schedule has a scalar quality cost and a scalar coverage shortfall measured on fixed scales.
All hard feasibility constraints are identical across compared schedules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark output is the nondominated set \(P=\{x\in X:\nexists y\in X,\ f(y)\leq f(x),\ g(y)\leq g(x),\ (f(y),g(y))\neq(f(x),g(x))\}\).
review_flags: No supplied source specifies the intended quality, coverage, dominance, or scalarization conventions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the schedule-coverage tradeoff by its Pareto set rather than a hidden weighted sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the schedules satisfying all hard constraints, let \(f(x)\) be schedule-quality cost, and let \(g(x)\geq0\) be coverage shortfall. Schedule \(y\) dominates \(x\) when \(f(y)\leq f(x)\), \(g(y)\leq g(x)\), and at least one inequality is strict. The benchmark output is the nondominated set \(P=\{x\in X:\nexists y\in X\text{ that dominates }x\}\), or an approximation evaluated by a declared multiobjective indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The benchmark treats schedule quality and coverage shortfall as separate objectives and reports nondominated feasible schedules or a declared approximation measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Schedule-Coverage Tradeoff Benchmarks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto-set representation fits the comparison leaf, but the quality, coverage, dominance, approximation, and evaluation conventions are not supported by a cited source.

children.title: Transportation Benchmarks

assumptions_latex: The transportation network is directed and finite.
Supplies balance demands, and all arc costs and capacities are declared instance data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The benchmark optimum is \(\min\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a:0\leq x_a\leq u_a,\ \operatorname{div}_x(v)=b_v\ \forall v\in V\}\).

notation.meaning: flow, capacity, and unit cost on arc a

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A transportation benchmark is a directed network \(G=(V,A)\) with integer or real supplies \(b_v\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), arc capacities \(u_a\geq0\), and unit costs \(c_a\). A feasible flow \(x\) satisfies \(0\leq x_a\leq u_a\) and \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\) for every \(v\in V\). The benchmark objective is \(\min\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transportation benchmark routes balanced supply to demand through a capacitated network while minimizing total linear shipping cost.

children.title: Resource-Allocation Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Capacity, assignment, budget, plus shared-resource allocation corpora.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark instance is finite and all capacities, demands, and costs are explicitly encoded.
Feasibility and objective values are evaluated using the same declared numerical tolerance for every solver.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solver output is benchmark-valid exactly when it satisfies the displayed capacity and demand constraints; its reported score is the displayed total allocation cost.

notation.meaning: allocation of resource r to activity j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite capacitated allocation instances, optionally represented as discrete network-optimization models.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.4 Discrete Network Optimization Problems p. 19
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A resource-allocation benchmark instance consists of finite sets of resources \(R\) and activities \(J\), capacities \(b_r\geq 0\), demands \(d_j\geq 0\), admissible pairs \(E\subseteq R\times J\), and costs \(c_{rj}\). Its feasible set is
\[X=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}:\sum_{j:(r,j)\in E}x_{rj}\leq b_r\ \forall r\in R,\quad \sum_{r:(r,j)\in E}x_{rj}\geq d_j\ \forall j\in J\right\}.\]
The benchmark objective is \(\min_{x\in X}\sum_{(r,j)\in E}c_{rj}x_{rj}\); an integral variant additionally requires \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{E}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark specifies capacities, demands, admissible allocations, and costs; valid solutions meet all constraints and are compared by total cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Allocation Benchmarks

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.4 Discrete Network Optimization Problems p. 19
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A coupled transport-allocation benchmark is a tuple \((F,X,T,A,Q,c_F,c_X)\), where \(F\) is a transportation-feasible set, \(X\) is a resource-allocation-feasible set, and \(T:F\to Q\) and \(A:X\to Q\) map decisions to a common finite-dimensional interface. Its feasible solutions are

children.title: Scheduling Relaxation Validation
children.top_down_role: Empirical validation of scheduling relaxations, their bounds, plus their instance-dependent strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Relaxation Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation certificate for a minimization scheduling formulation and its declared relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_I\) be the integer feasible set, let \(X_R\supseteq X_I\) be its declared relaxation, let \(c\) be the scheduling objective, and let \(\varepsilon\geq 0\). A relaxation-validation certificate is a tuple \((x_R,z_R,x_I,z_I)\) satisfying \(x_R\in X_R\), \(x_I\in X_I\), \(\lvert c(x_R)-z_R\rvert\leq\varepsilon\), \(\lvert c(x_I)-z_I\rvert\leq\varepsilon\), and \(z_R\leq z_I+\varepsilon\). If an independent optimality certificate establishes \(z_R=\min_{x\in X_R}c(x)\), then \(z_R\leq z^\star\), where \(z^\star=\min_{x\in X_I}c(x)\). Validation reports membership, objective-consistency, ordering, and relaxed-optimality failures separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validation checks relaxed and integral feasibility, recomputes their objectives, checks their ordering, and treats the relaxed value as a certified lower bound only when relaxed optimality is independently certified.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling formulation is a minimization problem with integer feasible set \(X_I\) and declared relaxation \(X_R\supseteq X_I\).
Objective values are recomputed using one declared tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple \((x_R,z_R,x_I,z_I)\) validates the submitted relaxed and integer points when the membership, objective-consistency, and ordering checks pass; it certifies a lower bound on \(z^\star\) only when optimality over \(X_R\) is independently certified.

notation.meaning: reported relaxed and integer objective values

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: relaxation validation uses feasibility, objective recomputation, and the minimization lower-bound relation

children.title: Scheduling Approximation-Guarantee Validation
children.top_down_role: Benchmark evidence concerning claimed approximation quality across scheduling regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Approximation-Guarantee Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori multiplicative guarantee validation for nonnegative minimization scheduling objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^\star\) be the optimum scheduling cost and let \(\varepsilon\geq 0\). A guarantee-validation certificate comprises a feasible schedule \(x\), its recomputed value \(U=c(x)\), a checkable lower-bound certificate establishing \(0\leq L\leq z^\star\), and a claimed factor \(\alpha\geq 1\). It passes when all constituent certificates are valid and \[U\leq\alpha L+\varepsilon.\] Consequently, \(U\leq\alpha z^\star+\varepsilon\). When \(L=0\), the ratio \(U/L\) is undefined, so the benchmark reports the additive inequality; a purely multiplicative guarantee from this certificate is available only when \(\varepsilon=0\) and \(U=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible schedule, a certified lower bound, and the checked inequality validate a multiplicative-plus-additive approximation guarantee; a zero lower bound does not itself define a ratio.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling objective is nonnegative and minimized over a finite nonempty feasible set.
The claimed approximation factor satisfies \(\alpha\geq 1\), and \(L\) is a certified lower bound on the optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The submitted schedule satisfies the validated guarantee \(U\leq\alpha z^\star+\varepsilon\) whenever feasibility, the lower-bound certificate, and \(U\leq\alpha L+\varepsilon\) are independently verified.

notation.meaning: certified lower bound on the optimum

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a feasible upper bound and certified lower bound imply a multiplicative-plus-additive minimization guarantee

children.title: Relaxation-Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance families exposing weak, tight, or unstable relaxation gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative integrality-gap classification for scheduling minimization instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\) with integer optimum \(z^\star(I)\) and relaxation optimum \(z_R(I)>0\), define \(g(I)=z^\star(I)/z_R(I)\geq 1\). Assign \(g(I)=+\infty\) when \(z_R(I)=0<z^\star(I)\), and assign \(g(I)=1\) when \(z_R(I)=z^\star(I)=0\). For a benchmark family \(\mathcal{I}\), let \(G=\sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}}g(I)\). The family is exact when \(G=1\), bounded but nonexact when \(1<G<+\infty\), and unbounded when \(G=+\infty\). If a numerical threshold \(\gamma\geq 1\) is declared, the statement that the family has gap at most \(\gamma\) means \(G\leq\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using explicit conventions for zero relaxation values, benchmark families are classified as exact, bounded but nonexact, or unbounded by the supremum of their integrality-gap ratios.
assumptions_latex: Each instance is a nonnegative minimization problem with finite integer optimum \(z^\star(I)\).
Its relaxation has a certified optimum \(z_R(I)\leq z^\star(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value \(G\) places every nonempty benchmark family into exactly one of the exact, bounded-but-nonexact, or unbounded regimes.

notation.meaning: supremal gap over the benchmark family

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integrality-gap regimes are defined from integer and relaxation optima

children.title: Guarantee-Violation Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Benchmark conditions associated with apparent failures of reported approximation guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Guarantee-Violation Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-checkable diagnostics for failed scheduling approximation-certificate checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a submitted schedule \(x\), reported value \(\widehat U\), certified lower bound \(L\), claimed factor \(\alpha\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq 0\), define \(D_F=[x\notin X_I]\), \(D_O=[\lvert c(x)-\widehat U\rvert>\varepsilon]\), \(D_L=[L\text{ lacks a valid certificate establishing }L\leq z^\star]\), and \(D_G=[c(x)-\alpha L>\varepsilon]\). The diagnostic output is \((D_F,D_O,D_L,D_G,r)\), where \(r=c(x)-\alpha L\). When \(D_F=D_O=D_L=0\) and \(D_G=1\), the submitted certificate fails its claimed guarantee test. This failure alone does not establish \(c(x)>\alpha z^\star+\varepsilon\), because \(L\) may be strictly smaller than \(z^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four checks distinguish infeasibility, a misreported objective, an invalid lower bound, and failure of the submitted lower-bound-based guarantee test; the last is not automatically a violation relative to the unknown optimum.
assumptions_latex: A minimization benchmark declares \(\alpha\), \(\varepsilon\geq 0\), a proposed certified lower bound \(L\), and a submitted pair \((x,\widehat U)\).
All feasibility, objective, and lower-bound-certificate checks are reproducible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagnostic vector localizes failures of feasibility, objective reporting, lower-bound certification, and the certificate inequality without overstating certificate failure as a proven violation relative to \(z^\star\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: diagnostic residuals separate independently verifiable certificate failures

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-oracle model for finite submodular set functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A value-oracle submodular instance consists of a finite ground set \(V\) and an oracle \(\mathcal{O}_f\) that returns \(f(S)\) for every queried \(S\subseteq V\), where
\[f(A)+f(B)\geq f(A\cup B)+f(A\cap B)\qquad\forall A,B\subseteq V.\]
Equivalently, for \(A\subseteq B\subseteq V\) and \(e\in V\setminus B\), the marginal values satisfy \(f(A\cup\{e\})-f(A)\geq f(B\cup\{e\})-f(B)\). The benchmark exposes no representation of \(f\) beyond \(\mathcal{O}_f\), and records each oracle invocation and queried set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A submodular function is accessed only through exact set-value queries, whose number is measured independently from running time.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Oracle Submodular Instances

For a directed graph \(G=(W,E,c;s,t)\) with \(c_e\geq 0\), define \(V=W\setminus\{s,t\}\) and
\[f(S)=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(S\cup\{s\})}c_e\qquad(S\subseteq V).\]
Then \(f\) is a submodular set function. A graph-representable benchmark instance supplies \(G\), the identification of \(V\), and the source-side convention; evaluating \(f(S)\) means summing capacities of arcs leaving \(S\cup\{s\}\). Any additional constant or modular term must be encoded and reported separately.
