children.title: Lower-Bound Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks focused on reported lower bounds relative to trusted references.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality lower-bound certificate for a minimization linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z^*=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\), let \(\hat y\) satisfy \(\hat y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\hat y\le c\). Then \(L=b^{\mathsf T}\hat y\) is an independently verifiable lower bound: every primal-feasible \(x\) satisfies \(L\le c^{\mathsf T}x\), and hence \(L\le z^*\) whenever the primal optimum is finite. Validation requires recomputing both dual feasibility and \(L\) from the recorded instance data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective value of any independently verified dual-feasible vector is a valid lower bound on a finite minimization optimum.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual use the displayed sign conventions.
\(\hat y\) passes exact dual-feasibility validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=b^{\mathsf T}\hat y\le z^*\).

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

children.title: Upper-Bound Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks focused on reported upper bounds relative to trusted references.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal objective upper-bound certificate for a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^*=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(P\) is the exact primal feasible set. If an independently checked candidate \(\hat x\) satisfies \(\hat x\in P\), then \(U=c^{\mathsf T}\hat x\) is a verifiable upper bound on the optimum: \(z^*\le U\). Validation requires recomputing feasibility and the objective from the instance data. If only relaxed feasibility is established, \(U\) is not an exact upper-bound certificate unless a separate correction argument is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective of an exactly primal-feasible minimization candidate is an upper bound; relaxed feasibility alone does not certify that bound.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem with nonempty feasible set \(P\).
\(\hat x\) passes exact primal-feasibility validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*\le U=c^{\mathsf T}\hat x\).

source_refs.locator: 5.2 The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 105

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 The Primal-Dual Algorithm p. 105

children.title: Dual-Bound Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency relationships between dual outputs and claimed bound values.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Bound Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency test for independently certified minimization bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a validated lower bound and \(U\) a validated upper bound for the same minimization instance. Exact consistency holds precisely when \(L\le U\). For tolerances \(\varepsilon_a,\varepsilon_r\ge0\), declared numerical consistency holds when \(L-U\le\varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_r\max\{1,|L|,|U|\}\). If \(L>U\) in exact arithmetic, at least one certificate, instance identifier, objective convention, or arithmetic computation is invalid. When \(U-L\le\varepsilon\), the certified absolute optimality gap is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid lower and upper bounds must be ordered; their difference also certifies the remaining absolute optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) and \(U\) refer to the same minimization instance and objective convention.
Both bounds were independently validated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le z^*\le U\), and therefore \(0\le U-z^*\le U-L\).

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact ordering and absolute-gap claims are standard and fit a consistency condition, but the cited primal-dual section does not specifically support the declared absolute-relative numerical consistency formula. Because that formula is part of the mathematical validation predicate and is protocol-dependent, a direct source or benchmark specification is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Certificate Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual exact optimality certificate for a standard linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,\ y\ge0\}\), a pair \((\hat x,\hat y)\) is an exact optimality certificate when both vectors are feasible and \(c^{\mathsf T}\hat x=b^{\mathsf T}\hat y\). Independent validation of these predicates proves that \(\hat x\) and \(\hat y\) are optimal and that their common value equals the optimum. Equality may equivalently be established by exact complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible primal and dual solutions with equal objective values independently certify both solutions as optimal.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual use the displayed mutually dual forms.
Feasibility and objective values are checked independently using certified arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}\hat x=b^{\mathsf T}\hat y=z^*\).

source_refs.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

source_witnesses.locator: 5.13 Primal-dual methods p. 72

children.title: Infeasibility Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation of solver outputs claiming that no feasible solution exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-type certificate for infeasibility of linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the system \(Ax\le b\) with unrestricted \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), a vector \(y\) is an exact infeasibility certificate when \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). These relations are independently checkable and imply that no \(x\) can satisfy \(Ax\le b\). Conversely, if the system is infeasible, such a vector exists. A numerical certificate must replace strict negativity by a certified separation from zero that dominates all stated arithmetic-error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative multiplier annihilating the constraint matrix and yielding a negative weighted right-hand side certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) are finite-dimensional real data.
The variable \(x\) is unrestricted in sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional Farkas certificate and its converse are correctly signed for the displayed system, and certificate fits the leaf. No source is supplied, however, and the numerical separation requirement additionally depends on an unspecified certified-arithmetic protocol.

children.title: Unboundedness Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation of solver outputs claiming that the objective is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-direction certificate for an unbounded minimization linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\), a pair \((x^0,d)\) certifies unboundedness below when \(Ax^0\ge b\), \(x^0\ge0\), \(Ad\ge0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Indeed, \(x^0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\), while \(c^{\mathsf T}(x^0+td)\to-\infty\). All feasibility, recession, and strict-descent predicates must be independently validated; a direction without a feasible base point does not certify unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible base point plus a feasible recession direction with negative cost certifies that a minimization problem is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: The linear program has the displayed minimization form.
Strict descent is established exactly or with a certified error margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}=-\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-base-point and improving-recession-direction certificate is mathematically correct for the displayed minimization LP, and certificate is the appropriate content kind. An authoritative recession-cone locator and a source for the certified strict-descent protocol are missing.

children.title: Status-Separation Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Cases testing whether infeasibility, unboundedness, plus ambiguous statuses remain distinguishable.

knowledge_statements.title: Status-Separation Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation of optimal, infeasible, and unbounded-below linear-program statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed exact minimization linear program, define three validated statuses: optimal when a feasible primal-dual pair has zero objective gap; infeasible when a valid alternative-system certificate is present; and unbounded below when a feasible point and a strict improving recession direction are present. No two of these statuses can simultaneously possess valid exact certificates. Thus simultaneous acceptance of two statuses diagnoses an error in the instance identity, sign convention, certificate checker, or arithmetic rather than a legitimate optimization outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact certificates for optimality, infeasibility, and unboundedness are mutually exclusive; accepting two statuses reveals a validation error.
assumptions_latex: All certificates concern identical exact instance data and objective sense.
Each component certificate has passed independent validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#\{s\in\{\mathrm{optimal},\mathrm{infeasible},\mathrm{unbounded}\}:s\text{ has a valid certificate}\}\le1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mutual-exclusivity property is correct under the stated identical-instance and exact-validation assumptions, and property fits the diagnostic leaf. No citation supports the combined status-alternative claim or fixes the precise certificate forms on which it depends.

children.title: Near-Boundary Misclassification
children.top_down_role: Numerically or structurally marginal cases associated with incorrect status reports.

assumptions_latex: The exact optimization instance has a well-defined status in \(\{\mathrm{feasible},\mathrm{infeasible},\mathrm{unbounded}\}\).
The validator uses absolute feasibility tolerance \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_{\tau}(I)\ne s_0(I)\) can occur only within the declared boundary regime \(0<\delta(I)\le \tau\).

notation.meaning: exact minimum constraint or certificate margin relevant to status separation

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes misclassification caused by accepting residuals that straddle an exact optimization-status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be an optimization instance, and let \(\delta(I)\ge 0\) be the smallest exact violation or certificate margin separating its true status \(s_0(I)\) from another status. A tolerance-based validator reports \(s_{\tau}(I)\) by treating every relevant residual of magnitude at most \(\tau\) as zero. Near-boundary misclassification is the event \(s_{\tau}(I)\ne s_0(I)\) with \(0<\delta(I)\le \tau\). Instances satisfying \(\delta(I)>\tau\) are outside this particular failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misclassification is near-boundary when the exact margin separating two statuses is positive but no larger than the validator's tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Boundary Misclassification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the proposed universal status-margin model. The exact status set also conflates feasibility with unboundedness, and the problem-class-specific residuals defining delta are not specified sufficiently to justify the claimed boundary.

assumptions_latex: The problem is minimization with nonnegative objective values.
The candidate \(x\) is independently verified feasible, and \(L>0\) is a verified lower bound on the optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\le \rho L\Rightarrow f(x)\le \rho f^*\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative validation for nonnegative minimization; additive or sign-indefinite objectives require a different certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f^*=\min\{f(y):y\in F\}\) with \(f(y)\ge 0\) for every \(y\in F\). To validate a claimed \(\rho\)-approximation, independently verify \(x\in F\), \(0<L\le f^*\), and \(f(x)\le \rho L\), where \(\rho\ge 1\). These checks certify \(f(x)\le \rho f^*\). Failure of any check rejects the certificate but does not by itself prove that the candidate lacks a \(\rho\)-approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution is certified rho-approximate when its value is at most rho times an independently verified positive lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Guarantee Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate is mathematically sufficient for nonnegative minimization and the content kind fits, but no inspectable source supports this approximation-validation rule in the benchmark context.

assumptions_latex: Each solver receives the same canonical instance and declared numerical policy.
Every returned solution or certificate can be checked independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A test fails when \(R_i\not\sim R_j\) for some \(i\ne j\), unless independent validation identifies an invalid result.

notation.meaning: problem-specific semantic equivalence relation on validated results

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares semantic outcomes, not solver-specific logs, internal states, or raw floating-point strings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \(I\), solvers \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\), and a semantic equivalence relation \(\sim\), run \(R_i=S_i(I)\) under matched limits and numerical policies. Independently validate every reported status, solution, objective value, and certificate. If all validated results satisfy \(R_i\sim R_j\) for every \(i,j\), record agreement. Otherwise emit the tuple \((I,R_1,\ldots,R_k)\) as a differential failure, annotated with which independent checks failed or which validated outcomes disagree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run multiple solvers on one canonical instance, validate their outputs independently, and flag any unexplained semantic disagreement.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Solver Differential Testing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A differential-testing source is required. The conclusion exempts disagreements when validation identifies an invalid result, whereas the stated algorithm treats failed independent checks as differential failures; the intended failure semantics must be resolved from a source.

assumptions_latex: Two formulations encode the same feasible objects through explicit maps.
Objective values and status meanings are preserved by those maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Validated outputs must satisfy \(R_P\sim_{\phi,\psi}R_Q\); otherwise the paired test exposes a formulation-dependent discrepancy.

notation.meaning: equivalence induced by the formulation maps

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires explicit correspondence between feasible objects and objectives; merely similar formulations are insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) have feasible sets \(F_P,F_Q\), with maps \(\phi:F_P\to F_Q\) and \(\psi:F_Q\to F_P\) preserving feasibility and objective value. Solve both formulations and independently validate results \(R_P,R_Q\). Compare statuses, mapped solutions, and objective values under the induced relation \(\sim_{\phi,\psi}\). Report failure if the validated results are not equivalent, including the formulations, maps, outputs, and numerical policies as a reproducible witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve two provably equivalent formulations and compare independently validated statuses, mapped solutions, and objective values.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Formulation Testing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the testing protocol. Feasibility and objective preservation alone do not fully specify status and certificate correspondence, so the hypotheses defining equivalent formulations require authoritative clarification.

assumptions_latex: The transformation has a specified relation between source and transformed optima.
Candidate solutions can be mapped between the two instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The test accepts exactly when validated outputs satisfy the transformation relation \(\mathcal R_T\).

notation.meaning: specified relation between corresponding validated results

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers transformations with known output relations, including relabeling, scaling, augmentation, or decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an instance \(I\), construct \(I'=T(I)\) together with a declared result relation \(\mathcal R_T\). Solve \(I\) and \(I'\), independently validate both outputs, and map their feasible solutions and certificates as prescribed by \(T\). Accept the test exactly when the validated statuses, mapped objective values, and certificates satisfy \(\mathcal R_T\); otherwise return \((I,I',R,R')\) and the violated component of \(\mathcal R_T\) as a failure witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transform an instance using a known semantic relation, solve both versions, and check that validated outputs obey that relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Transformation Testing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits the testing leaf, but the generic relation R_T leaves the actual status, objective, solution, and certificate obligations transformation-dependent. A metamorphic-testing source is needed.

children.title: Representation-Invariance Testing
children.top_down_role: Tests comparing equivalent encodings, layouts, formats, or data representations.

assumptions_latex: Each encoding decodes to the same exact mathematical instance.
Solver limits and validation tolerances are fixed across encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(E_1)=D(E_2)=I\Rightarrow R(E_1)\sim R(E_2)\) is the tested invariance condition.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tests invariance under semantically neutral serialization, ordering, naming, and exact coefficient representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be encodings with \(D(E_1)=D(E_2)=I\) under an exact decoder \(D\). Under identical resource limits and numerical policies, independently validated solver results should satisfy \(R(E_1)\sim R(E_2)\), where \(\sim\) compares status, feasibility, objective value, and certificate meaning rather than byte identity. A violation is representation-induced and must record both encodings, decoded equality, solver configuration, and validation outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different exact encodings of the same instance should produce semantically equivalent validated outcomes under matched policies.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Invariance Testing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The leaf is a testing procedure, while the record is classified as a property. Moreover, exact-equivalent encodings need not yield equivalent termination classifications under finite resource limits, so a source must specify the tested oracle and admissible outcome relation.

children.title: Precision-Sensitivity Testing
children.top_down_role: Tests comparing behavior across numeric precision levels and arithmetic formats.

assumptions_latex: A finite ordered set of arithmetic precisions is available.
All nonprecision settings and the exact decoded instance remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sensitivity is witnessed by \(R_{p_i}\not\sim R_{p_j}\) or by nonmonotone validated error as \(p_i<p_j\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Varies arithmetic precision while holding the decoded instance, stopping rules, tolerances, and resource policy fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For precision levels \(p_1<\cdots<p_m\), run the same decoded instance with identical nonprecision settings and obtain independently validated results \(R_{p_1},\ldots,R_{p_m}\). Record status, residuals, objective bounds, certificates, and termination reason. Report precision sensitivity if \(R_{p_i}\not\sim R_{p_j}\) for some \(i,j\), or if a declared validation error fails its expected monotonic relation as precision increases. Output the smallest tested precision pair witnessing the discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve one exact instance at several arithmetic precisions and report the smallest pair producing incompatible validated behavior.
knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Sensitivity Testing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No numerical-testing source is cited. Increasing arithmetic precision does not generally guarantee monotone validated error for a full solver, so the expected monotonic relation requires an explicitly sourced metric and algorithmic hypothesis.

children.title: Encoding-Precision Interactions
children.top_down_role: Tests targeting behavior caused jointly by data encoding choices and numeric precision.

assumptions_latex: Encodings preserve a common intended exact instance or have quantified perturbations.
At least two arithmetic precisions are tested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta\ne 0\) identifies behavior not attributable to encoding or precision alone under the chosen response metric.

notation.meaning: scalar validated response for encoding e and precision p

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a factorial second difference to separate joint encoding-precision effects from marginal effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose encodings \(e_1,e_2\), precisions \(p_1,p_2\), and a scalar validated response \(Y(e,p)\), such as residual, objective error, or failure indicator. Define \(\Delta=Y(e_1,p_1)-Y(e_1,p_2)-Y(e_2,p_1)+Y(e_2,p_2)\). Encoding and precision have no interaction for this response when \(\Delta=0\). A reproducible value \(\Delta\ne 0\), exceeding the declared measurement uncertainty, is evidence that their joint effect is not explained by their separate effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero factorial second difference shows that changing precision affects two encodings differently beyond their separate effects.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Precision Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The second difference is a standard two-factor interaction contrast, but no source is supplied and its interpretation depends on the response scale, replication, and uncertainty model. In particular, a failure indicator requires care beyond an unqualified scalar equality.

children.title: Representation-Induced Divergence
children.top_down_role: Cases where equivalent representations produce materially different outcomes.

assumptions_latex: Two encodings represent the same intended instance under a declared decoder.
Results are independently validated under matched resource and numerical policies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(E_1)=D(E_2)\) and \(R(E_1)\not\sim R(E_2)\) constitute a divergence witness.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates semantic divergence from harmless differences in logs, tie-breaking, or alternative optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Representation-induced divergence occurs when \(D(E_1)=D(E_2)\) for two encodings but independently validated results satisfy \(R(E_1)\not\sim R(E_2)\) under matched policies. The equivalence relation \(\sim\) must permit distinct optimal solutions having the same certified status and value. Thus divergence requires a discrepancy in validated status, feasibility, objective guarantee, certificate validity, or termination classification, not merely different search paths, identifiers, or byte-level outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divergence occurs when exact-equivalent encodings yield substantively incompatible validated results under the same testing policy.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Induced Divergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but no source establishes the proposed divergence criterion. The semantic equivalence relation and treatment of resource-limit termination must be specified authoritatively.

assumptions_latex: The relevant nonzero numerical data are finite real numbers.
A common physical or mathematical unit is used within each compared coefficient class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is in the declared large-dynamic-range regime exactly when \(\kappa_{\mathrm{data}}>K\).

notation.meaning: multiset of relevant nonzero coefficient magnitudes

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a benchmark regime; the threshold and coefficient classes must be declared before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be the multiset of absolute values of all relevant nonzero coefficients after fixing units and excluding structural zeros. Define \(\kappa_{\mathrm{data}}=\max M/\min M\). For a benchmark threshold \(K>1\), the instance has large dynamic range when \(\kappa_{\mathrm{data}}>K\). If coefficients belong to dimensionally distinct classes, compute the ratio separately within each class and declare the regime when at least one class exceeds its specified threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance has large dynamic range when the ratio of its largest to smallest relevant nonzero coefficient exceeds a declared threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Large Dynamic Range

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition defines a possible benchmark regime, but neither the coefficient classes nor threshold K have sourced conventions. The ratio is representation- and scaling-dependent even after fixing physical units, so its benchmark interpretation needs support.

children.title: Near-Degenerate Instances
children.top_down_role: Benchmark instances with nearly redundant, tied, singular, or weakly separated structures.

assumptions_latex: The instance depends continuously on numerical data in a normed parameter space.
A precisely specified ill-posed set \(\Sigma\) represents degeneracy or a status boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Near-degeneracy at scale \(\varepsilon\) is the predicate \(0<\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: set of degenerate or ill-posed data

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines proximity to a problem-specific degeneracy set in a declared data norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) denote the numerical data of an optimization instance in a normed space, and let \(\Sigma\) be the closed set of data for which the chosen regularity property fails or the exact status is not locally stable. The instance is near-degenerate at scale \(\varepsilon>0\) when \(0<\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\le\varepsilon\), where \(\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)=\inf_{z\in\Sigma}\|d-z\|\). The norm, data normalization, and set \(\Sigma\) are part of the test specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance is near-degenerate when its normalized data lie within a declared positive distance of the problem's degeneracy set.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Degenerate Instances

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distance-to-ill-posedness formulation is plausible, but the applicable degeneracy set, norm, normalization, and regularity property are problem-class-specific and unsupported by a cited condition-analysis source.

children.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases near thresholds used to classify feasibility.

assumptions_latex: Feasibility is expressed by inequalities \(g_i(x)\le 0\) and equalities \(h_j(x)=0\).
The validator uses a common absolute tolerance \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance changes at tolerance values in \(\{\max_i(g_i(x))_+,\max_j|h_j(x)|\}\), with the combined boundary \(\tau=r(x)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-tolerance form; scaled or relative residual tests have analogous boundaries after normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate \(x\), define \(r(x)=\max\{\max_i(g_i(x))_+,\max_j|h_j(x)|\}\). A tolerance validator accepts \(x\) as feasible exactly when \(r(x)\le\tau\). Hence \(\tau=r(x)\) is its feasibility-tolerance boundary: every \(\tau<r(x)\) rejects and every \(\tau\ge r(x)\) accepts. Candidates with \(r(x)\) close to the configured \(\tau\) are tolerance-sensitive and must retain unrounded residuals for independent validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate crosses the feasibility decision boundary when the configured tolerance reaches its maximum independently computed constraint residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No numerical-feasibility source is supplied. The maxima need nonempty index sets or explicit empty-family conventions, and the conclusion incorrectly suggests that both component residuals are acceptance-change values; with one common tolerance, the combined decision changes at their maximum r(x).

children.title: Optimality-Tolerance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases near thresholds used to classify optimality.

assumptions_latex: A minimization problem has feasible set \(F\), objective \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}\), and known reference value \(f^*\).
A validator accepts objective tolerance \(\tau_o\ge 0\) and computes a reported value \(\widehat f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validation result can change when the tolerance crosses an observed optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute objective-gap boundary for validating a reported minimizer against a trusted reference value.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate \(x\in F\), define the optimality validator by \(V_{\tau_o}(x)=1\) exactly when \(|\widehat f(x)-f^*|\le \tau_o\). If \(g(x)=|\widehat f(x)-f^*|>0\), then \(V_{\tau_o}(x)=0\) for every \(0\le \tau_o<g(x)\), while \(V_{\tau_o}(x)=1\) for every \(\tau_o\ge g(x)\). Thus \(\tau_o=g(x)\) is an optimality-tolerance boundary: an arbitrarily small tolerance change across it reverses the accepted optimality status without changing the instance or candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate switches from rejected to accepted exactly when the objective tolerance reaches its reported gap from the trusted optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Tolerance Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Tolerance-Sensitive Status Changes
children.top_down_role: Outcome changes associated with alternative tolerance settings.

assumptions_latex: Let \(d\ge 1\), let \(\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be the set of admissible tolerance vectors, and fix a norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
A deterministic validator maps each instance-output pair \((I,y)\) and tolerance vector \(\tau\in\mathcal{T}\) to a status \(C(I,y;\tau)\) in a finite set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A status change caused solely by changing \(\tau\) exposes tolerance-sensitive classification.

notation.meaning: validator status at tolerance vector tau

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status instability under tolerance changes with the instance, output, platform, and validator otherwise fixed.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((I,y)\) has a tolerance-sensitive status change at \(\tau^*\in\mathcal{T}\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(\tau^-,\tau^+\in\mathcal{T}\) such that \(\|\tau^- -\tau^*\|<\varepsilon\), \(\|\tau^+ -\tau^*\|<\varepsilon\), and \(C(I,y;\tau^-)\ne C(I,y;\tau^+)\). The instance, reported output, platform, and validation rules other than their numerical tolerances remain fixed. Such a point is a classification failure boundary when the benchmark specification does not determine a unique status throughout any admissible neighborhood of \(\tau^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A status is tolerance-sensitive at an admissible tolerance vector when arbitrarily close admissible tolerances assign different classifications to the same fixed instance and output.
knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Sensitive Status Changes

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Integer Overflow
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by arithmetic values exceeding supported integer ranges.

assumptions_latex: Let \(w\ge 2\) be an integer. Signed \(w\)-bit two's-complement arithmetic represents exactly the integers in \(R_w=[-2^{w-1},2^{w-1}-1]\).
An implementation evaluates integer addition using wraparound modulo \(2^w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact positive sum can be represented as a negative value and reverse a comparison.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete wraparound counterexample for fixed-width signed integer arithmetic.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=2^{w-1}-1\). The exact sum of the representable operands \(M\) and \(1\) is \(M+1=2^{w-1}\notin R_w\). Under the assumed wraparound arithmetic, \(\operatorname{fl}_w(M+1)=-2^{w-1}\). Consequently, the mathematically true predicate \(M+1>0\) is evaluated as false when the comparison uses the wrapped result. Any combinatorial algorithm that accumulates weights or capacities and branches on this sign can therefore select a different branch from its exact-integer specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a signed word of at least two bits, adding one to the largest representable integer wraps to the smallest negative integer and can reverse an algorithmic comparison.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer Overflow

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Floating-Point Precision Loss
children.top_down_role: Outcome degradation caused by rounding, cancellation, or insufficient floating-point precision.

assumptions_latex: Floating-point arithmetic rounds to nearest with unit roundoff \(u\).
Choose a representable positive number \(a\) whose successor spacing exceeds \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Distinct exact quantities can become identical in floating-point arithmetic and invalidate a strict comparison.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absorption counterexample showing loss of a small objective or distance increment.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the distance from \(a\) to the next larger floating-point number is greater than \(2\), rounding to nearest gives \(\operatorname{fl}(a+1)=a\), although the exact inequality \(a+1>a\) holds. Hence the computed increment \(\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(a+1)-a)\) equals \(0\) rather than \(1\). A shortest-path, local-search, or bound-update implementation that tests whether this computed quantity is strictly positive may therefore suppress a genuine improvement solely because the working precision cannot resolve the increment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At sufficiently large magnitude, adding one may leave a floating-point value unchanged, hiding a genuine strict improvement.
knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Precision Loss

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Fixed-Width Accumulator Failures
children.top_down_role: Cases exposing range limits in counters, sums, costs, capacities, or indices.

assumptions_latex: An accumulator uses signed \(w\)-bit integers with representable range \(R_w=[-2^{w-1},2^{w-1}-1]\).
Each summand \(a_i\) is individually representable and the accumulator wraps modulo \(2^w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Individually valid inputs do not prevent failure when an intermediate partial sum leaves \(R_w\).

notation.meaning: exact partial sum after k terms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intermediate-sum range boundary for fixed-width objective, capacity, or cost accumulation.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The fixed-width accumulation is exact through step \(k\) only if every exact partial sum \(S_j=\sum_{i=1}^j a_i\) belongs to \(R_w\) for \(1\le j\le k\). If some first index \(j\) satisfies \(S_j\notin R_w\), then wraparound yields \(\widehat S_j\equiv S_j\pmod{2^w}\) with \(\widehat S_j\ne S_j\). Later cancellation may place the final exact total back in \(R_w\), but it does not restore correctness of branches, bounds, or comparisons already computed from \(\widehat S_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-width sum fails at the first out-of-range partial sum, even when every input and the final exact total are representable.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Width Accumulator Failures

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Precision-Loss Propagation
children.top_down_role: How local numeric degradation affects classifications, objectives, bounds, or certificates.

assumptions_latex: A computation has exact scalar intermediates \(z_k=\phi_k(z_{k-1})\) and computed intermediates \(\widehat z_k=\phi_k(\widehat z_{k-1})+\delta_k\).
Each map \(\phi_k\) is Lipschitz on the relevant domain with constant \(L_k\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local arithmetic errors propagate according to a product-sum bound and may be amplified by later operations.

notation.meaning: local rounding error at step k
Lipschitz constant of the kth update

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic forward-error propagation for a scalar chain of finite-precision updates.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(e_k=|\widehat z_k-z_k|\), Lipschitz continuity and the triangle inequality give \(e_k\le L_k e_{k-1}+|\delta_k|\). Iteration yields \[e_n\le \left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}L_j\right)e_0+\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\delta_i|\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}L_j.\] Thus errors introduced early are multiplied by all subsequent sensitivity factors. If several relevant products exceed \(1\), small local precision losses can become large enough to reverse a discrete comparison or termination test downstream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each local numerical error is multiplied by the sensitivity of later updates, so small early errors can alter downstream discrete decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Loss Propagation

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

assumptions_latex: Two conforming platforms execute the same deterministic source program and input but may use different permitted evaluation precisions, contraction rules, or reduction orders.
The program contains a branch whose floating-point comparison lies within the resulting rounding uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Permitted platform arithmetic can produce different traces, outputs, or reported statuses.

notation.meaning: exact real value of the branch expression

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-platform divergence caused by permitted differences in finite-precision evaluation.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let platforms \(p\) and \(p'\) compute approximations \(\widehat q_p\) and \(\widehat q_{p'}\) to the same exact branch quantity \(q\), with valid error bounds \(|\widehat q_p-q|\le e_p\) and \(|\widehat q_{p'}-q|\le e_{p'}\). If the comparison threshold \(t\) lies in both uncertainty intervals, the guarantees permit \(\widehat q_p<t\) and \(\widehat q_{p'}\ge t\). The executions may then take different branches, so \(R_p(I)\ne R_{p'}(I)\) despite identical source code and input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a branch threshold lies inside platform-specific rounding uncertainty, conforming platforms may follow different traces and report different results.
knowledge_statements.title: Platform-Dependent Numerical Behavior

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Nontermination
children.top_down_role: Runs that fail to reach a terminal solver status.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic algorithm induces states \(s_0,s_1,\ldots\) through a transition map \(T\), with \(s_{k+1}=T(s_k)\).
A terminal-state predicate \(H\) specifies successful or declared unsuccessful termination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An infinite execution avoiding \(H\) is nonterminating.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition-system definition for deterministic combinatorial optimization implementations.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The execution from \(s_0\) is nonterminating if it defines \(s_k\) for every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and satisfies \(H(s_k)=0\) for every \(k\). This definition excludes merely slow executions that eventually reach a terminal state. For benchmark observation under a finite resource limit \(B\), failure to terminate by \(B\) is only a censored observation of nontermination unless an invariant, repeated deterministic state, or other certificate establishes that no later state can satisfy \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nontermination is an infinite valid execution that never reaches a terminal state; exceeding a finite timeout alone does not prove it.
knowledge_statements.title: Nontermination

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Algorithmic Cycling
children.top_down_role: Runs that repeatedly revisit states, bases, partitions, or configurations.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic algorithm has a state space \(S\), a transition map \(T:S\to S\) on complete states including all tie-breaking and internal control data, and a terminal-state predicate \(H:S\to\{0,1\}\).
Starting from \(s_0\in S\), every nonterminal state satisfies \(s_{k+1}=T(s_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repetition of a nonterminal complete state forces an infinite periodic execution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated-state certificate for cycling in a deterministic state-transition implementation.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose there exist indices \(0\le i<j\) such that \(s_i=s_j\) and \(H(s_k)=0\) for every integer \(k\) with \(i\le k<j\). Determinism implies \(s_{i+r}=s_{j+r}\) for every \(r\ge0\). Hence the execution repeats with period \(p=j-i\) and never terminates. The pair \((i,j)\), together with the recorded complete states and verified transitions \(s_{k+1}=T(s_k)\) for \(i\le k<j\), is a finite certificate of algorithmic cycling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a deterministic implementation, repeating the same complete state after a nonterminal segment certifies that the intervening cycle will recur forever.
knowledge_statements.title: Algorithmic Cycling

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Progress Stalling
children.top_down_role: Runs that continue executing while producing negligible measurable progress.

assumptions_latex: An iterative algorithm has a state space \(S\) and produces states \(s_k\in S\) for \(k\in\mathbb{N}\).

A nonnegative progress measure \(P:S\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) is specified, smaller values represent progress, and termination requires \(P(s_k)\le\varepsilon\) for a prescribed threshold \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Persistent failure to decrease \(P\) detectably while it remains above \(\varepsilon\) constitutes progress stalling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable stalling condition relative to a declared progress measure and threshold.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a prescribed observation-window length \(m\ge1\) and detectable-decrease threshold \(\eta>0\), progress stalls at iteration \(k\) when \(P(s_k)>\varepsilon\) and \(P(s_k)-P(s_{k+r})<\eta\) for every integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le m\). Infinite stalling occurs if there is an index \(k_0\) such that \(P(s_k)>\varepsilon\) and \(P(s_k)-P(s_{k+1})<\eta\) for every \(k\ge k_0\). This condition does not require exact state repetition and therefore distinguishes stalling from cycling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Progress stalls when the declared measure remains above its termination threshold but fails to decrease by the detectable amount over the specified observation window.
knowledge_statements.title: Progress Stalling

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Termination-Detection Failures
children.top_down_role: Cases where stopping logic fails to recognize completion or lack of progress.

assumptions_latex: A specification defines a true terminal predicate \(H:S\to\{0,1\}\).
An implementation uses a computed predicate \(\widehat H:S\to\{0,1\}\), possibly from rounded residuals, counters, or distributed state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disagreement between \(H\) and \(\widehat H\) is a termination-detection failure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: False-positive and false-negative detection relative to a specified terminal predicate.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a reachable state \(s\), a false-positive termination detection occurs when \(\widehat H(s)=1\) but \(H(s)=0\); the implementation stops before the specified terminal condition holds. A false-negative detection occurs when \(\widehat H(s)=0\) but \(H(s)=1\); the implementation continues after termination is warranted. The failure boundary is the set \(\{s\in S:H(s)\ne\widehat H(s)\}\), including states where rounding, stale data, or counter overflow changes the implemented predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Termination detection fails whenever the implemented stopping predicate disagrees with the specification, causing either premature stopping or unnecessary continuation.
knowledge_statements.title: Termination-Detection Failures

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2.1 Termination Properties of the Simplex Method p. 187
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

assumptions_latex: For each instance-output pair \((I,y)\), a benchmark specification assigns a reference status \(C^*(I,y)\) in a finite status set \(S\).
The tested implementation reports \(\widehat C(I,y)\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A mismatch between reported and reference statuses is an incorrect status classification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark-oracle definition covering optimal, feasible, infeasible, unbounded, unknown, and error statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incorrect status classification occurs precisely when \(\widehat C(I,y)\ne C^*(I,y)\). A false assertion is a mismatch with \(\widehat C(I,y)\in\{\mathrm{optimal},\mathrm{feasible},\mathrm{infeasible},\mathrm{unbounded}\}\), because it claims a mathematical property not assigned by the reference. A false refusal is a mismatch with \(\widehat C(I,y)\in\{\mathrm{unknown},\mathrm{error}\}\) while \(C^*(I,y)\) assigns a conclusive status. The comparison is meaningful only when both classifiers use the same instance semantics, tolerances, and status vocabulary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classification is incorrect when an implementation's status differs from the benchmark reference under the same semantics, tolerances, and status vocabulary.
knowledge_statements.title: Incorrect Status Classification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The benchmark-oracle mismatch definition is coherent and the definition kind fits the topic, but the record supplies no citation at all. Its expanded status taxonomy and false-assertion versus false-refusal classification require an inspectable authoritative source before candidate-review acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Solution or Certificate Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational validity boundary for optimization-solver outputs checked by an independent verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance be \(x\), its feasible set be \(F(x)\), and \(V(x,y,c)\in\{0,1\}\) be an independent verifier for proposed solution \(y\) and certificate \(c\). An output \((s,y,c)\), with status \(s\), crosses the invalid-output boundary if it reports feasibility or optimality while \(y\notin F(x)\), if its claimed certificate satisfies \(V(x,y,c)=0\), or if it reports infeasibility or unboundedness without a certificate accepted by the corresponding status verifier. Numerical tolerances used by every verifier must be fixed before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver output is invalid when its claimed solution is infeasible, its certificate fails independent verification, or its terminal status lacks a valid certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)\) and all certificate verifiers are specified independently of the tested solver.
All numerical acceptance tolerances are fixed before testing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Invalid}(s,y,c;x)=1\) whenever any asserted status or certificate fails its prescribed independent check.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the terminal container, but no cited source supports the proposed verifier model or the claim that every infeasibility or unboundedness report must carry a certificate accepted by a corresponding verifier. That requirement is solver and problem-class dependent, so source uncertainty affects the mathematical scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Performance Cliffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abrupt resource degradation under small, declared changes in instance size or structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an algorithm, resource statistic \(R(x)>0\), instance metric \(d\), neighborhood radius \(\varepsilon>0\), and cliff factor \(C>1\). A performance cliff occurs on a benchmark domain \(D\) when there exist \(x,y\in D\) with \(d(x,y)\leq\varepsilon\) but \(R(y)/R(x)\geq C\). For a size-indexed family \((x_n)\), an asymptotic cliff occurs when \(R(x_{n+1})/R(x_n)\) is unbounded along a subsequence. Timeouts are assigned the predetermined censoring value or treated separately, never silently discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A performance cliff is a large or unbounded resource increase caused by a small declared change in an otherwise comparable instance.
assumptions_latex: \(R\), \(d\), \(\varepsilon\), and \(C\) are fixed before examining results.
Compared runs use the same resource-accounting and timeout policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x,y\in D:\ d(x,y)\leq\varepsilon\ \wedge\ R(y)\geq C R(x)\) certifies a finite-scale cliff.

notation.meaning: measured time, memory, work, or another fixed resource statistic

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local topic match, but the finite-scale ratio criterion and the asymptotic adjacent-instance ratio criterion are bespoke definitions without cited support. A source is needed to justify these precise notions of a performance cliff and their treatment of censored runs.

children.title: Nondeterministic Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures whose occurrence or output varies across nominally identical runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondeterministic Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intermittent validity or progress failure under repeated nominally identical executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed instance \(x\), configuration \(c\), random seed \(r\), and declared environment \(e\), let \(Y\) be the run outcome induced only by uncontrolled execution variation. Let \(G(Y)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate termination with a valid status and output. A nondeterministic failure regime exists when \(0<\Pr[G(Y)=0]<1\): identical declared inputs sometimes pass and sometimes fail. Estimation must report the repetition count and the empirical failure frequency rather than replacing repeated outcomes by a single favorable run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondeterministic failure occurs when nominally identical runs have both positive success probability and positive failure probability.
assumptions_latex: The instance, configuration, seed, and declared environment are identical across repetitions.
Outcome validity is decided by a fixed predicate \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\Pr[G(Y)=0]<1\) identifies an intermittent nondeterministic failure regime.

notation.meaning: outcome of a nominally identical run

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, and the variables are introduced consistently. However, no source supports modeling uncontrolled execution variation by a probability law or defining the regime exactly by a failure probability strictly between zero and one.

children.title: Concurrency Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures arising from parallel execution, shared state, scheduling, or synchronization.

knowledge_statements.title: Concurrency Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safety or progress failure caused by an admissible parallel execution schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Model a parallel algorithm by states \(S\), admissible schedules \(\Sigma_p\) for \(p\geq2\) workers, a safety invariant \(I:S\to\{0,1\}\), and a progress predicate \(P\). A concurrency failure exists if some \(\sigma\in\Sigma_p\) reaches a state \(s\) with \(I(s)=0\), or produces an infinite execution for which \(P\) is never satisfied, while every admissible serial execution on the same input terminates with the invariant preserved. This definition includes deadlock, livelock, lost updates, and corrupted shared state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concurrency fails when an admissible parallel schedule violates safety or progress although the corresponding serial executions remain correct.
assumptions_latex: Parallel and serial executions start from the same input state.
Admissible schedules and the safety and progress predicates are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\sigma\in\Sigma_p\) causing \(\neg I\) or permanent \(\neg P\) establishes a concurrency failure.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected kind fits the failure-regime leaf, but the safety/progress model has no supporting citation. In particular, satisfaction of a state predicate P is not by itself a complete liveness semantics, and the serial-correctness restriction is not inherent in every standard definition of concurrency failure.

children.title: Race-Condition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Workloads that expose timing-sensitive access to shared data or solver state.

knowledge_statements.title: Race-Condition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schedule-sensitive failure arising from unsynchronized conflicting accesses to shared state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two concurrent operations access the same shared location, with at least one operation writing, and suppose no synchronization order requires one access to precede the other. This conflicting pair constitutes a race. It forms a race-condition failure regime when two admissible schedules \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\) order the pair differently and yield observably inequivalent outcomes \(Y(\sigma_1)\not\sim Y(\sigma_2)\), with at least one outcome violating validity or progress. The equivalence relation \(\sim\) must incorporate all permitted numerical and ordering tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A race-condition regime exists when unsynchronized conflicting accesses admit schedules with inequivalent outcomes, at least one of which is invalid or nonprogressing.
assumptions_latex: The memory and synchronization semantics determine which schedules are admissible.
Outcome equivalence \(\sim\) and validity are fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(\sigma_1)\not\sim Y(\sigma_2)\) after opposite orderings of a conflicting pair certifies schedule-sensitive behavior.

notation.meaning: admissible schedules ordering conflicting accesses differently

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement defines a race-condition failure regime only when at least one inequivalent outcome violates validity or progress, but the conclusion says that inequivalence alone certifies schedule-sensitive behavior. That conclusion does not certify the stated failure regime. A supporting source is also absent, so the intended race semantics and corrected certification criterion cannot be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Parallel Reproducibility
children.top_down_role: Repeatability of results across thread counts, schedules, platforms, or execution orders.

assumptions_latex: The instance, configuration, seed, worker count, and declared environment are fixed.
The equivalence relation \(\sim\) is fixed and includes declared numerical tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall \sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\Sigma_p,\;Y(x,c,r,p,e,\sigma_1)\sim Y(x,c,r,p,e,\sigma_2)\).

notation.meaning: admissible schedules for the fixed worker count
observable status, solution, objective, and certificate output

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schedule-invariant outcome condition for a fixed parallel algorithm configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance \(x\), algorithm configuration \(c\), seed \(r\), worker count \(p\), declared environment \(e\), admissible schedule set \(\Sigma_p\), and acceptable-outcome equivalence relation \(\sim\). Parallel reproducibility holds exactly when \(Y(x,c,r,p,e,\sigma_1)\sim Y(x,c,r,p,e,\sigma_2)\) for all \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\in\Sigma_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel execution is reproducible when all admissible schedules produce equivalent status, objective, certificate, and solution outputs under fixed declared conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Reproducibility
Toy-Instance Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Benchmark distortion caused by excessive weight on instances below a declared difficulty threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) carry evaluation weights \(w_i\geq0\) summing to one, and let \(T\subseteq B\) be the instances classified as toy-sized by a predeclared difficulty rule. Toy-instance dominance at level \(\alpha\) occurs when \(\sum_{i\in T}w_i\geq\alpha\). It becomes an evaluation failure when some algorithms \(a,b\) satisfy \(S_B(a)>S_B(b)\) but \(S_{B\setminus T}(a)<S_{B\setminus T}(b)\), using renormalized weights on the non-toy subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Toy instances dominate when they receive excessive benchmark weight and reverse an algorithm ranking relative to the non-toy instances.
assumptions_latex: Toy status and the threshold \(\alpha\) are declared before scoring.
Subset scores use the same metric and renormalized benchmark weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in T}w_i\geq\alpha\) together with a ranking reversal identifies toy-dominance failure.

notation.meaning: score of algorithm a on instance set D

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role matches the leaf, but neither the threshold-weight definition nor the additional ranking-reversal requirement has cited support. The title could denote excessive toy-instance weight without requiring a reversal, so a source is needed to establish the intended exact boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Obsolete or Saturated Corpora
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of benchmark discrimination after instances cease to challenge contemporary algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a corpus, \(\mathcal A\) a declared comparison class, and \(L_B(a)\) its aggregate loss under a fixed resource budget. The corpus is \(\varepsilon\)-saturated for \(\mathcal A\) when \(\max_{a,b\in\mathcal A}|L_B(a)-L_B(b)|\leq\varepsilon\). It is obsolete relative to target distribution \(Q\) when it is saturated while \(\max_{a,b\in\mathcal A}|L_Q(a)-L_Q(b)|>\varepsilon\). Thus the corpus cannot discriminate differences that remain material on the target population.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A corpus is obsolete when it barely distinguishes current algorithms although those algorithms still differ materially on the target population.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm class, resource budget, loss, and tolerance \(\varepsilon\) are fixed beforehand.
Benchmark and target losses use compatible validity and timeout rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diam}L_B(\mathcal A)\leq\varepsilon<\operatorname{diam}L_Q(\mathcal A)\) identifies obsolescence relative to \(Q\).

notation.meaning: aggregate benchmark loss of algorithm a

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits a benchmark failure boundary, but the proposed definition equates obsolescence with small loss diameter on the corpus plus a larger target-distribution diameter. This is a plausible operational criterion rather than a standard consequence, and no source supports its exact scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Instance Duplication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ranking distortion from undisclosed repeated or equivalently transformed benchmark instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) and let \(\equiv\) be a declared equivalence relation identifying exact duplicates or transformations that preserve the tested optimization content. Hidden duplication occurs when some equivalence class has multiplicity greater than one but multiplicities are undisclosed in scoring. It becomes an evaluation failure if the ordinary instance-weighted scores rank algorithms \(a,b\) differently from scores assigning equal total weight to every equivalence class. Duplicate detection and class balancing must precede final aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hidden duplication fails evaluation when undisclosed equivalent instances receive repeated weight and alter the algorithm ranking compared with class-balanced scoring.
assumptions_latex: The equivalence relation \(\equiv\) preserves the optimization content relevant to evaluation.
Both scoring rules use the same per-instance metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{instance}}(a,b)\neq\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{class}}(a,b)\) certifies duplication-induced ranking distortion.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and topic alignment are appropriate. A source is required for the content-preserving equivalence criterion, equal-total-weight class correction, and use of ranking reversal as the precise evaluation-failure boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Unrepresentative Generator Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-induced evaluation bias relative to a declared target instance population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_G\) be the distribution induced by a benchmark generator, \(Q\) the declared target distribution, and \(\ell(a,x)\in[0,1]\) the evaluation loss. For algorithm class \(\mathcal A\), the generator is \(\varepsilon\)-unrepresentative when \(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}|\mathbb E_{P_G}\ell(a,X)-\mathbb E_Q\ell(a,X)|>\varepsilon\). A ranking failure occurs when some \(a,b\in\mathcal A\) are ordered oppositely by their expected losses under \(P_G\) and \(Q\). Generator parameters must be included in the definition of \(P_G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generator is unrepresentative when algorithm risks or rankings under its output distribution materially differ from those under the declared target population.
assumptions_latex: \(P_G\), \(Q\), \(\mathcal A\), \(\ell\), and \(\varepsilon\) are specified independently of observed rankings.
The loss is measurable and bounded in \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}|R_{P_G}(a)-R_Q(a)|>\varepsilon\) establishes distributional unrepresentativeness.

notation.meaning: instance distribution induced by the generator
expected loss of algorithm a under distribution P

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distributional formula is internally coherent and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but it is a particular uniform-risk discrepancy criterion over an algorithm class. No cited source establishes that this criterion, rather than a distribution distance or task-specific representativeness test, is the intended definition.

children.title: Metric Gaming
children.top_down_role: Evaluation practices that improve reported metrics without corresponding algorithmic value.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Gaming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Improvement of the reported metric at the expense of declared target utility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(a)\) be a benchmark metric to maximize and \(U(a)\) the independently declared target utility. Metric gaming is possible when the metric is not order-preserving for utility: there exist admissible algorithms \(a,b\) such that \(M(a)>M(b)\) but \(U(a)<U(b)\). It becomes an observed evaluation failure when selection or tuning chooses \(a\) over \(b\) because of \(M\), thereby decreasing \(U\). Validity failures cannot be offset by superior metric values unless the protocol explicitly defines such a tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric gaming occurs when benchmark-driven selection improves the reported score while worsening independently declared target utility.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark metric and target utility are declared before algorithm selection.
Compared algorithms satisfy the same validity requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(a)>M(b)\ \wedge\ U(a)<U(b)\) demonstrates metric-utility misalignment.

notation.meaning: reported benchmark metric for algorithm a

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits Metric Gaming, but the exact order-reversal definition and independently declared scalar utility model have no cited support. A source is needed to distinguish metric misalignment from observed gaming caused by adaptive selection or strategic optimization.

children.title: Benchmark Overfitting
children.top_down_role: Solver design or tuning specialized excessively to a fixed benchmark corpus.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Overfitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive benchmark selection producing a material fresh-sample generalization gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) be a repeatedly inspected benchmark, \(\mathcal A\) a candidate class, and \(\widehat a\) an algorithm selected adaptively using results on \(B\). For bounded loss \(\ell\), define \(\widehat R_B(a)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(a,X_i)\) and target risk \(R_Q(a)=\mathbb E_Q\ell(a,X)\). Benchmark overfitting at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) occurs when \(|R_Q(\widehat a)-\widehat R_B(\widehat a)|>\varepsilon\), as estimated on an independent fresh sample from \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benchmark overfitting occurs when adaptively selected performance on a reused corpus differs materially from performance on independent target-distribution instances.
assumptions_latex: Benchmark reuse or inspection influences selection of \(\widehat a\).
Fresh evaluation instances are independent draws from the declared target distribution \(Q\).
The loss is measurable and bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|R_Q(\widehat a)-\widehat R_B(\widehat a)|>\varepsilon\) identifies benchmark overfitting at tolerance \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: algorithm adaptively selected using benchmark results

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record appropriately uses a failure boundary and gives a coherent empirical-versus-target risk gap. However, no source supports the exact attribution of any such gap above tolerance to adaptive benchmark overfitting; sampling variability and the fresh-sample estimation procedure require sourced qualification.

children.title: Metric-Corpus Exploitation
children.top_down_role: Cases where metric choices amplify corpus-specific optimization behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Corpus Exploitation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete failure caused by selecting an algorithm specifically for the reported metric and benchmark corpus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the benchmark distribution \(P\) be concentrated on instance \(a\), and let the deployment distribution \(Q\) be concentrated on instance \(b\). For loss \(\ell\in[0,1]\), suppose two algorithms satisfy \(\ell(A_1,a)=0\), \(\ell(A_1,b)=1\), \(\ell(A_2,a)=1\), and \(\ell(A_2,b)=0\). Benchmark minimization selects \(A_1\), attaining benchmark risk \(R_P(A_1)=0\), although its deployment risk is \(R_Q(A_1)=1\), while \(R_Q(A_2)=0\). Thus perfect reported performance need not imply out-of-corpus performance when selection exploits corpus-specific metric behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting for a fixed benchmark can yield perfect reported loss yet maximal deployment loss when the deployment corpus differs.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\delta_a\) and \(Q=\delta_b\).
\(R_D(A)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}[\ell(A,x)]\) for \(\ell\in[0,1]\).

notation.meaning: expected loss of algorithm A under distribution D

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-instance counterexample is mathematically coherent and fits a failure-boundary container, but no cited source supports the benchmark-exploitation interpretation.

children.title: Out-of-Corpus Generalization
children.top_down_role: Performance transfer from development corpora to unseen instance families.

knowledge_statements.title: Out-of-Corpus Generalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional generalization of a benchmark-selected algorithm to an independently specified deployment corpus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be an instance space, \(\mathcal A\) an algorithm class, \(P\) a benchmark distribution on \(\mathcal X\), and \(S=(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\sim P^n\). Let \(\widehat A:\mathcal X^n\to\mathcal A\) be a benchmark-based selection rule, let \(Q\) be a deployment distribution fixed independently of \(S\), and let \(\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal A\) be nonempty. For a loss \(\ell:\mathcal A\times\mathcal X\to[0,1]\), define \(R_Q(A)=\mathbb E_{X\sim Q}[\ell(A,X)]\). For \(\varepsilon\geq0\) and \(\delta\in[0,1]\), the selection rule has \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) out-of-corpus generalization from \(P\) to \(Q\) relative to \(\mathcal A_0\) when \(\Pr_{S\sim P^n}\!\left(R_Q(\widehat A(S))\leq\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_0}R_Q(A)+\varepsilon\right)\geq1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark-based selection rule has epsilon-delta out-of-corpus generalization when, with probability at least one minus delta over the benchmark sample, its deployment risk is within epsilon of the best deployment risk in the stated nonempty reference class.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(S\sim P^n\), and \(Q\) is fixed independently of \(S\).
\(\widehat A:\mathcal X^n\to\mathcal A\), \(\varnothing\neq\mathcal A_0\subseteq\mathcal A\), and \(\ell:\mathcal A\times\mathcal X\to[0,1]\).
\(\varepsilon\geq0\) and \(\delta\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr_{S\sim P^n}\!\left(R_Q(\widehat A(S))\leq\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_0}R_Q(A)+\varepsilon\right)\geq1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: algorithm selected from benchmark corpus S
expected deployment loss of algorithm A

review_flags: authoritative source required for the reference-class and distribution-shift convention

children.title: Performance Evaluation View Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Resource, work, outcome, scaling, profile, and statistical views used to analyze benchmark results.

children.title: Wall-Clock Time
children.top_down_role: End-to-end calendar duration observed by benchmark users.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elapsed real time for one benchmark run under a specified timing boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a benchmark run with a designated start event occurring at monotonic-clock reading \(t_{\mathrm{start}}\) and a designated completion event at reading \(t_{\mathrm{stop}}\), its wall-clock time is \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=t_{\mathrm{stop}}-t_{\mathrm{start}}\). The interval includes every delay between those events, including computation, blocking, scheduling, communication, and input/output. For repeated runs \(r=1,\ldots,m\), the benchmark must report a stated statistic of \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}^{(r)}\), together with the timing boundary and treatment of setup and teardown.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wall-clock time is monotonic elapsed real time between declared start and completion events, including delays and waiting.
assumptions_latex: \(t_{\mathrm{start}}\) and \(t_{\mathrm{stop}}\) are readings from the same monotonic clock.
\(t_{\mathrm{stop}}\geq t_{\mathrm{start}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=t_{\mathrm{stop}}-t_{\mathrm{start}}\geq0\).

notation.meaning: monotonic-clock readings at the timing boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is precise and matches the wall-clock-time leaf, but the reporting requirements and inclusion of all intervening delays have no cited, inspectable source.

children.title: CPU Time
children.top_down_role: Processor time consumed by a benchmarked process or execution group.

knowledge_statements.title: CPU Time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Processor time charged to the benchmarked process or declared process set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a run interval and a declared set \(J\) of processes or threads. If \(U_j\) and \(K_j\) denote, respectively, user-mode and kernel-mode processor time charged to execution context \(j\in J\), then total CPU time is \(T_{\mathrm{CPU}}=\sum_{j\in J}(U_j+K_j)\). This sum measures consumed processor time rather than elapsed real time; simultaneous execution on multiple cores contributes additively. A benchmark report must state \(J\) and whether child processes and kernel time are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CPU time sums charged user and kernel processor time over the declared processes or threads, including simultaneous core use additively.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is fixed by the benchmark accounting convention.
\(U_j,K_j\geq0\) are measured over the same run interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{CPU}}=\sum_{j\in J}(U_j+K_j)\geq0\).

notation.meaning: charged user-mode and kernel-mode processor times

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional operating-system CPU accounting definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently describes aggregate charged processor time and correctly distinguishes it from elapsed time, but no authoritative CPU-accounting source is cited.

children.title: Elapsed-Time Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Breakdowns of elapsed duration into computation, waiting, input/output, plus framework overhead.

knowledge_statements.title: Elapsed-Time Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive partition of a run’s elapsed time into mutually exclusive execution states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the measured wall-clock interval \([t_0,t_1)\) into measurable, pairwise disjoint state sets \(I_{m compute}\), \(I_{m io}\), \(I_{m comm}\), \(I_{m sync}\), and \(I_{m sched}\), whose union is \([t_0,t_1)\). Writing \(T_k=\mu(I_k)\) for interval length, the elapsed-time decomposition is \[T_{\mathrm{wall}}=T_{\rm compute}+T_{\rm io}+T_{\rm comm}+T_{\rm sync}+T_{\rm sched}.\] Categories may be refined, but additivity requires exclusive attribution; overlapping per-thread or per-device times do not directly form this decomposition.
