knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wall time equals the sum of durations assigned to mutually exclusive compute, I/O, communication, synchronization, and scheduling states.
assumptions_latex: The state sets are measurable and pairwise disjoint.
Their union equals the complete measured interval \([t_0,t_1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\sum_k\mu(I_k)\).

notation.meaning: portion of the elapsed interval attributed to state k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite additivity over an exclusive time partition
category taxonomy requires authoritative benchmarking source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive identity is valid under the explicit measurable-partition assumptions and representation is the correct kind, but the particular execution-state taxonomy lacks a cited source.

children.title: Time-Measure Divergence
children.top_down_role: Benchmark regimes where wall-clock, CPU, or decomposed elapsed measures yield different conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Measure Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies disagreement between elapsed time and aggregate processor time under concurrency or waiting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a completed run with \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}>0\), define the time-measure ratio \(\rho=T_{\mathrm{CPU}}/T_{\mathrm{wall}}\) and divergence \(D=T_{\mathrm{CPU}}-T_{\mathrm{wall}}\). Sequential full utilization ideally gives \(\rho\approx1\). Parallel execution can give \(\rho>1\) because processor times across cores add, whereas blocking or descheduling can give \(\rho<1\). Consequently neither time measure determines the other without assumptions on parallelism, utilization, and accounting scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CPU and wall time diverge under parallelism, blocking, or scheduling, so either can misrepresent the other without execution context.
assumptions_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}>0\).
CPU and wall measurements use the same run boundaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho=T_{\mathrm{CPU}}/T_{\mathrm{wall}}\) may be less than, equal to, or greater than \(1\).

notation.meaning: signed difference between CPU and wall time

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: processor-time accounting under waiting and multicore execution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly allows the CPU-to-wall-time ratio to lie below, at, or above one under differing utilization and concurrency regimes, but the accounting interpretation is unsupported by a citation.

children.title: Memory Footprint
children.top_down_role: Resident, peak, working-set, plus retained-memory measurements.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Footprint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resident volatile-memory usage of a benchmarked execution over its declared run interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M(t)\) be the number of bytes of volatile memory resident and attributable to the declared benchmark scope at time \(t\in[t_0,t_1]\). The instantaneous memory footprint is \(M(t)\), the peak footprint is \(M_{\max}=\sup_{t\in[t_0,t_1]}M(t)\), and the time-averaged footprint is \(\overline M=(t_1-t_0)^{-1}\int_{t_0}^{t_1}M(t)\,dt\). The accounting convention must state whether shared pages, mapped files, allocator reserves, and child processes are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory footprint is attributable resident volatile memory over time, commonly summarized by its peak or time average under a declared accounting convention.
assumptions_latex: \(M(t)\geq0\) is measurable under a fixed accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\max}=\sup_t M(t)\) and \(\overline M=(t_1-t_0)^{-1}\int_{t_0}^{t_1}M(t)\,dt\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: peak and average resource-occupancy measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The peak and time-average formulas are coherent, but identifying memory footprint specifically with attributable resident volatile memory is convention-dependent and requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Allocation Activity
children.top_down_role: Allocation volume, frequency, lifetime, plus reclamation behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Allocation Activity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic allocation and deallocation events attributable to one benchmark run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run, let \(E^+\) be its multiset of successful allocation events and \(E^-\) its multiset of deallocation events. If event \(e\) requests or releases \(b(e)\geq0\) bytes, allocation activity is summarized by \(N_{m alloc}=|E^+|\), \(B_{m alloc}=\sum_{e\in E^+}b(e)\), \(N_{m free}=|E^-|\), and \(B_{m free}=\sum_{e\in E^-}b(e)\). These cumulative quantities need not equal peak footprint because storage may be repeatedly allocated and released.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocation activity counts allocation and release events and their cumulative bytes; repeated reuse can make it much larger than peak memory.
assumptions_latex: Events are observed within fixed run and process boundaries.
\(b(e)\geq0\) uses one declared requested-size or actual-size convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{m alloc}=\sum_{e\in E^+}b(e)\) and \(B_{m free}=\sum_{e\in E^-}b(e)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: event-count and cumulative-byte resource measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event counts and cumulative-byte measures fit allocation activity, but requested-versus-actual sizes and allocation-event attribution are source-dependent conventions with no citation.

children.title: Storage Consumption
children.top_down_role: Persistent or temporary storage used by instances, logs, checkpoints, or intermediate artifacts.

knowledge_statements.title: Storage Consumption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent or external storage occupied or transferred by a benchmark run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(t)\) be the bytes of persistent or external storage attributable to the benchmark at time \(t\in[t_0,t_1]\), and let \(r(e)\) and \(w(e)\) be bytes read and written by input/output event \(e\). Storage consumption comprises occupancy measures \(S_{\max}=\sup_t S(t)\) and \(S_{m final}=S(t_1)\), together with traffic measures \(B_{m read}=\sum_e r(e)\) and \(B_{m write}=\sum_e w(e)\). Occupancy and traffic are distinct and must not be reported interchangeably.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Storage consumption separates occupied persistent bytes from cumulative bytes read or written during the run.
assumptions_latex: Storage scope and run boundaries are fixed.
\(S(t),r(e),w(e)\geq0\) follow a declared logical- or physical-byte convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\max}=\sup_t S(t)\), \(B_{m read}=\sum_e r(e)\), and \(B_{m write}=\sum_e w(e)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distinction between occupancy and traffic measures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record clearly distinguishes storage occupancy from I/O traffic, but treating both as components of storage consumption requires an authoritative measurement source and inspectable locator.

children.title: Memory-Storage Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Benchmark regimes where in-memory retention competes with external or persistent storage.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Storage Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto comparison of volatile-memory and persistent-storage resources at fixed solution quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance set, solution-quality requirement, and execution environment. For each admissible algorithm configuration \(a\), let \(M(a)\) be peak volatile-memory footprint and \(S(a)\) be a declared storage measure. Configuration \(a\) dominates \(b\) when \(M(a)\leq M(b)\) and \(S(a)\leq S(b)\), with at least one strict inequality. The memory-storage tradeoff frontier is the set of configurations not dominated by any admissible configuration. A scalar score \(\lambda M(a)+(1-\lambda)S(a)\) is meaningful only after normalization and specification of \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The memory-storage frontier contains configurations for which neither resource can be reduced without worsening the other among admissible alternatives.
assumptions_latex: All configurations satisfy the same correctness and solution-quality requirements.
\(M(a)\) and \(S(a)\) use fixed accounting conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) is frontier-optimal exactly when no \(b\) satisfies \(M(b)\leq M(a)\), \(S(b)\leq S(a)\), with one strict inequality.

notation.meaning: peak volatile-memory footprint of configuration a
declared storage consumption of configuration a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto-frontier property is mathematically precise and fits the tradeoff leaf, but its application to benchmark memory and storage measures has no cited algorithm-engineering source.

children.title: Communication Cost
children.top_down_role: Data-transfer volume, frequency, latency, plus topology-sensitive communication burden.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Message and data-transfer resources consumed by a distributed benchmark run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a distributed run, let \(E\) be the multiset of inter-participant communication events and let \(b(e)\) be the payload bytes of event \(e\in E\). Its communication volume is \(V=\sum_{e\in E}b(e)\), and its message count is \(N=|E|\). Under a latency-bandwidth model, a serialized sequence of these messages has modeled communication cost \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}=\alpha N+\beta V\), where \(\alpha\geq0\) is the per-message latency and \(\beta\geq0\) is the time per byte. Concurrent transfers require an explicitly stated aggregation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication cost records message count and transferred bytes; under a latency-bandwidth model, serialized transfers are priced by nonnegative per-message and per-byte coefficients.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) contains exactly the communication events attributed to the run.
\(b(e)\geq0\) follows a fixed payload-byte or wire-byte convention.
\(\alpha\geq0\) and \(\beta\geq0\), and the modeled transfers are serialized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=|E|\), \(V=\sum_{e\in E}b(e)\), and \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}=\alpha N+\beta V\).

notation.meaning: per-message latency and per-byte transfer coefficients

children.title: Synchronization Cost
children.top_down_role: Waiting, barriers, locking, coordination, plus contention overhead.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delay and event counts caused by coordination constraints in a distributed or parallel run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be the finite set of synchronization events in a run and \(P\) the finite set of participating execution contexts. For each event \(k\in B\), let \(\varnothing\neq P_k\subseteq P\) be its participant set. For every \(p\in P_k\), let \(a_{p,k}\) be the arrival time and \(r_{p,k}\geq a_{p,k}\) the release time. The aggregate synchronization waiting cost is \(W_{\mathrm{sync}}=\sum_{k\in B}\sum_{p\in P_k}(r_{p,k}-a_{p,k})\), while the synchronization span is \(L_{\mathrm{sync}}=\sum_{k\in B}\left(\max_{p\in P_k}r_{p,k}-\min_{p\in P_k}a_{p,k}\right)\). These measure different quantities and require a declared event-attribution rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization cost may be measured as total waiting across participants or as the sum of synchronization-event spans; these quantities are generally different.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) and \(P\) are finite, and \(\varnothing\neq P_k\subseteq P\) for every \(k\in B\).
\(r_{p,k}\geq a_{p,k}\) for every \(k\in B\) and \(p\in P_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{\mathrm{sync}}=\sum_{k\in B}\sum_{p\in P_k}(r_{p,k}-a_{p,k})\geq0\).

notation.meaning: synchronization events, execution contexts, and the participants in event k
arrival and release times for participant p at event k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: waiting-time aggregation over synchronization events
authoritative distributed-performance source required for the event-span convention

children.title: Energy Consumption
children.top_down_role: Energy use attributable to benchmark execution across supported hardware scopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy Consumption
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational energy measure for one distributed solver run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a run interval \([t_0,t_1]\) and a finite set \(D\) of measured devices. If \(P_d(t)\) is the device-level power trace, define raw run energy by \[E_{\mathrm{raw}}=\sum_{d\in D}\int_{t_0}^{t_1}P_d(t)\,dt.\] If the benchmark prespecifies idle baselines \(P_d^{\mathrm{idle}}(t)\), it may instead report net energy \[E_{\mathrm{net}}=\sum_{d\in D}\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\bigl(P_d(t)-P_d^{\mathrm{idle}}(t)\bigr)\,dt.\] The report must identify the device boundary, sampling or integration rule, interval endpoints, baseline convention, and energy unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run energy is integrated device power over a fixed measurement interval, optionally corrected by a prespecified idle baseline.
assumptions_latex: \(P_d:[t_0,t_1]\to[0,\infty)\) is integrable for every \(d\in D\).
The measured device set \(D\) and run boundaries are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{\mathrm{raw}}\) or the explicitly declared \(E_{\mathrm{net}}\) is the run's energy-consumption measure.

notation.meaning: Set of measured computing, memory, network, or accelerator devices.
Measured power of device d at time t.
Energy attributed to the measured run.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational definition obtained by integrating measured power over a declared run boundary
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The operational definition and definition content kind fit the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the measurement-boundary, integration, and idle-baseline conventions.

children.title: Communication-Energy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes where data movement affects total energy use or energy efficiency.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Energy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto and scalarized comparison of communication and energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be the configurations that solve the same benchmark task under one declared correctness and solution-quality criterion. For \(a\in\mathcal A\), let \(C(a)\ge 0\) be communication cost and \(E(a)\ge 0\) energy consumption. Configuration \(b\) dominates \(a\) when \(C(b)\le C(a)\), \(E(b)\le E(a)\), and at least one inequality is strict. The communication-energy frontier is \[\mathcal F_{CE}=\{a\in\mathcal A:\nexists b\in\mathcal A\text{ dominating }a\}.\] With fixed positive references \(C_0,E_0\), a scalarized operating point minimizes \(J_\lambda(a)=\lambda C(a)/C_0+(1-\lambda)E(a)/E_0\) for a reported \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff is the nondominated frontier of communication cost and energy among configurations meeting the same solution criterion.
assumptions_latex: Every \(a\in\mathcal A\) is evaluated on the same instance set and solution criterion.
\(C_0>0\) and \(E_0>0\) whenever scalarization is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{CE}\) contains exactly the observed communication-energy Pareto-efficient configurations.

notation.meaning: Declared communication cost of configuration a.
Measured energy consumption of configuration a.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto formulation is mathematically coherent and fits the tradeoff leaf, but no source supports the selected communication metric, frontier convention, or scalarization protocol.

children.title: Synchronization-Energy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes where coordination overhead affects energy use or useful-work efficiency.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization-Energy Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto and scalarized comparison of synchronization and energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) contain configurations satisfying one fixed correctness and solution-quality criterion. For \(a\in\mathcal A\), let \(S(a)\ge0\) be a declared synchronization cost and \(E(a)\ge0\) its energy consumption. Configuration \(b\) dominates \(a\) if \(S(b)\le S(a)\), \(E(b)\le E(a)\), and at least one inequality is strict. Define \[\mathcal F_{SE}=\{a\in\mathcal A:\nexists b\in\mathcal A\text{ dominating }a\}.\] Given fixed \(S_0,E_0>0\), scalarization may use \(J_\lambda(a)=\lambda S(a)/S_0+(1-\lambda)E(a)/E_0\), with the chosen \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) reported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tradeoff is the nondominated frontier of synchronization cost and energy for configurations satisfying an identical solution criterion.
assumptions_latex: All configurations use the same benchmark instances, stopping rule, and solution criterion.
The synchronization event counted by \(S\) is fixed across configurations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{SE}\) contains exactly the observed synchronization-energy Pareto-efficient configurations.

notation.meaning: Measured energy consumption of configuration a.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto formulation is coherent and the definition kind fits the leaf, but the synchronization metric and scalarization conventions lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Iteration Counts
children.top_down_role: Counts of repeated top-level or nested iterative units.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Protocol-defined count of repeated algorithmic state transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run represented by states \(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_K\), fix an iteration-boundary predicate \(B\) before measurement. A transition \(x_{k-1}\mapsto x_k\) contributes one iteration exactly when it crosses one boundary recognized by \(B\). The iteration count is \[N_{\mathrm{iter}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf 1\{B(x_{k-1},x_k)=1\}.\] If outer and inner loops coexist, report their counts separately as \(N_{\mathrm{outer}}\) and \(N_{\mathrm{inner}}\); they must not be added unless a prespecified weighting converts both to a common work unit. Aborted or partial transitions are counted only if the protocol explicitly includes them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration count is the number of protocol-recognized transitions across fixed iteration boundaries, with nested loop levels reported separately.
assumptions_latex: The boundary predicate \(B\) is deterministic and fixed across compared runs.
The observed execution trace has finitely many recorded transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{iter}}\) is the reproducible iteration count under boundary convention \(B\).

notation.meaning: Benchmark predicate recognizing a completed iteration boundary.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: event count induced by a fixed iteration-boundary predicate
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The protocol-defined event count is precise and appropriate as a definition, but no citation supports the treatment of boundaries, nested loops, or partial transitions.

children.title: Phase Counts
children.top_down_role: Counts of major execution stages, restarts, rounds, or epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Phase Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Count of completed coarse-grained algorithmic phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an execution trace be partitioned by a prespecified phase-boundary rule into consecutive nonempty segments \(I_1,\ldots,I_P\), each carrying a phase label from a finite set \(\Phi\). The phase count is \[N_{\mathrm{phase}}=P.\] For label \(\phi\in\Phi\), define \(N_\phi=\sum_{j=1}^{P}\mathbf 1\{I_j\text{ has label }\phi\}\), so that \(N_{\mathrm{phase}}=\sum_{\phi\in\Phi}N_\phi\). Adjacent segments with the same label are merged unless the protocol declares a restart or another event that creates a new phase. An incomplete terminal segment is reported separately unless inclusion was fixed beforehand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase count is the number of coarse execution segments produced by a fixed boundary and labeling rule.
assumptions_latex: The trace partition and phase labels are uniquely determined by the declared protocol.
Each counted segment is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{phase}}\) equals the sum of the per-label phase counts \(N_\phi\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: trace partition induces a reproducible coarse-grained event count
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The phase-count definition is internally consistent and fits the terminal container, but its segmentation, merging, and incomplete-phase conventions are unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Primitive-Operation Counts
children.top_down_role: Counts of designated low-level operations used as implementation-independent work proxies.

knowledge_statements.title: Primitive-Operation Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector and weighted count of declared elementary operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite operation alphabet \(\Omega\) whose elements are benchmark-declared primitive operations. For an execution trace \(T=(o_1,\ldots,o_m)\) with \(o_j\in\Omega\), define the count of primitive \(\omega\in\Omega\) by \[N_\omega(T)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf 1\{o_j=\omega\}.\] The primitive-operation profile is \(N(T)=(N_\omega(T))_{\omega\in\Omega}\). If fixed nonnegative weights \(w_\omega\) represent a common work unit, the weighted count is \[W(T)=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w_\omega N_\omega(T).\] The alphabet, instrumentation level, weights, and treatment of vectorized or batched operations must remain identical across compared runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primitive work is reported as counts of fixed elementary operation types, optionally aggregated using prespecified nonnegative weights.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is finite and fixed before collecting compared traces.
Every counted trace event has exactly one primitive label in \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(T)\) is the primitive-operation profile, and \(W(T)\) is its declared weighted aggregation.

notation.meaning: Benchmark alphabet of primitive operation types.
Number of trace events labeled by primitive omega.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: categorical event-count vector with an optional fixed linear aggregation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vector and weighted counts are well defined and fit the leaf, but the primitive-operation and instrumentation conventions have no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An implementation-independent first approximation to computational work; it is not a bit-complexity or precision-sensitive cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm is a finite collection of programming-language-style instructions, such as arithmetic operations, conditional statements, and input-output instructions. Its computational work may be approximated by counting designated primitive operations, including additions, multiplications, divisions, and comparisons. This count abstracts from programming and hardware details but does not reflect the greater cost of arithmetic on large integers or high-precision floating-point numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm is a finite collection of programming-language-style instructions. A first, implementation-independent estimate of its work counts primitive arithmetic and comparison operations. This estimate ignores that operations on large integers or high-precision numbers can cost more than operations on small or fixed-precision values.
assumptions_latex: \text{The computation is specified by a finite set of executable instructions.}
\text{Additions, multiplications, divisions, and comparisons are treated as primitive operations.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The number of primitive operations is a first-order, implementation-independent proxy for computational work, but it ignores operand-size and precision costs.}

source_evidence.locator: Introduction / 1.6. Algorithms and operation counts / Definition 1.6-extra-1

source_refs.locator: Introduction / 1.6. Algorithms and operation counts / Definition 1.6-extra-1

knowledge_statements.title: Algorithms and primitive-operation counts

source_witnesses.locator: Introduction / 1.6. Algorithms and operation counts / Definition 1.6-extra-1

children.title: Cross-Level Work Attribution
children.top_down_role: Relationships among primitive activity, phase structure, plus aggregate iteration counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Level Work Attribution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistent attribution of primitive work to phases and iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(O\) be the finite set of recorded primitive-operation events. Let \(\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal I\) be the recorded phases and iterations, and assign every \(o\in O\) to exactly one phase \(p(o)\in\mathcal P\) and either one iteration \(i(o)\in\mathcal I\) or the distinguished value \(\bot\) for work outside iterations. For nonnegative event weights \(w(o)\), define \[W_p=\sum_{o:p(o)=p}w(o),\qquad W_i=\sum_{o:i(o)=i}w(o),\qquad W_\bot=\sum_{o:i(o)=\bot}w(o).\] Conservation requires \[\sum_{o\in O}w(o)=\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}W_p=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}W_i+W_\bot.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each primitive event is assigned to one phase and to one iteration or an outside-iteration bucket, preserving total attributed work.
assumptions_latex: Every recorded event receives exactly one phase assignment.
Iteration assignments are exclusive, with \(\bot\) covering all events outside iterations.
Event weights satisfy \(w(o)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The phase-level and iteration-level attributions both reconcile with total recorded work.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: disjoint event attribution yields additive conservation identities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly expresses exclusive attribution and additive reconciliation, but no source supports this cross-level trace-accounting convention.

children.title: Oracle-Call Counts
children.top_down_role: Counts of value, gradient, separation, independence, or other designated oracle queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query-complexity measure for a declared solver oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an oracle \(\mathcal O\) with declared query domain \(Q\) and response space \(R\). A run produces a transcript \(\tau=((q_1,r_1),\ldots,(q_m,r_m))\), where \(q_j\in Q\) is submitted and \(r_j=\mathcal O(q_j)\in R\) is returned. Its completed oracle-call count is \[N_{\mathcal O}(\tau)=m.\] Calls submitted but not completed are reported separately. If one interface invocation contains a batch \((q_{j1},\ldots,q_{jb_j})\), the benchmark must declare whether it counts one invocation or \(b_j\) logical queries. Different oracle types are represented by separate coordinates rather than silently summed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call count is the number of completed query-response pairs, with oracle types and batching conventions declared explicitly.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface, query semantics, and response semantics are fixed across runs.
The transcript records every completed query-response pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathcal O}(\tau)\) is the run's completed call count for oracle \(\mathcal O\).

source_refs.locator: The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26

source_witnesses.locator: The Running Time of Oracle Algorithms p. 26

children.title: Relaxation-Solve Counts
children.top_down_role: Counts of relaxation constructions, resolutions, or related solver invocations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Solve Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Count of completed relaxation-solver invocations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run, let \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) be the recorded invocations of a declared relaxation solver, each associated with a relaxation model, parameter state, start event, termination status, and optional warm start. Define \[N_{\mathrm{relax}}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf 1\{e_j\text{ reaches a protocol-recognized termination status}\}.\] Attempted but interrupted invocations are counted separately as \(N_{\mathrm{abort}}\). Reoptimization of a modified relaxation contributes a new solve exactly when the protocol records a new invocation; internal iterations of one invocation do not. Counts should be stratified by relaxation class or termination status when those categories differ materially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation-solve count records completed solver invocations, separating aborted attempts and treating reoptimization according to a fixed invocation rule.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation class and recognized termination statuses are declared before comparison.
Every solver invocation has a unique recorded start and final status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{relax}}\) is the number of completed relaxation solves under the declared event convention.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: completed solver invocations form a protocol-defined event count
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The completed-invocation count fits the leaf and is mathematically coherent, but the termination, reoptimization, warm-start, and abort conventions lack a source.

children.title: Cut-Generation Counts
children.top_down_role: Counts of generated, accepted, active, or rejected cutting structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Generation Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate counts of generated, accepted, and added cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) be the sequence of cut candidates emitted by all declared separators during a run. Define the generated-cut count by \(N_{\mathrm{gen}}=m\). If \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) indexes candidates passing the solver's acceptance filter and \(L\subseteq A\) indexes accepted cuts actually inserted into a relaxation, define \[N_{\mathrm{acc}}=|A|,\qquad N_{\mathrm{add}}=|L|.\] Hence \(0\le N_{\mathrm{add}}\le N_{\mathrm{acc}}\le N_{\mathrm{gen}}\). Duplicate rediscovery is counted in \(N_{\mathrm{gen}}\) unless deduplication precedes the recorded generation event. Counts must be stratified by separator family when multiple families are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut activity is reported separately as generated candidates, accepted candidates, and cuts actually added to relaxations.
assumptions_latex: Every emitted candidate has a unique event identifier.
Acceptance and relaxation insertion are recorded as distinct events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{add}}\le N_{\mathrm{acc}}\le N_{\mathrm{gen}}\) under the declared cut-event pipeline.

notation.meaning: Number of cuts inserted into relaxations.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nested cut-processing event sets induce ordered counts

children.title: Search-Node Counts
children.top_down_role: Counts of explored, expanded, pruned, queued, or revisited search nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Node Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event counts for nodes in an explicit search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be the set of unique search nodes created during a run of an explicit tree-search algorithm. Let \(P\subseteq V\) contain nodes selected for processing, and let \(F\subseteq P\) contain nodes whose processing finishes under a declared terminal disposition such as pruning, fathoming, or branching. Define \[N_{\mathrm{gen}}=|V|,\qquad N_{\mathrm{proc}}=|P|,\qquad N_{\mathrm{fin}}=|F|.\] Then \(N_{\mathrm{fin}}\le N_{\mathrm{proc}}\le N_{\mathrm{gen}}\). The root is included unless explicitly excluded. Reprocessing one node does not create another generated node but may be reported as an additional processing event in a separate event count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search-node reporting distinguishes unique generated nodes, nodes selected for processing, and nodes reaching a terminal disposition.
assumptions_latex: Every generated search node has a unique identifier.
Processing and terminal-disposition events are recorded consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{fin}}\le N_{\mathrm{proc}}\le N_{\mathrm{gen}}\) for unique-node counts.

notation.meaning: Set of unique generated search nodes.
Processed nodes reaching a terminal disposition.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nested search-node event sets induce ordered cardinalities
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested unique-node counts are coherent and fit the leaf, but the root, reprocessing, terminal-disposition, and parallel-duplicate conventions lack a citation.

children.title: Work-Count Normalization
children.top_down_role: Comparable reporting conventions for heterogeneous oracle, relaxation, cut, or search activity.

knowledge_statements.title: Work-Count Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensionless normalization of heterogeneous solver-event counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For benchmark instance \(x\), let \(N_k(x)\ge0\) be the count of work event type \(k\in K\), and let fixed weights \(w_k\ge0\) convert event types to a declared reference-work unit. Given a prespecified positive exposure \(D(x)>0\), define \[W_{\mathrm{norm}}(x)=\frac{\sum_{k\in K}w_kN_k(x)}{D(x)}.\] Valid choices of \(D(x)\) include a declared input-size statistic, number of solved instances, or reference-solver work, but different denominators define different measures and cannot be pooled silently. For an instance set \(X\), aggregate the instance-level values with a prespecified statistic rather than taking an unweighted ratio of pooled counts unless pooling is intended.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized work is a fixed weighted event count divided by a positive, prespecified exposure, with aggregation performed at a declared level.
assumptions_latex: The event set \(K\), weights \(w_k\), and exposure \(D\) are fixed across compared algorithms.
\(D(x)>0\) for every reported instance \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_{\mathrm{norm}}(x)\) is a dimensionless or declared-unit normalized work measure for instance \(x\).

notation.meaning: Count of work event type k on instance x.
Positive normalization exposure for instance x.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalization is a fixed weighted count divided by positive exposure
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization representation is mathematically consistent and appropriate for the leaf, but no source supports the weighting, exposure, or cross-instance aggregation conventions.

children.title: Feasibility Quality
children.top_down_role: Quality of solution status relative to the benchmark feasibility requirements.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark instance specifies constraints \(g_i(x)\le 0\) for \(i\in I\), equalities \(h_j(x)=0\) for \(j\in J\), and positive tolerances \(\tau_i,\sigma_j\).
The reported candidate \(x\) belongs to the ambient representation domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)=1\) exactly when every normalized residual is at most one.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Feasibility is benchmarked by comparing normalized constraint residuals with declared tolerances.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-aware feasibility measure for reported benchmark solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[R_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)=\max\!\left\{\max_{i\in I}\frac{[g_i(x)]_+}{\tau_i},\;\max_{j\in J}\frac{|h_j(x)|}{\sigma_j}\right\},\qquad [t]_+=\max\{t,0\}.\] The feasibility quality is \(Q_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)=\mathbf 1\{R_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)\le 1\}\). Thus the candidate passes the benchmark feasibility test precisely when every inequality and equality residual lies within its declared tolerance; the numerical residual \(R_{\mathrm{feas}}(x)\) retains the severity of failure when the indicator is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility quality records whether every normalized constraint residual satisfies its declared tolerance, while the maximum residual quantifies the severity of failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally plausible, but the tolerance normalization and maximum-residual convention are protocol-specific and have no cited source. The behavior when I or J is empty is also unspecified.

children.title: Constraint-Violation Quality
children.top_down_role: Magnitude, distribution, plus severity of residual constraint violations.

assumptions_latex: Constraints and positive scaling values \(s_k\) are fixed for the benchmark instance.
Each constraint has a nonnegative violation residual \(r_k(x)\), equal to zero exactly when that constraint is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smaller \(V_p(x)\) denotes better constraint-violation quality, and \(V_p(x)=0\) exactly when all measured constraints are satisfied.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Constraint violation is commonly summarized by normalized residual norms, but the aggregation convention must be fixed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-based quality measure for infeasible candidates under a fixed scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in[1,\infty)\), define \[V_p(x)=\left(\sum_k\left(\frac{r_k(x)}{s_k}\right)^p\right)^{1/p},\] and define \(V_\infty(x)=\max_k r_k(x)/s_k\). Constraint-violation quality is ordered inversely by this aggregate: candidate \(x\) is at least as good as candidate \(y\) when \(V_p(x)\le V_p(y)\), provided both are evaluated with identical residual definitions, scales, and \(p\). Moreover, \(V_p(x)=0\) if and only if every measured constraint is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-violation quality ranks candidates by a fixed norm of scaled nonnegative residuals; zero aggregate violation is equivalent to satisfying all measured constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Violation Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Normalized residual norms are standard, but the selected scales, p-norm aggregation, and comparison convention require authoritative support. The constraint index set and its finiteness are not explicitly introduced.

children.title: Integrality-Violation Quality
children.top_down_role: Magnitude plus prevalence of violations affecting discrete-variable requirements.

assumptions_latex: The index set \(B\) identifies variables required to be integral.
Positive scales \(s_i\) and an integrality tolerance \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_\infty(x)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\) exactly when every designated variable is integral within tolerance.

notation.meaning: Distance from a scalar to the nearest integer

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Distance to the nearest integer is the standard residual for integrality requirements.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-aware integrality residual for mixed-integer benchmark solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a candidate \(x\), define \[I_\infty(x)=\max_{i\in B}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x_i,\mathbb Z)}{s_i},\qquad \operatorname{dist}(t,\mathbb Z)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z}|t-z|.\] Its integrality-violation quality improves as \(I_\infty(x)\) decreases. The candidate is integral within the benchmark tolerance when \(I_\infty(x)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\). Comparisons are valid only when the designated index set, scales, and tolerance are identical; otherwise the resulting integrality-quality values are not directly comparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrality-violation quality is the maximum scaled distance of a designated integer variable from its nearest integer, judged against a fixed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Violation Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Nearest-integer distance is mathematically appropriate, but scaling it before applying a single integrality tolerance is a benchmark-specific convention without evidence. The maximum is undefined if B is empty unless a convention is supplied.

children.title: Feasibility-Violation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Outcome comparisons where aggregate feasibility labels obscure differing violation profiles.

assumptions_latex: All candidates are evaluated using the same feasibility indicator and scalar violation measure \(V(x)\ge 0\).
Objective values are compared only among candidates admitted by the same feasibility convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nondominated set contains exactly the candidates for which no other candidate improves feasibility status or violation without worsening the other component.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Pareto dominance provides a convention-independent description of tradeoffs between feasibility status and violation magnitude.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto comparison of feasibility status and violation magnitude before objective quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate with each candidate the vector \(q(x)=(1-F(x),V(x))\), where \(F(x)\in\{0,1\}\) and smaller components are preferred. Candidate \(x\) dominates \(y\) when \(q(x)\le q(y)\) componentwise and \(q(x)\ne q(y)\). Consequently, a feasible candidate with zero violation dominates every infeasible candidate with positive violation. Among infeasible candidates, dominance reduces to comparing \(V\). A benchmark may impose a lexicographic order, but any such scalar ordering must be reported separately from the nondominated feasibility-violation relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility and violation form a two-component outcome: feasible zero-violation candidates dominate infeasible ones, while remaining tradeoffs are represented by Pareto nondominance.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Violation Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto construction fits the tradeoff leaf, but no source supports this particular outcome vector. If feasibility is defined by zero violation, its two components are redundant, so the intended benchmark interpretation needs authoritative clarification.

children.title: Objective-Value Quality
children.top_down_role: Quality of reported objective values relative to trusted or best-known references.

assumptions_latex: The optimization sense is fixed and a candidate \(x\) is feasible under the benchmark convention.
A finite reference value \(f_{\mathrm{ref}}\) and positive scale \(s_f\) are declared before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smaller \(E_f(x)\) means better reference-relative objective-value quality, with zero denoting equality to the reference value.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Objective outcomes require a fixed optimization sense, feasibility convention, reference value, and normalization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reference-relative objective quality for feasible benchmark candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=1\) for minimization and \(d=-1\) for maximization. Define the normalized objective error \[E_f(x)=\frac{d\bigl(f(x)-f_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr)}{s_f}.\] Candidate \(x\) has at least as good objective-value quality as candidate \(y\) when \(d f(x)\le d f(y)\), assuming both are feasible. The value \(E_f(x)=0\) indicates agreement with the reference, while its sign records whether the reported objective is worse or better than that reference under the declared optimization sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-value quality compares feasible candidates in the declared optimization direction and reports normalized signed error relative to a fixed reference value.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization-sense ordering is correct, but the signed reference-relative error and its normalization are protocol choices not supported by any citation.

children.title: Bound Quality
children.top_down_role: Strength plus validity of reported lower or upper bounds.

assumptions_latex: The instance has finite optimum \(f^*\), and the optimization sense is fixed.
The reported value \(b\) is claimed as a valid global bound on \(f^*\).
A finite reference bound \(b_{\mathrm{ref}}\) and positive scale \(s_b\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound has better reference-relative quality when it is valid and lies no farther from \(f^*\) in the direction opposite the primal objective.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Bound quality is determined by validity and tightness in the optimization-specific direction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and tightness of global bounds under a declared optimization sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, validity requires \(b\le f^*\), and larger valid bounds are tighter; define \(Q_b(b)=(b-b_{\mathrm{ref}})/s_b\). For maximization, validity requires \(b\ge f^*\), and smaller valid bounds are tighter; define \(Q_b(b)=(b_{\mathrm{ref}}-b)/s_b\). Thus larger \(Q_b\) denotes greater improvement over the same reference bound. A numerically tight but invalid value is not assigned bound quality as a certificate of global performance and must instead be flagged as inconsistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound quality combines validity with tightness: lower bounds improve upward for minimization, while upper bounds improve downward for maximization.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The validity and tightness directions are correct, but the proposed reference-relative score is an unsupported benchmark convention. It is also unclear whether the reference bound must itself be valid.

children.title: Optimality-Gap Quality
children.top_down_role: Quality of reported absolute, relative, normalized, or reference-based gaps.

assumptions_latex: A feasible incumbent has finite objective value \(z\), and \(b\) is a valid finite global bound.
A positive denominator floor \(\delta\) is fixed for all compared runs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}\ge0\), \(G_{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\), and either gap equals zero exactly when \(z=b\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Absolute and denominator-protected relative primal-bound gaps are standard solver outcome measures.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and relative gaps between a feasible incumbent and a valid global bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the absolute optimality gap by \[G_{\mathrm{abs}}=|z-b|\] and the denominator-protected relative gap by \[G_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac{|z-b|}{\max\{|z|,|b|,\delta\}}.\] Under bound validity, these quantities are nonnegative and vanish exactly when the incumbent value equals the bound, thereby certifying optimality up to the numerical conventions used to validate both values. Gap-quality comparisons require the same absolute or relative convention, denominator floor, feasibility tolerance, and bound-validity tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimality-gap quality measures the absolute or normalized distance between a feasible incumbent and a valid global bound under fixed numerical conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Gap Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute gap is sound under the assumptions, but relative-gap denominators vary across solver and benchmarking protocols. The selected symmetric denominator and floor therefore require a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Objective-Bound Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency of incumbent objectives with reported bounds.

assumptions_latex: The reported incumbent value \(z\) comes from a candidate accepted as feasible.
The reported bound \(b\) is intended to bound the same objective under the same optimization sense.
A nonnegative consistency tolerance \(\eta\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((z,b)\) is consistent exactly when the optimization-specific primal-bound inequality holds within \(\eta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Weak duality fixes the required ordering between a feasible objective value and a valid global bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical consistency condition linking incumbent objectives and global bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, objective-bound consistency is the condition \(b\le z+\eta\). For a maximization problem, it is the condition \(z\le b+\eta\). The incumbent and bound must refer to the same objective function, scaling, optimization sense, and instance. If the applicable inequality fails, the pair cannot support an optimality-gap claim: at least one of feasibility, objective evaluation, bound validity, numerical tolerance, or instance identity is inconsistent with the report.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent and global bound are consistent when their optimization-specific ordering holds within tolerance and both refer to the same instance and objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Bound Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization-specific ordering is mathematically appropriate, but the additive consistency tolerance and its placement are protocol-specific and uncited.

children.title: Gap-Reporting Regimes
children.top_down_role: Comparability of gap measures across objective scales, signs, statuses, or reference choices.

assumptions_latex: An incumbent value \(z\) and bound \(b\) may be finite, infinite, or unavailable.
Feasibility, bound validity, and numerical tolerances are declared independently of the gap formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A numerical relative gap is reportable only in the finite consistent regime; other regimes require explicit categorical status.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Missing incumbents, missing bounds, inconsistent pairs, and finite valid pairs require distinct reporting regimes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Categorical regimes governing when an optimality gap is numerically meaningful.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S_{\mathrm{gap}}\) by the mutually exclusive regimes: \(\mathrm{NO\_INCUMBENT}\) if no feasible finite \(z\) exists; \(\mathrm{NO\_BOUND}\) if no valid finite \(b\) exists; \(\mathrm{INCONSISTENT}\) if finite \(z\) and \(b\) violate objective-bound consistency; and \(\mathrm{FINITE}\) otherwise. A numerical absolute or relative gap may be reported only when \(S_{\mathrm{gap}}=\mathrm{FINITE}\). Infinite or unavailable values must retain their categorical status and must not be converted to an arbitrary percentage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gap reporting distinguishes absent incumbents, absent bounds, inconsistent pairs, and finite valid pairs; only the last regime supports a numerical gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Reporting Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The categorical reporting idea fits the leaf, but the stated regimes are not mutually exclusive: both NO_INCUMBENT and NO_BOUND apply when neither finite value exists unless precedence is explicitly defined. A source is needed to determine the intended categories or precedence.

assumptions_latex: The instance has finite optimum \(f^*\), and \(x\) is feasible.
The approximation factor satisfies \(\rho\ge1\).
Objective values are nonnegative in the multiplicative convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A smaller certified \(\rho\) represents stronger multiplicative approximation quality, with \(\rho=1\) denoting optimality.

notation.meaning: Objective value of the reported solution

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Multiplicative approximation factors are standard for nonnegative combinatorial optimization objectives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative approximation quality for nonnegative minimization and maximization objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization, a feasible solution \(x\) has multiplicative approximation quality \(\rho\) when \(f(x)\le\rho f^*\). For maximization, it has quality \(\rho\) when \(f(x)\ge f^*/\rho\). The smallest certified factor is preferred, and \(\rho=1\) means that \(x\) is optimal. This multiplicative measure is not invariant under additive shifts of the objective; instances permitting zero, negative, or sign-changing objective values require a separately declared additive or normalized-error convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation quality is the smallest certified multiplicative factor relating a feasible solution value to the optimum, with factor one indicating optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimization and maximization inequalities are standard under the stated nonnegativity assumptions, and definition is an appropriate kind. Nevertheless, no inspectable source supports the approximation convention or its benchmark interpretation.

children.title: Certificate Quality
children.top_down_role: Completeness, strength, compactness, plus diagnostic value of reported certificates.

assumptions_latex: A certificate \(c\) claims a property \(P(x)\) for instance \(I\).
A deterministic verifier \(V\) and encoding convention are fixed.
Certificate size and verification cost are measured in the declared computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Certificate quality improves with stronger certified claims and lower normalized verification resources, subject to verifier acceptance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Certificate assessment separates acceptance, claim strength, encoding size, and verification cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quality profile combining certificate strength, size, and verification cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quality profile of certificate \(c\) is defined only when \(V(I,x,c)=1\) and is the tuple \[Q_{\mathrm{cert}}(c)=\bigl(S(c),-|c|,-T_V(I,x,c)\bigr),\] where \(S(c)\) is the declared strength of the verified claim, \(|c|\) is encoded length, and \(T_V\) is verification cost. Profiles are compared by Pareto dominance unless the benchmark declares a scalarization. A rejected certificate has no certified strength, regardless of its claimed objective, bound, or feasibility quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate quality jointly evaluates the strength of an accepted claim, encoded certificate size, and verification cost, using Pareto comparison unless a scalar rule is declared.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed Pareto profile is a substantive benchmark design choice without evidence. The domain and ordering of S(c) are not defined, so Pareto comparison of the first coordinate is not yet mathematically well specified.

children.title: Certificate Verifiability
children.top_down_role: Independent checkability of certificates using available data, formats, plus trusted validators.

assumptions_latex: The instance \(I\), candidate \(x\), certificate \(c\), and verifier specification are explicitly encoded.
The verifier \(V\) is deterministic and terminates on every admissible encoding.
Verifier acceptance is sound for the claimed predicate \(P(I,x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance \(V(I,x,c)=1\) is a reproducible certificate of \(P(I,x)\) under the fixed encoding and verifier specification.

notation.meaning: Claim certified about the instance and candidate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: A certificate is independently verifiable when a terminating sound verifier accepts its explicit encoding.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent deterministic verification of an explicitly encoded optimization certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The certificate \(c\) is verifiable for claim \(P(I,x)\) when the independently executable procedure \(V\) terminates and returns \(V(I,x,c)=1\), and soundness guarantees \[V(I,x,c)=1\;\Longrightarrow\;P(I,x).\] Reproducible verification additionally requires a fixed input encoding, arithmetic model, tolerance policy, and verifier version. Verification failure or nontermination does not by itself refute \(P(I,x)\); it establishes only that the supplied certificate-verifier pair does not certify the claim under the declared protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate is verifiable when a fixed terminating sound verifier accepts its explicit encoding; rejection does not necessarily make the underlying claim false.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Verifiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement describes a verifiability condition or definition, not a certificate object, so content_kind certificate does not fit this leaf. The soundness, reproducibility, and protocol requirements also lack an authoritative citation; source-backed revision is required.

children.title: Certificate-Portability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Certificate usability across solvers, platforms, numeric formats, or interchange representations.

assumptions_latex: Instances are encoded by a fixed, publicly specified format.
The verifier is independent of the solver and receives only the instance, claimed outcome, and certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Portability holds precisely when the common verifier accepts the transported certificate without solver-specific state.

notation.meaning: certificate produced by solver implementation s for instance I
set of solver implementations in the portability regime

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational benchmark definition based on solver-independent verification
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines portability relative to a common instance format and independent verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a collection of solver implementations using a common instance encoding, and let \(V(I,z,y)\in\{0,1\}\) be an independently specified verifier for claimed objective value \(z\) and certificate \(y\). The collection is in a certificate-portable regime when every solver output \((z_s(I),y_s(I))\) can be exported in a common certificate format and satisfies \(V(I,z_s(I),y_s(I))=1\) whenever the solver reports a certified outcome. Portability excludes dependence on private solver state, undocumented tolerances, or implementation-specific reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificates are portable when every solver exports them in a common format that an independent verifier can check without private solver state.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate-Portability Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the certificate-portability leaf and is internally coherent, but no inspectable source supports this particular common-format, independent-verifier regime.

children.title: Unverifiable-Certificate Failures
children.top_down_role: Outputs whose certificates cannot be checked because of missing, ambiguous, or incompatible evidence.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark requires a solver-independent verifier with a fixed acceptance rule.
A solver reports a claimed objective value together with a purported certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reported certified outcome is unusable for certified comparison whenever independent acceptance is undefined or fails.

notation.meaning: independent verifier, possibly undefined on malformed certificates

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: failure is defined by inability to reproduce certificate acceptance
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates an objective claim from independently reproducible certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\), reported pair \((z,y)\), and independent verifier \(V\), an unverifiable-certificate failure occurs if \(V(I,z,y)\) is undefined, cannot be executed under the benchmark specification, or equals \(0\). Typical mechanisms include a malformed certificate, omitted reconstruction data, dependence on hidden solver state, incompatible numeric conventions, or tolerance-sensitive acceptance. Such a report may remain a feasible incumbent observation, but it must not be counted as a certified bound, optimum, or approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certification fails when the independent verifier cannot run or rejects the certificate; the associated objective claim cannot count as a certified result.
knowledge_statements.title: Unverifiable-Certificate Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the rule excluding rejected or unexecutable certificates from certified bounds, optima, and approximation guarantees requires a benchmark-methodology source.

assumptions_latex: All runs use a common time origin and resource limit.
For minimization, the incumbent value is recorded only after feasibility has been verified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The anytime profile is the best verified incumbent value available by each time, with lower values preferred for minimization.

notation.meaning: set of verified feasible solutions produced by time t
objective function for a minimization problem

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional best-so-far profile for an anytime minimization algorithm
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the minimization convention; maximization reverses the extremum and monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance and time \(t\ge 0\), let \(F(t)\) be the verified feasible solutions emitted no later than \(t\). Define the anytime solution-quality profile by \(q(t)=\inf\{f(x):x\in F(t)\}\), with \(q(t)=+\infty\) when \(F(t)=\varnothing\). Then \(q(t_2)\le q(t_1)\) whenever \(t_2\ge t_1\). Comparisons may use the entire right-continuous profile or a prespecified functional such as time-integrated normalized gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anytime quality is the best verified objective value found by each time; for minimization, this best-so-far curve cannot increase.
knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Solution Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The best-so-far minimization profile is standard and fits the topic, but no source is supplied, and right-continuity does not follow without assumptions excluding accumulating output times or specifying a profile convention.

assumptions_latex: A benchmark family supplies instances indexed by a declared size statistic.
All non-size factors designated as controls follow a fixed sampling protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input-size scaling is the conditional resource profile obtained by varying the declared size statistic under the fixed protocol.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines empirical scaling, not a worst-case asymptotic complexity theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n(I)\in\mathbb{N}\) be a prespecified input-size statistic and \(R(I)\ge 0\) a measured resource such as time, memory, or node expansions. Under a fixed instance-generation and censoring protocol, input-size scaling is the function \(S_R(n)=T(R(I)\mid n(I)=n)\), where \(T\) is a prespecified statistic, such as a median or quantile. Any fitted law \(S_R(n)\approx g(n;\theta)\) must report the fitted range, controls, uncertainty, and treatment of unsuccessful runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Input-size scaling summarizes resource use at each declared instance size while holding the benchmark generation and censoring protocol fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Input-Size Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly concerns empirical rather than worst-case scaling, but the conditional summary, censoring, fitting, and reporting conventions have no inspectable methodology source.

children.title: Density Scaling
children.top_down_role: Performance trends as graph, matrix, constraint, or interaction density changes.

assumptions_latex: Instances share a common combinatorial representation.
Size and other designated structural covariates are controlled or explicitly conditioned upon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Density scaling is the conditional performance profile across prescribed density levels.

notation.meaning: number of represented elements or vertices
number of represented relations, edges, or constraints

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: controlled benchmark scaling along a density coordinate
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density must be representation-specific and cannot be inferred from size alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each instance \(I\), define a representation-specific density \(d(I)\), for example \(d(I)=m(I)/n(I)\) or \(d(I)=2m(I)/(n(I)(n(I)-1))\) for a simple undirected graph. Given performance measure \(R(I)\), density scaling is \(S_R(d)=T(R(I)\mid d(I)=d,\ C(I)\in\mathcal{C})\), where \(C\) contains controlled size and structural covariates. The density formula, admissible range, conditioning scheme, and aggregation statistic \(T\) are part of the benchmark specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Density scaling measures performance as a declared edge, relation, or constraint density changes while size and specified structural factors are controlled.
knowledge_statements.title: Density Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation-specific definition fits Density Scaling, but the conditional scaling framework and required controls are unsupported by a cited benchmark source.

children.title: Structural-Parameter Scaling
children.top_down_role: Performance trends across width, depth, rank, sparsity pattern, or decomposition parameters.

assumptions_latex: A structural statistic is computable identically for every benchmark instance.
The sampling design distinguishes the structural statistic from input size and density.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Structural-parameter scaling is the conditional resource profile obtained as the chosen structural statistic varies.

notation.meaning: declared structural parameter of instance I

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional empirical scaling by a declared structural parameter
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to parameters such as width, degeneracy, rank, or decomposition depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k(I)\) be a prespecified structural parameter, such as treewidth, degeneracy, rank, or decomposition depth, and let \(C(I)\) contain size, density, and other controlled covariates. For a performance outcome \(R(I)\), structural-parameter scaling is \(S_R(k)=T(R(I)\mid k(I)=k,\ C(I)\in\mathcal{C})\). The benchmark must state whether \(k(I)\) is exact, bounded, or estimated and must not interpret variation in \(S_R\) as structural causation unless the sampling design identifies that effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural-parameter scaling summarizes performance as a chosen structural statistic varies, conditional on size, density, and other declared controls.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural-Parameter Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits structural-parameter scaling and appropriately distinguishes exact, bounded, and estimated parameters, but its modeling and causal-interpretation requirements lack a source.

children.title: Density-Structure Interactions
children.top_down_role: Scaling behavior when density varies within distinct structural regimes.

assumptions_latex: Density and structural parameters are measured under fixed definitions.
The benchmark design contains sufficient joint variation to distinguish main effects from interactions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero interaction term records that density sensitivity changes with structure, rather than being an additive density effect.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard conditional-response decomposition for benchmark interactions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interaction is defined relative to a declared response scale and fitted model class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(I)\) be a prespecified transformation of runtime, resource consumption, or solution quality. A density-structure response model may be represented as \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid d,k,C]=\alpha+h_d(d)+h_k(k)+h_{dk}(d,k)+\gamma^{\mathsf T}C\), subject to stated identifiability constraints on the component functions. Density and structure interact when \(h_{dk}\) is not identically zero on the benchmark domain. Equivalently, where derivatives exist, interaction is witnessed by \(\partial^2\mathbb{E}[Y\mid d,k,C]/(\partial d\,\partial k)\ne 0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Density and structure interact when their joint performance effect cannot be represented by separate additive effects on the declared response scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Density-Structure Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the interaction leaf, but the asserted equivalence with a nonzero mixed derivative requires domain, smoothness, and identifiability conditions not stated here; a modeling source is needed to fix the exact formulation.

children.title: Structure-Driven Performance Cliffs
children.top_down_role: Abrupt performance changes associated with structural transitions in benchmark instances.

assumptions_latex: Instances approach a structural threshold while size, density, and implementation remain controlled.
Performance is summarized by a positive resource statistic or success probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A performance cliff occurs when an arbitrarily small structural change near the threshold causes a benchmark-significant discontinuity or unbounded relative deterioration.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational threshold definition for abrupt empirical degradation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires replicated evidence near the threshold; an isolated outlier is not a cliff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(k)>0\) summarize conditional resource use at structural level \(k\), with all declared controls fixed. A structure-driven performance cliff at \(k_0\) is present when there exist sequences \(k_j^-\to k_0\) and \(k_j^+\to k_0\) from opposite sides such that \(S(k_j^+)/S(k_j^-)\ge c\) for a prespecified practically significant \(c>1\), or this ratio diverges. For success probability, replace the ratio criterion by a prespecified discontinuous drop. Replication and uncertainty intervals must exclude ordinary sampling variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural performance cliff is a replicated, practically significant abrupt deterioration near a structural threshold, under controlled size, density, and implementation.
knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Driven Performance Cliffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the one-sided ratio criterion, direction convention, significance threshold, and replication rule constitute a particular operational definition without supporting methodology evidence.

children.title: Coefficient-Magnitude Scaling
children.top_down_role: Performance trends as coefficient ranges or dynamic ranges increase.

assumptions_latex: The combinatorial support and coefficient precision are held fixed.
Arithmetic and overflow conventions are identical across runs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coefficient-magnitude scaling is the conditional performance profile obtained by varying the maximum absolute coefficient.

notation.meaning: numeric coefficients in the encoded instance

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: controlled scaling by coefficient magnitude
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates numerical magnitude from precision and encoded bitlength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance \(I\) with numeric coefficients \(a_1,\ldots,a_p\), define \(M(I)=\max_{1\le j\le p}|a_j|\). Under fixed support, dimensions, coefficient precision, arithmetic model, and encoding convention, coefficient-magnitude scaling is \(S_R(M)=T(R(I)\mid M(I)=M,\ C(I)\in\mathcal{C})\). Rescaling all coefficients is an admissible magnitude experiment only when the benchmark also records whether mathematical equivalence is preserved and whether stopping tolerances or overflow behavior change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient-magnitude scaling measures performance as the largest absolute coefficient changes while structure, precision, arithmetic, and encoding are controlled.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient-Magnitude Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition appropriately separates magnitude from precision and encoding length, but the controls and admissibility conditions for rescaling experiments require an inspectable numerical-benchmark source.

children.title: Numeric-Precision Scaling
children.top_down_role: Performance trends as input precision or arithmetic precision changes.

assumptions_latex: The instance family has fixed combinatorial structure and a declared exact reference representation.
The solver's arithmetic and feasibility tolerances are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Numeric-precision scaling is the conditional performance and correctness profile as the retained precision varies.

notation.meaning: number of retained binary fractional digits or another declared precision index
coefficient quantization operator at precision p

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: controlled benchmark scaling under coefficient quantization
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision scaling includes both resource use and changes to feasibility or optimality outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_p(a)\) quantize each exact reference coefficient \(a\) to a declared precision level \(p\), and let \(I_p=Q_p(I)\). Numeric-precision scaling is the profile \(S_R(p)=T(R(I_p)\mid C(I_p)\in\mathcal{C})\) under fixed combinatorial structure, magnitude regime, solver configuration, and verification rule. The benchmark must separately report resource consumption and semantic distortion, including changed feasibility, objective ordering, optimal value, or certificate acceptance caused by replacing \(I\) with \(I_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numeric-precision scaling varies coefficient quantization while tracking both computational performance and any resulting change in feasibility, optimality, or verification.
knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Precision Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits numeric-precision scaling, but its quantization-based formulation and semantic-distortion reporting requirements have no cited numerical-analysis or benchmark source.

children.title: Coefficient-Bitlength Scaling
children.top_down_role: Performance trends organized by encoded coefficient bitlength.

assumptions_latex: Coefficients are encoded as signed integers or rationals under a fixed canonical convention.
Combinatorial dimensions and structural controls are recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coefficient-bitlength scaling is the conditional resource profile across declared coefficient encoding lengths.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of an integer coefficient
maximum coefficient bitlength in instance I

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional binary encoding length used in complexity experiments
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Makes the encoding contribution to input length explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer coefficient \(a\), let \(\ell(a)=1+\lceil\log_2(1+|a|)\rceil\), including one sign bit, and define \(L(I)=\max_j\ell(a_j)\). For rational coefficients, the benchmark must specify separate numerator and denominator lengths. Coefficient-bitlength scaling is \(S_R(L)=T(R(I)\mid L(I)=L,\ C(I)\in\mathcal{C})\) under a fixed encoding and arithmetic model. The total encoded input length must also be reported when coefficient counts vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coefficient-bitlength scaling measures resource use as canonical binary coefficient lengths change, while separately recording structure and total encoded input length.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient-Bitlength Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits coefficient-bitlength scaling, but the stated signed-integer length convention is not universal and needs a source or explicit benchmark standard with a locator.

children.title: Magnitude-Precision Interactions
children.top_down_role: Behavior arising from combined coefficient range plus precision requirements.

assumptions_latex: Magnitude and precision indices vary jointly over a prespecified benchmark grid.
Structural variables, arithmetic, tolerances, and solver configuration are controlled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Magnitude and precision interact when the effect of changing one depends on the level of the other on the declared response scale.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: factorial response decomposition for two numeric scaling factors
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers runtime, numerical failures, and certificate acceptance under joint numeric variation.
