knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For magnitude index \(M\), precision index \(p\), controls \(C\), and response \(Y\), represent the conditional response as \(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid M,p,C]=\alpha+h_M(M)+h_p(p)+h_{Mp}(M,p)+\gamma^{\mathsf T}C\), with declared identifiability constraints. A magnitude-precision interaction exists when \(h_{Mp}\) is not identically zero. The benchmark must report the joint design domain because large magnitude and low precision may jointly alter coefficient ordering, feasibility tolerances, overflow risk, or certificate acceptance even when neither marginal profile predicts that change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Magnitude and precision interact when their joint effect on performance or correctness cannot be explained by adding their separate effects.
knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude-Precision Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the interaction leaf, but the additive decomposition, identifiability constraints, and claimed numerical mechanisms require an inspectable factorial-modeling or numerical-benchmark source.

children.title: Parallel Speedup
children.top_down_role: Runtime improvement as processing resources increase relative to a stated baseline.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Speedup
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wall-clock speedup for a fixed algorithm, instance, platform, and processor count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_p(x)>0\) be the elapsed time required to solve instance \(x\) using \(p\in\mathbb{N}_{+}\) processing elements under a fixed implementation and stopping rule. The parallel speedup relative to one processing element is \[S_p(x):=\frac{T_1(x)}{T_p(x)}.\] More generally, relative to a baseline count \(p_0\), define \(S_{p_0\to p}(x):=T_{p_0}(x)/T_p(x)\). Speedup is linear when \(S_p(x)=p\), sublinear when \(S_p(x)<p\), and superlinear when \(S_p(x)>p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel speedup is baseline runtime divided by runtime with more processing elements, with linear speedup equal to the processor count.
assumptions_latex: \(T_p(x)\) uses identical instances, correctness criteria, and stopping rules for every \(p\).
Runtime measurements use a fixed implementation and platform configuration.

notation.meaning: elapsed runtime on instance x with p processing elements
speedup relative to one processing element

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Parallel Speedup leaf and are mathematically standard, but the record provides no inspectable citation. An authoritative parallel-performance source with a section or page locator is required.

children.title: Parallel Efficiency
children.top_down_role: Useful scaling benefit relative to the amount of parallel resources employed.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Efficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Processor-use efficiency derived from speedup under a fixed-size experiment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an execution on \(p\in\mathbb{N}_{+}\) processing elements with speedup \(S_p(x)\), its parallel efficiency is \[E_p(x):=\frac{S_p(x)}{p}=\frac{T_1(x)}{pT_p(x)}.\] Relative to a baseline using \(p_0\) processing elements, the incremental efficiency is \(E_{p_0\to p}(x):=S_{p_0\to p}(x)/(p/p_0)\). Thus \(E_p(x)=1\) denotes linear speedup, while \(E_p(x)<1\) quantifies the fraction of ideal aggregate processing capacity realized by the measured run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel efficiency is speedup per processing element; efficiency one corresponds to linear speedup.
assumptions_latex: All runs use the same instance and solution criterion.

notation.meaning: parallel efficiency on p processing elements
elapsed runtime with p processing elements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is standard and the definition kind fits, but no source is supplied. The description of efficiency below one as a realized fraction also needs source-qualified wording because measured efficiency can exceed one under superlinear speedup.

children.title: Strong-Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parallel behavior for fixed benchmark workloads across increasing resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-instance scaling as the allocated parallelism increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance \(x\) and vary the processor count \(p\). The resulting measurements form a strong-scaling regime. For a processor range \(P\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{+}\), scaling is ideal on \(P\) when \(T_p(x)=T_1(x)/p\) for every \(p\in P\), equivalently \(S_p(x)=p\). It is efficiency-preserving at level \(\eta\in(0,1]\) when \(E_p(x)\geq\eta\) throughout \(P\). A strong-scaling saturation point at threshold \(\eta\) is the least tested \(p\) for which \(E_p(x)<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong scaling fixes the problem instance and measures how runtime, speedup, or efficiency changes as processor count grows.
assumptions_latex: The same fixed instance \(x\), implementation, and stopping rule are used for all tested \(p\).
\(P\) is a finite set of tested positive processor counts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ideal strong scaling satisfies \(T_p(x)=T_1(x)/p\), equivalently \(S_p(x)=p\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-instance definition matches strong scaling, but there is no cited source. In addition, the least tested processor count with efficiency below the threshold exists only if the corresponding subset of the tested set is nonempty.

children.title: Weak-Scaling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parallel behavior when workload grows with available resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling with increasing processor count and proportionally controlled workload per processor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_p\) be the instance assigned to \(p\) processing elements, chosen so that a declared workload measure \(n(x_p)/p\) is constant. These runs form a weak-scaling regime. Relative to baseline \(p_0\), define weak-scaling efficiency by \[E^{\mathrm{weak}}_{p_0\to p}:=\frac{T_{p_0}(x_{p_0})}{T_p(x_p)}.\] Weak scaling is ideal over a tested range when \(T_p(x_p)=T_{p_0}(x_{p_0})\) throughout that range. The workload measure must be reported because equal input counts need not imply equal computational work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak scaling increases total problem size with processor count while holding a declared workload per processor constant.
assumptions_latex: \(n(x_p)/p=n(x_{p_0})/p_0\) for every tested \(p\).
Runs use a common implementation, platform policy, and correctness criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ideal weak scaling satisfies \(T_p(x_p)=T_{p_0}(x_{p_0})\).

notation.meaning: instance selected for processor count p
weak-scaling efficiency relative to the baseline

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly distinguishes weak scaling by a declared per-processor workload measure, and definition is the appropriate kind. An authoritative weak-scaling citation is nevertheless required to support the chosen efficiency convention and hypotheses.

children.title: Parallel Scaling Limits
children.top_down_role: Resource levels where coordination, imbalance, serial work, or contention erodes scaling benefits.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Scaling Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work–span upper bounds on attainable speedup for a fixed computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the work–span model, let \(T_1(x)\) be the computation's work and \(T_\infty(x)\) its span, both measured in compatible operation units. Any schedule on \(p\) identical processing elements satisfies \[T_p(x)\geq\max\!\left\{\frac{T_1(x)}{p},T_\infty(x)\right\}.\] Consequently, \[S_p(x)\leq\min\!\left\{p,\frac{T_1(x)}{T_\infty(x)}\right\}.\] Thus adding processors cannot overcome either the total-work bound or the critical-path bound; communication, synchronization, and scheduling overhead can only lower realized speedup further.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Speedup cannot exceed either the processor count or the computation's work-to-span parallelism.
assumptions_latex: The computation is represented by a finite dependency directed acyclic graph.
Processing elements are identical, and each operation is executed exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_p(x)\leq\min\{p,T_1(x)/T_\infty(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: execution time on p processing elements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The work-span lower bounds and resulting speedup bound fit the Parallel Scaling Limits leaf and complexity_bound kind, but no inspectable work-span source is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-to-Experiment Complexity Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Log-ratio diagnostics comparing observed resource growth with a theoretical asymptotic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(n)>0\) be a measured resource statistic for instances of declared size \(n\), and let \(g(n)>0\) be the theoretical comparison function. For two tested sizes \(n_i<n_j\), define the empirical growth exponent relative to \(g\) by \[q_{ij}:=\frac{\log(R(n_j)/R(n_i))}{\log(g(n_j)/g(n_i))},\] whenever the denominator is nonzero. Equivalently, normalized residuals are \(r_i:=R(n_i)/g(n_i)\). Approximate constancy of \(r_i\), or values \(q_{ij}\) near one across increasing size ranges, is empirical consistency with \(R(n)=\Theta(g(n))\), but does not establish an asymptotic bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare measured growth with theory using normalized residuals or log-ratio exponents; finite experiments indicate consistency but cannot prove asymptotic complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(R(n_i)>0\) and \(g(n_i)>0\) at every tested size.
Instances and measurement procedures are comparable across sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constant \(R(n_i)/g(n_i)\), equivalently \(q_{ij}\approx1\), is a finite-sample diagnostic for the model \(R(n)=\Theta(g(n))\).

notation.meaning: measured resource statistic at size n
empirical growth exponent relative to g

source_refs.locator: Time and Space Complexity p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Time and Space Complexity p. 23

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited book locator concerns time and space complexity but does not directly support the proposed finite-sample log-ratio and residual diagnostics. Moreover, approximate residual constancy and q-values near one are not equivalent without quantitative tolerances and control of the denominator. A direct empirical-complexity source is needed.

children.title: Runtime Profiles
children.top_down_role: Performance-profile views based on measured execution duration.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dolan–Moré performance profiles instantiated with elapsed runtime as the cost metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite problem set \(P\) and solver set \(S\), let \(t_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be solver \(s\)'s runtime on problem \(p\), with failure represented by \(\infty\). Define \(r_{p,s}:=t_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}t_{p,u}\) and, for \(\tau\geq1\), \[\rho_s^{\mathrm{time}}(\tau):=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|.\] Then \(\rho_s^{\mathrm{time}}(1)\) is the fraction of problems on which \(s\) is fastest, while \(\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\rho_s^{\mathrm{time}}(\tau)\) is its success fraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A runtime profile gives the fraction of benchmark problems on which a solver runs within a factor of the fastest solver.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(S\) are finite and nonempty.
Every problem has at least one solver with finite runtime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s^{\mathrm{time}}(\tau)=|\{p:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}|/|P|\).

notation.meaning: runtime of solver s on problem p
runtime ratio to the best solver on problem p
runtime performance profile of solver s

children.title: Work-Unit Profiles
children.top_down_role: Performance-profile views based on iterations, evaluations, nodes, primitives, or other work proxies.

knowledge_statements.title: Work-Unit Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance profiles using a platform-independent declared operation or oracle count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite problem set \(P\) and solver set \(S\), let \(w_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be the number of declared work units used by solver \(s\) on problem \(p\), assigning \(\infty\) to failure. Define \(q_{p,s}:=w_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}w_{p,u}\). The work-unit profile is \[\rho_s^{\mathrm{work}}(\tau):=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:q_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] The work-unit definition and counting boundary must be identical for all solvers being compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A work-unit profile measures how often each solver's declared operation count lies within a factor of the benchmark minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(S\) are finite and nonempty.
Work units are counted by one common, deterministic convention.
Every problem has at least one finite work count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s^{\mathrm{work}}(\tau)=|\{p:q_{p,s}\leq\tau\}|/|P|\).

notation.meaning: work ratio to the least-work solver

children.title: Time-Work Profile Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparisons of solver rankings under elapsed-time versus work-unit measures.

assumptions_latex: The runtime and work profiles use the same finite, nonempty problem set \(P\) and solver set \(S\).
For every \(p\in P\) and \(s\in S\), the paired measurements satisfy \(t_{p,s},w_{p,s}\in(0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(t_{p,s}=c_p w_{p,s}\) for all \(p\in P\) and \(s\in S\), then \(\rho_s^{\mathrm{time}}(\tau)=\rho_s^{\mathrm{work}}(\tau)\) for every \(s\in S\) and \(\tau\geq1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(S\) be finite, nonempty problem and solver sets, and suppose \(t_{p,s},w_{p,s}\in(0,\infty)\) for every \(p\in P\) and \(s\in S\). Define \(r_{p,s}:=t_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}t_{p,u}\) and \(q_{p,s}:=w_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}w_{p,u}\). If for each \(p\in P\) there exists \(c_p>0\) such that \(t_{p,s}=c_p w_{p,s}\) for every \(s\in S\), then \(r_{p,s}=q_{p,s}\) for all \(p\in P\) and \(s\in S\), and hence \[\rho_s^{\mathrm{time}}(\tau)=\rho_s^{\mathrm{work}}(\tau)\] for every \(s\in S\) and \(\tau\geq1\). Consequently, if the paired profiles differ for some solver and threshold, then no such family of solver-independent, per-problem conversion factors \(\{c_p:p\in P\}\) exists for all paired measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finite paired measurements, time and work profiles coincide when every runtime is a problem-specific positive constant times the corresponding work count. If the profiles differ, no such solver-independent conversion factor exists for all paired measurements.

children.title: Platform-Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where runtime profiles vary across platforms while work-unit profiles remain comparatively stable.

knowledge_statements.title: Platform-Sensitivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A checkable criterion for invariance of runtime profiles across computing platforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t^{(h)}_{p,s}>0\) denote runtime on platform \(h\), and let \(r^{(h)}_{p,s}:=t^{(h)}_{p,s}/\min_u t^{(h)}_{p,u}\). A benchmark is runtime-profile invariant over a platform set \(H\) when \[r^{(h)}_{p,s}=r^{(h')}_{p,s}\] for all \(h,h'\in H\), problems \(p\), and solvers \(s\). A sufficient condition is \(t^{(h)}_{p,s}=a_{h,p}w_{p,s}\) with \(a_{h,p}>0\) independent of \(s\). Platform sensitivity occurs whenever normalized ratios, and consequently some profile values, vary with \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime profiles are platform invariant exactly when all normalized solver runtime ratios remain unchanged across platforms.
assumptions_latex: All platforms use the same problem set, solver versions, parameters, and stopping rules.
Every included problem has at least one successful solver on each platform.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Platform invariance requires \(r^{(h)}_{p,s}=r^{(h')}_{p,s}\) for all indexed comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Quality Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance profiles formed from a nonnegative solution-loss metric rather than resource consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite problem set \(P\) and solver set \(S\), let \(\ell_{p,s}\in[0,\infty]\) be a declared solution-quality loss, with smaller values better and failure assigned \(\infty\). Fix \(\epsilon>0\) and define \(r^{Q}_{p,s}:=(\ell_{p,s}+\epsilon)/(\min_{u\in S}\ell_{p,u}+\epsilon)\). The solution-quality profile is \[\rho_s^{Q}(\tau):=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r^{Q}_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] The offset \(\epsilon\), loss normalization, resource budget, and treatment of infeasible solutions must be fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution-quality profile reports the fraction of problems on which a solver's loss is within a factor of the best observed loss.
assumptions_latex: All quality values are evaluated under one fixed resource budget and loss convention.
\(P\) and \(S\) are finite, and each problem has one finite loss.
\(\epsilon>0\) is fixed independently of the solver.

notation.meaning: fixed positive offset preventing division by zero

children.title: Memory Profiles
children.top_down_role: Performance-profile views based on peak, resident, retained, or working-set memory.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance profiles using peak allocated or resident memory as the resource metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite problem set \(P\) and solver set \(S\), let \(m_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be solver \(s\)'s memory consumption on problem \(p\), measured by one declared convention, with failure assigned \(\infty\). Define \(r^{M}_{p,s}:=m_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}m_{p,u}\). The memory profile is \[\rho_s^{M}(\tau):=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r^{M}_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] Hence \(\rho_s^{M}(1)\) is the fraction of problems for which \(s\) attains the least measured memory consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A memory profile gives the fraction of problems on which a solver uses memory within a factor of the least-consuming solver.
assumptions_latex: All solvers use the same memory metric, such as peak resident set size.
\(P\) and \(S\) are finite and nonempty.
Every problem has at least one finite memory measurement.

notation.meaning: memory ratio to the least-consuming solver

children.title: Storage Profiles
children.top_down_role: Performance-profile views based on persistent or temporary storage consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Storage Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dolan–Moré profile specialized to persistent-storage consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite nonempty benchmark set and \(S\) a finite solver set. For each \((p,s)\), let \(d_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be the measured persistent-storage consumption, with \(d_{p,s}=\infty\) for an unsuccessful run. Define \(d_p^*=\min_{u\in S}d_{p,u}\), assuming \(d_p^*<\infty\), and \(r_{p,s}=d_{p,s}/d_p^*\). The storage performance profile of solver \(s\) is \[\rho_s^{\mathrm{stor}}(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] Storage consumption must use one fixed statistic, such as peak allocated disk bytes or total bytes written, for every run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile gives the fraction of instances on which a solver uses at most a factor τ more persistent storage than the benchmark minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(S\) are finite, with \(P\neq\varnothing\).
\(d_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) is measured by a common storage statistic.
\(\min_{s\in S}d_{p,s}<\infty\) for every \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s^{\mathrm{stor}}:[1,\infty)\to[0,1]\) is the storage profile of \(s\).

notation.meaning: Persistent-storage consumption of solver s on instance p.
Storage ratio relative to the best observed solver on p.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the storage-specific extension of Dolan–Moré profiles.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the Storage Profiles leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator supports extending Dolan–Moré profiles to the selected persistent-storage statistics and failure convention.

children.title: Energy Profiles
children.top_down_role: Performance-profile views based on energy consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dolan–Moré profile specialized to run-level energy consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite nonempty benchmark set and \(S\) a finite solver set. For each run, let \(e_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be its measured energy consumption, with \(e_{p,s}=\infty\) for failure. Define \(e_p^*=\min_{u\in S}e_{p,u}\), assuming \(e_p^*<\infty\), and \(r_{p,s}=e_{p,s}/e_p^*\). The energy performance profile is \[\rho_s^{\mathrm{energy}}(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] Every run must use the same energy boundary, including the same choice of processor, accelerator, memory, and idle-energy accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile reports the fraction of instances whose measured energy is within factor τ of the lowest energy observed among solvers.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(S\) are finite, with \(P\neq\varnothing\).
\(e_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) uses a common system boundary and measurement protocol.
\(\min_{s\in S}e_{p,s}<\infty\) for every \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s^{\mathrm{energy}}:[1,\infty)\to[0,1]\) is the energy profile of \(s\).

notation.meaning: Energy consumed by solver s on instance p.
Energy ratio relative to the best observed solver on p.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the energy-specific profile and measurement convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Energy Profiles leaf, but the energy-specific extension and prescribed system boundary and idle-energy accounting lack an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Communication Profiles
children.top_down_role: Performance-profile views based on data movement, message counts, or communication time.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dolan–Moré profile for a fixed communication-cost statistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite nonempty benchmark set and \(S\) a finite solver set. Let \(q_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be a fixed communication statistic for a run, such as transmitted bytes or message count, and assign \(q_{p,s}=\infty\) to failure. Set \(q_p^*=\min_{u\in S}q_{p,u}\), assuming \(q_p^*<\infty\), and \(r_{p,s}=q_{p,s}/q_p^*\). The communication performance profile is \[\rho_s^{\mathrm{comm}}(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] The statistic and the boundaries across which communication is counted must remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile measures how often a solver's communication cost lies within factor τ of the least observed communication cost.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(S\) are finite, with \(P\neq\varnothing\).
\(q_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) uses one communication statistic and boundary.
\(\min_{s\in S}q_{p,s}<\infty\) for every \(p\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s^{\mathrm{comm}}:[1,\infty)\to[0,1]\) is the communication profile of \(s\).

notation.meaning: Communication cost of solver s on instance p.
Communication ratio relative to the best observed solver on p.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the communication-specific profile and accounting boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is internally consistent and locally appropriate, but no cited source establishes this communication-profile definition or the proposed statistic and accounting-boundary convention.

children.title: Composite Resource Profiles
children.top_down_role: Profile views combining multiple resource dimensions through stated comparison criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Resource Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalarized performance profile combining multiple normalized resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(S\) be finite, with \(P\neq\varnothing\), and let \(c_{p,s,j}\in(0,\infty]\) denote resource \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Put \(b_{p,j}=\min_{u\in S}c_{p,u,j}>0\). Choose a fixed componentwise nondecreasing scalarization \(\Phi:[1,\infty]^m\to(0,\infty]\), and define \(z_{p,s}=\Phi((c_{p,s,j}/b_{p,j})_{j=1}^m)\), \(z_p^*=\min_{u\in S}z_{p,u}\), and \(r_{p,s}=z_{p,s}/z_p^*\). The composite resource profile is \[\rho_s^{\Phi}(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] The same resources and scalarization must be used for all runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize each resource, combine the normalized values with a fixed monotone scalarization, then profile each solver against the best composite value.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq2\), and all finite resource measurements are positive.
\(\Phi\) is fixed and componentwise nondecreasing.
Every instance has at least one solver with finite composite cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s^{\Phi}:[1,\infty)\to[0,1]\) is the scalarization-dependent composite resource profile.

notation.meaning: Consumption of resource j by solver s on instance p.
Composite resource profile induced by the scalarization.

review_flags: The path does not determine a canonical composite-resource scalarization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is mathematically plausible and definition is an appropriate kind, but the taxonomy does not determine this particular normalize-then-scalarize procedure. A source must establish the intended composite-resource construction and assumptions on the scalarization.

children.title: Stratified Profiles
children.top_down_role: Profiles partitioned by instance class, scale, structure, provenance, or difficulty.

knowledge_statements.title: Stratified Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance profiles computed separately on predefined benchmark strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\bigsqcup_{g\in G}P_g\) be a partition into nonempty strata, fixed independently of solver outcomes, and let \(S\) be finite. Given positive extended costs \(c_{p,s}\), define \(c_p^*=\min_{u\in S}c_{p,u}<\infty\) and \(r_{p,s}=c_{p,s}/c_p^*\). For solver \(s\), stratum \(g\), and \(\tau\geq1\), its stratified performance profile is \[\rho_{s,g}(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P_g|}\left|\{p\in P_g:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|.\] The family \((\rho_{s,g})_{g\in G}\), together with the stratum sizes, is the stratified profile; pooling it requires explicitly chosen stratum weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stratified profile applies the usual performance-profile calculation separately to each predetermined, nonempty class of benchmark instances.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\bigsqcup_{g\in G}P_g\) is a fixed partition with \(P_g\neq\varnothing\).
\(S\) is finite and each instance has a finite reference cost.
Stratum membership does not depend on measured solver outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\rho_{s,g})_{g\in G}\) is the stratum-indexed performance-profile family for solver \(s\).

notation.meaning: Profile of solver s restricted to stratum g.

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this stratified extension of performance profiles.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separate within-stratum profiles are coherent and fit the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports this precise stratified-profile convention, the outcome-independent partition requirement, or the treatment of pooling weights.

children.title: Pairwise Solver Profiles
children.top_down_role: Profiles restricted to direct comparisons between selected solver pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Solver Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance profile whose reference set contains exactly two solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be finite and nonempty, and choose distinct solvers \(a\) and \(b\). For positive extended costs \(c_{p,a}\) and \(c_{p,b}\), suppose \(m_p=\min\{c_{p,a},c_{p,b}\}<\infty\) for every \(p\). Define \(r_{p,s}^{a,b}=c_{p,s}/m_p\) for \(s\in\{a,b\}\). The pairwise solver profiles are \[\rho_s^{a,b}(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}^{a,b}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad s\in\{a,b\},\quad\tau\geq1.\] Costs from solvers outside the pair do not enter either the denominator or the empirical distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two solvers are profiled using, on every instance, only the better cost achieved by that pair as the reference.
assumptions_latex: \(P\neq\varnothing\) is finite.
\(a\neq b\), and costs lie in \((0,\infty]\).
At least one of \(a,b\) has finite cost on every instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\rho_a^{a,b},\rho_b^{a,b})\) is the pairwise performance-profile comparison of \(a\) and \(b\).

notation.meaning: Best cost within the selected solver pair on instance p.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the pair-restricted reference convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pair-restricted formula is precise and fits Pairwise Solver Profiles, but no source establishes that this leaf uses a two-solver reference minimum rather than another pairwise comparison construction.

children.title: Stratum-Specific Rank Reversals
children.top_down_role: Cases where aggregate solver ordering changes within benchmark strata.

knowledge_statements.title: Stratum-Specific Rank Reversals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance ordering reverses between two benchmark strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_g\) and \(P_h\) be two nonempty strata, and let \(\rho_{s,g}\) and \(\rho_{s,h}\) be the corresponding profiles. Distinct solvers \(a,b\) exhibit a stratum-specific rank reversal when one solver weakly profile-dominates in one stratum and the other weakly profile-dominates in the other, with both comparisons strict somewhere: \[\bigl(\forall\tau\geq1:\rho_{a,g}(\tau)\geq\rho_{b,g}(\tau)\bigr)\land\bigl(\exists\tau\geq1:\rho_{a,g}(\tau)>\rho_{b,g}(\tau)\bigr),\] \[\bigl(\forall\tau\geq1:\rho_{b,h}(\tau)\geq\rho_{a,h}(\tau)\bigr)\land\bigl(\exists\tau\geq1:\rho_{b,h}(\tau)>\rho_{a,h}(\tau)\bigr).\] This condition concerns full-profile dominance rather than a reversal at only one selected threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank reversal occurs when solver a profile-dominates b in one stratum, while b profile-dominates a in another.
assumptions_latex: \(P_g\) and \(P_h\) are nonempty strata.
The same cost statistic, solver set, and failure convention define both profile families.
\(a\neq b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed opposing dominance relations constitute a stratum-specific rank reversal between \(a\) and \(b\).

notation.meaning: Performance profile of solver s in stratum g.

review_flags: The literature may use scalar rankings rather than full-profile dominance; no relevant locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed condition consistently defines reversal of full-profile dominance and condition is a suitable content kind. A source is required because rank reversal may instead refer to a scalar rank, selected threshold, or summary statistic.

children.title: Pairwise Intransitivity
children.top_down_role: Comparison patterns where pairwise advantages do not induce a stable global ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Intransitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cyclic majority preference induced by pairwise benchmark outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be finite and nonempty and let costs \(c_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be compared using a fixed tie rule. For distinct solvers \(a,b\), define their pairwise win score by \[W(a,b)=\frac{1}{|P|}\sum_{p\in P}\left(\mathbf{1}\{c_{p,a}<c_{p,b}\}+\frac12\mathbf{1}\{c_{p,a}=c_{p,b}\}\right),\] and write \(a\succ b\) when \(W(a,b)>1/2\). Pairwise intransitivity occurs if there exist distinct solvers \(a,b,c\) such that \[a\succ b,\qquad b\succ c,\qquad c\succ a.\] Thus no single transitive ordering can reproduce all three pairwise majority comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise intransitivity is a cycle: a beats b on a majority basis, b beats c, and c beats a.
assumptions_latex: \(P\neq\varnothing\) is finite.
All comparisons use one cost statistic and one tie convention.
\(a,b,c\) are distinct solvers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\succ b\succ c\succ a\) certifies intransitivity of the pairwise preference relation.

notation.meaning: Tie-adjusted fraction of instances on which a beats b.
Solver a has pairwise win score greater than one half against b.

review_flags: The node path does not specify whether pairwise preference uses wins, profile dominance, or another score.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Condorcet-cycle condition is mathematically coherent, but the parent context of pairwise performance profiles does not establish that pairwise preference is the tie-adjusted majority of raw instance wins. An authoritative locator is needed for this choice.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Set Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Profile conclusions can change when the comparison solver set changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq R'\) be finite solver reference sets, let \(a,b\in R\), and define \(m_p(R)=\min_{u\in R}c_{p,u}\), \(r_{p,s}^{R}=c_{p,s}/m_p(R)\), and \(\rho_s^{R}(\tau)=|P|^{-1}|\{p:r_{p,s}^{R}\leq\tau\}|\). Reference-set instability at threshold \(\tau\geq1\) occurs when \[\operatorname{sgn}\!\left(\rho_a^{R}(\tau)-\rho_b^{R}(\tau)\right)\neq\operatorname{sgn}\!\left(\rho_a^{R'}(\tau)-\rho_b^{R'}(\tau)\right).\] It can occur because adding a solver lowers \(m_p\) by instance-dependent factors, thereby changing the empirical ratios of solvers already present.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding reference solvers can reverse or create a threshold-based profile ordering between two solvers that were already compared.
assumptions_latex: \(P\neq\varnothing\), and \(R\subseteq R'\) are finite.
\(a,b\in R\).
Every instance has positive finite reference minima under both sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A change in the displayed sign is a threshold-specific reference-set instability.

notation.meaning: Best cost on instance p among solvers in reference set R.
Profile of solver s computed using reference set R.
Sign function, including zero for a tie.

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this formal instability criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent threshold-specific failure phenomenon and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No source supports this exact sign-change criterion or establishes that it is the intended meaning of Reference-Set Instability.

children.title: Failure Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Profile changes caused by solver errors, invalid outputs, or unsolved instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of profiles to the numerical encoding of unsuccessful runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq P\times S\) be the set of unsuccessful runs. A failure encoding \(E\) assigns each \((p,s)\in F\) an extended cost \(E_{p,s}\), while successful costs remain fixed. Let \(\rho_s^{E}\) be the resulting profile. For two admissible encodings \(E,E'\), define solver-level failure sensitivity by \[\Delta_s(E,E')=\sup_{\tau\geq1}\left|\rho_s^{E}(\tau)-\rho_s^{E'}(\tau)\right|.\] A reported profile conclusion is failure-sensitive over a class \(\mathcal E\) if some \(E,E'\in\mathcal E\) change that conclusion; \(\sup_{E,E'\in\mathcal E}\Delta_s(E,E')\) quantifies curve sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure sensitivity measures how much a solver's profile or inferred comparison changes when unsuccessful runs receive different admissible cost encodings.
assumptions_latex: The successful-run costs and benchmark set are fixed.
Every encoding in \(\mathcal E\) uses positive extended costs and yields finite instance reference minima.
Profiles use the same solver set under all encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_s(E,E')\in[0,1]\) measures the maximum profile displacement caused by changing failure encoding.

notation.meaning: An admissible numerical encoding of failures.
Supremum-norm displacement between two encoded profiles.

review_flags: No supplied locator defines an admissible failure-encoding class or sensitivity metric.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source defines the admissible failure-encoding class or the proposed supremum-distance functional. The leaf denotes a sensitivity phenomenon, so failure_boundary or property may be more appropriate than definition depending on the sourced intended meaning.

children.title: Timeout Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Profile changes caused by cutoff choices or censored runtimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Timeout Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of profiles to the selected run-time cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t_{p,s}\in(0,\infty]\) be uncensored run time and let \(T>0\) be a cutoff. Under a fixed timeout penalty rule \(h_T\), define the recorded cost by \(c_{p,s}^{T}=t_{p,s}\) when \(t_{p,s}\leq T\), and \(c_{p,s}^{T}=h_T(t_{p,s})\) otherwise. Let \(\rho_s^{T}\) be the induced profile. For cutoffs \(T,T'>0\), define \[\Delta_s(T,T')=\sup_{\tau\geq1}\left|\rho_s^{T}(\tau)-\rho_s^{T'}(\tau)\right|.\] A profile conclusion is timeout-sensitive on \(\mathcal T\) if it changes for some \(T,T'\in\mathcal T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Timeout sensitivity records how much a profile or comparison changes when the cutoff varies while the timeout-penalty rule remains fixed.
assumptions_latex: The underlying runs, benchmark set, and solver set are fixed.
\(h_T\) is specified for every considered cutoff.
Every induced profile has finite instance reference minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_s(T,T')\in[0,1]\) is the maximum profile displacement between cutoffs \(T\) and \(T'\).

notation.meaning: Fixed rule for encoding runs exceeding cutoff T.
Profile displacement caused by changing the cutoff.

review_flags: No supplied locator specifies the timeout-penalty convention or sensitivity functional.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed curve-displacement measure depends on an unsourced cutoff-indexed penalty family and on uncensored runtimes for timed-out runs. A source must determine the intended timeout model, sensitivity functional, and whether the terminal container calls for a failure boundary rather than a definition.

children.title: Tie Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Profile changes caused by equal, rounded, or tolerance-equivalent performance values.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of profile comparisons to numerical tie tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\rho_a\) and \(\rho_b\) be two profiles and let \(w\) be a nonnegative integrable weight on \([1,\tau_{max}]\) with positive integral. For tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), define the tie-adjusted comparison score \[D_{a,b}(\varepsilon)=\frac{\int_1^{\tau_{\max}}w(\tau)\,\psi_\varepsilon(\rho_a(\tau)-\rho_b(\tau))\,d\tau}{\int_1^{\tau_{\max}}w(\tau)\,d\tau},\] where \(\psi_\varepsilon(x)=1\) if \(x>\varepsilon\), \(0\) if \(|x|\leq\varepsilon\), and \(-1\) if \(x<-\varepsilon\). The comparison is tie-sensitive on a tolerance set \(E\) when \(\operatorname{sgn}D_{a,b}(\varepsilon)\) is not constant over \(\varepsilon\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tie sensitivity occurs when varying the tolerance used to regard profile differences as ties changes the inferred ordering of two solvers.
assumptions_latex: \(1<\tau_{\max}<\infty\).
\(w\geq0\) is integrable and has positive integral.
The profiles and integration range remain fixed as \(\varepsilon\) varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Variation of \(\operatorname{sgn}D_{a,b}(\varepsilon)\) over \(E\) certifies tie sensitivity.

notation.meaning: Tolerance below which a profile difference is treated as a tie.

review_flags: The path does not determine a canonical tie rule or profile-ranking functional.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted integral score is one possible tie-sensitive ranking functional, but neither the path nor any citation selects it, its weight, or its finite threshold range. The intended tie rule and the suitable role—likely a sensitivity property or failure boundary—require sourced clarification.

children.title: Failure-Penalty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Alternative treatments of failed runs within profile construction.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark set \(P\) and solver set \(S\) are finite.
Each run has measured cost \(t_{p,s}\), timeout limit \(T_p\), and success indicator \(z_{p,s}\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting profile is conditional on the selected failure penalty and should be compared across plausible values of \(M\).

notation.meaning: finite penalty assigned to an unsuccessful run

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite penalties make performance profiles computable with failed runs, but rankings may depend on the penalty convention
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-penalty treatment of failed runs in Dolan–Moré-style profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(p\in P\) and \(s\in S\), define \(\widetilde t_{p,s}^{(M)}=t_{p,s}\) when \(z_{p,s}=1\), and \(\widetilde t_{p,s}^{(M)}=M T_p\) otherwise. Set \(r_{p,s}^{(M)}=\widetilde t_{p,s}^{(M)}/\min_{u\in S}\widetilde t_{p,u}^{(M)}\) and \(\rho_s^{(M)}(\tau)=|P|^{-1}|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}^{(M)}\leq\tau\}|\). Because changing \(M\) can move failed observations across a threshold \(\tau\), solver orderings derived from \(\rho_s^{(M)}\) need not be invariant in \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failed runs receive a finite multiple of the timeout. Changing that multiple can alter profile values and solver rankings.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure-Penalty Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports this particular finite-penalty regime or the ranking-sensitivity claim. The ratio also requires a strictly positive denominator, which is not guaranteed by the stated assumptions.

children.title: Timeout-Tie Interactions
children.top_down_role: Profile behavior when cutoff censoring produces equal or indistinguishable recorded outcomes.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark set \(P\) and solver set \(S\) are finite.
A common timeout convention and a deterministic tie tolerance \(\varepsilon_p\geq0\) are fixed for every problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Timeout and tie rules must be varied jointly when assessing the robustness of profile-based solver rankings.

notation.meaning: reported or penalized cost for problem p and solver s

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: censoring and tie tolerances jointly determine best-run denominators and threshold membership
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint sensitivity of performance-profile outcomes to censoring and tie conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(m_p=\min_{u\in S}\widetilde t_{p,u}\) and \(B_p=\{s\in S:\widetilde t_{p,s}\leq m_p+\varepsilon_p\}\). If a timeout or failure penalty changes \(m_p\), then both \(B_p\) and every ratio \(r_{p,s}=\widetilde t_{p,s}/m_p\) may change. Consequently, even a solver whose own uncensored runtime is unchanged can enter or leave \(\{p:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\). Thus timeout handling and tie tolerance generally have a nonseparable effect on the empirical profile \(\rho_s(\tau)=|P|^{-1}|\{p:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Timeout handling can change the best observed cost, thereby changing both declared ties and every solver's performance ratio.
knowledge_statements.title: Timeout-Tie Interactions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is plausible for this sensitivity leaf, but the joint timeout-tie formulation has no cited support. The additive tolerance defines membership in a best-solver set while the profile still uses exact ratios, so the precise intended tie-aware profile convention is unclear.

assumptions_latex: The problem set \(P\) is finite, and each problem \(p\) has dimension or scaling factor \(n_p+1>0\).
For solver \(s\), \(t_{p,s}\in[0,\infty]\) is the evaluations needed to satisfy a fixed success test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(d_s\) is the empirical fraction of problems solved within normalized budget \(\alpha\).

notation.meaning: evaluation count required by solver s on problem p

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard normalized-budget empirical data-profile definition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation-budget data profiles with dimension normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\geq0\), the data profile of solver \(s\) is \[d_s(\alpha)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\left\{p\in P:\frac{t_{p,s}}{n_p+1}\leq\alpha\right\}\right|.\] An unsuccessful run has \(t_{p,s}=+\infty\). Hence \(d_s(\alpha)\in[0,1]\), is nondecreasing and right-continuous, and measures the fraction of benchmark problems on which \(s\) meets the common success test using at most \(\alpha(n_p+1)\) evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A data profile is the empirical fraction of problems solved within a dimension-normalized evaluation budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Data Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind match standard dimension-normalized data profiles, and the mathematics is internally coherent, but no authoritative source with a section, definition, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark set \(P\) is finite and a common budget \(B\) is imposed.
Each run yields a nonnegative error measure \(e_{p,s}(B)\), with smaller values preferred.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(A_s(\epsilon;B)\) summarizes the distribution of achieved accuracy at budget \(B\).

notation.meaning: error achieved by solver s on problem p at budget B

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: empirical attainment fractions provide a mathematically explicit accuracy profile
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical attainment profile over accuracy tolerances at a fixed budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For solver \(s\), budget \(B\), and tolerance \(\epsilon\geq0\), define \[A_s(\epsilon;B)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\left\{p\in P:e_{p,s}(B)\leq\epsilon\right\}\right|.\] The same error normalization and failure convention must be used for all solvers. Then \(A_s(\epsilon;B)\in[0,1]\) is nondecreasing and right-continuous in \(\epsilon\); larger values mean that the solver attains the requested accuracy on a larger fraction of problems by budget \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accuracy profile reports the fraction of benchmark problems whose error is at most each tolerance under a common budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for the leaf, but the proposed empirical attainment function is not established as the intended meaning of "Accuracy Profiles" by any cited source. The cross-problem error normalization is also left abstract, making the exact mathematical object source-dependent.

children.title: Convergence Traces
children.top_down_role: Trajectories of residual, gap, objective, or accuracy measures toward a reference outcome.

assumptions_latex: A run is observed over resource values \(b\in[0,B]\).
A scalar quality measure \(q_s(b)\) is recorded using a fixed direction of preference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trace \(b\mapsto q_s(b)\) represents the run's quality evolution over consumed resource.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convergence traces represent observed quality as a function of consumed resource
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-run resource-versus-quality trace, independent of monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convergence trace for solver \(s\) is the function \(q_s:[0,B]\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) defined by a fixed logging convention: at each resource value \(b\), \(q_s(b)\) is the quality statistic available at or immediately before \(b\). For event times \(0=b_0<b_1<\cdots<b_K\leq B\), the usual event-log representation is \(q_s(b)=q_{s,k}\) for \(b_k\leq b<b_{k+1}\), with the final value extended through \(B\). Comparisons require a common resource scale and quality normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergence trace records a run's solution-quality statistic against consumed time, evaluations, nodes, or another common resource.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence Traces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits convergence traces, but the specific left-continuous event-log convention and extended-real codomain have no source support. An inspectable benchmarking reference is required to establish that this is the intended local convention.

children.title: Incumbent-Progress Traces
children.top_down_role: Trajectories showing improvements in the best available solution over budget.

assumptions_latex: The optimization direction is fixed.
At resource value \(b\), the set \(F_s(b)\) contains all feasible solutions found by solver \(s\) no later than \(b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incumbent trace is monotone: nonincreasing for minimization and nondecreasing for maximization.

notation.meaning: feasible solutions found by budget b

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: an incumbent is the best feasible solution observed so far
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-so-far feasible objective values along a solver run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, define \[I_s(b)=\inf\{f(x):x\in F_s(b)\},\] with \(I_s(b)=+\infty\) when \(F_s(b)=\varnothing\). Since \(F_s(b_1)\subseteq F_s(b_2)\) whenever \(b_1\leq b_2\), one has \(I_s(b_2)\leq I_s(b_1)\). For maximization, replace the infimum by a supremum and use \(-\infty\) before the first feasible solution; the trace is then nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incumbent-progress trace records the best feasible objective found so far and is monotone under a fixed optimization direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent-Progress Traces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, and the best-feasible-so-far monotonicity statement is mathematically standard. However, no authoritative locator supports the definition or its benchmarking interpretation.

children.title: Bound-Progress Traces
children.top_down_role: Trajectories showing changes in reported bounds over budget.

assumptions_latex: A minimization problem has optimal value \(f^*\).
At each resource value \(b\), solver \(s\) reports a valid global lower bound \(L_s(b)\leq f^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The best-so-far bound trace is nondecreasing and remains a valid lower bound on \(f^*\).

notation.meaning: reported valid lower bound at resource b

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: best-so-far valid bounds yield monotone bound-progress traces
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-so-far valid global bounds for minimization; reverse inequalities for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the best-so-far lower-bound trace by \[\overline L_s(b)=\sup_{0\leq u\leq b}L_s(u).\] For \(0\leq b_1\leq b_2\leq B\), it satisfies \(\overline L_s(b_1)\leq\overline L_s(b_2)\leq f^*\). Thus temporary deterioration in raw reported bounds does not affect \(\overline L_s\). For maximization with valid upper bounds, use \(\overline U_s(b)=\inf_{0\leq u\leq b}U_s(u)\), which is nonincreasing and satisfies \(f^*\leq\overline U_s(b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound-progress trace records the strongest valid global bound seen so far, producing a monotone approach toward the optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Progress Traces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role and best-so-far bound formulas fit the leaf and are internally consistent, but the record has no inspectable source for this trace convention or its minimization/maximization variants.

children.title: Stagnation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Trace segments with negligible improvement despite continuing resource consumption.

assumptions_latex: A trace \(q:[0,B]\to\mathbb R\) uses a quality scale on which larger values are better.
A minimum meaningful improvement \(\delta\geq0\) and duration threshold \(\Delta>0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stagnation regime is any interval satisfying the displayed improvement predicate.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stagnation requires explicit improvement and duration thresholds
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-based stagnation intervals for a larger-is-better progress trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interval \([a,c]\subseteq[0,B]\) is a \((\delta,\Delta)\)-stagnation interval when \(c-a\geq\Delta\) and \[\sup_{b\in[a,c]}q(b)-q(a)\leq\delta.\] A maximal interval satisfying this predicate is a stagnation regime. For a smaller-is-better trace, replace the improvement term by \(q(a)-\inf_{b\in[a,c]}q(b)\). The pair \((\delta,\Delta)\) is part of the definition; without it, stagnation is not a reproducible property of a trace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stagnation is an interval of sufficient duration during which recorded quality improves by no more than a declared tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Stagnation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is suitable, but this threshold-based stagnation predicate is an application-dependent choice rather than a uniquely standard definition. A source is needed to justify the predicate and the use of maximal qualifying intervals as regimes.

children.title: Nonmonotone Progress
children.top_down_role: Trajectories containing regressions, oscillations, resets, or unstable quality measures.

assumptions_latex: A raw trace \(q:[0,B]\to\mathbb R\) is sampled under a fixed larger-is-better quality convention.
The logged statistic need not be an incumbent or best-so-far value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Raw nonmonotone traces must not be interpreted as best-so-far convergence without applying an explicit envelope transformation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: current-state statistics can deteriorate, whereas best-so-far envelopes are monotone
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes raw current-state progress from monotone best-so-far progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonmonotone progress occurs when there exist \(0\leq b_1<b_2\leq B\) such that \(q(b_2)<q(b_1)\). This can arise from current-iterate quality, noisy estimates, changing penalties, or nonnested bounds. The best-so-far transformation \[q^{\uparrow}(b)=\sup_{0\leq u\leq b}q(u)\] is nondecreasing and removes downward excursions, but it represents attainment rather than the raw state. For a smaller-is-better measure, use \(q^{\downarrow}(b)=\inf_{0\leq u\leq b}q(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A raw progress statistic may worsen. Its best-so-far envelope is monotone but answers a different, attainment-based question.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Progress

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the warning against interpreting raw state as best-so-far progress. The envelope formulas are coherent, but no source supports the stated causes, terminology, or benchmarking interpretation.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark set \(P\) is finite.
For solver \(s\), \(T_{p,s}\in[0,\infty]\) is the first resource value at which a fixed target is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The profile \(H_s\) is the empirical cumulative distribution of target-attainment resources.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: time-to-target profiles are empirical distributions of first hitting times
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical first-hitting-time profile for a common quality target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_{p,s}(u)\) be a larger-is-better progress statistic and let \(\theta_p\) be the target for problem \(p\). Define \[T_{p,s}=\inf\{u\geq0:q_{p,s}(u)\geq\theta_p\},\] with \(T_{p,s}=+\infty\) if the target is never reached. The time-to-target profile is \[H_s(b)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:T_{p,s}\leq b\}\right|.\] It is nondecreasing and right-continuous; larger \(H_s(b)\) means more problems attain their targets by resource \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A time-to-target profile is the empirical distribution of the resource first needed to attain a common problem-specific target.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-to-Target Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role and empirical first-hitting-time formula fit the leaf, but no authoritative source is cited. The phrase "common problem-specific target" also requires a declared target-construction protocol to ensure solver-independent comparison.

assumptions_latex: The benchmark set \(P\) is finite and all solvers receive a common budget \(B\).
Each run yields a normalized loss \(\ell_{p,s}(B)\in[0,\infty]\), with smaller values better.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(Q_s(\eta;B)\) compares solvers through the empirical distribution of fixed-budget loss.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-budget quality profiles are empirical attainment distributions under equal resource limits
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical loss distribution after an equal resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For budget \(B\) and loss threshold \(\eta\geq0\), define \[Q_s(\eta;B)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\left\{p\in P:\ell_{p,s}(B)\leq\eta\right\}\right|.\] Unsuccessful runs receive a declared worst-case loss, possibly \(+\infty\). The profile is nondecreasing and right-continuous in \(\eta\). Comparability requires the same budget unit, quality normalization, and failure convention for all solvers; otherwise differences in \(Q_s\) may reflect protocol rather than algorithmic quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-budget quality profile reports the fraction of problems whose normalized loss is below each threshold after equal resource expenditure.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Budget Quality Profiles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate, but no source establishes this empirical loss CDF as the intended fixed-budget quality profile. The normalized loss and optional worst-case failure value are protocol-dependent and require explicit sourced definitions.

children.title: Distributional Summaries
children.top_down_role: Location, spread, quantile, tail, plus shape summaries for benchmark outcomes.

assumptions_latex: Observations \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R\) are produced under one declared benchmark protocol.
Missing, censored, and failed runs are handled by a fixed reporting rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The empirical distribution together with declared location, spread, and quantiles forms a reproducible distributional summary.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: empirical distributions, quantiles, and robust spread statistics are standard distributional summaries
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample summaries of repeated-run or across-instance performance observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The empirical distribution is \[\widehat F_n(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{X_i\leq x\}.\] Its generalized empirical quantile is \(\widehat Q_n(u)=\inf\{x:\widehat F_n(x)\geq u\}\) for \(u\in(0,1)\). A distributional summary should report at least a location statistic, such as \(\widehat Q_n(1/2)\), and a spread statistic, such as \(\operatorname{IQR}=\widehat Q_n(3/4)-\widehat Q_n(1/4)\), together with \(n\) and the censoring or failure convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributional summaries describe benchmark observations through their empirical distribution, sample size, location, spread, quantiles, and failure-handling convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Summaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role broadly fits distributional summaries, and the empirical CDF and generalized quantile formulas are standard. No source supports the normative claim about what must be reported, and merely declaring a censoring rule does not establish that the ordinary empirical CDF is appropriate for censored observations.

children.title: Sampling Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty attributable to finite selections of instances, seeds, or runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample uncertainty of a benchmark statistic under repeated sampling from a specified instance-and-run population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) be benchmark observations sampled according to a fixed design from a population distribution \(P\), and let \(T_n=t(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\) estimate \(\theta(P)\). Sampling uncertainty is the dispersion of the sampling distribution \(\mathcal L_P(T_n)\). It may be summarized by \(\operatorname{SE}_P(T_n)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_P(T_n)}\) or by a confidence set \(C_n\) whose coverage satisfies \(P\{\theta(P)\in C_n\}\geq 1-\alpha\). It excludes variation caused solely by an unmodeled measurement mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sampling uncertainty is the variation of a benchmark estimator across repeated samples drawn under the same design and population.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) follow the declared benchmark sampling design.
\(T_n\) and the target functional \(\theta(P)\) are measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L_P(T_n)\), its standard error, or a calibrated confidence set quantifies finite-sample uncertainty.

notation.meaning: Population distribution induced by the benchmark sampling design.
Statistic computed from the sampled observations.
Confidence set for the target performance functional.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports benchmark sampling uncertainty or the stated coverage formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the benchmark sampling model or confidence-set coverage formulation. An authoritative statistics source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Measurement Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty attributable to timing noise, instrumentation, platforms, or recorded measurements.

knowledge_statements.title: Measurement Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncertainty introduced when an observed benchmark metric imperfectly measures its latent performance quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For experimental unit \(i\), let the recorded performance be \(Y_i=g(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\), where \(X_i\) is the latent performance quantity, \(g\) is the declared measurement scale, and \(\varepsilon_i\) represents instrumentation, timing, logging, or quantization error. Measurement uncertainty is the conditional distribution \(\mathcal L(Y_i\mid X_i)\), commonly summarized by conditional bias \(b(x)=\mathbb E[Y_i-g(x)\mid X_i=x]\) and conditional variance \(v(x)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i=x)\). It is distinct from variation in \(X_i\) across instances, seeds, or sampled runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measurement uncertainty is variation or bias added while converting latent algorithm performance into a recorded benchmark value.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_i\) and \(X_i\) are defined on a common probability space.
The measurement scale \(g\) is fixed for the compared observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L(Y_i\mid X_i)\), together with \(b(x)\) and \(v(x)\), characterizes measurement uncertainty.

notation.meaning: Latent performance quantity for experimental unit i.

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses statistical measurement-error models for algorithm benchmarks.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is locally appropriate, but no cited source supports this measurement-error model or its benchmark interpretation.

children.title: Heavy-Tail Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Distributional behavior dominated by rare, extreme, or highly variable outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tail Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical conditions warning that runtime or cost observations have tail behavior incompatible with stable moment-based summaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n>0\) be repeated performance observations, with order statistics \(Y_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq Y_{(n)}\). For a chosen \(k<n\), define the Hill diagnostic \(\widehat\xi_k=k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\log\!\bigl(Y_{(n-j+1)}/Y_{(n-k)}\bigr)\). A benchmark exhibits a heavy-tail warning when estimates \(\widehat\xi_k\) remain materially positive over a prespecified stable range of \(k\), while upper empirical quantiles or the sample mean change substantially under deletion or censoring of a few largest observations. Values \(\widehat\xi_k\geq 1/2\) warn that finite variance is unsupported; values at least \(1\) warn that a finite mean is unsupported under a Pareto-tail model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable positive tail-index estimates plus strong sensitivity to extreme observations warn that ordinary mean and variance summaries may be unreliable.
assumptions_latex: The observations are positive and identically distributed within the diagnosed regime.
The upper tail is provisionally modeled as regularly varying.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagnostic flags unsupported finite-moment assumptions; it does not by itself establish an exact tail law.

notation.meaning: Number of upper-order observations used for tail estimation.
Hill estimate of the extreme-value tail index.

review_flags: The supplied locators do not support extreme-value diagnostics.
Threshold stability and sensitivity criteria require benchmark-specific calibration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hill formula, stability diagnostic, and moment-warning thresholds require an extreme-value-theory source with a precise locator.

children.title: Paired Performance Analysis
children.top_down_role: Within-instance comparisons that preserve benchmark pairing across solvers or configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Performance Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of two algorithms using matched observations from the same benchmark units or controlled run conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matched benchmark units \(i=1,\ldots,n\), let \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) be performance measurements for algorithms \(A\) and \(B\) under the same pairing key, and define \(D_i=X_i-Y_i\) for a metric to be minimized. Paired performance analysis estimates a functional of the within-pair distribution, such as \(\Delta=\mathbb E[D_i]\), the median of \(D_i\), or \(p=\Pr(D_i<0)+\tfrac12\Pr(D_i=0)\). Statistical uncertainty is computed from the paired differences \(D_i\), not by treating the two marginal samples as independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paired analysis compares algorithms through within-unit differences, preserving shared instance or run conditions and estimating uncertainty from those differences.
assumptions_latex: Each \((X_i,Y_i)\) uses a declared common pairing key.
Pairs are sampled independently or their dependence is explicitly modeled.
Smaller metric values indicate better performance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The comparative estimand is determined by the distribution of \(D_i=X_i-Y_i\).

notation.meaning: Probability that A wins a pair, with ties split equally.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports paired statistical comparison in algorithm benchmarking.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the paired estimands or the requirement to compute uncertainty from within-pair differences.

children.title: Rank Analysis
children.top_down_role: Solver ordering based on per-instance or aggregate ranks.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of algorithms through within-block ordinal positions rather than raw performance magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the performance of algorithm \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) on benchmark block \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with smaller values preferred. Define \(R_{ij}\) as the rank of \(Y_{ij}\) among \(Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{im}\), assigning tied values their average occupied rank. Rank analysis summarizes algorithm \(j\) by \(\bar R_j=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}R_{ij}\) and orders algorithms by increasing \(\bar R_j\). Inference must use the joint within-block rank vectors because \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}R_{ij}=m(m+1)/2\) makes ranks within a block dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank analysis orders algorithms by their average within-instance ranks while retaining the dependence among algorithms evaluated on the same blocks.
assumptions_latex: Every included block evaluates the same \(m\) algorithms.
The performance direction and tie rule are fixed before ranking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Algorithm \(j\) receives summary rank \(\bar R_j\), with smaller values indicating better ordinal performance.

notation.meaning: Performance of algorithm j on block i.
Within-block rank with average ranks for ties.

review_flags: The supplied combinatorial rank locator concerns matroid rank, not statistical rank analysis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inventory's rank source concerns matroid rank, not statistical ranking. A benchmark-comparison or blocked-rank-analysis source is required.

children.title: Dominance Analysis
children.top_down_role: Comparisons based on consistent advantages across outcomes, instances, or resource criteria.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise ordering based on the probability and magnitude of one algorithm outperforming another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For paired performance variables \(X\) and \(Y\) of algorithms \(A\) and \(B\), with smaller values preferred, define the win probability \(p_{AB}=\Pr(X<Y)+\tfrac12\Pr(X=Y)\). Algorithm \(A\) probabilistically dominates \(B\) when \(p_{AB}>1/2\). A stronger first-order dominance relation holds when \(F_X(t)\geq F_Y(t)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\), with strict inequality for at least one \(t\), where \(F_X\) and \(F_Y\) are the marginal distribution functions. The chosen dominance relation and pairing convention must be reported because they define different orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dominance analysis orders algorithms using pairwise win probabilities or, more strongly, uniform ordering of their performance distributions.
assumptions_latex: The compared measurements use the same performance scale and direction.
For \(p_{AB}\), the joint law of the paired measurements is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declared win-probability or first-order criterion determines whether \(A\) dominates \(B\).

notation.meaning: Tie-adjusted probability that A outperforms B.
Marginal cumulative distribution functions of the performances.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports probabilistic or first-order dominance in empirical performance analysis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record combines win-probability ordering and first-order stochastic dominance. A source must support the terminology and distinguish these relations.

children.title: Rank-Dominance Disagreement
children.top_down_role: Cases where rank summaries conflict with dominance relationships.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Dominance Disagreement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regime in which average ranks and pairwise dominance induce conflicting comparative conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar R_A\) and \(\bar R_B\) be average within-block ranks, with smaller ranks preferred, and let \(p_{AB}=\Pr(X_A<X_B)+\tfrac12\Pr(X_A=X_B)\) be the paired win probability. A rank-dominance disagreement occurs when \(\bar R_A<\bar R_B\) but \(p_{AB}<1/2\), or when \(\bar R_A>\bar R_B\) but \(p_{AB}>1/2\). Such disagreement is possible because ranks depend on all algorithms present in each block, whereas \(p_{AB}\) depends only on the joint pair \((X_A,X_B)\). Therefore neither ordering may be substituted for the other without additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average ranks and pairwise win probabilities can favor opposite algorithms because ranks depend on the full competitor set while dominance is pairwise.
assumptions_latex: Ranks and win probabilities use the same benchmark blocks and performance direction.
Ties are assigned consistently in both summaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same nonzero sign of \(\bar R_A-\bar R_B\) and \(p_{AB}-1/2\) certifies rank-dominance disagreement.

notation.meaning: Average within-block ranks of algorithms A and B.
Tie-adjusted paired win probability for A against B.

review_flags: No supplied source directly documents the corrected disagreement criterion or its benchmark interpretation.

children.title: Pairing-Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Changes in conclusions caused by missing pairs, filtering, aggregation, or pairing choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairing-Sensitivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which comparative conclusions change materially with the benchmark pairing rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be a set of admissible matching rules between observations from algorithms \(A\) and \(B\). For each \(\pi\in\Pi\), let \(D_i^{(\pi)}=X_i-Y_{\pi(i)}\) and let \(T(\pi)\) be a declared paired summary, such as the mean difference or tie-adjusted win probability. The comparison is pairing-sensitive at tolerance \(\delta\geq0\) when \(\sup_{\pi,ho\in\Pi}|T(\pi)-T(\rho)|>\delta\); it is direction-sensitive when there exist \(\pi,\rho\in\Pi\) for which the centered summaries have opposite signs. Admissible rules must preserve declared blocking constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A comparison is pairing-sensitive when admissible ways of matching runs materially change the estimated effect, especially when they reverse its direction.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\pi\in\Pi\) is a bijection satisfying the declared blocking constraints.
The summary \(T\) and tolerance \(\delta\) are fixed before comparing pairings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The spread of \(T(\pi)\) over \(\Pi\) determines magnitude sensitivity, and a sign reversal determines direction sensitivity.

notation.meaning: Comparative summary under pairing rule pi.

review_flags: No supplied locator supports a formal sensitivity analysis over admissible benchmark pairings.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formal supremum-based sensitivity predicate and admissible-pairing framework have no supporting citation.

children.title: Performance Variance
children.top_down_role: Variation in benchmark outcomes across repeated runs or sampled instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Performance Variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance decomposition for repeated performance measurements under a declared experimental design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be a scalar performance measurement and let \(I,S,O,W\) denote instance, random seed, run order, and initial machine state. The total performance variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) under the declared joint design distribution. When second moments exist, the instance decomposition is \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y\mid I])+\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid I)]\). Further components may be defined by a specified random-effects or functional-ANOVA model involving \(S,O,W\) and their interactions; without such a model, those components are not uniquely identifiable from the total variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Performance variance is the dispersion of repeated benchmark outcomes under a declared design; attributing it to factors requires an explicit decomposition model.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) has a finite second moment.
The joint experimental distribution of \((I,S,O,W)\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\) quantifies total variability, while conditional decompositions separate modeled sources.

notation.meaning: Instance, seed, run-order, and warm-state factors.

review_flags: The supplied sensitivity-analysis locator does not establish this statistical variance decomposition for experiments.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical decomposition is standard, but no relevant statistics source with a specific locator is supplied; the listed optimization sensitivity section is insufficient.

children.title: Random-Seed Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Outcome changes attributable to pseudorandom seed selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Seed Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of randomized-algorithm performance on the pseudorandom seed under fixed benchmark conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(i,s)\) be the performance obtained on instance \(i\) with random seed \(s\), all other controlled conditions fixed, and let \(S\) follow the declared seed-sampling distribution. Seed sensitivity on instance \(i\) is the conditional dispersion \(V_S(i)=\operatorname{Var}_S(Y(i,S)\mid I=i)\), when finite.
