A scale-free alternative is \(V_S(i)/\mathbb E_S[Y(i,S)\mid I=i]^2\) when the denominator is nonzero. Aggregate sensitivity must specify how \(V_S(i)\) is weighted across instances and must not conflate seed variation with instance variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-seed sensitivity measures how much a randomized algorithm's performance changes across seeds while the instance and other experimental conditions remain fixed.
assumptions_latex: Seeds are sampled from a declared distribution independently of uncontrolled conditions.
Repeated seeded runs begin from equivalent controlled states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_S(i)\) isolates within-instance performance variation attributable to the seed distribution.

notation.meaning: Performance on instance i using seed s.
Random seed drawn from the experimental seed distribution.
Conditional seed variance on instance i.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly addresses random-seed effects in empirical algorithm benchmarking.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports treating conditional seed variance and its normalized form as benchmark seed-sensitivity measures.

children.title: Run-Order Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Outcome changes attributable to benchmark execution sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Run-Order Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of measured performance on a run's position or predecessor within an experimental sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_{i,r}\) be the measured performance of treatment \(i\) when executed at sequence position \(r\), and let \(Z_{i,r}\) contain the intended benchmark factors. Define \(m_i(r,z)=\mathbb E[Y_{i,r}\mid Z_{i,r}=z]\). Treatment \(i\) is run-order sensitive over positions \(\mathcal R\) at tolerance \(\delta\geq0\) when \(\sup_{r,q\in\mathcal R}|m_i(r,z)-m_i(q,z)|>\delta\) for some controlled condition \(z\). Randomizing or counterbalancing order supports estimation but does not redefine the sensitivity predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run-order sensitivity occurs when expected measured performance changes materially with sequence position after intended benchmark factors are held fixed.
assumptions_latex: Sequence position is recorded for every run.
The conditional means are identifiable under the allocation or randomization design.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A conditional mean range exceeding \(\delta\) certifies run-order sensitivity within the studied positions.

notation.meaning: Measured performance of treatment i at position r.
Conditional mean performance at position r.

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports the stated conditional criterion for run-order effects.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-mean range criterion and its design interpretation require a source on order effects or experimental design.

children.title: Warm-State Carryover
children.top_down_role: Run-order effects arising from caches, memory state, adaptive tuning, or retained solver state.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-State Carryover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual influence of preceding runs on current performance through persistent machine or software state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_r\) be the performance of the current treatment at run \(r\), let \(H_{r-1}\) encode the preceding run or retained machine state, and let \(Z_r\) contain the current intended benchmark factors. Define \(m(h,z)=\mathbb E[Y_r\mid H_{r-1}=h,Z_r=z]\). Warm-state carryover is present at tolerance \(\delta\geq0\) when \(\sup_{h,h'}|m(h,z)-m(h',z)|>\delta\) for some \(z\). A reset protocol removes material carryover only if this bound is at most \(\delta\) over the admissible predecessor states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warm-state carryover exists when retained state from earlier runs materially changes current expected performance despite identical current benchmark factors.
assumptions_latex: Predecessor state or an adequate state proxy is recorded.
The design permits predecessor-state effects to be separated from current treatment effects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditional mean variation across predecessor states exceeding \(\delta\) certifies material warm-state carryover.

notation.meaning: Recorded predecessor history or retained state.

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses carryover effects or reset validation in performance experiments.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the conditional carryover predicate or the stated reset-validation criterion.

children.title: Seed-Variance Interactions
children.top_down_role: Variation patterns attributable to differing seed effects across instances or configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Seed-Variance Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interaction decomposition for randomized-algorithm performance across benchmark instances and random seeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_{isr}\in\mathbb R\) be the performance measured on instance \(i\), seed \(s\), and replicate \(r\). In the random-effects model \[Y_{isr}=\mu+u_i+v_s+w_{is}+\varepsilon_{isr},\] assume the centered effects are pairwise uncorrelated, with variances \(\sigma_I^2,\sigma_S^2,\sigma_{IS}^2,\sigma_E^2\). Then \[\operatorname{Var}(Y_{isr})=\sigma_I^2+\sigma_S^2+\sigma_{IS}^2+\sigma_E^2.\] A nonzero \(\sigma_{IS}^2\) means that seed sensitivity depends on the instance; it cannot be represented solely by an instance-independent seed effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A seed–instance interaction is present when the performance effect of changing a random seed varies across instances; its variance is a distinct component of total variability.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_{isr}\) has finite second moment.
The random effects are centered and pairwise uncorrelated.
Replicates follow the stated additive random-effects model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_{isr})=\sigma_I^2+\sigma_S^2+\sigma_{IS}^2+\sigma_E^2\), with \(\sigma_{IS}^2>0\) identifying seed–instance interaction.

notation.meaning: observed performance for instance, seed, and replicate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variance decomposition and content kind fit the leaf, but no evidence supports the particular crossed random-effects model or the interpretation of its interaction component.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Feature Performance Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supervised representation of conditional algorithm performance using measurable instance features.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathcal X\) be an instance, \(\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p\) a fixed feature map, and \(Y_a\in\mathbb R\) the performance of algorithm \(a\). Under squared-error loss, the population instance-feature performance model is \[m_a(z)=\mathbb E[Y_a\mid \phi(X)=z],\] whenever the conditional expectation exists. An estimated predictor \(\widehat m_a\) maps features to predicted performance \(\widehat Y_a=\widehat m_a(\phi(X))\). For a finite portfolio \(\mathcal A\), feature-based selection returns \[\widehat a(X)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathcal A}\widehat m_a(\phi(X)),\] when smaller performance values are preferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance-feature model predicts each algorithm’s conditional performance from measurable instance features and may select the algorithm with the smallest predicted cost.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_a\) is integrable for every \(a\in\mathcal A\).
\(\phi\) is measurable.
\(\mathcal A\) is finite when the selection rule is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_a(\phi(X))\) represents conditional mean performance, and \(\widehat a(X)\) minimizes predicted performance over the portfolio.

notation.meaning: conditional mean performance function for algorithm a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the topic, but a source is required for the modeling convention and selection rule. The conditional mean as a function of z is generally defined only up to feature-distribution-null sets unless a regular version is specified.

children.title: Run-Time Survival Curves
children.top_down_role: Survival-oriented summaries of unresolved runs across time or resource budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Run-Time Survival Curves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Survival-function representation of time until a specified algorithmic termination event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\Omega\to[0,\infty]\) be the time until a prespecified termination event, such as finding a target-quality solution. Its run-time survival curve is \[S(t)=\Pr(T>t),\qquad t\ge 0.\] Thus \(S\) is nonincreasing and right-continuous, with \(S(0)=\Pr(T>0)\). Given observations \((Y_i,\delta_i)\), where \(Y_i=\min(T_i,C_i)\) and \(\delta_i=\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}\), the Kaplan–Meier estimator is \[\widehat S(t)=\prod_{j:t_j\le t}\left(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\right),\] where \(d_j\) events occur among \(n_j\) runs at risk at event time \(t_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run-time survival curve gives the probability that the specified termination event has not occurred by time t; censored samples can be summarized by Kaplan–Meier estimation.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a nonnegative extended-valued random variable.
For Kaplan–Meier estimation, censoring is independent of \(T\) conditional on the modeled design variables.
Event times and risk sets are recorded consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(t)=\Pr(T>t)\), with \(\widehat S(t)\) given by the product-limit estimator under independent censoring.

notation.meaning: time to the specified termination event

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The survival-function definition and product-limit formula fit the leaf and are internally consistent, but the estimator and censoring assumptions require an inspectable survival-analysis source.

children.title: Right-Censored Runs
children.top_down_role: Runs whose outcomes remain unresolved at a stopping limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Right-Censored Runs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observed-data representation when execution stops before the event time is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_i\in[0,\infty]\) be run \(i\)'s event time and \(C_i\in[0,\infty)\) its observation limit. The right-censored observation is \[(Y_i,
\delta_i)=\left(\min\{T_i,C_i\},\mathbf 1\{T_i\le C_i\}\right).\] If \(\delta_i=1\), the event time is observed as \(T_i=Y_i\). If \(\delta_i=0\), the observation determines only \(T_i>Y_i=C_i\). Treating \(Y_i\) as an uncensored event time when \(\delta_i=0\) replaces a lower bound on runtime by an equality and changes the estimand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run is right-censored when observation ends before its event; the data reveal only that its event time exceeds the recorded cutoff.
assumptions_latex: Each run has a well-defined event time \(T_i\) and observation limit \(C_i\).
The convention records an event at the limit when \(T_i=C_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_i=0\) implies only \(T_i>Y_i\), whereas \(\delta_i=1\) implies \(T_i=Y_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and consistently uses the convention that an event at the observation limit is observed, but that convention and the observed-data formulation lack cited support.

children.title: Competing Termination Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Distinct termination causes that alter interpretation of run completion.

knowledge_statements.title: Competing Termination Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competing-risks representation for mutually exclusive algorithm termination causes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_k\in[0,\infty]\) be the latent time to termination cause \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\). The observed termination time and cause are \[T=\min_{1\le k\le K}T_k,
\qquad J\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\le k\le K}T_k,\] with a fixed tie rule. Cause \(k\)'s cumulative incidence function is \[F_k(t)=\Pr(T\le t,J=k).\] If \(S(t)=\Pr(T>t)\) and cause-specific hazards \(\lambda_k\) exist, then \[F_k(t)=\int_0^t S(u-)\lambda_k(u)\,du.\] Termination from one cause precludes observing termination from every other cause in that run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Competing termination outcomes are mutually exclusive causes of stopping. Each cause has a cumulative incidence that accounts for the possibility of earlier stopping by another cause.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many mutually exclusive recorded causes.
A deterministic rule resolves simultaneous latent termination times.
Cause-specific hazards exist for the hazard representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_k(t)=\Pr(T\le t,J=k)=\int_0^t S(u-)\lambda_k(u)\,du\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and cumulative-incidence formulation fit the leaf, but the latent-time construction and hazard representation require a specific competing-risks source.

children.title: Censoring Bias Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Checks for performance conclusions distorted by incomplete run observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Censoring Bias Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable implications of noninformative censoring in benchmark runtime data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be event time, \(C\) censoring time, \(X\) recorded design covariates, and \(G\) an algorithm or treatment label. Conditional noninformative censoring requires \[T\mathbin{\perp\!\!\!\perp}C\mid(X,G).\] A diagnostic compares censoring distributions through \[H_0:G_C(t\mid X,G=g)=G_C(t\mid X,G=g')\] for relevant groups \(g,g'\), and tests whether the censoring indicator or censoring time remains associated with pre-censoring performance summaries after conditioning on \((X,G)\). Rejection or systematic residual association falsifies the corresponding observable implication, but failure to reject does not establish conditional independence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagnostics compare censoring across groups and test residual associations with observed history. Detected associations contradict noninformative censoring, but their absence cannot prove it.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) contains the design variables on which independence is asserted.
The compared runs use consistently defined events and censoring limits.
The diagnostic model permits the associations being tested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A rejected observable implication is evidence against \(T\mathbin{\perp\!\!\!\perp}C\mid(X,G)\); nonrejection is not a certificate of independence.

notation.meaning: conditional survival function of censoring time

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Conditional independence of T and C given (X,G) does not imply equal censoring distributions across different values of G. Because G is conditioned upon, censoring may legitimately vary by group. Thus rejection of the displayed group-equality null does not by itself falsify noninformative censoring.

children.title: Reproducible Benchmarking Infrastructure
children.top_down_role: Artifacts, execution environments, reporting interfaces, replication, and continuous benchmark stewardship.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Common infrastructure, shared data, formats, machines, and comparison protocols
Downloads, supplementary data, run scripts, and solution checker

children.title: Source Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Versioned source materials required to inspect or reconstruct solver implementations.

knowledge_statements.title: Source Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Content-addressed source inputs to a reproducible benchmark build.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A source artifact is a tuple \[A_S=(B_S,h_S,m_S),\] where \(B_S\in\{0,1\}^*\) is an immutable byte sequence containing source code or build input, \(h_S=H(B_S)\) is its digest under a declared hash function \(H\), and \(m_S\) records its format, origin, version identifier, and applicable build path. Two archived source artifacts are identical for the benchmark record only when their declared identity fields and verified byte digests agree. A mutable repository branch name without a resolved revision and archived bytes does not uniquely specify \(A_S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source artifact is an immutable, versioned build input identified by archived bytes, a declared digest, and metadata sufficient to interpret and build it.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) and its encoding are explicitly declared.
Metadata fields used for artifact identity are fixed by the benchmark protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_S\) uniquely denotes archived source bytes and their benchmark-relevant identity metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is an appropriate role for the leaf, but the tuple schema, identity fields, and byte-digest identity rule are protocol-dependent and have no supporting standard or benchmark specification.

children.title: Binary Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Executable deliverables preserved for direct benchmark reuse.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Content-addressed executable outputs used to run benchmark experiments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary artifact is a tuple \[A_B=(B_B,h_B,p_B,m_B),\] where \(B_B\in\{0,1\}^*\) is an executable or loadable byte sequence, \(h_B=H(B_B)\) is its digest, \(p_B\) specifies the target execution platform and application-binary interface, and \(m_B\) records its format and runtime dependencies. A benchmark run uses the recorded binary artifact only if the executed bytes verify against \(h_B\) and the execution environment satisfies \(p_B\) and the declared dependencies. A filename or semantic version alone is not a binary identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary artifact is an executable byte sequence identified by a verified digest and accompanied by platform and runtime-dependency metadata.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) and its digest encoding are declared.
The execution platform and runtime dependencies are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A benchmark run is attributable to \(A_B\) only when its executed bytes and compatibility metadata match the record.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the leaf, but the proposed binary identity and attribution criteria are protocol-dependent and unsupported by a cited standard or specification.

children.title: Build Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Compiler outputs, build records, packaging metadata, and intermediate products supporting reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.title: Build Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persisted records and intermediate outputs of a source-to-binary build execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given source artifact \(A_S\), build specification \(R\), and build environment \(E\), a build execution produces \[(A_B,A_L)=\operatorname{Build}(A_S,R,E),\] where \(A_B\) is the resulting binary artifact and \(A_L\) is a build artifact containing persisted intermediate outputs or records needed to audit the transformation. At minimum, \(A_L\) identifies the inputs, toolchain, dependency resolutions, commands, environment parameters, exit status, and output digests. Reproducibility is tested by rerunning the declared transformation and comparing output digests under the protocol's stated equivalence criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build artifacts record the toolchain, dependencies, commands, environment, intermediate evidence, status, and output digests connecting source inputs to binaries.
assumptions_latex: Source and output artifacts have stable identities.
The benchmark protocol declares which environment fields affect build equivalence.
Build commands and dependency resolutions are recordable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_L\) supplies an auditable record of \(\operatorname{Build}(A_S,R,E)=(A_B,A_L)\).

notation.meaning: persisted build record and intermediate artifacts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the build-artifact leaf, but the asserted minimum record fields and reproducibility criterion depend on a particular build protocol and require a supporting source.

children.title: Source-to-Binary Traceability
children.top_down_role: Links among source revisions, build records, and released executables.

knowledge_statements.title: Source-to-Binary Traceability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable provenance certificate linking source bytes, build execution, and executable bytes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_S\) and \(A_B\) have verified digests \(h_S\) and \(h_B\). A source-to-binary traceability certificate is \[\tau=(h_S,h_R,h_E,h_L,h_B),\] together with retrievable source, recipe, environment, and build-record artifacts whose digests are the first four entries. Verification accepts when every digest matches, the build record identifies these inputs and output, and either a replay produces bytes with digest \(h_B\) or an authenticated build attestation binds the same digests. Acceptance certifies provenance under the declared build model; it does not by itself certify semantic equivalence, correctness, or absence of malicious tooling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A traceability certificate binds source, recipe, environment, build record, and binary digests. Replay or authenticated attestation verifies provenance, but not program correctness.
assumptions_latex: All referenced artifacts are retrievable and digest-verifiable.
The verification protocol declares acceptable replay equivalence or attestation trust roots.
The hash function is treated as collision resistant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance of \(\tau\) certifies that \(h_B\) is linked to \(h_S\) by the recorded build process under the declared trust model.

notation.meaning: digests of recipe, environment record, and build record

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the correct content kind, and the stated limitation to provenance is appropriate. The certificate structure, replay alternative, authenticated-attestation alternative, and trust assumptions nevertheless require a cited provenance standard or protocol.

children.title: Instance Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Concrete benchmark inputs preserved with stable identities and formats.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immutable, parseable representations of benchmark problem instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance domain \(\mathcal I\), an instance artifact is a tuple \[A_I=(B_I,h_I,f_I,v_I),\] where \(B_I\in\{0,1\}^*\) is an immutable serialization, \(h_I=H(B_I)\) its digest, and \((f_I,v_I)\) identifies the format and schema version. A declared parser \(P_{f_I,v_I}\) must satisfy \[P_{f_I,v_I}(B_I)=I\in\mathcal I.\] The benchmark identity is byte-level unless the protocol additionally declares a canonicalization map; semantic equivalence of differently serialized instances does not otherwise make their artifacts identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance artifact is an immutable, hashed serialization with a declared format, schema version, and parser that yields a valid benchmark instance.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) and its digest encoding are declared.
The parser and schema version are fixed by the benchmark protocol.
Parser acceptance implies membership in \(\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid \(A_I\) verifies its bytes and parses to a well-defined instance \(I\in\mathcal I\).

notation.meaning: parser for the declared format and version

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the instance-artifact leaf, but byte-level identity, parser validity, schema versioning, and canonicalization rules are benchmark-protocol choices requiring an inspectable source.

children.title: Generator Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Generator implementations, parameterizations, and release records used to produce instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Generator Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Executable, versioned specifications for deterministic or randomized benchmark-instance generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generator artifact is a tuple \[A_G=(B_G,h_G,\Theta,\mathcal S,P),\] where \(B_G\) is immutable generator code or executable specification with digest \(h_G=H(B_G)\), \(\Theta\) is its parameter space, \(\mathcal S\) its seed space, and \(P\) its declared execution protocol. For parameters \(\theta\in\Theta\) and seed \(s\in\mathcal S\), execution defines \[G_{A_G,P}(\theta,s)=A_I\] or a recorded failure. Reproducible generation requires that the protocol fix all nondeterministic inputs affecting the produced instance artifact, including pseudorandom-number implementation and relevant environment state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generator artifact fixes generator bytes, parameters, seeds, and execution protocol so that each declared invocation yields a traceable instance artifact or recorded failure.
assumptions_latex: Generator bytes and protocol components have stable identities.
The protocol records every nondeterministic input affecting generation.
Produced outputs are represented as instance artifacts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each declared pair \((\theta,s)\) determines a traceable output \(A_I\) or an explicit failure under \(P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the generator-artifact leaf, but the tuple schema and claim that recorded protocol state makes each invocation deterministic require a cited reproducibility protocol specifying all relevant nondeterministic inputs.

children.title: Certificate Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Machine-checkable evidence supporting reported feasibility, optimality, or failure outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-checkable evidence for the validity or quality of a benchmark solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an optimization instance \(I\) with feasible set \(F(I)\) and objective \(f_I\), a certificate artifact is a tuple \(A=(d_I,x,b,w,V,d_V)\), where \(d_I\) identifies \(I\), \(x\) is a reported solution, \(b\) is a claimed bound, \(w\) is auxiliary evidence, and \(V\) is a versioned verifier with digest \(d_V\). It certifies the report when \(V(I,x,b,w)=1\). Verifier soundness requires \[V(I,x,b,w)=1\Longrightarrow x\in F(I)\ \text{and the claim encoded by }b\text{ holds}.\] For minimization, an optimality certificate may encode \(f_I(x)\le b\) together with a valid lower bound \(b\le \min_{y\in F(I)}f_I(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate artifact binds an instance and reported solution to machine-checkable evidence whose versioned verifier establishes feasibility, a bound, or optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) has a precisely specified feasible set and objective.
The verifier and its input serialization are deterministic and versioned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(I,x,b,w)=1\) certifies the claim represented by \((x,b,w)\) for \(I\).

notation.meaning: Content identifiers of the instance and verifier

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind fits this terminal container, and the formulation is mathematically plausible. However, no citation supports the proposed artifact tuple, verifier-soundness requirement, or optimality-certificate convention, so the record cannot be accepted at candidate-review level.

children.title: Generation Provenance
children.top_down_role: Traceability from generated instances to generator versions, parameters, and random inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Generation Provenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replayable provenance for generated benchmark instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generation-provenance record for an instance \(I\) is a tuple \(P=(d_G,\theta,s,r,D,d_I)\), where \(d_G\) identifies the exact generator implementation, \(\theta\) is its canonical parameter map, \(s\) is the random seed, \(r\) identifies the pseudorandom-number algorithm and version, \(D\) lists ordered parent-data identifiers, and \(d_I\) is the content digest of the serialized output. The record is replay-valid when execution in the declared generation environment satisfies \[\operatorname{digest}(G_{d_G}(\theta,s,r,D))=d_I.\] If the generator is nondeterministic beyond \(s\), the record must additionally identify every external random or mutable input needed to make this equality reproducible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generation provenance records the generator, parameters, randomness, inputs, and output digest needed to regenerate and identify an instance.
assumptions_latex: The output serialization and digest algorithm are fixed.
All generator inputs affecting the output are recordable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is replay-valid exactly when regeneration yields the recorded output digest \(d_I\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is an appropriate content kind for Generation Provenance and the statement matches the local artifact-chain context. The exact tuple, replay-validity equation, and treatment of nondeterministic inputs are nevertheless uncited locally invented conventions requiring an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Configuration Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Solver options, benchmark policies, and run-specific settings preserved for reuse.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical records of parameters controlling a benchmark execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A configuration artifact is a tuple \(C=(S,v,p,\delta,e,d_C)\), where \(S\) is a configuration schema, \(v\) its version, \(p\) a finite map from parameter names to explicitly serialized values, \(\delta\) records applied defaults, \(e\) records permitted external overrides, and \(d_C\) is the digest of the canonical serialization. It is complete for a program \(A\) when the effective parameter map is uniquely reconstructible as \[p_{\mathrm{eff}}=\operatorname{resolve}_S(p,\delta,e)\] and every configuration value read by \(A\) belongs to \(\operatorname{dom}(p_{\mathrm{eff}})\). Secrets may be replaced by stable references only when their behaviorally relevant versions are identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A configuration artifact canonically records explicit values, defaults, overrides, and schema information sufficient to reconstruct every effective runtime parameter.
assumptions_latex: Configuration resolution is deterministic under schema \(S\).
Canonical serialization fixes ordering and value representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Completeness implies that \(p_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is uniquely reconstructible from \(C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits the Configuration Artifacts leaf and its variables are introduced consistently. No source supports the selected tuple fields, completeness criterion, resolution semantics, or rule for secret references.

children.title: Environment Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Operating-system, hardware, runtime, and locale records associated with execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Environment Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recorded execution-platform state relevant to benchmark behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An environment artifact is a canonical record \(E=(H,O,K,U,L,R,	au,d_E)\), where \(H\) describes hardware and enabled features, \(O\) the operating-system image, \(K\) the kernel, \(U\) user-space settings, \(L\) locale and time-zone settings, \(R\) resource limits and scheduler or affinity controls, \(\tau\) time-source metadata, and \(d_E\) the record digest. For a declared observation map \(\Omega\), the record is behaviorally complete for executable \(A\) when \[E_1=E_2\Longrightarrow \Omega(A,E_1)=\Omega(A,E_2)\] up to stated nondeterminism and tolerances. Any omitted field must therefore be asserted irrelevant to \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An environment artifact identifies hardware, operating system, limits, clocks, and settings relevant to reproducing declared benchmark observations.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark declares its observable outputs and tolerances.
Environment fields have canonical identifiers or serializations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Behavioral completeness makes equality of recorded environments sufficient for equivalence under \(\Omega\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is a suitable role for Environment Artifacts, but the proposed behavioral-completeness condition is a substantive formalization rather than a standard uncontested definition. It has no citation, and the meaning of equality between environment records relative to omitted fields needs authoritative support.

children.title: Dependency Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Libraries, toolchains, packages, and resolved versions required by the benchmark stack.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Content-addressed representation of a benchmark's resolved software dependency closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dependency artifact represents the resolved software closure as a directed labeled graph \(D=(V,E,\lambda,\eta,d_D)\). Each vertex \(v\in V\) denotes an exact package, library, compiler, runtime, or build tool; \(\lambda(v)\) contains its version, source or binary digest, build options, and target platform. An edge \((u,v,k)\in E\) states that component \(u\) depends on \(v\) with dependency kind \(k\). The map \(\eta\) records the resolver and lock-file semantics. The representation is closed when \[u\in V\ \land\ u\text{ declares dependency }v\Longrightarrow v\in V\ \land\ (u,v,k)\in E.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dependency artifact is a content-addressed graph containing every resolved software component, its build identity, and all dependency edges.
assumptions_latex: Dependency declarations can be resolved to exact component identities.
Component and graph serializations are canonical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closure ensures that every resolved transitive dependency is represented in \(D\).

notation.meaning: Dependency graph with metadata and digest
Dependency kind, such as build or runtime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation correctly matches the graph-oriented Dependency Artifacts container. The graph schema and closure condition are not sourced, and the condition refers to a declared dependency kind k without explicitly quantifying or otherwise determining k for each declaration.

children.title: Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Environmental or dependency conditions under which preserved configurations cease to reproduce.

knowledge_statements.title: Compatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicate delimiting execution contexts supported by an artifact bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the set of execution contexts and let \(x_0\in X\) be the recorded reference context. For declared observations \(\Omega\), tolerances \(\varepsilon\), and required features \(Q\), define compatibility by \[\operatorname{Compat}(x;x_0,Q,\varepsilon)=1\iff Q(x)=1\ \land\ \operatorname{dist}(\Omega(A,x),\Omega(A,x_0))\le\varepsilon.\] A compatibility boundary is the frontier between \(C=\{x\in X:\operatorname{Compat}(x;x_0,Q,\varepsilon)=1\}\) and \(X\setminus C\), expressed through testable constraints on architecture, interfaces, dependency versions, numerical behavior, and resources. Outside \(C\), reproducibility is not asserted; a successful launch alone does not establish compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatibility boundary separates contexts satisfying required features and observational tolerances from contexts for which reproducibility is not claimed.
assumptions_latex: The observation distance and tolerances are declared.
Required platform and interface features are decidable from an environment record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in C\) exactly when all required features and observational tolerances hold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the appropriate mathematical role for Compatibility Boundaries. The compatibility predicate is locally invented and unsupported, and executable A appears inside the observation map without being introduced or quantified. An authoritative source is needed before choosing and repairing the exact formalization.

children.title: Raw Log Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Unprocessed textual or structured event records emitted during benchmark execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Raw Log Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immutable, minimally transformed records emitted during benchmark execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A raw log artifact is a tuple \(L=(R,m,d_L)\), where \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\) is the preserved sequence of emitted records, \(m\) specifies encoding, source streams, clock domains, buffering, and capture losses, and \(d_L\) is the digest of the captured bytes. Each record has the form \(r_i=(s_i,t_i,q_i,p_i)\), comprising source, source-local timestamp, source-local sequence number, and payload. The artifact is loss-accountable when every capture gap is represented in \(m\). Parsing, filtering, timestamp correction, or deduplication produces a derived artifact and must not replace \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A raw log artifact preserves emitted bytes and capture metadata, including ordering information and known losses, before parsing or correction.
assumptions_latex: Captured bytes have a fixed digest algorithm.
Each emitting source supplies a timestamp, sequence number, or both.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_L\) identifies the immutable captured record sequence and its capture metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits Raw Log Artifacts and distinguishes raw from derived data appropriately. No source supports this exact record schema or loss-accountability rule. Moreover, d_L is defined as a digest of captured bytes while the conclusion says it identifies both the record sequence and capture metadata, leaving the digest scope inconsistent.

children.title: Execution Trace Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Time-ordered records of solver activity, state transitions, or instrumentation events.

knowledge_statements.title: Execution Trace Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structured event representation of a benchmark execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An execution trace artifact is a labeled partially ordered event structure \(T=(E,\prec,\ell,\kappa,d_T)\). Each event \(e\in E\) has label \(\ell(e)\) containing its event type, actor, timestamp, and attributes. The relation \(\prec\) includes source order and recorded causal edges and must be acyclic. The clock metadata \(\kappa\) identifies timestamp domains and their calibrations; \(d_T\) identifies the canonical trace serialization. A linear display order \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\) is valid only if \[e_i\prec e_j\Longrightarrow i<j.\] Events inferred rather than directly observed must be marked with their inference rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An execution trace is a content-addressed, labeled partial order of observed or explicitly inferred runtime events with clock and causality metadata.
assumptions_latex: Event identities are unique within the execution.
Recorded causal and source-order edges are acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every valid trace serialization preserves the partial order \(\prec\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits the Execution Trace Artifacts leaf, and the partial-order presentation is coherent. The selected event model, clock metadata requirements, inference marking, and claim about every valid serialization have no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Performance Counter Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Hardware, operating-system, or process-level measurements collected during runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Performance Counter Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recorded counter measurements with sufficient semantics for valid comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A performance-counter artifact is \(P=(M,S,\sigma,d_P)\). Each measurement \(m\in M\) is a tuple \((c,a,[t_0,t_1],v,u,q)\) identifying counter \(c\), measured actor or resource \(a\), interval \([t_0,t_1]\), value \(v\), unit \(u\), and quality flags \(q\). The semantics map \(S\) records whether \(v\) is cumulative, sampled, or a delta, together with scaling, multiplexing, overflow, and reset rules. The acquisition specification \(\sigma\) records tool versions and sampling policy. A derived rate is valid only when elapsed time and counter correction share declared clock and scaling conventions, for example \[\rho=\frac{\operatorname{correct}_S(v)}{t_1-t_0}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A performance-counter artifact binds measurements to counters, scopes, intervals, units, acquisition policy, and correction semantics needed for valid derived metrics.
assumptions_latex: Counter identity and unit are stable over each measurement interval.
Overflow, reset, and multiplexing behavior are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Derived quantities from \(P\) are defined only through its recorded semantics \(S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is suitable for Performance Counter Artifacts and the formula is internally delimited and plausible. The measurement schema, correction semantics, and validity condition for derived rates require a specific authoritative citation, but source_refs is empty.

children.title: Telemetry Synchronization
children.top_down_role: Alignment of logs, traces, counters, timestamps, and run identities.

knowledge_statements.title: Telemetry Synchronization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clock-calibration condition for combining telemetry streams.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose telemetry source \(j\) uses local clock \(t_j\). A synchronization record supplies a map \(\phi_j(t)=a_jt+b_j\) to a reference clock and an error bound \(\epsilon_j\ge0\) such that every calibrated event time satisfies \[|t_{\mathrm{ref}}-\phi_j(t_j)|\le\epsilon_j.\] Two events \(e\) and \(f\) from sources \(j\) and \(k\) have a synchronization-certified order \(e<f\) only if \[\phi_j(t_e)+\epsilon_j<\phi_k(t_f)-\epsilon_k.\] Otherwise their relative order is indeterminate unless an independent causal edge orders them. Calibration epochs must be split whenever drift invalidates the stated affine map or error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Telemetry streams are synchronized by calibrated clock maps and error bounds; cross-stream order is certified only when their uncertainty intervals are disjoint.
assumptions_latex: Each calibration epoch admits a bounded-error affine clock map.
Timestamp acquisition errors are included in \(\epsilon_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disjoint calibrated uncertainty intervals certify order; overlapping intervals do not.

notation.meaning: Map from source clock to reference clock

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition correctly fits Telemetry Synchronization. The bounded affine-clock model and disjoint-interval ordering criterion are mathematically plausible, but their applicability and the epoch-splitting requirement depend on an uncited synchronization model; no source establishes the exact hypotheses or conclusion.

children.title: Analysis Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Scripts, notebooks, processed tables, and statistical outputs used to derive benchmark findings.

knowledge_statements.title: Analysis Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducible representation of transformations from benchmark results to reported statistics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An analysis artifact is a tuple \(A=(D,d_D,g,d_g,\theta,R,d_R)\), where \(D\) is the ordered collection of input datasets with identifiers \(d_D\), \(g\) is the analysis program with implementation identifier \(d_g\), \(\theta\) contains canonical analysis parameters, and \(R\) is the resulting tables, models, tests, or summary statistics with digest \(d_R\). It represents the transformation \[R=g(D;\theta).\] The artifact is replay-valid when executing the identified program under its recorded execution context reproduces \(d_R\), subject only to explicitly declared numerical tolerances or stochastic seeds. Exclusions and missing-data rules are components of \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An analysis artifact binds input data, versioned code, parameters, exclusions, and outputs into a replayable transformation producing reported statistics.
assumptions_latex: All analysis inputs have stable content identifiers.
Any stochastic analysis records its random-number implementation and seeds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replay validity requires regeneration of the recorded result digest \(d_R\) within declared conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate for Analysis Artifacts and matches the result-communication context. The proposed tuple and replay-validity criterion, particularly digest reproduction subject to numerical tolerances, need a precise source because digest equality and tolerance-based numerical equivalence are distinct notions.

children.title: Visualization Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Figures, dashboards, plotting specifications, and presentation-ready benchmark displays.

knowledge_statements.title: Visualization Artifacts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducible representation of rendered benchmark figures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A visualization artifact is a tuple \(V=(R,d_R,h,d_h,\psi,F,d_F)\), where \(R\) is an identified analysis result, \(h\) is a versioned renderer, \(\psi\) specifies data selections, transformations, scales, axes, encodings, aggregation, and style, and \(F\) is the rendered figure with digest \(d_F\). It represents \[F=h(R;\psi).\] The artifact is semantically complete when every displayed mark and annotation is determined by \(R\), \(h\), and \(\psi\), except elements explicitly labeled as manual. It is replay-valid when the recorded execution context regenerates \(d_F\), or an explicitly permitted canonical-equivalent rendering when byte identity is not guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A visualization artifact binds analysis results to renderer code, plotting specifications, and output, making every displayed mark reproducible or explicitly manual.
assumptions_latex: The input analysis result has a stable identifier.
The permitted rendering-equivalence criterion is declared when byte equality is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Semantic completeness makes each nonmanual figure element a determined function of \((R,h,\psi)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation fits Visualization Artifacts and appropriately links results, rendering specifications, and figures. No citation supports the tuple or semantic-completeness criterion, and canonical-equivalent rendering is left undefined, so the mathematical version cannot be accepted without a source and a precise equivalence relation.

children.title: Result-to-Figure Provenance
children.top_down_role: Traceability from reported visuals to processed results, analysis versions, and source data.

knowledge_statements.title: Result-to-Figure Provenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal lineage from benchmark results through analysis artifacts to plotted values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be immutable raw-result records, \(T\) an analysis transformation, and \(V\) a visualization transformation. Result-to-figure provenance is a manifest \(P=(h_R,h_T,h_V,m)\), where each \(h\) is a content identifier and \(m\) maps every displayed mark \(g\) to its contributing records and parameters. It must satisfy \[g=V(T(R);\theta_V),\qquad m(g)=(R_g,\theta_T,\theta_V),\quad R_g\subseteq R.\] Re-evaluating the identified transformations on the identified records must reproduce the plotted datum, up to a declared numerical and rendering tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each plotted mark identifies its raw records, analysis and visualization transformations, parameters, and declared reproduction tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and transformation specifications are immutable or content-addressed.
All filtering, aggregation, and plotting parameters are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every displayed mark has a replayable lineage to contributing raw-result records.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports formal result-to-figure provenance requirements.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the artifact-lineage leaf, and the statement is internally coherent, but no cited source supports the proposed manifest fields, mark-level mapping, or replay-tolerance requirement. The unrelated local inventory cannot establish this formalization.

children.title: Execution Environment Capture
children.top_down_role: Records of machine, operating-system, runtime, locale, and process context for benchmark runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Execution Environment Capture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical record of the software, hardware, operating-system, and runtime context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For benchmark execution \(e\), an environment capture is a canonical record \[C(e)=(H,O,R,A,L),\] where \(H\) describes hardware and firmware, \(O\) identifies the operating system and kernel, \(R\) records language runtimes and process settings, \(A\) identifies the executed artifact, and \(L\) contains locale, time-zone, and relevant environment variables. Every component must be serialized deterministically, with unavailable fields explicitly marked. Two captures are environment-equivalent under projection \(\pi\) precisely when \(\pi(C(e_1))=\pi(C(e_2))\), where \(\pi\) is declared before comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An execution capture canonically records hardware, system, runtime, artifact, and relevant process settings, with an explicit comparison projection.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark declares which environment fields can affect its observations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(e)\) is a deterministic, comparable representation of the declared execution environment.
review_flags: No supplied source locator defines execution-environment capture.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits an execution-environment capture record. However, no source supports the asserted canonical field set, deterministic serialization requirement, or projection-based equivalence relation, and the available inventory is unrelated.

children.title: Dependency Resolution Capture
children.top_down_role: Resolved package, library, toolchain, and transitive dependency states.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency Resolution Capture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-verifiable certificate of the dependency graph selected for an execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(D,E)\) be the fully resolved dependency graph of an executable artifact. A dependency-resolution certificate records, for every \(d\in D\), its name, exact version or content identifier, source, platform variant, and integrity digest, and records every resolution edge in \(E\). The certificate is valid when all digests verify, each edge's declared constraint is satisfied by its selected target, and reinstalling under the recorded platform selects a graph \(G'\) canonically isomorphic to \(G\). Unresolved, optional, vendored, and dynamically loaded dependencies must be represented explicitly rather than omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The certificate fixes the complete selected dependency graph and permits verification of identities, constraints, integrity, and reconstruction.
assumptions_latex: Dependency identities and constraints admit canonical serialization.
Integrity digests are computed over the installed or retrieved artifacts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid certificate verifies the exact resolved dependency graph used by the execution.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports dependency-lock certificate semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is a plausible terminal kind because the record is presented as machine-verifiable evidence of a resolved dependency graph. A source is required for the completeness obligations, validity conditions, canonical graph-isomorphism requirement, and treatment of optional or dynamic dependencies.

children.title: Environment Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Use of captured context to recreate a compatible benchmark execution setting.

knowledge_statements.title: Environment Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic reconstruction from captured execution and dependency records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an environment capture \(C\), dependency certificate \(G\), artifact identifier \(a\), and reconstruction policy \(P\). Initialize an isolated empty environment. Provision the hardware abstraction and operating-system image required by \(P(C)\); fetch every artifact by recorded identifier; verify all integrity digests; install dependencies in a topological order of \(G\); then apply recorded runtime and process settings. Stop with failure upon any missing artifact, digest mismatch, unsatisfied constraint, or unsupported field. Otherwise output environment \(E'\) together with a comparison report asserting \(P(C(E'))=P(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reconstruct an isolated environment from captured metadata and locked dependencies, failing on any unverifiable mismatch.
assumptions_latex: The recorded dependency graph is acyclic after collapsing permitted dependency cycles.
All required artifacts remain retrievable or are archived.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(E'\) satisfying the declared reconstruction policy, or an explicit failure report.
review_flags: No supplied source locator specifies a formal environment-reconstruction algorithm.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the reconstruction leaf, but the proposed procedure and its guarantee are not source-supported. In particular, provisioning a hardware abstraction, topological installation, failure conditions, and equality under the combined policy/projection P require an inspectable authoritative reference.

children.title: Environment Drift Detection
children.top_down_role: Identification of context changes that can alter benchmark behavior or measurements.

knowledge_statements.title: Environment Drift Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicate detecting relevant change between canonical environment captures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_0\) be the approved baseline capture, \(C_1\) the current capture, \(\pi\) the declared relevance projection, and \(d\) a fieldwise discrepancy function with threshold \(\tau\geq 0\). Relevant environment drift is present exactly when \[D(C_0,C_1):=d\bigl(\pi(C_0),\pi(C_1)\bigr)>\tau.\] The comparison report must list every differing projected field and distinguish missing, added, and modified values. Exact drift detection is the special case in which \(d(x,y)=\mathbf{1}\{x\neq y\}\) and \(\tau=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Environment drift occurs when the declared discrepancy between relevant baseline and current fields exceeds a preselected threshold.
assumptions_latex: Captures use a common canonical schema.
The projection, discrepancy function, and threshold are fixed before observing benchmark outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(C_0,C_1)\) gives a reproducible predicate for relevant environment drift.
review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this drift predicate or threshold convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition fits a drift-detection predicate, and the notation is coherent. No source establishes that environment drift should be defined by this discrepancy-and-threshold convention or supports the required fieldwise report, so the mathematical version remains project-invented pending evidence.

children.title: Seed Recording
children.top_down_role: Capture and reporting of seeds associated with randomized benchmark runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Seed Recording
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness condition for replaying seeded pseudorandom benchmark executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stochastic execution \(e\), a seed record is complete when it stores \[S(e)=\bigl(A,v,\{(j,s_j,q_j)\}_{j\in J}\bigr),\] where \(A\) and \(v\) identify the pseudorandom generator and implementation version, \(J\) indexes all random streams, \(s_j\) is stream \(j\)'s initialization state or seed, and \(q_j\) is its stream-construction rule. If a seed is derived, the parent identifier and derivation function are also recorded. A bare integer seed is insufficient whenever generator identity, stream assignment, or derivation affects the generated sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete seed recording identifies every generator, version, stream seed or state, and stream-derivation rule used in an execution.
assumptions_latex: All controlled pseudorandom sources expose their initialization or serializable state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete \(S(e)\) determines every governed pseudorandom stream used by execution \(e\).

notation.meaning: initial state and construction rule for stream j

review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses pseudorandom seed-record completeness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition fits a completeness criterion for seed recording. The listed generator, version, stream-state, and derivation requirements are plausible but uncited, and no supplied locator supports the conclusion that the record determines every governed stream.

children.title: Random Stream Governance
children.top_down_role: Allocation, naming, versioning, and reuse policies for pseudorandom streams.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Stream Governance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic assignment and separation of pseudorandom streams across experimental units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be the set of experimental units and \(K\) the set of stochastic components. Random-stream governance specifies a versioned deterministic map \[g:U\times K\longrightarrow \mathcal{S},\] where \(\mathcal{S}\) is a family of identified pseudorandom streams. The map, generator family, and derivation rule are fixed before outcomes are observed. Distinct pairs must receive either disjoint streams or streams whose permitted sharing is explicitly declared. Every random draw must be attributable to one assigned stream, and rerunning the same unit under the same governance record must reproduce the same governed draw sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A versioned rule assigns every stochastic component an attributable stream, controls sharing, and reproduces governed draws on rerun.
assumptions_latex: Each stochastic component obtains randomness only through the governance interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(g\) makes stream allocation explicit, auditable, and replayable.
review_flags: No supplied source locator defines benchmark random-stream governance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Principle is an appropriate role for a governance rule. The deterministic assignment map, stream-disjointness alternative, attribution requirement, and replay guarantee need an authoritative source; none is cited and the local inventory is unrelated.

children.title: Replicate Stream Independence
children.top_down_role: Separation of random streams across repetitions, solvers, instances, or experimental blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Replicate Stream Independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic independence requirement for random streams assigned to distinct replicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For replicates \(r=1,\ldots,n\), let \(X_r=(X_{r,1},X_{r,2},\ldots)\) denote the random sequence consumed by replicate \(r\). Replicate streams are independent when, for every finite choice of indices \(I_r\) and measurable sets \(B_r\), \[\Pr\!\left(\bigcap_{r=1}^{n}\{(X_{r,i})_{i\in I_r}\in B_r\}\right)=\prod_{r=1}^{n}\Pr\!\left((X_{r,i})_{i\in I_r}\in B_r\right).\] In pseudorandom implementations this is an experimental design requirement approximated by a documented generator construction with nonoverlapping substreams; distinct seed labels alone do not establish it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicate streams should be mutually independent; implementations justify this using documented nonoverlapping substream construction, not merely distinct seeds.
assumptions_latex: The idealized random streams are defined on a common probability space.
Each replicate consumes only its assigned stream.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite events determined by different replicate streams factor into the product of their probabilities.

Nevertheless, no source is supplied for either the probability-space formulation or the benchmark-specific claim that documented nonoverlapping pseudorandom substreams approximate the requirement while distinct seeds do not establish it.

children.title: Residual Nondeterminism
children.top_down_role: Uncontrolled variability arising outside explicitly managed random streams.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Nondeterminism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variation remaining after controlled inputs, environment, and pseudorandom streams are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(e)\) be the observable output of execution \(e\), and let \(C(e)\) contain all declared controlled inputs, environment fields, and random-stream states. Residual nondeterminism is present if there exist executions \(e_1,e_2\) such that \[C(e_1)=C(e_2)\quad\text{but}\quad d_Y\bigl(Y(e_1),Y(e_2)\bigr)>\varepsilon,\] for a predeclared output metric \(d_Y\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\). Thus seed replay does not guarantee execution replay when uncontrolled scheduling, parallel reductions, races, clocks, device behavior, or external services can alter the output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual nondeterminism exists when identically controlled executions differ beyond a declared output tolerance because some causal input remains uncontrolled.
assumptions_latex: The output metric and tolerance are fixed before repeated executions.
Captured contexts are compared canonically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A witnessed pair \((e_1,e_2)\) satisfying the displayed predicate refutes deterministic replay under the declared controls.

notation.meaning: declared controlled context of execution e

review_flags: No supplied source locator formalizes residual nondeterminism for benchmark replay.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct kind for variation remaining after declared controls are fixed. The witness predicate is coherent, but its tolerance-based definition and enumerated causal interpretation lack any cited, inspectable support.

children.title: Baseline Machine Calibration
children.top_down_role: Reference measurements used to characterize benchmark hosts before or during experiments.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Machine Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated reference workload measurement establishing an admissible host-performance baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a host \(h\), reference workload \(W\), warm-up rule, sample count \(n\), statistic \(T\), and admissible interval \(I\). Stabilize the host under the declared resource policy, execute warm-up trials, then collect measurements \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) under identical settings. Record host context, raw samples, and \(b=T(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). If diagnostics detect thermal, frequency, or contention violations, discard the affected samples according to a rule fixed in advance and repeat. Output calibration record \(B=(h,W,b,I)\); accept the host only when \(b\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run a fixed reference workload repeatedly under controlled conditions and accept the host only when its calibration statistic is admissible.
assumptions_latex: The reference workload and statistic are fixed before calibration.
The admissible interval is established independently of the benchmark outcomes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs an auditable baseline record and an acceptance decision \(b\in I\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator specifies host baseline-calibration methodology.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits a calibration procedure, but no source supports the particular warm-up, sampling, diagnostic rejection, repetition, record, and acceptance protocol. The admissible-interval methodology especially requires an authoritative benchmark-calibration reference.

children.title: Resource Contention Control
children.top_down_role: Management of competing CPU, memory, storage, accelerator, and network activity.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Contention Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admission criterion limiting interference from concurrent consumers of host resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_k(t)\) be monitored utilization by nonbenchmark workloads of resource \(k\) during measurement interval \(J\), and let \(c_k\) be its predeclared ceiling. A run satisfies resource-contention control when \[\sup_{t\in J}u_k(t)\leq c_k\quad\text{for every monitored resource }k,\] and the benchmark's processor affinity, memory allocation policy, storage target, and network-isolation policy equal their recorded settings. Any missing monitor data or ceiling violation invalidates the run unless a predeclared censoring rule explicitly permits it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run is admissible only when external resource use remains below fixed ceilings and all declared isolation settings hold.
assumptions_latex: Monitors distinguish benchmark consumption from relevant external consumption.
Resource ceilings and censoring rules are fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfying the predicate certifies compliance with the declared contention-control policy.

notation.meaning: external utilization of resource k at time t

review_flags: No supplied source locator supports this resource-contention admission condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition fits the resource-contention-control leaf. The supremum ceiling, mandatory isolation settings, treatment of missing monitor data, and censoring exception form a specific admission policy that is not supported by any supplied source locator.

children.title: Frequency Stability
children.top_down_role: Monitoring of clock variation, power modes, throttling, and boost behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Frequency Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admission criterion bounding processor-frequency variation during timed benchmark execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i(t)>0\) be the effective frequency of processor \(i\) assigned to a benchmark during measurement interval \(J\), and let \(f_i^\star\) be its calibrated target. Frequency stability at relative tolerance \(\delta\geq0\) holds when \[\max_i\sup_{t\in J}\frac{|f_i(t)-f_i^\star|}{f_i^\star}\leq\delta.\] The frequency governor, boost policy, processor affinity, and sampling method must be recorded. If effective frequency cannot be observed directly, the substituted proxy and its error bound must be declared before measurements are accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Processor frequency is stable when every assigned processor remains within a predeclared relative tolerance of its calibrated target.
assumptions_latex: Frequency samples or declared proxies cover the complete timed interval.
Targets and tolerance are fixed independently of measured benchmark performance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed bound gives a reproducible frequency-stability admission predicate.

notation.meaning: effective frequency of assigned processor i

review_flags: No supplied source locator establishes a benchmark frequency-stability criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition fits the frequency-stability leaf, and its variables are introduced consistently. No source establishes the maximum relative-deviation predicate, complete-interval coverage requirement, or proxy error-bound rule as a valid benchmark admission criterion.

children.title: Thermal Stability
children.top_down_role: Monitoring of temperature-dependent performance variation across benchmark runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Thermal Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational acceptance condition for thermally controlled benchmark runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run \(r\) over measurement interval \(I_r\), let \(T_r(t)\) be the monitored package temperature and let \(q_r(t)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate thermal throttling. Given limits \(T_{\max}\) and \(\varepsilon_T\), the host is thermally stable for \(r\) exactly when \[\sup_{t\in I_r}T_r(t)\le T_{\max},\qquad \sup_{t\in I_r}T_r(t)-\inf_{t\in I_r}T_r(t)\le\varepsilon_T,\qquad \sup_{t\in I_r}q_r(t)=0.\] Runs failing any predicate are excluded or explicitly labeled thermally unstable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark run is thermally stable when temperature stays below its limit, varies only within tolerance, and no thermal-throttling event occurs.
assumptions_latex: \(I_r\) excludes a declared warm-up interval.
Temperature and throttling telemetry are sampled throughout \(I_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) is accepted as thermally stable if and only if all three displayed predicates hold.

children.title: Cross-Host Calibration Drift
children.top_down_role: Loss of measurement comparability caused by changing or mismatched host baselines.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Host Calibration Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative drift of repeated calibration measurements across benchmark hosts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_{hj}>0\) be calibration metric \(j\) measured on host \(h\), with reference host \(h_0\), for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Define the multiplicative cross-host calibration drift by \[D(h,h_0)=\max_{1\le j\le m}\left|\log\frac{c_{hj}}{c_{h_0j}}\right|.\] For a declared tolerance \(\delta\ge0\), hosts \(h\) and \(h_0\) are calibration-compatible when \(D(h,h_0)\le\delta\). Calibration protocol, workload, aggregation rule, and measurement units must be identical across hosts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-host drift is the largest absolute log-ratio between corresponding positive calibration metrics; hosts are compatible when this drift is within a declared tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(c_{hj}>0\) for every compared host and metric.
All hosts use the same calibration protocol and aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is calibration-compatible with \(h_0\) exactly when \(D(h,h_0)\le\delta\).

notation.meaning: calibration metric j on host h

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Cross-Host Calibration Drift leaf and is mathematically coherent, but choosing the maximum absolute log-ratio as the drift measure and using a single tolerance are substantive, noncanonical modeling choices. No source supports this exact calibration metric or compatibility rule.

children.title: Containerized Execution
children.top_down_role: Benchmark runs performed within versioned container images and declared runtime constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Containerized Execution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducible execution with a content-addressed user-space environment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A containerized benchmark execution is a tuple \(C=(d,c,e,m,ho)\), where \(d\) is an immutable image digest, \(c\) is the command and arguments, \(e\) is the explicit environment map, \(m\) specifies mounted inputs, and \(\rho\) specifies resource limits. Executing workload \(x\) on host \(h\) produces \[\mathcal E(C,x,h)=(y,s,z),\] where \(y\) is captured output, \(s\) is termination status, and \(z\) is measured metadata. The container fixes declared user-space dependencies but does not, by itself, fix the host kernel, instruction set, firmware, or hardware.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Containerized execution fixes a digest-addressed user-space image, command, environment, mounts, and limits while recording outputs, status, and metadata; host-level dependencies remain external.
assumptions_latex: The image named by \(d\) is retrievable and digest-verified.
All undeclared network access is disabled or recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) identifies the preserved user-space execution specification for \(\mathcal E(C,x,h)\).

A container specification or reproducible-execution source with a precise locator is needed.

children.title: Archived Execution Environments
children.top_down_role: Long-term preservation of runnable environments, images, virtual machines, or system snapshots.

knowledge_statements.title: Archived Execution Environments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness criterion for a preserved benchmark execution environment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An archived execution environment is a finite bundle \(A=(B,L,S,K,Q,H)\) containing executable artifacts \(B\), dependency lock data \(L\), source snapshot \(S\), toolchain identifiers \(K\), execution configuration \(Q\), and cryptographic digest map \(H\). It is complete relative to dependency closure \(D\) when every \(d\in D\) is either included in \(A\) or referenced by an immutable, resolvable identifier, and every included byte sequence verifies against \(H\). Completeness is relative to declared external platform requirements and does not imply future executability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An archived environment preserves artifacts, dependencies, source, toolchains, configuration, and digests; it is complete when its dependency closure is immutable, resolvable, and verifiable.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the declared transitive dependency closure.
Digest functions in \(H\) are fixed by name and version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is complete relative to \(D\) exactly when all dependencies are preserved or immutably resolvable and all stored digests verify.

children.title: Runtime Portability Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks that preserved environments execute consistently across supported hosts and runtimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Portability Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional and metric validation across declared runtime platforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite set of target platforms and \(X\) a validation workload set. For execution specification \(C\), let \((y_{hx},s_{hx},z_{hx})=\mathcal E(C,x,h)\). Relative to reference \(h_0\), output equivalence \(\sim_x\), and metric tolerances \(\tau_k\), runtime portability is validated when, for every \(h\in H\) and \(x\in X\), \[s_{hx}=s_{h_0x},\qquad y_{hx}\sim_x y_{h_0x},\qquad |z_{hx,k}-z_{h_0x,k}|\le\tau_k\] for every metric designated portability-sensitive. Unsupported platforms and failed executions violate the condition unless explicitly excluded beforehand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A runtime is portable over declared platforms when statuses and outputs match the reference and each portability-sensitive metric remains within its stated tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(h_0\in H\) is the declared reference platform.
Each relation \(\sim_x\) and tolerance \(\tau_k\) is fixed before validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Runtime portability over \(H\times X\) is validated if and only if all displayed comparisons pass.

children.title: Preservation Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Host, architecture, runtime, licensing, or repository constraints that prevent future execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Preservation Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Host-level incompatibilities that environment archives cannot eliminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an archived environment contain a binary requiring instruction set \(S_B\), and let a future host implement \(S_h\). If \(S_B\nsubseteq S_h\) and no compatible emulator is preserved, then the archived execution cannot be reproduced on that host, even when every archived artifact passes digest verification. Likewise, preservation of user-space bytes cannot determine behavior depending on an unrecorded kernel interface, device, firmware state, external service, or nondeterministic source. Thus artifact integrity and dependency completeness are insufficient beyond the declared platform and external-state boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified archive can still be unusable when the host lacks required instructions or execution depends on unpreserved kernel, device, service, firmware, or nondeterministic state.
assumptions_latex: The binary requires at least one instruction in \(S_B\setminus S_h\).
No compatible emulator or binary translation layer is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Digest-valid archival preservation does not imply executable reproduction when \(S_B\nsubseteq S_h\) or required external state is absent.

notation.meaning: instruction set required by the archived binary
instruction set implemented by the host
