children.title: Workflow Orchestration
children.top_down_role: Coordination of benchmark jobs, resources, dependencies, retries, and collection activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Workflow Orchestration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency-respecting execution of a reproducible benchmark workflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), task specifications \(a_v\), and initial artifacts. Initialize every task as pending. Repeatedly select a pending vertex \(v\) whose predecessors have succeeded, resolve its inputs, execute \(a_v\), verify declared outputs, and record status, timestamps, environment identifier, input digests, and output digests. Mark \(v\) successful only after validation; on failure, mark every dependent task blocked unless a declared recovery rule applies. Stop when no task is runnable. Output the task-state map, produced artifacts, and run provenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The orchestrator executes ready tasks in dependency order, validates and records their artifacts, blocks affected descendants after failures, and returns states plus provenance.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and acyclic.
Each task specification \(a_v\) declares its inputs, outputs, and execution environment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every executed task follows all predecessors, and the output records a terminal state for every \(v\in V\).

children.title: Run Manifests
children.top_down_role: Machine-readable declarations of run identity, inputs, settings, resources, and expected outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Run Manifests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Immutable specification and outcome record for one benchmark run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A run manifest is a content-addressed record \(M=(u,w,i,a,e,p,r,o,s,t)\), where \(u\) is a unique run identifier, \(w\) identifies the workflow revision, \(i\) lists input digests, \(a\) gives algorithm and parameters, \(e\) identifies the execution environment, \(p\) records platform metadata, \(r\) records randomness controls, \(o\) lists output digests, \(s\) is the outcome status, and \(t\) contains timing metadata. A manifest is complete when every required field is present or explicitly null with a reason, and every referenced immutable object is digest-verifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A run manifest records the workflow, inputs, algorithm, parameters, environment, platform, randomness, outputs, status, and timing, with immutable references and explicit missing-value reasons.
assumptions_latex: The manifest schema fixes field types and required fields.
Every immutable artifact reference includes its digest algorithm.

children.title: Workflow-to-Run Provenance
children.top_down_role: Links from orchestration definitions to dispatched jobs, produced artifacts, and reported results.

knowledge_statements.title: Workflow-to-Run Provenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation connecting workflow tasks to concrete executions and artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For workflow graph \(G=(V,E)\) and run set \(R\), represent provenance by a directed labeled graph \(P=(N,A)\) with nodes \(N=V\cup R\cup I\cup O\cup Q\), where \(I\), \(O\), and \(Q\) are input-artifact, output-artifact, and environment nodes. Each \(r\in R\) has exactly one task edge \(r\to v\), one environment edge \(r\to q\), zero or more consumption edges \(i\to r\), and zero or more generation edges \(r\to o\). Every executed dependency \((u,v)\in E\) is realized by an artifact path from a run of \(u\) to a run of \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provenance is a labeled graph linking each concrete run to its workflow task, environment, consumed inputs, and generated outputs while realizing executed workflow dependencies.
assumptions_latex: Every \(r\in R\) instantiates exactly one workflow task.
Artifact and environment nodes have stable identifiers.

children.title: Partial Workflow Recovery
children.top_down_role: Resumption and reconciliation of interrupted, duplicated, or incompletely recorded benchmark workflows.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Workflow Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe reuse and selective recomputation after an interrupted workflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a workflow DAG \(G=(V,E)\), prior manifests, and stored artifacts. Mark task \(v\) reusable when its prior status is successful, all output digests verify, and its provenance fingerprint—computed from task specification, environment, parameters, and input digests—matches the current fingerprint. Let \(U\) contain every nonreusable task and all its descendants. Process \(U\) topologically, reusing verified outputs from \(V\setminus U\) and rerunning each task in \(U\). If a rerun fails, block its unexecuted descendants. Output updated manifests, artifacts, and provenance without altering prior records.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery reuses only successful, digest-valid tasks with matching provenance fingerprints, then reruns invalid tasks and their descendants in topological order.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and acyclic.
Task fingerprints cover every declared behavior-affecting input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only vertices in \(U\) are recomputed, while every reused vertex has verified artifacts and an unchanged provenance fingerprint.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Readable Result Schemas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed validation contract for automated benchmark-result exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A machine-readable result schema is a tuple \(S=(F,T,R,C,V)\), where \(F\) is a finite field-name set, \(T:F\to\mathcal T\) assigns data types, \(R\subseteq F\) is the required-field set, \(C\) is a finite collection of cross-field constraints, and \(V\) is a version identifier. children.title: Aggregate Performance Profiles
children.top_down_role: Cross-instance summaries comparing relative solver performance over a benchmark corpus.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Performance Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines normalized empirical performance profiles over a common finite benchmark set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite solver set, \(P\) a finite instance set, and \(m_{p,s}>0\) a performance metric for every completed run. Define \(b_p=\min_{u\in S}m_{p,u}\), \(r_{p,s}=m_{p,s}/b_p\), and assign a declared penalty \(r_{p,s}=r_{\max}\) to each unsuccessful run. The aggregate performance profile of solver \(s\) is the empirical distribution function \[\rho_s(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq \tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq 1.\] The report shall state the metric, penalty convention, benchmark population, and treatment of ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A performance profile reports, for each solver and factor, the fraction of instances solved within that factor of the best recorded performance.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(P\) are finite and nonempty.
Completed-run metric values are strictly positive.
Every unsuccessful run receives a declared finite or infinite penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s(\tau)=|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}|/|P|\) is a nondecreasing empirical distribution on \([1,\infty]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The empirical-versus-asymptotic distinction is sensible, but no source supports the prescribed contents, uncertainty, censoring, or fitting requirements. As a reporting interface, this may be a representation rather than a mathematical definition.

children.title: Stratified Aggregate Reports
children.top_down_role: Aggregate results partitioned by benchmark family, feature group, difficulty class, or experimental condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Stratified Aggregate Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines aggregate benchmark summaries conditioned on prespecified instance or run strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a finite run set and let \(z:R\to Z\) assign each run exactly one declared stratum. For a solver \(s\), metric \(m_r\), and stratum \(h\in Z\), a stratified aggregate report gives \[A_{s,h}=T\bigl(\{m_r:r\in R,\ s_r=s,\ z(r)=h,\ o_r\in O_{\mathrm{inc}}\}\bigr),\] together with the denominator, missing-outcome counts, and uncertainty measure. Stratum definitions, inclusion set \(O_{\mathrm{inc}}\), and statistic \(T\) shall be identical across compared solvers unless differences are explicitly disclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stratified report computes the same declared aggregate separately within each prespecified subgroup and exposes subgroup denominators, missing outcomes, and uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: Every analyzed run has one declared stratum label.
The aggregate statistic and inclusion convention are fixed across comparisons.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_{s,h}\) compares solvers only within the common stratum \(h\) and declared included-outcome set.

notation.meaning: aggregate for solver s within stratum h

review_flags: No supplied source specifies stratified benchmark aggregation.
Methodological source and conventions require review.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No evidence supports the proposed stratification, inclusion, uncertainty, or cross-solver comparability conventions. The report-oriented terminal container may call for content_kind representation rather than definition.

children.title: Aggregation Sensitivity Reports
children.top_down_role: Comparisons showing how grouping, weighting, filtering, or normalization choices affect conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Sensitivity Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines robustness reports comparing conclusions under prespecified aggregation choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a fixed benchmark dataset and \(\mathcal A\) a finite, prespecified family of admissible analysis specifications, each fixing an aggregation functional, failure treatment, transformation, weighting, and uncertainty procedure. For solver \(s\), define \(q_s^{(a)}=a(D,s)\) for \(a\in\mathcal A\). An aggregation sensitivity report presents all \(q_s^{(a)}\), induced solver orderings, and any conclusion whose truth changes with \(a\). It shall not change the underlying run population except where population variation is itself a declared sensitivity dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sensitivity report recomputes benchmark conclusions under declared aggregation choices and identifies rankings or claims that change with those choices.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark data are fixed and traceable.
The admissible analysis family is declared before interpreting sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(\{q_s^{(a)}:a\in\mathcal A\}\) exposes dependence of reported conclusions on aggregation choices.

notation.meaning: reported quantity for solver s under specification a

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this robustness-report specification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The admissible analysis family and required sensitivity outputs are methodological choices without cited support. A benchmarking-methodology source is needed, and representation may fit this reporting-interface leaf better than definition.

children.title: Failure Reports
children.top_down_role: Categorized records of crashes, invalid outputs, resource errors, and other unsuccessful runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines accounting reports for attempted runs ending in non-timeout failure states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be the finite set of scheduled benchmark runs and let \(o:U\to O\) assign each run exactly one terminal outcome. Given a declared failure set \(F\subset O\) disjoint from timeout and exclusion outcomes, the failure report lists or aggregates \(R_F=\{r\in U:o(r)\in F\}\) by solver, instance, failure class, and diagnostic code. It reports \(|R_F|\), the denominator used for every rate, and whether partial outputs were validated; failures remain in outcome accounting even when omitted from performance aggregates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A failure report accounts for every attempted non-timeout failure, classifies its diagnostic, states rate denominators, and records treatment of partial outputs.
assumptions_latex: Each scheduled run receives exactly one terminal outcome.
Failure, timeout, exclusion, and successful-completion classes are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_F=\{r\in U:o(r)\in F\}\) is the complete set of declared non-timeout failures.

notation.meaning: declared set of non-timeout failure outcomes

review_flags: No supplied source defines benchmark failure accounting.
Outcome taxonomy and reporting standard require a source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes the proposed mutually exclusive failure taxonomy or mandatory report fields. Those choices determine the mathematical set being reported; representation may also be the better content kind for this report leaf.

children.title: Timeout Reports
children.top_down_role: Records of runs terminated at time or resource limits, including applicable cutoff context.

knowledge_statements.title: Timeout Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines accounting reports for runs terminated at declared resource limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite scheduled run set. For each run \(r\), let \(L_r>0\) be its declared resource limit, \(c_r\) its observed consumption, and \(o(r)\) its terminal outcome. The timeout set is \(R_T=\{r\in U:o(r)=\mathrm{timeout}\}\). A timeout report states the limited resource, limit-setting rule, enforcement mechanism, counts and rates with denominators, and the convention used when aggregating censored performance. A run may be labeled timeout only under the declared enforcement rule, including any stated tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A timeout report identifies runs stopped at declared limits and records the limited resource, enforcement rule, counts, denominators, and censoring treatment.
assumptions_latex: Every run has a declared terminal outcome.
Every timeout-eligible run has a positive declared resource limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T=\{r\in U:o(r)=\mathrm{timeout}\}\) contains exactly the runs classified by the declared limit-enforcement rule.

notation.meaning: resource limit declared for run r
observed resource consumption of run r

review_flags: No supplied locator supports timeout-report conventions.
Benchmark execution and censoring source required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the timeout classification, enforcement-tolerance, or censoring conventions. The introduced consumption c_r does not participate in the classification formula, so the relationship between consumption, limit, and timeout remains unspecified.

children.title: Exclusion Reports
children.top_down_role: Records of omitted instances, runs, solvers, or measurements with stated exclusion reasons.

knowledge_statements.title: Exclusion Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reports accounting for scheduled runs removed from a declared analysis population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be the finite scheduled run universe and \(I\subseteq U\) the runs included in a specified analysis. The exclusion set is \(E=U\setminus I\). An exclusion report records every \(r\in E\) with a prespecified reason code, the stage at which exclusion occurred, and whether the run was attempted. It reports exclusion counts by solver and stratum and states the resulting denominator \(|I|\). A failed or timed-out attempted run is not an exclusion merely because an aggregate statistic cannot use its metric value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exclusion report enumerates scheduled runs omitted from an analysis, gives prespecified reasons and stages, and distinguishes exclusions from attempted failures or timeouts.
assumptions_latex: The scheduled run universe and analysis population are identifiable.
Each excluded run has at least one declared reason code.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=I\mathbin{\dot\cup}E\), where every member of \(E\) is explicitly accounted for.

notation.meaning: runs included in the specified analysis

review_flags: No supplied source defines exclusion-report accounting.
A reproducible-benchmarking reporting source is needed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between exclusions and attempted unsuccessful runs is plausible but uncited and convention-dependent. Evidence is required for the accounting rules; representation may fit the report leaf better than definition.

children.title: Outcome Accounting Reconciliation
children.top_down_role: Reconciliation of successful, failed, timed-out, excluded, and missing outcomes against the planned experiment.

knowledge_statements.title: Outcome Accounting Reconciliation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the partition and count identities required for complete benchmark outcome accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be the finite scheduled run universe, partitioned into excluded runs \(E\), successful completed runs \(C\), timeout runs \(T\), and other failed runs \(F\). Outcome accounting is reconciled exactly when \[U=E\mathbin{\dot\cup}C\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\mathbin{\dot\cup}F\qquad\text{and}\qquad |U|=|E|+|C|+|T|+|F|.\] For every solver, instance stratum, and reported subtotal, the same identities must hold after restriction. Any duplicate identifier, missing scheduled run, or discrepancy between detailed records and reported totals violates reconciliation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outcome accounting reconciles when exclusions, successes, timeouts, and other failures form a disjoint exhaustive partition globally and within every reported subtotal.
assumptions_latex: Every scheduled run has a stable identifier.
Outcome classes are declared and mutually exclusive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=E\mathbin{\dot\cup}C\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\mathbin{\dot\cup}F\) and all corresponding count identities hold.

notation.meaning: timeout runs and other failed runs

review_flags: The partition identity is elementary, but the selected benchmark outcome taxonomy lacks supplied evidence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition identity is elementary and condition is the correct content kind, but the particular four-class benchmark taxonomy and its required application to every subtotal lack supporting evidence.

children.title: Provenance Reports
children.top_down_role: Lineage records connecting benchmark inputs, executions, transformations, artifacts, and published results.

knowledge_statements.title: Provenance Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines lineage reports connecting benchmark results to inputs, transformations, executions, and artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A provenance report represents a benchmark study by a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\). Each vertex identifies an immutable or content-addressed entity or activity, including source instances, preprocessing steps, solver executions, environments, and result artifacts. An edge \((u,v)\in E\) declares that \(v\) used, generated, or was derived from \(u\), with the relation type recorded. Every published aggregate must be reachable from the run records it summarizes, and every run record must be reachable from its instance, executable, configuration, and environment metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A provenance report gives a traceable lineage graph from source instances, software, configurations, and environments through executions to published aggregates.
assumptions_latex: Reported entities and activities have stable identifiers.
Declared derivation edges are acyclic and relation-typed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every reported aggregate has a directed provenance path from each class of artifact required to reproduce its contributing runs.

notation.meaning: typed dependency or derivation from u to v

review_flags: No supplied source supports this provenance model.
A provenance or reproducible-computing standard is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No provenance standard is cited. Requiring every provenance report to be a DAG and imposing the stated reachability obligations are substantive modeling choices that cannot be accepted without an authoritative provenance source.

children.title: Version Reports
children.top_down_role: Release, revision, image, toolchain, schema, and dataset identifiers associated with a study.

knowledge_statements.title: Version Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines reports fixing the identities and versions of benchmark software and data artifacts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the finite set of artifacts required by a benchmark study. A version report assigns every \(a\in A\) an artifact class, canonical identifier, version label, and immutable digest \(h(a)\) whenever the artifact is available as bytes. For source-controlled artifacts it additionally records the repository identifier, revision, and dirty-state indicator. Two reported environments are version-equivalent on \(A\) only if their canonical identifiers and digests agree for every required artifact; equality of human-readable version labels alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A version report identifies every required software and data artifact using versions, revisions, dirty-state information, and immutable digests where available.
assumptions_latex: The required artifact set is finite and declared.
The digest function and canonicalization procedure are identified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Version equivalence requires \(h_1(a)=h_2(a)\) and matching canonical identifiers for every \(a\in A\).
review_flags: No supplied locator addresses software or dataset version reporting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports digest equality as the defining criterion for version equivalence. The conclusion also introduces h_1 and h_2 without defining them, while the statement defines only h.

children.title: Configuration Reports
children.top_down_role: Reported solver settings, benchmark policies, resource limits, and run-specific overrides.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration Reports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines canonical reports of solver, instance, resource, and execution configuration values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be the finite set of configuration keys that can affect benchmark execution or interpretation. A configuration report is a total mapping \(c:K\to V\) recording, for each key, its typed value, unit when applicable, origin, and scope. It includes solver parameters, random seeds, preprocessing choices, resource limits, concurrency, hardware allocation, and environment variables declared relevant. Defaults must be materialized rather than inferred. A canonical serialization \(\sigma(c)\) and digest \(h(\sigma(c))\) identify the exact reported configuration used by each run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A configuration report materializes all relevant settings and defaults as typed values with origins and scopes, then canonically identifies the resulting configuration.
assumptions_latex: The set of configuration keys affecting execution or interpretation is declared.
Canonical serialization and digest procedures are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each run references one total configuration \(c\) identified by \(h(\sigma(c))\).
review_flags: No supplied source specifies reproducible configuration reporting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the asserted exhaustive key set, mandatory materialization of defaults, or digest-based identity rule. Calling c:K→V typed also requires a defined value universe or key-dependent type discipline.

children.title: Metadata Consistency Audits
children.top_down_role: Checks for conflicting, incomplete, or mismatched provenance, version, or configuration records.

knowledge_statements.title: Metadata Consistency Audits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States machine-checkable consistency conditions across reproducibility metadata reports and run records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be the run-record set, \(A\) the artifact registry, and \(C\) the configuration registry. A metadata consistency audit passes exactly when every foreign reference from \(R\) resolves uniquely in \(A\cup C\), every referenced digest recomputes to its recorded value, required fields satisfy their declared types and units, and shared identifiers have equal values wherever repeated. Additionally, every published result references contributing runs, and every run references an instance, executable version, configuration, and execution environment. The audit output lists each violated predicate and the affected identifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metadata audit checks referential integrity, digests, types, units, repeated values, and complete links from published results to reproducible runs.
assumptions_latex: Metadata schemas identify required fields, types, units, and reference targets.
Referenced artifacts remain available for digest verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The audit passes if and only if all declared integrity predicates hold for \(R\), \(A\), and \(C\).
review_flags: No supplied source defines these metadata integrity predicates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is an appropriate content kind, but no schema or reproducibility standard supports these exact integrity predicates. The requirement that every foreign reference resolve in A∪C also appears too narrow unless all other referenced entities are explicitly included in those registries.

assumptions_latex: A benchmark specification fixes an instance set, solver configuration, random-seed policy, resource limits, and reported statistics.
The replicating team does not reuse unpublished execution outputs from the original team.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The study is an independent replication precisely when the independence and protocol-conformance predicates both hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational definition for computational combinatorial-optimization benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a benchmark study conducted under protocol \(P\). A study \(R\) is an independent replication of \(B\) if a team organizationally independent of the authors of \(B\) reconstructs the executable experiment from the public artifacts specified by \(P\), runs the prescribed instances and configurations, and evaluates the same declared response variables. Independence requires that implementation, execution, and analysis decisions not be determined by unpublished outputs of \(B\). Replication success is assessed against tolerances fixed by \(P\), rather than by exact equality of timings or stochastic trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent team reconstructs and reruns a public benchmark protocol, then compares the prescribed outputs using predeclared tolerances rather than exact execution equality.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent Replication

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Independent Replication container and is internally coherent, but it makes substantive operational choices about organizational independence, reconstruction from public artifacts, unpublished outputs, and tolerance-based success without any cited source. The unrelated local inventory cannot support these choices.

children.title: Cross-Machine Replication
children.top_down_role: Replication across hosts with differing processors, memory systems, accelerators, or storage configurations.

assumptions_latex: Both machines execute the same solver artifact, benchmark instances, configuration, seed policy, and measurement protocol.
Machine-dependent resource quantities are either normalized by a declared rule or excluded from equivalence testing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-machine replication holds when every declared invariant response agrees within its specified tolerance on the two machines.

notation.meaning: response vector for instance i in environment e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardware changes while the software platform and benchmark protocol remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each benchmark instance \(i\), let \(Y_i(e)\) contain the responses declared invariant under a machine change, such as feasibility status, certified objective value, or normalized resource statistics. Cross-machine replication between \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) holds under componentwise tolerances \(\varepsilon_i\geq 0\) exactly when \[|Y_{ij}(e_1)-Y_{ij}(e_2)|\leq \varepsilon_{ij}\] for every numeric component \(j\), and every categorical component agrees under the protocol's declared equivalence relation. Raw wall-clock equality is not required unless explicitly designated invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With software and protocol fixed, machine-specific runs replicate when all declared invariant outputs agree under predefined numeric and categorical tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Machine Replication

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits Cross-Machine Replication, and the variables and componentwise test are defined. An authoritative source is required for the proposed invariant-response model, normalization rule, categorical equivalence treatment, and exclusion of raw wall-clock equality.

children.title: Cross-Platform Replication
children.top_down_role: Replication across operating systems, architectures, runtimes, compilers, or container platforms.

assumptions_latex: The same benchmark instances, solver semantics, configuration, and seed policy are used on both software platforms.
The protocol declares which outputs must be invariant and how unsupported features are classified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-platform replication holds exactly when all required semantic outputs are equivalent and all platform-specific deviations remain within declared tolerances.

notation.meaning: two operating-system, compiler, runtime, or library platforms
observable benchmark result on platform p
protocol-declared equivalence relation for instance i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Software-platform changes may include operating system, compiler, runtime, and dependency versions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every instance \(i\), let \(O_i(p)\) record termination status, feasibility or certificate status, objective value, and other protocol-designated observables on platform \(p\). A run on \(p_2\) cross-platform replicates a reference run on \(p_1\) if \(O_i(p_1)\sim_i O_i(p_2)\) for every required instance \(i\). The relation \(\sim_i\) must be fixed before execution and may combine exact equality for discrete semantic outputs with tolerance intervals for floating-point or performance outputs. A missing required platform feature is a replication failure, not an equivalent observation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runs across operating systems or software stacks replicate when predeclared semantic outputs match and numerical differences stay within platform-aware tolerances.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Platform Replication

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits Cross-Platform Replication and the statement is internally consistent. No source supports the particular equivalence relation, the mixture of exact and tolerant comparisons, or the rule that a missing platform feature necessarily constitutes replication failure.

children.title: Portability Discrepancy Analysis
children.top_down_role: Investigation of behavioral or performance differences observed across machines or platforms.

assumptions_latex: Paired observations are available for the same instances and configurations in a reference and a target environment.
Each response component has a declared scale, tolerance, and missing-data rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a componentwise discrepancy table and an aggregate portability assessment determined solely by the declared normalization and aggregation rules.

notation.meaning: reference and target response for instance i and component j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired discrepancy analysis for machine or software-platform changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given paired responses, set \(d_{ij}=|y^{(1)}_{ij}-y^{(0)}_{ij}|/s_{ij}\) for numeric components, where \(s_{ij}>0\) is fixed by the protocol; set \(d_{ij}=0\) or \(1\) for equivalent or nonequivalent categorical components. Mark a component discrepant when \(d_{ij}\) exceeds its declared threshold. Partition discrepancies by changed environment factors, report every instance-component violation, and aggregate only with a predeclared statistic such as a maximum or quantile. Missing, crashed, or invalid runs receive the protocol's explicit failure value and are never silently discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize paired output differences, flag threshold violations, attribute them to changed environment factors, and aggregate them using a rule fixed before inspection.
knowledge_statements.title: Portability Discrepancy Analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is a suitable kind for this discrepancy-analysis procedure, but the normalization, binary encoding of categorical discrepancies, factor attribution, aggregation choices, and failure-value treatment are protocol-dependent and uncited. The available source inventory is unrelated.

children.title: Replication Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which cross-system results are no longer treated as comparable replications.

assumptions_latex: Replication equivalence is defined by a fixed set of observables and tolerances.
At least one unmodeled environment change can affect a declared observable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalence is guaranteed only inside the declared environment domain; outside it, even semantically valid executions may cease to be replication-equivalent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of claims based on a declared environment class and tolerance model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A replication claim over \(\mathcal E\) has boundary \(\partial\mathcal E\) determined by the protocol's supported hardware, software, arithmetic, and resource regimes. The implication \[e_1,e_2\in\mathcal E\Longrightarrow O(e_1)\sim O(e_2)\] makes no assertion when either environment lies outside \(\mathcal E\). Equivalence can fail beyond this boundary through unsupported instructions, changed numerical semantics, nondeterministic parallel schedules, resource exhaustion, or altered dependency behavior. Consequently, observing equivalence on finitely many environments does not establish universal portability; it supports only the sampled domain and the explicitly justified interpolation region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replication equivalence applies only within declared hardware, software, arithmetic, and resource regimes; observations on finitely many environments do not prove universal portability.
knowledge_statements.title: Replication Equivalence Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary fits the terminal container, but the statement introduces a topological boundary notation without specifying a topology and refers to an explicitly justified interpolation region without defining it. A source is also needed for the portability-boundary characterization and finite-environment inference claim.

assumptions_latex: A baseline and candidate solver are evaluated on matched instances under the same declared protocol.
The regression thresholds and treatment of timeouts, failures, and stochastic variation are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The candidate has a benchmark regression exactly when at least one protected response violates its predeclared noninferiority threshold.

notation.meaning: baseline and candidate response on instance i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matched benchmark comparison for detecting solver performance or correctness regressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every protected instance or aggregate \(i\), compute the protocol-declared loss \(L_i(Y_i^{(1)},Y_i^{(0)})\), oriented so that larger values are worse. The candidate exhibits a regression if \[L_i(Y_i^{(1)},Y_i^{(0)})>\delta_i\] for at least one protected \(i\), after applying the declared uncertainty adjustment for repeated stochastic runs. Correctness failures, invalid certificates, or newly unsolved required instances are regressions independently of runtime improvement. A comparison is inconclusive, rather than passing, when required observations are missing and the protocol provides no conservative failure encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver version regresses when a matched correctness or performance response exceeds a predeclared loss threshold after the specified uncertainty adjustment.
knowledge_statements.title: Regression Benchmarking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Regression Benchmarking, and the loss-threshold formulation is coherent. The universal any-protected-response rule, uncertainty adjustment, correctness overrides, and inconclusive handling are substantive protocol choices with no supporting citation.

assumptions_latex: Solver versions are archived and evaluated using a versioned benchmark protocol.
Responses are comparable directly or are transformed by a documented calibration linking protocol revisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting version-by-instance response history supports reproducible trend and change-point analyses without conflating solver changes with undocumented benchmark changes.

notation.meaning: recorded response for version t on instance i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Version-indexed representation of solver behavior across a maintained benchmark suite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Longitudinal solver tracking represents benchmark history as a partially observed array \(Y=(Y_{t,i})_{t=1,
\ldots,T,\,i\in I}\) accompanied by solver artifact identifiers, protocol versions, environment descriptors, and uncertainty summaries. Each entry records correctness status and the declared performance responses for version \(v_t\) on instance \(i\). Comparisons across \(t\) are admissible only when protocols are identical or a documented calibration maps their responses to a common scale. Failures and missing runs remain explicit states. Trend statistics must preserve the version order and identify benchmark-set changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Track each archived solver version in a version-by-instance response array, retaining protocol, environment, uncertainty, failure, and benchmark-change metadata.
knowledge_statements.title: Longitudinal Solver Tracking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is appropriate for the version-by-instance tracking container. The admissibility of calibrated cross-protocol comparisons and the required metadata and trend constraints are not supported by a cited longitudinal benchmarking source.

children.title: Community Challenge Protocols
children.top_down_role: Shared task scope, eligibility, benchmark access, evaluation windows, and participation policies.

assumptions_latex: The challenge organizer publishes the task, benchmark partitions, resource model, submission rules, and scoring rule before evaluation.
A hidden test partition is inaccessible to participants until submissions are frozen.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A challenge run conforms to the protocol only when validation, execution, scoring, and disclosure follow the published deterministic rules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Protocol-level definition for reproducible community solver challenges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A community challenge protocol \(P\) is a preregistered tuple specifying eligible submissions \(\mathcal S_P\), training and test instance partitions, execution environments, resource limits, correctness checks, failure handling, score map \(S_P\), tie rules, submission limits, and disclosure schedule. An execution conforms to \(P\) when each accepted submission is validated before scoring, run on the frozen hidden test set under identical resource accounting, and ranked solely by \(S_P\) and the declared tie rules. Any post hoc change requires a versioned amendment and separate reporting of affected results.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A community challenge freezes eligibility, data partitions, resources, validation, scoring, ties, and disclosure; conforming runs apply those rules uniformly to hidden tests.
knowledge_statements.title: Community Challenge Protocols

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits Community Challenge Protocols, but the asserted required tuple, hidden-test procedure, identical resource accounting, amendment policy, and conformity criterion are governance conventions rather than source-free mathematical facts. No relevant source is cited.

children.title: Shared Leaderboard Governance
children.top_down_role: Publication, moderation, correction, versioning, and retention policies for comparative rankings.

assumptions_latex: Leaderboard rules, benchmark versions, and scoring code are publicly versioned.
Every material administrative action is recorded in an append-only audit log.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The published ranking remains auditable because every displayed score and governance intervention is reproducible from immutable submissions, rules, and logged decisions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auditability and change control for a shared computational leaderboard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Shared leaderboard governance requires that \(\pi_F\) be computed from immutable validated submissions \(\mathcal S\) using a published version of \(F\). Rule, benchmark, or scoring changes create a new leaderboard version unless a preregistered correction procedure applies. Conflicts of interest, disqualifications, reruns, appeals, and corrections must be decided under published criteria and entered in an append-only log. Historical rankings remain accessible with their original rule and benchmark identifiers. Thus no displayed rank may depend on an undocumented manual adjustment or a silently replaced submission.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared leaderboard is auditable when immutable submissions, versioned scoring, published decision rules, and append-only records determine every current and historical rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Leaderboard Governance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Principle is a suitable role for Shared Leaderboard Governance. The immutability, versioning, appeal, audit-log, and historical-access requirements are normative claims and need an authoritative governance or benchmark-competition source.

children.title: Submission Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks on submitted systems, result files, execution evidence, and policy compliance.

assumptions_latex: The challenge publishes a machine-checkable submission schema and deterministic admissibility rules.
Reference validators and instance-level correctness checkers are versioned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validation record is a reproducible certificate of admissibility or a localized explanation of rejection; it is not a certificate of optimality unless separately checked.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-verifiable admissibility certificate for competition submissions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a submission \(s\), define \(C(s)=(h(s),v,(V_j(s))_{j=1}^k)\), where \(h(s)\) is a cryptographic artifact identifier, \(v\) identifies the validator version, and each \(V_j\) checks one published requirement, including schema, executability, resource declarations, output syntax, and instance-level feasibility or certificate validity. The submission is admissible exactly when \(V_j(s)=1\) for all \(j\). Because each predicate is deterministic and versioned, an independent party can recompute \(C(s)\). A failed record must identify the first or complete set of violated predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validation certificate binds an artifact to a validator version and reproducible predicate results, proving challenge admissibility or identifying exact rejection causes.
knowledge_statements.title: Submission Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The terminal container is Submission Validation, while the selected certificate kind narrows it to a validation record and does not describe the validation procedure itself. Moreover, the claim that the predicates are deterministic and independently recomputable, and the asserted admissibility equivalence, require a source before the mathematical role and formulation can be settled.

children.title: Ranking Stability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of leaderboard positions to benchmark composition, scoring choices, uncertainty, or updates.

assumptions_latex: The same admissible solvers are rescored under two permitted benchmark samples or perturbations.
Scores are oriented so that smaller values are better, with a fixed tie rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ranking is stable at radius \(\eta\) when every permitted perturbation within that radius leaves the induced weak order unchanged.

notation.meaning: score of solver a under evaluation condition E

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic order stability under declared resampling or benchmark perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the weak order \(\preceq_E\) satisfy \(a\preceq_E b\) exactly when \(S_a(E)\leq S_b(E)\), after applying the fixed tie rule. The leaderboard is stable at radius \(\eta\geq0\) around \(E\) if, for every permitted \(E'\) with \(d(E,E')\leq\eta\), \[a\preceq_E b\Longleftrightarrow a\preceq_{E'} b\] for all solver pairs \(a,b\). Pairwise stability may instead be reported locally: pair \((a,b)\) is stable when the sign of \(S_a(E')-S_b(E')\) cannot change over the permitted perturbation set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A leaderboard is stable when all permitted benchmark perturbations within a declared radius preserve every pairwise ordering under the fixed tie rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Ranking Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition fits Ranking Stability, but no source supports this strong all-perturbations weak-order invariance definition. The phrase after applying the fixed tie rule is also insufficient to determine whether score equality or a tie-breaking order defines the displayed relation, which affects the biconditional.

children.title: Leaderboard Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Gaming, leakage, unverifiable submissions, stale results, or incomparable tracks that undermine rankings.

assumptions_latex: Leaderboard scores are estimated from a finite benchmark sample.
Participants may adapt repeatedly to publicly revealed scores or the benchmark may poorly represent the target population.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without independence, adequate coverage, and uncertainty control, displayed rank need not estimate population performance and may reverse under fresh evaluation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalization boundary for finite, public, and adaptively queried leaderboards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A leaderboard order based on \(\widehat S_D\) is not guaranteed to represent the population order based on \(S_{\mathcal P}\) when \(D\) is unrepresentative, too small, publicly overused, or adaptively queried without correction. In particular, there may exist solvers \(a,b\) such that \[\widehat S_D(a)<\widehat S_D(b)\quad\text{but}\quad S_{\mathcal P}(a)>S_{\mathcal P}(b).\] The same failure can arise from hidden correctness errors, inconsistent resource accounting, excessive missingness, or score aggregation dominated by a small instance subset. Therefore rank is meaningful only within the benchmark population, protocol, and uncertainty regime actually justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite leaderboard ranks can reverse on the target population through sampling error, adaptive overfitting, hidden invalidity, inconsistent accounting, missingness, or unrepresentative aggregation.
knowledge_statements.title: Leaderboard Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct kind and the rank-reversal formula is plausible, but the generalization, adaptive-overfitting, missingness, accounting, and aggregation claims require relevant statistical or leaderboard-overfitting evidence. None of the inventoried combinatorial-optimization sources supports them.
